Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Large and Small Spur Gear Pair Showing Speed DifferenceSubject: Engineering - Mechanical EngineeringExperiment Objective: To observe the speed difference and rotation direction of a large and small spur gear meshing on parallel shafts, and understand the relationship between gear tooth number and rotational speed.II. Experimental EquipmentLarge spur gear (one), small spur gear (one), two parallel shafts with bearings, simple gear mounting frame or test rig, hand crank or direct hand rotation, marker pen (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Mount the large and small spur gears on two parallel shafts. Adjust the center distance so the gears mesh correctly with full tooth engagement.2. Initial Check: Ensure both shafts rotate freely without jamming. Optionally mark one tooth on each gear for easier observation.3. Core Operation: Use your hand to slowly rotate the larger gear in a steady direction.4. Observation: Keep rotating the larger gear and observe the rotation direction and speed of the smaller gear.5. Completion: Stop rotation and inspect the meshing condition; ensure no tooth skipping occurred.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. When the larger gear is rotated by hand, the smaller gear rotates automatically.2. The smaller gear rotates in the opposite direction to the larger gear.3. The smaller gear completes more revolutions in the same time, showing a higher rotational speed.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleIn a spur gear pair on parallel shafts, meshing gears transmit motion through tooth contact. The rotational speed is inversely proportional to the number of teeth. Since the smaller gear has fewer teeth, it rotates faster than the larger gear. The meshing also causes the two gears to rotate in opposite directions.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Metal Spoon vs Wooden Spoon in Hot WaterI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Heat Transfer in Metal and Wooden Spoons2. Subject: Engineering – Mechanical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate differences in heat transfer rates caused by different material thermal conductivities by observing butter melting on spoon handles.II. Experimental EquipmentClear heat-resistant container (1), hot water (about 70–80°C), metal spoon (1), wooden spoon (1), butter pats of equal size (2), thermometer (optional), camera or smartphone with fixed focus and time-lapse function.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Pour hot water into the clear container, filling it to a level below the spoon handles. Prepare two equal-sized butter pats.2. Placement: Place the metal spoon and wooden spoon side by side in the same container, with spoon bowls submerged and handles extending above the water line.3. Butter Setup: Place one butter pat on each spoon handle at the same height above the water surface.4. Recording: Fix the camera position and focus; start time-lapse recording.5. Observation: Allow heat to transfer from the hot water through the spoons to the handles until clear melting differences are observed.6. Completion: Stop recording once the butter on the metal spoon has clearly melted more than that on the wooden spoon.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both butter pats are solid and identical in size and shape.2. During Heating: Butter on the metal spoon softens and melts noticeably faster than butter on the wooden spoon.3. Final State: Butter on the metal spoon may drip or fully melt, while butter on the wooden spoon remains partially solid or melts much more slowly.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesMetal has a much higher thermal conductivity than wood. Heat from the hot water is conducted efficiently along the metal spoon to the handle, raising its temperature quickly and melting the butter. Wood is a poor thermal conductor, so heat transfer along the wooden spoon is slower, resulting in delayed butter melting.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Different materials have different thermal conductivities, affecting heat transfer rates. Minimum assumptions: hot water provides a constant heat source; metal conducts heat better than wood; butter visibly melts when heated. Phased storyline: (1) Initial setup with identical butter pats on spoon handles above water; (2) Heat flows from hot water into spoons; (3) Rapid temperature rise along metal spoon causes early butter melting; (4) Wooden spoon shows delayed or reduced melting. Visibility constraints: camera must clearly show both spoon handles and butter simultaneously, with a fixed viewpoint to verify relative melting progression.

Fix the metal rod horizontally on the left and the glass rod horizontally on the right, ensuring equal length and similar diameter.2. Attach several identical metal pins along each rod at equal spacing using small amounts of wax.3. Light the flame and heat both rods steadily without changing position.6. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Reaction Between Sodium Peroxide and WaterI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Reaction Between Sodium Peroxide and WaterSubject: Engineering - Chemical EngineeringObjective: To observe oxygen generation and alkalinity when sodium peroxide reacts with water, and to verify the reaction using a glowing splint and phenolphthalein.II. Experimental EquipmentTest tube, test tube rack, dropper, small amount of pale yellow sodium peroxide powder, distilled water, glowing splint, phenolphthalein solution, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear safety goggles. Place a clean, dry test tube on a rack. Add a small amount of pale yellow sodium peroxide powder to the bottom of the test tube.2. Water Addition: Using a dropper, carefully add a small volume of distilled water into the test tube.3. Gas Test: Immediately insert a glowing splint into the mouth of the test tube.4. Indicator Test: Add 1–2 drops of phenolphthalein solution into the reaction mixture.5. Finish: Observe the results, then place the test tube back on the rack and allow the reaction to complete.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Upon adding water, vigorous bubbling occurs in the test tube.2. The glowing splint relights or burns more brightly, indicating oxygen evolution.3. After adding phenolphthalein, the solution turns pink, indicating an alkaline environment.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSodium peroxide reacts with water to form sodium hydroxide and hydrogen peroxide: Na2O2 + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2O2. The hydrogen peroxide further decomposes to produce oxygen gas: 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2↑. The released oxygen supports combustion, relighting the glowing splint, while the formed sodium hydroxide makes the solution alkaline, turning phenolphthalein pink.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Reaction of sodium peroxide with water producing oxygen and an alkaline solution. Minimum assumptions: sodium peroxide is pale yellow solid; water addition initiates reaction; oxygen supports combustion; phenolphthalein indicates alkalinity. Phased storyline: (1) Initial static setup with solid in test tube; (2) Water addition causing bubbling; (3) Glowing splint insertion leading to brightening; (4) Phenolphthalein addition causing pink coloration. Visibility constraints: close-up of test tube mouth for splint effect; clear view of solution color change; continuous perspective to verify causal sequence.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Electrolysis of Copper Chloride SolutionI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Electrolysis of Copper Chloride SolutionSubject: Engineering – Chemical EngineeringExperiment Objective: To observe and understand the electrode reactions during electrolysis of copper chloride solution using graphite electrodes, and to relate observed phenomena to electrochemical principles.II. Experimental EquipmentBeaker (100–250 mL), copper chloride solution (blue-green, appropriate concentration), two graphite electrodes, DC power supply, connecting wires with clips, electrode holder or clamp, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Pour copper chloride solution into the beaker to a suitable level. Put on safety goggles.2. Electrode Setup: Insert two graphite electrodes vertically into the solution without touching each other.3. Circuit Connection: Connect the anode to the positive terminal of the DC power supply and the cathode to the negative terminal.4. Electrolysis Operation: Switch on the power supply. Adjust to a low, stable voltage.5. Observation and Recording: Focus the camera on the electrodes and perform time-lapse photography to record changes over time.6. Completion: After sufficient observation, turn off the power supply, disconnect electrodes, and clean equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The solution is uniformly blue-green; electrodes are clean and dark.2. During Electrolysis: Reddish-brown copper gradually deposits on the cathode surface; bubbles of gas evolve at the anode; the solution color becomes lighter near the cathode.3. Over Time (Time-lapse): Copper layer thickens on the cathode, and continuous gas evolution is visible at the anode.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesElectrolysis uses electrical energy to drive non-spontaneous redox reactions. In copper chloride solution, Cu2+ ions gain electrons at the cathode and are reduced to metallic copper (Cu2+ + 2e− → Cu). At the anode, chloride ions lose electrons to form chlorine gas (2Cl− → Cl2 + 2e−). Graphite electrodes act as inert conductors, allowing electron transfer without participating in the reaction.

Minimum assumptions include correct electrode polarity, presence of Cu2+ and Cl− ions, and visible electrochemical reactions.Expected phased storyline: (1) Static setup phase showing beaker, blue-green solution, and correctly connected graphite electrodes; (2) Power-on phase where electrolysis begins; (3) Progressive reaction phase where copper deposition appears on the cathode and gas bubbles evolve at the anode; (4) Accelerated time-lapse phase emphasizing thickening copper layer and continuous gas evolution. manual: Experiment Title: Temperature Sensor Activating a Cooling FanSubject: Engineering – Mechatronics & RoboticsI. Experiment ObjectiveTo demonstrate how a temperature sensor detects temperature changes near a metal plate and triggers a controller to activate or deactivate a cooling fan when a heat source is moved toward or away from the plate.II. Connect the sensor to the controller, and connect the controller output to the cooling fan. Power on the system.2. Initial State Check: Ensure the heat source is far from the metal plate. Observe that the fan is off, indicating normal temperature below the set threshold.3. Heating Operation: Slowly move the heat source toward the metal plate. Allow heat to transfer to the plate and sensor.4. Observation During Heating: When the sensed temperature exceeds the preset threshold, observe the controller output signal and the cooling fan turning on.5. Cooling Operation: Gradually move the heat source away from the metal plate.6. Observation During Cooling: As the temperature drops below the threshold, observe the controller stopping the output and the cooling fan turning off.7. Shutdown: Turn off the power supply after confirming repeated and stable operation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial state: Fan is stationary when the heat source is far away.2. Heating phase: As the heat source approaches, the metal plate warms up and the fan starts rotating.3. Cooling phase: When the heat source is removed, the plate cools down and the fan gradually stops.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe temperature sensor converts temperature changes of the metal plate into electrical signals. The controller compares the signal with a preset temperature threshold. When the temperature exceeds the threshold, the controller activates the cooling fan; when it falls below the threshold, the fan is deactivated. This demonstrates a basic closed-loop temperature control system in mechatronics.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Mass–Spring System Oscillating After Being Stretched and ReleasedI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Oscillation of a Mass–Spring System After Vertical Stretching2. Subject: Engineering – Systems Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the dynamic behavior of a mass–spring system when a hanging weight is pulled straight down from rest and released, and to relate the observed oscillation to restoring force and equilibrium.II. Experiment Objective: To qualitatively detect chloride ions in a food-related sample by observing the precipitation reaction between chloride ions and silver nitrate, and to understand the basic principle of precipitation reactions used in food analysis.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (1 tube, clean and dry), test tube rack, graduated dropper or pipette, salt solution (sodium chloride aqueous solution, representing food sample extract), silver nitrate solution (AgNO₃, dilute), glass rod (optional), safety goggles and gloves.III. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Parallel Circuit Voltage Law ExperimentI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Parallel Circuit Voltage Law ExperimentSubject: Engineering - Electrical EngineeringExperiment Objective: To verify that in a parallel circuit, the voltage across each branch is equal to the power supply voltage by measuring the voltage of the power supply, bulb L1, and bulb L2.II. Experimental EquipmentDC power supply (low voltage), switch, two identical light bulbs (L1 and L2), voltmeter, connecting wires.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ensure the power supply is turned off. Check that the two bulbs are identical and the voltmeter is set to the appropriate DC voltage range.2. Circuit Connection: Connect bulbs L1 and L2 in parallel to the power supply through the switch. Ensure all connections are firm and correct.3. Measuring Supply Voltage: Connect the voltmeter in parallel across the power supply terminals.4. Switch Operation: Close the switch to energize the circuit and record the power supply voltage reading.5. Measuring Bulb L1 Voltage: Keep the switch closed, move the voltmeter probes to both ends of bulb L1, and record the voltage.6. Measuring Bulb L2 Voltage: Move the voltmeter probes to both ends of bulb L2 and record the voltage.7. End Operation: Open the switch and disconnect the circuit.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. After the switch is closed, both bulbs L1 and L2 light up simultaneously with similar brightness.2. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesIn a parallel circuit, each branch is directly connected to the power supply. Therefore, the voltage across each branch component is equal to the power supply voltage. This experiment confirms the parallel circuit voltage law: U = U1 = U2, where U is the supply voltage, and U1 and U2 are the voltages across bulbs L1 and L2 respectively.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Turning a Rotary Potentiometer to Smoothly Vary a Lamp’s BrightnessI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Using a Rotary Potentiometer to Smoothly Control Lamp Brightness2. Subject: Engineering – Electrical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how a rotary potentiometer connected in series can continuously adjust the brightness of an incandescent lamp; to understand the relationship between resistance, current, and luminous intensity; and to practice basic circuit operation and observation skills.II. Experimental EquipmentRotary potentiometer (one, with knob clearly marked), small low-voltage incandescent lamp (one), DC power supply or battery pack (matched to lamp rating), connecting wires, tabletop or flat working surface, fixed camera or tripod (for time-lapse recording), switch (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the power supply, potentiometer, and lamp on the tabletop. Ensure the power is turned off. Fix the camera position and focus so that the potentiometer knob, lamp, and hand operation are all clearly visible.2. Circuit Connection: Connect the potentiometer in series with the incandescent lamp and the power supply, ensuring all connections are firm and correct.3. Initial State Check: Set the potentiometer knob to one extreme position (maximum or minimum resistance). Turn on the power supply.4. Core Operation: Slowly and smoothly rotate the potentiometer knob in one direction using your hand. After reaching the end position, slowly rotate the knob back in the opposite direction. Maintain a steady speed suitable for time-lapse recording.5. Completion: After observing the full range of brightness changes, return the knob to the initial position and turn off the power supply.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: When the power is turned on, the lamp is either dim or bright depending on the initial knob position.2. During Rotation: As the knob is slowly turned, the lamp brightness changes smoothly and continuously, becoming gradually brighter or dimmer without sudden jumps.3. Reverse Rotation: When the knob is turned back, the lamp brightness correspondingly decreases or increases smoothly, showing a reversible and continuous control effect.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe potentiometer acts as a variable resistor in the circuit. Rotating the knob changes the effective resistance in series with the lamp. According to Ohm’s law (I = V/R), increasing resistance reduces the current through the lamp, causing lower brightness, while decreasing resistance increases current, making the lamp brighter. The smooth mechanical rotation of the potentiometer results in continuous electrical resistance change, producing a smooth variation in lamp brightness.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the supply voltage does not exceed the lamp’s rated voltage.2. Rotate the potentiometer slowly to avoid sudden current changes.3. Check wiring before powering on to prevent short circuits.4. Keep the camera fixed to ensure consistent visual comparison in time-lapse recording.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: continuous control of electrical current using a rotary potentiometer to vary incandescent lamp brightness. Minimum assumptions: a low-voltage DC source, a potentiometer functioning as a variable resistor, and an incandescent lamp whose brightness visibly depends on current.Phased storyline: (1) Static setup on a tabletop with lamp and potentiometer wired in series, camera focus fixed; (2) Power on with an initial lamp brightness; (3) Hand slowly rotates the potentiometer knob, causing a gradual, continuous brightness increase or decrease; (4) Knob reverses direction and brightness smoothly reverses; (5) System returns to rest. Visibility constraints: the knob rotation, hand movement, and lamp filament brightness must remain in frame simultaneously to verify causal linkage.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Paper Glider Nose-Up vs Nose-Down Trim Glide ComparisonI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Glide Behavior of Paper Gliders with Different Trim Angles2. Subject: Engineering - Aerospace Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe how trim angle (nose-up vs nose-down) affects glide path, descent rate, and stability when two identical paper gliders are released from the same height without initial push.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical paper gliders made from the same paper and design; indoor hall with sufficient height and still air; step ladder or balcony for equal-height release; optional floor markers for landing observation.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Construct two identical paper gliders. Adjust one to a slight nose-up trim and the other to a slight nose-down trim while keeping mass distribution the same.2. Positioning: Stand in a large indoor hall. Hold both gliders side by side at the same height, wings level, noses pointing forward.3. Release: Simultaneously release both gliders with open hands, applying no forward or downward push.4. Observation: Track each glider visually from release to floor contact, focusing on glide angle, speed, and stability.5. Completion: Allow both gliders to land naturally and mark approximate landing positions if needed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both gliders start from the same height with no initial velocity.2. During Glide: The nose-up trimmed glider descends more slowly with a flatter glide path and greater pitch angle; the nose-down trimmed glider descends faster with a steeper glide path.3. Final State: The nose-down glider typically reaches the floor first, landing closer to the release point vertically; the nose-up glider lands later and farther away horizontally.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesTrim angle determines the angle of attack of the glider. A nose-up trim increases angle of attack, producing more lift but also more drag, resulting in slower, flatter glide. A nose-down trim reduces angle of attack, decreasing lift-to-drag ratio and causing a faster, steeper descent. This experiment demonstrates the balance of lift, drag, and gravity in unpowered flight.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure both gliders are structurally identical except for trim; release simultaneously without push; conduct experiment in still air to avoid airflow interference.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Uneven Dye Spreading in Water vs OilI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Uneven Dye Spreading in Water vs Oil2. Subject: Engineering - Chemical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how liquid polarity affects the diffusion and miscibility of substances by visually comparing the spreading behavior of food coloring in water and cooking oil.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical clear glass containers, water, cooking oil, food coloring (single color), dropper, flat stable surface, camera or smartphone with fixed focus and time-lapse function.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place the two identical clear glass containers side by side on a flat surface. Pour equal volumes of water into one container and cooking oil into the other. Ensure both liquids are still and at room temperature.Camera Setup: Position the camera directly in front of the containers, ensuring both are fully in frame. Fix the focus and exposure, and enable time-lapse recording.Core Operation: Using a dropper, simultaneously release one drop of food coloring into the center of each container, avoiding contact with container walls.Recording: Allow the camera to record continuously as the dye spreads in each liquid for a short period.Completion: Stop recording once the contrast in spreading behavior is clearly visible.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both liquids are transparent and colorless before dye addition.After Dropping Dye: In water, the food coloring quickly disperses and diffuses throughout the liquid. In cooking oil, the dye remains mostly intact, spreading very slowly or forming localized droplets.Final State: The water becomes uniformly colored, while the oil shows minimal color diffusion.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on polarity and miscibility principles in chemical engineering. Water is a polar solvent, and food coloring is generally water-soluble, allowing rapid diffusion. Cooking oil is non-polar, making it immiscible with the polar dye. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure containers are identical to avoid geometric bias. Add dye drops simultaneously for fair comparison. Avoid shaking or disturbing the liquids during observation.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Sodium Alginate Droplets Forming Gel Beads in Calcium Chloride SolutionI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Formation of Calcium Alginate Gel BeadsSubject: Engineering – Biomedical EngineeringExperiment Objective: To demonstrate ionic crosslinking hydrogel formation by observing sodium alginate droplets forming gel beads in calcium chloride solution.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsBeaker (100–250 mL), calcium chloride solution (0.1–0.2 M, clear and colorless), sodium alginate solution (1–2%, viscous), plastic pipette or dropper, glass rod or gentle swirling by hand, lab bench, gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a beaker containing calcium chloride solution on the lab bench; ensure the solution is clear and still.2. Loading: Draw sodium alginate solution into a pipette, avoiding air bubbles.3. Droplet Addition: Hold the pipette vertically above the beaker and slowly release sodium alginate droplets into the calcium chloride solution.4. Gentle Swirling: Gently swirl the beaker as more droplets are added to prevent beads from sticking together.5. Completion: After adding several droplets, stop swirling and allow beads to settle at the bottom of the beaker.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Calcium chloride solution is clear and colorless.During Addition: Each sodium alginate droplet forms a spherical gel bead immediately upon contact with the solution.After Swirling: Beads remain discrete, soft, and translucent, settling gently at the bottom.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSodium alginate is a polysaccharide that undergoes ionic crosslinking in the presence of divalent calcium ions. When alginate droplets enter calcium chloride solution, Ca2+ ions replace Na+ ions and crosslink alginate chains, forming insoluble calcium alginate hydrogel beads. This principle is widely used in biomedical engineering for cell encapsulation and drug delivery.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Addition Reaction of Ethylene with Bromine WaterI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Addition Reaction of Ethylene with Bromine Water2. Subject: Engineering - Chemical Engineering (Organic Chemistry Fundamentals)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the addition reaction between ethylene and bromine, verify the unsaturated nature of ethylene through the decolorization of bromine water, and understand the basic reaction characteristics of alkenes.II. Experimental Equipment and Reagents1. Test tube (1 tube, 15×150 mm)2. Test tube rack3. Gas delivery tube (glass tube with rubber tubing)4. Ethylene gas source (prepared in advance)5. Bromine water (orange-yellow, approximately 10 mL)6. Rubber stopper with hole (optional, to fix the delivery tube)7. Safety goggles and glovesIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place a clean test tube on the test tube rack. Wear safety goggles and gloves. Use a measuring cylinder to measure 10 mL of bromine water and pour it into the test tube. Observe that the solution is orange-yellow and clear.2. Equipment Setup: Insert one end of the gas delivery tube into the test tube so that the tube opening is below the surface of the bromine water but does not touch the tube wall or bottom. Connect the other end to the ethylene gas source.3. Core Operation: Slowly introduce ethylene gas into the test tube. Control the gas flow to ensure steady bubbling through the bromine water.4. Observation: Continue introducing ethylene gas while closely observing the color change of the bromine water.5. Completion: When the bromine water becomes completely colorless, stop the ethylene gas flow. Remove the delivery tube from the test tube, place the test tube back on the rack, and record the final state.6. Cleanup: Dispose of the reaction mixture according to chemical waste regulations. Clean and return all equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The bromine water in the test tube is orange-yellow and transparent.2. During Gas Introduction: As ethylene gas bubbles through the solution, the orange-yellow color gradually fades.3. Final State: The bromine water becomes colorless, indicating that bromine has been consumed in the reaction.V. Summary of Experimental Principle1. Core Principle: Ethylene (C2H4) is an unsaturated hydrocarbon containing a carbon–carbon double bond. It can undergo an addition reaction with bromine.2. Reaction Equation: C2H4 + Br2 → C2H4Br23. Principle Analysis: When ethylene is introduced into bromine water, bromine molecules add across the double bond of ethylene, forming 1,2-dibromoethane. As bromine is consumed, its characteristic orange-yellow color disappears. The decolorization of bromine water is direct evidence of the addition reaction and confirms the presence of a carbon–carbon double bond in ethylene.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Bromine water is corrosive and volatile; avoid direct contact and inhalation.2. Introduce ethylene gas slowly to prevent solution splashing.3. Ensure good ventilation during the experiment.4. Strictly follow waste disposal regulations for bromine-containing solutions.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Mass–Spring Oscillator Released from Different Initial DisplacementsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Mass–Spring Oscillator Released from Different Initial Displacements2. Subject: Engineering – Systems Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that for two identical mass–spring oscillators, different initial displacements affect the amplitude of motion but not the oscillation period, and to understand the basic dynamic behavior of simple harmonic motion.II. Experimental EquipmentVertical spring–mass oscillator set (2 identical sets, each including a fixed support, identical spring, and identical mass), rigid lab bench, ruler or scale (for measuring displacement), smartphone or camera (for motion recording), marker or tape (to mark equilibrium position).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the two identical vertical spring–mass oscillators side by side on a stable lab bench. Ensure the springs and masses are identical and freely hanging without obstruction. Mark the equilibrium position of each mass when at rest.2. Initial Displacement Setup: Gently pull the left mass downward to a larger displacement below its equilibrium position. Pull the right mass downward to a smaller displacement. Ensure both masses are held still and aligned vertically.3. Release Operation: Simultaneously release both masses from rest without giving any initial push, ensuring only gravitational and spring forces act on the masses.4. Recording and Observation: Record the motion of both oscillators using a camera or observe directly from the side, keeping both oscillators in the same field of view.5. Completion: Allow both oscillators to oscillate for several cycles, then let them come to rest naturally.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both masses start from rest at different vertical positions, with the left mass displaced farther than the right.2. During Motion: After release, both masses oscillate up and down along the vertical direction. The left mass shows a larger oscillation amplitude, while the right mass shows a smaller amplitude.3. Comparative Observation: Despite the difference in amplitudes, both masses complete each oscillation cycle in the same time, repeatedly passing through the equilibrium position together.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates simple harmonic motion in identical mass–spring systems. For an ideal mass–spring oscillator, the period of oscillation depends only on the mass and spring constant, not on the initial displacement (amplitude). When released from rest, different initial displacements result in different amplitudes, but the oscillation frequency and period remain the same, illustrating the linear restoring force described by Hooke’s law.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both springs and masses are identical to guarantee a fair comparison.2. Release both masses simultaneously and without any extra force.3. Keep the setup stable to avoid external vibrations or disturbances.4. Observe from a safe distance to avoid interference with the oscillating masses.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: identical mass–spring oscillators undergoing simple harmonic motion, where amplitude depends on initial displacement but period depends only on mass and spring constant. Minimum assumptions: springs are identical and linear, masses are equal, motion is vertical, and both are released from rest without external forces. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) setup phase showing two identical vertical oscillators side by side at rest; (2) initial condition phase where the left mass is pulled farther down than the right; (3) release phase with simultaneous release from rest; (4) motion phase where both masses oscillate vertically, the left with larger amplitude; (5) comparison phase showing both oscillators passing equilibrium together repeatedly, indicating equal periods. Visibility constraints: both oscillators must remain in the same frame with a clear side view to compare amplitude and timing.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: LED Response When Bridged by Graphite Pencil Lead and Wooden StickSubject: Engineering - Materials Science & EngineeringObjective: To demonstrate the difference in electrical conductivity between graphite and wood by observing whether an LED in a simple battery-powered circuit turns on or remains off when a visible gap is bridged with different materials.II. Experiment Title: Steel Ball Pressed into Aluminum vs Steel under the Same Load2. Subject: Engineering - Materials Science & Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To compare the deformation behavior of aluminum and steel under identical loading conditions, and to understand the relationship between material hardness, yield strength, and plastic deformation.II. manual: Experiment Title: Timer Compare Match PWM Control of LED BrightnessSubject: Engineering – Mechatronics & RoboticsExperiment Objective: To understand how a microcontroller uses a timer compare match to generate a PWM signal, and how adjusting a potentiometer changes the PWM duty cycle to control LED brightness.Experimental Equipment: Microcontroller development board (with timer/PWM capability), LED (1), current-limiting resistor (220–330 ohms), potentiometer (10k ohms), breadboard, jumper wires, USB power cable, computer with programming software.Experimental Procedure:1. Preparation: Connect the microcontroller to the computer via USB. Fix the camera focus and position to clearly capture the LED and potentiometer for time-lapse recording.2. Circuit Setup: Connect the LED in series with the resistor to a PWM-capable output pin and ground. Connect the potentiometer ends to Vcc and GND, with the wiper connected to an analog input pin.3. Program Loading: Upload a program that configures a hardware timer in PWM mode. Set the compare register value based on the analog reading from the potentiometer.4. Core Operation: Power the system. Slowly rotate the potentiometer knob while observing the LED.5. Completion: After observing the full brightness range, stop the system and disconnect power.Observation of Experimental Phenomena:- Initial State: LED emits dim or medium light at the starting potentiometer position.- During Rotation: As the potentiometer is rotated, the LED brightness gradually increases or decreases smoothly.- Final State: At extreme positions, the LED reaches minimum (almost off) or maximum brightness.Summary of Experimental Principle:The microcontroller timer operates in PWM mode, repeatedly counting and comparing its value with a compare register. When the timer value is below the compare value, the output is high; otherwise, it is low. Changing the compare value alters the duty cycle of the PWM signal. The potentiometer provides an analog voltage that is converted into a digital value, which updates the compare register. A higher duty cycle delivers more average current through the LED, increasing brightness, while a lower duty cycle reduces brightness.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Sulfate Detection in Food (Barium Chloride Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Sulfate Detection in Food by Barium Chloride Method2. Subject: Engineering – Food and Bioprocess Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To qualitatively detect sulfate ions in a food-related sample by observing the formation of a white precipitate after adding barium chloride solution, and to understand the basic principle of precipitation reactions used in food analysis.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (1), test tube rack, measuring pipette or dropper, sulfate-containing mineral water sample, barium chloride solution (BaCl2, aqueous), safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube on the test tube rack and wear safety goggles.2. Sample Addition: Use a measuring pipette to transfer 2 ml of sulfate-containing mineral water into the test tube.3. Reagent Addition: Using a dropper, slowly add several drops of barium chloride solution into the test tube containing the mineral water.4. Mixing and Observation: Gently shake the test tube to mix the solutions and immediately observe the changes in the liquid.5. Completion: Place the test tube back on the rack for final observation and dispose of waste solution according to laboratory regulations.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The mineral water is colorless and transparent, with no visible solid.2. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on a classic precipitation reaction used in food and water analysis. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Fatigue Failure of a Notched Aluminum StripSubject: Engineering – Materials Science & EngineeringExperiment Objective: To demonstrate metal fatigue and stress concentration by repeatedly bending a notched aluminum strip clamped in a bench vise, and to understand how cyclic loading leads to fracture.II. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Simply Supported Beam on Two Rollers with a Center LoadI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Simply Supported Beam on Two Rollers with a Center Load2. Subject: Engineering – Mechanical Engineering (Strength of Materials)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the deformation behavior of a straight beam simply supported on two identical rollers under a single central load, verify elastic deformation and recovery, and understand the relationship between load and deflection.II. Experimental EquipmentStraight slender beam (metal or plastic), two identical cylindrical rollers (supports), loading device or standard weights, loading hanger, flat base or frame, ruler or dial gauge (optional), camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the two identical rollers on a horizontal base with equal spacing. Lay the straight beam horizontally on the rollers so that it is free to rotate and translate slightly at the supports.2. Alignment: Mark the exact midpoint of the beam. Fix the camera position and focus to capture the entire beam and supports; do not change focus during the experiment.3. Loading: Slowly apply a single vertical load at the exact midpoint of the beam using a loading hanger or weight. Increase the load gradually to avoid impact.4. Observation: Maintain the load briefly while observing the beam deformation.5. Unloading: Slowly remove the load completely and continue recording to capture the recovery of the beam.6. Completion: Stop recording, remove equipment, and restore the setup.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The beam is straight and horizontal, resting symmetrically on the two rollers.2. During Loading: As the central load is applied, the beam bends downward smoothly, with the maximum deflection occurring at the midpoint; deformation is symmetric about the center.3. During Unloading: After the load is removed, the beam gradually returns to its original straight shape, showing elastic recovery.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesA simply supported beam on rollers can freely rotate at the supports, producing zero bending moment at both ends. When a concentrated load is applied at the midpoint, internal bending moments develop, causing elastic deformation. According to elementary beam theory, the maximum bending moment and deflection occur at the center. If the load is within the elastic limit of the material, removal of the load results in full recovery of the original shape.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Apply and remove the load slowly to avoid dynamic effects.2. Ensure the load is applied exactly at the midpoint for symmetry.3. Keep the camera fixed to ensure consistent time-lapse observation.4. Do not exceed the elastic limit of the beam material.

Experiment Title: Thermistor Reacting to Warm vs Cold Objects with Visible LED Indication2. Subject: Engineering - Electrical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how a thermistor responds to temperature changes by observing visible changes in LED brightness when exposed to warm and cold objects.II. Experimental EquipmentThermistor (NTC type recommended), LED (any visible color), battery (3–9 V), connecting wires, resistor (current limiting for LED), breadboard or taped connections, steaming mug of hot water, bowl of ice water, tabletop, camera fixed on tripod.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the battery, thermistor, resistor, and LED on a tabletop and connect them in series so that the LED lights under normal room temperature.2. Warm Object Test: Slowly bring a steaming mug close to the thermistor without touching it; hold for several seconds while observing the LED.4. Cold Object Test: Remove the mug, allow the system to stabilize briefly, then bring a bowl of ice water close to the thermistor and observe the LED again.5. Alternation: Repeat the warm and cold approach once more to confirm repeatability.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: At room temperature, the LED maintains a steady baseline brightness.2. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Mass–Spring–Damper Oscillation Matched to RLC Circuit Oscillation (LED Brightness)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Analogy Between Mass–Spring–Damper Oscillation and RLC Circuit Oscillation2. Subject: Engineering – Systems Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the dynamic analogy between a mechanical mass–spring–damper system and an electrical RLC circuit by observing synchronized decaying oscillations of mechanical displacement and LED brightness.II. Experimental EquipmentMass–spring–damper apparatus (mass block, spring, damper, vertical or horizontal guide), rigid support frame, ruler or scale; RLC circuit board with resistor, inductor, capacitor, DC power source, switch, and visible LED; connecting wires; stable bench; camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse or continuous recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the mass–spring–damper system on the left side of the bench and the RLC circuit with LED on the right. Ensure both systems are at rest. Fix the camera focus and framing so both systems are clearly visible.2. Initial Setup: Displace the mass slightly from its equilibrium position and hold it stationary. Keep the circuit switch open; the LED should be off.3. Core Operation: Start recording. Simultaneously release the mass and close the circuit switch.4. Observation: Allow both systems to evolve freely without further interference until oscillations visibly decay.5. Completion: Stop recording after the motion and LED brightness have nearly ceased. Reset equipment if needed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The mass is displaced and stationary; the LED is off.2. After Release and Switching: The mass begins oscillating about equilibrium with gradually decreasing amplitude; the LED turns on and its brightness oscillates or pulses, also gradually decreasing.3. Final State: Both mechanical motion and LED brightness decay toward steady equilibrium or off state.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe experiment demonstrates the analogy between mechanical and electrical second-order systems. The mass–spring–damper system and the RLC circuit are governed by mathematically similar differential equations. Mechanical displacement corresponds to electrical charge or current, damping corresponds to resistance, and both systems exhibit decaying oscillations when released from an initial energy state. The LED brightness provides a visual indicator of electrical oscillation energy decay, matching the mechanical motion trend.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Latex Bead Agglutination with Specific Antibodies in LiquidI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Latex Bead Agglutination with Specific Antibodies in Liquid2. Subject: Engineering – Biomedical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate antigen–antibody specific binding using latex bead agglutination, and to visually compare agglutination versus non-specific control under identical conditions.II. Experimental Materials and Equipment- Clear reaction plate or slide with two wells- Colored latex bead suspension (uniform concentration)- Specific anti-bead antibody solution- Buffer solution (e.g., PBS) as negative control- Micropipettes and tips- Lab bench with uniform lighting- Camera mounted above the wells (fixed focus) for time-lapse recordingIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clear reaction plate on the lab bench. Ensure both wells are clean and dry. Fix the camera focus and framing to include both wells.2. Loading Beads: Using a micropipette, add equal volumes of identical colored latex bead suspension into the left and right wells.3. Reagent Addition: Add a defined volume of specific anti-bead antibodies to the left well. Add an equal volume of buffer solution to the right well as a control.4. Mixing: Gently swirl the plate to mix contents in both wells without splashing.5. Recording and Observation: Keep the camera focus fixed and record the wells over time to capture dynamic changes.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both wells show uniformly dispersed colored latex beads with no visible clumps.2. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Reducing Sugar Detection in Food (Fehling’s Reagent Method)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Reducing Sugar Detection in Apple Juice by Fehling’s Reagent MethodSubject: Engineering – Food and Bioprocess EngineeringExperiment Objective: To detect the presence of reducing sugars in apple juice by observing the reaction between reducing sugars and Fehling’s reagent under heating conditions, and to understand the basic principle of redox reactions used in food analysis.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (15×150 mm), test tube rack, graduated dropper or pipette, beaker, boiling water bath, hot plate, apple juice (filtered if necessary), Fehling’s reagent A (copper sulfate solution), Fehling’s reagent B (alkaline sodium potassium tartrate solution), test tube holder.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube on the rack. Use a pipette to add 2 mL of apple juice into the test tube.2. Reagent Addition: Add 1 mL of Fehling’s reagent A into the test tube, then add 1 mL of Fehling’s reagent B. Gently shake the test tube to mix; the solution appears blue.3. Heating: Place the test tube into a boiling water bath and heat for approximately 2 minutes using a test tube holder.4. Observation: Remove the test tube carefully and observe the color and state of the solution.5. Ending: After observation, place the test tube back on the rack, allow it to cool, and dispose of waste according to laboratory rules.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The mixed solution of apple juice and Fehling’s reagents is blue.During Heating: With heating in the boiling water bath, the blue color gradually fades.Final State: A yellow, orange, or brick-red precipitate appears, indicating a positive result for reducing sugars.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesFehling’s reagent contains Cu2+ ions in an alkaline medium. Reducing sugars in apple juice contain aldehyde or ketone groups that can reduce Cu2+ to Cu2O under heating conditions. Cu2O forms a yellow to brick-red precipitate. The appearance of this precipitate indicates the presence of reducing sugars in the food sample.

Visibility requirements: close-up view of test tube color before and after heating, clear sequence of actions without time reversal.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Graph Breadth-First Search (BFS) DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Graph Breadth-First Search (BFS) Demonstration2. Subject: Engineering - Computer Science - Data Structures and Algorithms3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the BFS algorithm on a simple graph, understand level-order traversal, queue-based processing, and the visited mechanism.II. Experimental Materials and Environment1. Digital canvas with white background2. Six circular nodes labeled A, B, C, D, E, F3. Straight lines representing edges between nodes4. Color scheme: red (current start), blue (discovered neighbors), gray (visited/processed)5. Queue visualization panel displayed on the sideIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Draw six labeled nodes (A–F) on a white background and connect them with lines to form a simple connected graph. Initialize all nodes as unvisited.2. Initialization: Select node A as the BFS start node. Highlight node A in red and enqueue A in the queue visualization.3. Core Operation: Dequeue node A. Highlight all unvisited adjacent nodes of A in blue and enqueue them in left-to-right order. After processing, fade node A to gray.4. Iteration: Repeatedly dequeue the front node in the queue, discover its unvisited neighbors (turn them blue and enqueue), then mark the dequeued node as gray.5. Termination: Continue until the queue is empty and all reachable nodes are visited.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Node A turns red first, indicating the BFS start.2. Neighboring nodes of A turn blue simultaneously, forming the first level.3. Nodes are processed in queue order, level by level.4. Each processed node fades to gray, indicating it has been visited.5. The queue visualization updates dynamically with enqueue and dequeue operations.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesBFS is a graph traversal algorithm that explores nodes in increasing order of distance from a start node. It uses a queue to ensure first-in-first-out processing, guaranteeing level-order traversal. Color changes represent node states: red for current start, blue for discovered but not processed, and gray for fully processed nodes.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Sphalerite Zinc Ion Detection (Dithizone Color Development Method)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Sphalerite Zinc Ion Detection by Dithizone Color DevelopmentSubject: Engineering – Geotechnical Engineering (Mineral Analysis)Objective: To qualitatively detect zinc ions released from sphalerite by observing the color development of the zinc–dithizone complex.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsColorimetric tube (1), dropper, glass rod or tube stopper, sphalerite powder (small amount), dilute nitric acid, dithizone reagent, protective gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Sample Preparation: Place a small amount of sphalerite powder into a clean colorimetric tube.2. Dissolution: Add an appropriate amount of dilute nitric acid into the tube until the powder is submerged. Gently shake to promote dissolution and release zinc ions.3. Color Development: Using a dropper, add exactly two drops of dithizone reagent into the tube.4. Mixing: Stopper the tube and shake gently for several seconds to ensure thorough mixing.5. Observation: Place the tube upright and observe the color change of the solution.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Sphalerite appears as a grayish powder; the acid solution is colorless.After Dissolution: The solid partially or fully dissolves, forming a clear or slightly colored solution containing Zn2+.After Adding Dithizone and Shaking: The solution develops a distinct orange-red to reddish color, indicating the formation of a zinc–dithizone complex.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSphalerite (ZnS) reacts with dilute nitric acid to release zinc ions into solution. Dithizone is a selective organic reagent that forms a colored chelate complex with Zn2+. Upon shaking, the zinc–dithizone complex forms, producing a characteristic red or orange-red color. The appearance of this color confirms the presence of zinc ions derived from sphalerite.VI. PrecautionsUse dilute nitric acid carefully to avoid splashing; add dithizone in controlled drops; dispose of waste solutions according to laboratory safety regulations.

Experiment Objective: To demonstrate mechanical-to-electrical energy conversion using a handheld piezoelectric igniter by observing visible electrical sparks during repeated press–release actions; to document the phenomenon using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Acid–Base Neutralization Monitored by Light Bulb Brightness2. Subject: Engineering – Chemical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how acid–base neutralization affects solution conductivity by observing changes in the brightness of an incandescent bulb connected to a simple electrical circuit.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass beaker (250 mL), aqueous acid solution (e.g., dilute HCl), aqueous base solution (e.g., dilute NaOH), battery (low-voltage DC), small incandescent bulb, connecting wires, two inert metal electrodes (e.g., graphite or stainless steel), glass stirring rod, camera with fixed focus for time-lapse recording, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clear beaker on a stable surface. Pour a fixed volume of aqueous acid into the beaker. Ensure the solution is clear and colorless. Put on safety goggles.2. Circuit Setup: Insert the two metal electrodes into the acid solution without touching each other. Connect the electrodes in series with the battery and the small incandescent bulb using wires, forming a closed circuit.3. Initial Observation: Switch on the circuit and observe the initial brightness of the bulb, which indicates the conductivity of the acidic solution.4. Neutralization Operation: While keeping the circuit connected, steadily pour the aqueous base into the beaker in small increments. Gently stir the solution continuously with a glass rod to ensure uniform mixing.5. Recording: Keep the camera focus fixed and record the entire process using time-lapse photography as the base is added and the bulb brightness changes.6. Completion: Stop adding base when the brightness change becomes stable. Disconnect the power, remove electrodes, and clean the apparatus.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The bulb glows with a certain brightness when the electrodes are in the acidic solution.2. During Base Addition: As the base is added and the solution is stirred, the bulb brightness gradually changes (typically decreases) as neutralization proceeds.3. Near Neutralization: When the acid is largely neutralized, the bulb becomes noticeably dimmer, indicating reduced ionic concentration and lower conductivity.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAcid–base neutralization converts hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions into water, reducing the total concentration of mobile ions in solution. Electrical conductivity depends on the presence of these ions. As neutralization progresses, conductivity decreases, leading to reduced current in the circuit and a corresponding decrease in the brightness of the incandescent bulb.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Sequential Stack Push and Pop Operation Principle DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Sequential Stack Push and Pop Operation Principle Demonstration2. Subject: Engineering - Computer Science3. Experiment Objective: To understand the Last In First Out (LIFO) property of a stack by visually demonstrating sequential push and pop operations using labeled elements.II. Experimental Equipment1. Computer or display device2. Stack operation animation or simulation environment3. Three colored square elements labeled A, B, and CIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Display a dark background with a vertical empty stack positioned at the center, clearly labeled Last In First Out.2. Push Operation Demonstration: Push square A from the top into the stack; then push square B onto the top of A; finally push square C onto the top of B, forming a vertical stack.3. Pop Operation Demonstration: Perform a pop operation to remove the top element C; perform a second pop to remove B; perform a third pop to remove A, returning the stack to empty.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The stack is empty and labeled Last In First Out.2. During Push Operations: Each pushed square appears on the top of the stack, increasing its height in the order A, then B, then C.3. During Pop Operations: Squares are removed from the top in reverse order, first C, then B, then A.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesA stack is a linear data structure that follows the Last In First Out principle. The push operation adds an element to the top of the stack, and the pop operation removes the element currently at the top. Because only the top element can be accessed, the last element pushed is always the first one popped, which is visually confirmed in this experiment.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Milk Casein Curdling After Adding AcidI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Milk Casein Curdling After Adding Acid2. Subject: Engineering – Chemical Engineering (Food/Chemical Processes)3. Experiment Objective: To observe acid-induced coagulation of milk casein, understand pH-triggered protein denaturation and aggregation, and visually record the process using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass bowl (1), milk (200–300 mL, preferably whole milk), lemon juice or vinegar (10–20 mL), spoon or glass stirrer, heat source or warm water bath, thermometer (optional), camera or phone on tripod with fixed focus.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Pour milk into a clear glass bowl. Warm the milk to approximately 40–60°C (warm but not boiling). Place the bowl on a stable surface.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera facing the bowl. Fix focus and framing to include the entire bowl. Start time-lapse recording.3. Acid Addition: Slowly add lemon juice (or vinegar) to the warm milk while gently stirring for 5–10 seconds to distribute the acid evenly.4. Resting: Stop stirring and leave the mixture undisturbed for several minutes.5. Completion: Continue recording until visible separation stabilizes. Stop recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Milk appears uniform, opaque white.2. After Acid Addition and Stirring: Small white particles begin to appear.3. During Resting: White curds aggregate and separate from a translucent yellow-green liquid (whey), forming visible layers or clusters.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleMilk contains casein proteins stabilized in micelles at near-neutral pH. Adding an acid lowers the pH toward casein’s isoelectric point (~4.6), neutralizing surface charges and destabilizing micelles. Casein proteins denature and aggregate into insoluble curds, while the remaining liquid phase becomes whey. Gentle stirring promotes uniform acid distribution; resting allows gravity-driven aggregation and separation.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Do not overheat milk to avoid boiling artifacts.2. Stir gently to avoid breaking forming curds.3. Use a clear glass container for visibility.4. Keep camera focus fixed to ensure consistent time-lapse observation.

Phased storyline: (1) Stable opaque milk in clear glass bowl; (2) visible addition of lemon juice while gently stirred; (3) early particulate formation; (4) undisturbed resting with accelerated time-lapse; (5) clear emergence of white curds and translucent whey. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Battery Powers a Light Bulb that Dims When a Second Bulb Is Switched OnI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Battery Powering a Light Bulb that Visibly Dims When a Second Bulb Is Switched OnSubject: Engineering – Electrical EngineeringExperiment Objective: To observe how adding an identical bulb in parallel affects the brightness of an incandescent bulb powered by a single battery, and to understand the role of internal resistance and load in simple circuits.II. Experimental EquipmentSingle dry-cell battery (e.g., 1.5 V), two identical small incandescent bulbs, bulb holders, connecting wires, one toggle switch, stable power base, camera or smartphone on tripod (focus fixed for time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the battery on a stable surface. Fix the camera position and manually lock focus so that bulb brightness changes can be clearly recorded.2. Initial Circuit: Connect one incandescent bulb directly to the battery using wires to form a closed circuit. Ensure the bulb lights steadily.3. Parallel Branch Setup: Prepare a second branch consisting of an identical bulb in series with a toggle switch. Do not connect it yet.4. Parallel Connection: Connect the second branch in parallel with the first bulb across the battery terminals, keeping the toggle switch in the OFF position.5. Core Operation: Start recording. Switch the toggle switch ON to connect the second bulb in parallel. After a short observation, switch it OFF again.6. Completion: Stop recording, disconnect the circuit, and allow bulbs to cool.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: With only one bulb connected, it glows at normal brightness.2. Switch ON: When the second identical bulb is switched on in parallel, both bulbs light, but the original bulb becomes visibly dimmer.3. Switch OFF: When the second bulb is switched off, the original bulb returns to its initial brighter state.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleA real battery has internal resistance. When only one bulb is connected, the current is relatively small and the terminal voltage is higher. Adding a second identical bulb in parallel increases the total current drawn from the battery, causing a larger voltage drop across the battery’s internal resistance. As a result, the terminal voltage decreases and both bulbs receive less voltage, so their brightness is reduced. Removing the second bulb lowers the current and restores the brightness of the first bulb.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstrate the effect of increased load in a parallel circuit powered by a single real battery, emphasizing internal resistance. Minimum assumptions: one battery with non-negligible internal resistance, two identical incandescent bulbs, true parallel wiring, and a functioning toggle switch.Phased storyline: (1) Initial phase – one bulb connected, steady bright glow. (2) Transition – toggle switch turned ON, second bulb joins in parallel. (3) Effect phase – immediate visible dimming of the first bulb and lighting of the second. (4) Recovery – switch turned OFF, second bulb goes dark and first bulb brightens again. Camera must remain fixed and in focus throughout to verify brightness changes and causal order.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Acrylamide Detection in Food (Colorimetric Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Acrylamide Detection in Fried Food by Colorimetric Method2. Subject: Engineering – Food and Bioprocess Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To detect the presence of acrylamide in fried French fries extract using a colorimetric reaction, and to understand the basic operation steps and reaction principle of acrylamide colorimetric analysis.II. Experimental Reagents and EquipmentTest tube (15×150 mm), test tube rack, dropper, water bath (temperature adjustable), thermometer, fried French fries extract, potassium bromide–potassium bromate solution, fuchsin sulfite reagent, protective gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean, dry test tube on the rack. Wear protective goggles and gloves.2. Sample Addition: Use a pipette to add 2 mL of fried French fries extract into the test tube.3. Reagent Addition: Add 1 drop of potassium bromide–potassium bromate solution into the test tube, then add 1 drop of fuchsin sulfite reagent.4. Heating: Place the test tube into a water bath maintained at 40℃. Heat gently and keep the temperature constant.5. Observation: After heating for a short time, remove the test tube and observe the color change of the solution.6. Completion: Record observations, then dispose of the reaction mixture according to laboratory waste regulations and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The fried French fries extract is light yellow to colorless and transparent.2. After Reagent Addition: The solution remains clear or slightly colored without obvious change.3. After Heating at 40℃: If acrylamide is present, the solution gradually develops a pink to reddish coloration; the color intensity correlates with acrylamide content.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAcrylamide in food extracts reacts under oxidative bromination conditions provided by the potassium bromide–potassium bromate system. The reaction products further react with fuchsin sulfite reagent to form a colored compound. The appearance and intensity of the pink-red color serve as the basis for qualitative or semi-quantitative detection of acrylamide. Heating at 40℃ accelerates the reaction, enabling visible color development within a short time.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Magnesium Detection in Food (Magneson Reagent Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Magnesium Detection in Food by Magneson Reagent Method2. Subject: Engineering – Food and Bioprocess Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To qualitatively detect magnesium ions in food samples by observing the color reaction between magnesium ions and magneson reagent under strongly alkaline conditions, and to master the basic operation of alkaline adjustment and reagent addition.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (15×150 mm), test tube rack, measuring pipette or dropper, laver extract (food sample extract), sodium hydroxide solution (approx. 1–2 mol/L), magneson reagent solution, pH paper or indicator (optional), safety gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube on the rack. Wear safety goggles and gloves. Ensure the laver extract is clear and free of large particles.2. Sample Addition: Use a pipette to accurately transfer 2 mL of laver extract into the test tube.3. Alkaline Adjustment: Add sodium hydroxide solution dropwise to the test tube while gently shaking. Use pH paper to confirm that the pH is adjusted to greater than 10.4. Reagent Addition: Add several drops (2–3 drops) of magneson reagent to the alkaline solution and gently shake to mix.5. Observation: Allow the solution to stand briefly and observe any color change.6. Finishing: Record the result. Dispose of the solution according to laboratory waste regulations and clean the apparatus.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The laver extract is light-colored or slightly greenish and transparent or slightly turbid.2. After NaOH Addition: The solution remains clear or slightly turbid, with no obvious color change.3. After Magneson Reagent Addition: If magnesium ions are present, the solution gradually develops a blue to blue-purple coloration, indicating a positive result.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleMagneson reagent specifically reacts with magnesium ions under strongly alkaline conditions (pH >10) to form a stable colored complex. Sodium hydroxide provides the alkaline environment required for the reaction. The appearance of a blue or blue-purple color confirms the presence of magnesium ions in the food extract. The intensity of the color qualitatively reflects the relative magnesium content.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Industrial Robotic Arm Pick-and-Place of a Small CubeSubject: Engineering – Mechatronics & RoboticsExperiment Objective: To demonstrate the basic pick-and-place operation of a multi-jointed industrial robotic arm using a gripper, and to observe motion sequencing and end-effector control under a fixed camera focus suitable for time-lapse recording.II. Experimental EquipmentMulti-jointed industrial robotic arm (6-DOF or similar); two flat table locations (A and B); small solid cube (uniform color, e.g., blue); parallel-jaw gripper; robot controller and teach pendant or PC; fixed-position camera with locked focus; safety enclosure or emergency stop.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Power on the robot and controller; ensure emergency stop is released. Place the cube at table location A. Fix the camera position and lock focus for time-lapse photography.2. Teaching/Programming: Define waypoints for approach, grasp, lift, transfer, and place above table location B. Set appropriate gripper open/close commands.3. Core Operation: Start the program. The arm moves to the approach position above the cube, closes the gripper to grasp the cube, lifts it vertically, transfers it to table location B, and opens the gripper to release the cube.4. Completion: The arm retracts to a safe home position. Stop recording and power down if required.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The cube rests stationary at table location A; the gripper is open.During Operation: The arm joints move sequentially; the gripper closes around the cube, which remains stable during lifting and transfer.Final State: The cube is released and remains stationary at table location B; the gripper opens and the arm retreats.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on robotic kinematics and end-effector control. Joint motions are coordinated to position the gripper in Cartesian space. The gripper applies sufficient normal force to overcome gravity and friction, enabling stable grasping. The pick-and-place sequence demonstrates state–cause–effect logic: commanded joint motion causes gripper positioning, gripper actuation causes cube grasping, and release causes placement.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the workspace is clear of humans; verify gripper force is suitable for the cube; keep camera focus fixed to avoid visual inconsistency; use emergency stop in case of abnormal motion.

Experiment Objective: To observe that adding identical batteries in series increases the brightness of an incandescent bulb by increasing the circuit voltage; to understand basic series-circuit behavior.II. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Ice Cube Melting Faster on a Metal Block than on a Wooden BlockI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Ice Cube Melting Comparison on Metal and Wood2. Subject: Engineering - Nuclear Engineering (Heat Transfer Fundamentals)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the effect of thermal conductivity on heat transfer by observing that identical ice cubes melt faster on a metal block than on a wooden block under identical environmental conditions.II. Experimental EquipmentMetal block (flat surface), wooden block (flat surface, similar size), two identical ice cubes, tray or tabletop, camera or smartphone with time-lapse function, room-temperature indoor environment.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the metal block and wooden block side by side on a flat surface in the same room. Ensure both blocks have been in the room long enough to reach room temperature.2. Setup: Position the camera directly facing the blocks, ensuring both blocks and their top surfaces are clearly visible. Fix the camera focus and do not move it during recording.3. Core Operation: Simultaneously place one identical ice cube on the center of the metal block and the other on the center of the wooden block.4. Recording: Start time-lapse recording immediately after placement. Leave the setup undisturbed while the ice cubes melt.5. Completion: Stop recording once a clear difference in melting extent is observed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both ice cubes are the same size and shape; no visible melting at placement.2. Over Time: The ice cube on the metal block develops water around it and shrinks faster than the ice cube on the wooden block.3. Final State: The metal-side ice cube is significantly smaller or nearly melted, while the wooden-side ice cube remains larger.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleMetal has a much higher thermal conductivity than wood, allowing it to transfer heat from the surrounding environment to the ice more efficiently. As a result, heat flows into the ice cube on the metal block at a faster rate, causing it to melt more quickly. Wood is a poor heat conductor, so the ice cube on wood receives heat more slowly and melts at a reduced rate.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Anti-seepage Performance Test of Geosynthetic Clay Liners (GCL)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Anti-seepage Performance Test of Geosynthetic Clay Liners (GCL)Subject: Engineering – Geotechnical EngineeringExperiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the anti-seepage performance of GCL by comparing seepage behavior in beakers with and without a GCL layer at the bottom.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent beakers (2 identical beakers), geosynthetic clay liner (GCL) sample sized to fit beaker bottom, colored aqueous solution (water with dye), graduated cylinder or cup for pouring, absorbent paper or tray.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place two clean, transparent beakers on a flat surface. Label one as GCL beaker and the other as control beaker.GCL Placement: Cut the GCL sample to fit the bottom of one beaker. Lay it flat and ensure it fully covers the bottom without wrinkles. Leave the other beaker unlined.Pouring Operation: Slowly pour equal volumes of colored aqueous solution into both beakers at the same time or sequentially with equal speed.Observation: Observe the bottom and sides of both beakers for colored water seepage or leakage over a short period.Completion: Stop pouring after reaching the same liquid level. Continue observing and record differences.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both beakers are empty and transparent; GCL beaker shows a visible liner at the bottom.After Pouring: In the control beaker, colored water quickly seeps through the bottom or spreads uniformly. Summary of Experimental PrincipleGCL contains bentonite clay that swells upon contact with water, forming a low-permeability barrier. This barrier effectively reduces or prevents water seepage. The experiment demonstrates the anti-seepage mechanism by comparing seepage behavior with and without the GCL layer under identical conditions.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: ECG Heart Signal Response to Light MovementI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: ECG Heart Signal Changes from Rest to Light Movement2. Subject: Engineering – Biomedical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe ECG heart signals obtained from chest electrodes in an adult subject, and to understand how light physical movement affects heart electrical activity.II. Experimental EquipmentClinical bed, adult volunteer, disposable chest ECG electrodes (3–5 leads), ECG lead wires, cardiac monitor with ECG display, adhesive tape, fixed-position camera for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the adult subject supine on a clinical bed. Clean the chest skin and attach ECG electrodes at standard chest positions. Connect electrodes to the cardiac monitor and confirm a stable ECG waveform. Fix the camera focus and position for time-lapse recording.2. Resting Baseline: Ask the subject to remain still and relaxed for a short period. Record the baseline ECG showing steady rhythmic peaks.3. Light Movement: Instruct the subject to perform brief light movement (such as gentle arm or leg motion) while remaining on the bed. Continue ECG recording during this phase.4. Return to Rest: Ask the subject to stop moving and rest again. Continue recording until the ECG stabilizes.5. Completion: Stop recording, gently remove electrodes, and power down equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. At rest, the ECG displays regular rhythmic electrical peaks with a stable heart rate.2. During light movement, the ECG shows an increased heart rate, with peaks occurring closer together.3. After returning to rest, the ECG gradually returns toward the baseline rhythm.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleECG electrodes detect bioelectric potentials generated by cardiac depolarization and repolarization. Light physical movement increases metabolic demand, activating the autonomic nervous system and increasing heart rate. This results in a higher frequency of rhythmic ECG peaks, which decreases again when the subject returns to rest.
