manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Electrolysis of Saturated Sodium Chloride SolutionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Electrolysis of Saturated Sodium Chloride Solution2. Subject: Engineering - Chemical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe electrode reactions during electrolysis of saturated sodium chloride solution using a graphite anode and iron cathode, identify the generation of alkaline environment and gases, and understand the electrochemical principles of brine electrolysis.II. Experimental EquipmentBeaker (250 mL), saturated sodium chloride solution, graphite rod (anode), iron strip (cathode), DC power supply, connecting wires with clips, phenolphthalein indicator, camera or microscope camera for focused time-lapse recording, safety goggles and gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear safety goggles and gloves. Pour saturated sodium chloride solution into the beaker until it is about 2/3 full.2. Electrode Setup: Insert the graphite rod and iron strip vertically into the solution, keeping them parallel and not touching. Connect the graphite rod to the positive terminal (anode) and the iron strip to the negative terminal (cathode).3. Indicator Addition: Add 2–3 drops of phenolphthalein to the solution and gently stir to distribute evenly. The solution should remain colorless initially.4. Core Operation: Turn on the DC power supply to apply a steady current. Adjust the camera to focus on the electrode region and start time-lapse or accelerated recording.5. Observation: Continuously observe and record the changes occurring around each electrode.6. Completion: After clear phenomena are observed, turn off the power supply, remove electrodes, dispose of solution properly, and clean all equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Solution is colorless and transparent; no bubbles at electrodes.2. After Power On: Bubbles appear at both electrodes. Near the iron cathode, the solution gradually turns pink, indicating an alkaline environment. Near the graphite anode, gas evolution is observed without color change.3. Continued Electrolysis: The pink region near the cathode becomes more distinct, and gas evolution becomes steadier at both electrodes.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesElectrolysis of saturated sodium chloride solution involves redox reactions at two electrodes. At the cathode (iron), water is reduced to produce hydrogen gas and hydroxide ions, increasing local pH and turning phenolphthalein pink: 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂↑ + 2OH⁻. At the anode (graphite), chloride ions are oxidized to chlorine gas: 2Cl⁻ − 2e⁻ → Cl₂↑. The experiment demonstrates electrode-specific reactions, ion migration, and the conversion of electrical energy into chemical energy.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Electrolysis of saturated sodium chloride solution using inert and active electrodes, highlighting electrode-specific redox reactions and indicator-based visualization of pH change.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: Presence of a DC power source, correct electrode polarity, sufficient ion concentration in saturated NaCl, and phenolphthalein responding only to alkaline conditions.Phased Storyline: (1) Static setup with colorless solution and inserted electrodes; (2) power applied causing immediate gas evolution; (3) localized pink color appears near cathode due to OH⁻ formation; (4) sustained bubbling and color contrast emphasized through focused, accelerated recording. Visibility must center on electrode regions, with stable framing to verify causal transitions.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Vitamin B6 Detection (Ninhydrin Colorimetric Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Detection of Vitamin B6 in Chicken Extract by Ninhydrin Colorimetric Method2. Subject: Engineering – Food and Bioprocess Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To qualitatively detect vitamin B6 in chicken extract using the ninhydrin colorimetric reaction and understand the principle of color development between ninhydrin and amino-containing compounds.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (15×150 mm), test tube rack, pipette or graduated dropper, water bath with temperature control, thermometer, chicken extract, ninhydrin reagent, heat-resistant gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube on the rack. Ensure the water bath is preheated and stabilized at 50℃.2. Sample Addition: Use a pipette to accurately add 2 mL of chicken extract into the test tube.3. Reagent Addition: Add 2 drops of ninhydrin reagent directly into the test tube containing the chicken extract.4. Heating: Place the test tube into the 50℃ water bath. Heat for a short period until color development is observed.5. Completion: Remove the test tube carefully and place it back on the rack for observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The chicken extract appears light yellow or pale brown and transparent to slightly turbid.2. During Heating: After adding ninhydrin and heating at 50℃, the solution gradually develops a purple or blue-purple coloration.3. Final State: The color stabilizes, indicating a positive ninhydrin reaction.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleNinhydrin reacts with free amino groups present in amino acids and vitamin B6-related compounds. Upon heating, this reaction produces a characteristic purple-blue compound (Ruhemann’s purple). Since chicken extract contains vitamin B6 and other amino-containing substances, heating with ninhydrin at 50℃ leads to visible color development, enabling qualitative detection.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Strictly control the volume of sample and number of reagent drops.2. Maintain the water bath temperature at approximately 50℃ to ensure proper reaction.3. Avoid direct contact with ninhydrin reagent and handle heated test tubes with care.4. Dispose of waste solutions according to laboratory regulations.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Enzymatic Soy Protein Hydrolysis Effect Detection (Solubility Method)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Enzymatic Soy Protein Hydrolysis Effect Detection (Solubility Method)Subject: Engineering – Food and Bioprocess EngineeringExperiment Objective: To demonstrate the effect of enzymatic hydrolysis on the solubility of soy protein by comparing unhydrolyzed soy protein suspension with neutral protease-treated soy protein solution through visual observation.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentTest tubes (2, identical), test tube rack, soy protein suspension (unhydrolyzed, containing visible precipitate), neutral protease-treated soy protein solution, dropper or measuring pipette, marker for labeling.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean test tubes on the test tube rack and label them as tube A and tube B.2. Sample Addition: Using a dropper, add an equal volume of unhydrolyzed soy protein suspension into tube A. Ensure visible precipitate is present. Add the same volume of neutral protease-treated soy protein solution into tube B.3. Core Operation: Hold both test tubes and shake them gently and simultaneously for several seconds to ensure mixing.4. Observation: Place the test tubes back on the rack and immediately observe the appearance of the solutions.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Tube A contains a turbid suspension with obvious precipitate; tube B contains a relatively uniform and less turbid solution.After Shaking: Tube A remains cloudy with precipitate settling or remaining suspended, while tube B appears clearer and more homogeneous, with little or no visible precipitate.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSoy protein molecules in their native or unhydrolyzed state have large molecular weights and strong intermolecular interactions, resulting in poor solubility and easy precipitation in water. After treatment with neutral protease, peptide bonds in soy protein are partially hydrolyzed, producing smaller peptides and amino acids. This enzymatic hydrolysis reduces molecular size and weakens protein–protein interactions, thereby increasing solubility and forming a more uniform solution. The difference in appearance between tube A and tube B visually reflects the effect of enzymatic hydrolysis on soy protein solubility.

Minimum assumptions: unhydrolyzed soy protein forms precipitate; hydrolyzed protein forms a clearer solution; shaking enables visual comparison. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Effervescent Tablet Dissolving in Cold vs Hot WaterI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Effervescent Tablet Dissolving in Cold vs Hot Water2. Subject: Engineering - Chemical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To compare the dissolution rate and reaction intensity of an effervescent tablet in hot and cold water through visual observation, and to understand the effect of temperature on reaction kinetics and mass transfer.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass beakers (2 identical beakers, 250 mL), hot water (about 60–70°C), cold water (about 5–10°C), effervescent tablets (2 identical tablets), thermometer (optional), stopwatch or time-lapse camera, heat-resistant gloves (optional).III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place two identical clear beakers side by side on a stable, well-lit surface. Pour equal volumes (about 200 mL) of hot water into one beaker and cold water into the other. Ensure both beakers are transparent and clearly labeled hot and cold.Camera Setup: Fix the camera position and focus to include both beakers in the same frame. Set time-lapse or continuous recording and do not change focus or zoom during the experiment.Core Operation: Hold two identical effervescent tablets above the beakers. Drop the tablets into the hot and cold water simultaneously and immediately start timing or recording.Observation: Observe and record the bubbling intensity, bubble size, dissolution speed, and the time required for each tablet to fully dissolve.Conclusion and Cleanup: After dissolution is complete, stop recording. Allow hot water to cool, then dispose of liquids safely and clean the beakers.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both beakers contain clear, colorless water; tablets are solid and intact.2. After Tablet Addition: Both tablets begin to release bubbles immediately. In hot water, bubbling is more vigorous with larger and more frequent bubbles; the tablet breaks apart and dissolves quickly. In cold water, bubbling is gentler and slower, and the tablet remains intact for a longer time.3. Final State: The tablet in hot water dissolves completely earlier than the tablet in cold water; bubbling in cold water persists longer.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesTemperature affects reaction kinetics and mass transfer. Higher temperature increases molecular motion, collision frequency, and diffusion rates, accelerating the chemical reaction between the effervescent tablet components and water, and speeding up carbon dioxide release. Lower temperature reduces these rates, resulting in slower dissolution and weaker effervescence.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use identical beakers, water volumes, and tablets to ensure fairness.2. Handle hot water carefully to avoid burns.3. Drop tablets simultaneously to ensure comparability.4. Keep camera fixed to ensure valid visual comparison.

Minimum assumptions: two identical tablets, equal water volumes, clear temperature contrast (hot vs cold), fixed camera perspective.Phased storyline: (1) Static setup with two clear beakers side by side labeled hot and cold; (2) simultaneous tablet drop into both beakers; (3) immediate effervescence in both, with hot water showing stronger, faster bubbling; (4) accelerated time-lapse showing quicker disappearance in hot water and prolonged bubbling in cold water. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Photodiode Light-Beam Interruption Triggering a Transparent Relay2. Subject: Engineering – Mechatronics & Robotics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how interruption of a light beam detected by a photodiode can trigger an electrical response, causing a transparent relay to actuate (and optionally a buzzer to sound), and to visually observe the sensing–actuation relationship.II. Experimental EquipmentLight source (LED or laser module with visible beam), photodiode sensor, resistor and power supply (5–12 V DC), transparent relay module (and/or small buzzer), connecting wires, breadboard, workbench, camera on tripod (fixed focus for time-lapse), safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place all components on the workbench. Mount the camera on a tripod, frame the entire setup, and fix the focus and exposure for time-lapse recording.2. Circuit Setup: Wire the photodiode in a light-detection circuit so that its output controls the transparent relay (and buzzer if used). Verify secure connections.3. Alignment: Position the light source so a steady, visible beam continuously shines onto the photodiode. Confirm the relay is in its default state when the beam is uninterrupted.4. Core Operation: Start recording. Use a hand to repeatedly interrupt the light beam between the source and the photodiode, then remove the hand to restore the beam. Repeat several cycles.5. Shutdown: Stop recording, turn off the power supply, and disconnect the circuit.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: With the light beam continuously shining on the photodiode, the transparent relay remains in its initial steady state (no movement or sound).2. During Interruption: Each time the hand blocks the light beam, the photodiode output changes, causing the relay armature inside the transparent casing to move (and the buzzer to sound, if connected).3. Restoration: When the hand is removed and the beam is restored, the relay returns to its original position (buzzer stops).V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates photoelectric sensing and electromechanical actuation. A photodiode converts incident light into an electrical signal. When the light beam is interrupted, the change in photodiode current alters the control signal to the relay driver circuit, energizing or de-energizing the relay coil. This causes a visible mechanical movement of the relay contacts, illustrating the sensing–decision–actuation chain fundamental to mechatronic systems.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Avoid direct eye exposure to intense light or laser beams.2. Ensure correct polarity and voltage to prevent component damage.3. Keep the camera fixed to maintain consistent time-lapse observation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstrate a mechatronic sensing–actuation loop where a photodiode detects light interruption and triggers a transparent relay. Minimum assumptions: a visible light beam aligned to a photodiode, a powered relay circuit, and a human hand capable of blocking the beam.Expected phenomena storyline: Phase 1 (steady state): continuous beam on photodiode, relay stationary. Phase 2 (cause): hand blocks beam. Phase 3 (effect): photodiode signal changes, relay actuates visibly (and buzzer sounds). Phase 4 (recovery): hand removed, beam restored, relay returns to initial state. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: RC Low-Pass Filter Smoothing a Noisy Voltage Driving an LEDI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: RC Low-Pass Filter Smoothing a Noisy Voltage Driving an LED2. Subject: Engineering - Electrical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how an RC low-pass filter smooths a rapidly varying or noisy voltage by comparing the brightness behavior of two identical LEDs, one driven directly by the source and one driven through an RC filter.II. Experimental EquipmentNoisy or rapidly switching voltage source (function generator or switched DC source), resistor (R), capacitor (C), two identical LEDs, current-limiting resistors (if required), breadboard and connecting wires, power supply, camera or smartphone with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the breadboard on a stable surface and fix the camera position and focus so both LEDs are clearly visible side by side.2. Direct LED Connection: Connect the first LED directly to the noisy voltage source through an appropriate current-limiting resistor.3. RC Filter Connection: Build an RC low-pass filter using a resistor in series with the source and a capacitor to ground; connect the second identical LED to the output of the RC filter.4. Verification: Check that both LEDs are correctly oriented and that the RC components are securely connected.5. Core Operation: Turn on the voltage source and rapidly switch or vary its voltage or frequency to introduce noise or fast changes.6. Recording: Record the LED behavior using time-lapse or continuous video while keeping the camera fixed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both LEDs are off or have the same steady brightness at constant input.2. During Rapid Variation: The directly driven LED flickers rapidly, reflecting the noisy voltage changes.3. Filtered Response: The LED connected through the RC low-pass filter changes brightness more slowly and smoothly, with reduced flicker.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAn RC low-pass filter attenuates high-frequency components of a voltage signal. When a noisy or rapidly changing voltage drives an LED directly, the LED brightness follows these fast variations. When driven through an RC filter, the capacitor charges and discharges gradually according to the time constant tau = R × C, smoothing the voltage and thus producing a steadier LED brightness.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure correct polarity of LEDs and capacitor; use appropriate resistor values to limit current; avoid short circuits; keep camera focus fixed to allow clear comparison.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: RC low-pass filtering and its smoothing effect on a noisy voltage as observed through LED brightness.Minimum Assumptions: Identical LEDs, a correctly connected RC filter, a rapidly varying voltage source, and a fixed camera viewpoint.Phased Storyline: (1) Stable setup with two LEDs side by side; (2) activation of noisy or rapidly switched voltage; (3) immediate flickering response of the direct LED; (4) delayed and smoothed brightness response of the RC-filtered LED. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Infrared Lamp Heating of Black vs White Surfaces with Wax MeltingI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Infrared Lamp Heating of Matte Black and Matte White Metal Plates2. Subject: Engineering - Chemical Engineering (Heat Transfer)3. Experiment Objective: To compare the heating effect of infrared radiation on surfaces with different colors and emissivities by observing the melting behavior of wax pellets; to understand the relationship between surface color, absorption of radiant heat, and temperature rise.II. Experimental EquipmentInfrared lamp (with stand and switch), two identical metal plates of the same material and size (one matte black, one matte white), wax pellets (same mass and size, 2-3 pellets per plate), heat-resistant base or stand, stopwatch or timer, ruler (for positioning), safety gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the matte black and matte white metal plates side by side on a heat-resistant base, ensuring equal distance and orientation relative to the infrared lamp. Wear safety goggles and gloves.2. Wax Placement: Place an equal number of wax pellets at the center of each metal plate, ensuring similar spacing and contact area.3. Lamp Positioning: Adjust the infrared lamp so that it is directly above the midpoint between the two plates, at a fixed height (e.g., 20-30 cm), ensuring both plates receive the same radiant exposure.4. Core Operation: Turn on the infrared lamp and start timing. Do not move the lamp or plates during heating.5. Observation and Recording: Continuously observe the wax pellets on both plates, noting the time when softening begins and when complete melting occurs.6. Completion: After clear differences are observed, turn off the infrared lamp. Allow the plates to cool naturally before handling or cleaning.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Wax pellets on both plates are solid, opaque, and maintain their original shape.2. During Heating: The wax on the matte black plate softens and begins to melt earlier than the wax on the matte white plate.3. Final State: Wax on the black plate shows more extensive melting or complete liquefaction, while wax on the white plate melts later or remains partially solid under the same heating time.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleInfrared radiation transfers energy primarily through radiation. Matte black surfaces have higher absorptivity and emissivity, allowing them to absorb more radiant energy and convert it into thermal energy, resulting in a faster temperature increase. Matte white surfaces reflect a larger portion of incident infrared radiation, absorbing less energy and heating more slowly. Therefore, under identical infrared exposure, the black plate reaches a higher temperature more quickly, causing the wax on it to melt sooner.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both plates are identical except for color to avoid material-related heat transfer differences.2. Keep lamp distance and angle constant to ensure fair comparison.3. Avoid touching heated plates directly to prevent burns.4. Conduct the experiment in a draft-free environment to minimize convective heat loss differences.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Infrared radiation heat transfer and the effect of surface color on absorptivity. Minimum assumptions: two identical metal plates differ only in surface color; infrared lamp provides uniform radiant energy; wax melting indicates relative temperature rise. Expected phased storyline: (1) Initial static setup with black and white plates side by side and solid wax pellets; (2) Lamp activation as the causal trigger; (3) Progressive heating where wax on the black plate softens and melts earlier; (4) Clear contrast stage showing greater melting on black plate than white. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Bromination Reaction of BenzeneI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Bromination Reaction of Benzene2. Subject: Engineering - Chemical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe the bromination reaction of benzene under catalytic conditions, understand electrophilic substitution reactions of aromatic compounds, and identify reaction phenomena through visual observation.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsThree-necked round-bottom flask, dropping funnel, condenser, thermometer, iron powder (catalyst), benzene (colorless liquid), liquid bromine (reddish-brown liquid), water bath or heating mantle, fume hood, protective gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the three-necked flask in a fume hood, connect the condenser and thermometer, and ensure all joints are sealed. Wear protective equipment.2. Addition of Reactants: Add a measured amount of benzene into the flask. Slowly add liquid bromine through the dropping funnel, observing the reddish-brown color of bromine in the mixture.3. Catalyst Introduction: Add a small amount of iron powder into the flask as a catalyst.4. Reaction: Gently heat or allow the mixture to react at room temperature. Swirl the flask slightly to ensure mixing.5. Observation: Observe the changes in the liquid inside the flask after the reaction proceeds for a short time.6. Completion and Cleanup: After observation, stop heating, allow the system to cool, and dispose of reaction waste according to safety regulations.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Benzene is colorless and transparent; bromine is reddish-brown.2. During Reaction: After adding iron powder, the reddish-brown color of bromine gradually fades.3. Final State: The liquid in the flask becomes lighter in color or nearly colorless, indicating consumption of bromine.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates an electrophilic aromatic substitution reaction. Iron reacts with bromine to form iron bromide (FeBr3), which acts as a catalyst to generate a stronger electrophile (Br+). Benzene undergoes substitution, forming bromobenzene and hydrogen bromide. The fading of bromine color indicates the progress of the reaction.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Hydrogen Evolution Corrosion of Steel (Iron Nail)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Hydrogen Evolution Corrosion of Steel (Iron Nail in Acidified Sodium Chloride Solution)2. Subject: Engineering – Chemical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe hydrogen evolution corrosion of steel in an acidic electrolyte environment, understand the electrochemical corrosion mechanism of iron, and recognize the role of acid and electrolyte in accelerating corrosion.II. Experimental EquipmentIron nail (clean and rust-free), beaker (100–250 mL), sodium chloride solution (approximately 3–5% NaCl), dilute hydrochloric acid (about 1 mol/L), glass rod, dropper, distilled water, safety goggles, gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear safety goggles and gloves. Clean the iron nail with distilled water and wipe dry to remove oil or rust.2. Solution Preparation: Pour an appropriate volume of sodium chloride solution into the beaker. Add a small amount of dilute hydrochloric acid dropwise and stir gently with a glass rod to obtain an acidified sodium chloride solution.3. Immersion Operation: Slowly place the iron nail completely into the prepared solution, ensuring it is fully submerged and not touching the beaker wall.4. Observation: Keep the beaker still and observe the surface of the iron nail for a short period.5. Completion: After observation, remove the iron nail, dispose of the solution according to laboratory regulations, and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The solution is colorless and transparent; the iron nail surface appears metallic gray.2. After Immersion: Fine bubbles gradually appear on the surface of the iron nail, especially at certain spots.3. Continued Observation: The bubbles increase slowly, indicating ongoing gas evolution; slight dulling of the nail surface may be observed.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates hydrogen evolution corrosion of steel in an acidic electrolyte. In acidified sodium chloride solution, iron undergoes electrochemical corrosion. Iron atoms lose electrons at anodic sites (Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻). The released electrons migrate to cathodic sites, where hydrogen ions in the acidic solution gain electrons and are reduced to hydrogen gas (2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂↑). The visible bubbles on the iron nail surface are hydrogen gas, indicating corrosion. Sodium chloride increases solution conductivity, accelerating the corrosion process.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Handle dilute hydrochloric acid carefully to avoid skin contact.2. Do not add excessive acid to prevent overly violent reactions.3. Ensure proper disposal of acidic waste solution.4. Perform the experiment in a well-ventilated area.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Dolomite and Calcite Differentiation by Alizarin Red StainingI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Dolomite and Calcite Differentiation Experiment (Alizarin Red Staining Method)2. Subject: Engineering – Geotechnical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To distinguish calcite and dolomite through their different staining responses to alizarin red solution, and to understand the mineralogical basis of carbonate identification.II. Experimental Materials and ReagentsWhite glass slides (2), dolomite powder (small amount), calcite powder (small amount), alizarin red S solution (0.2%–1%, prepared in weakly acidic aqueous solution), dropper.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean white glass slides side by side on a flat surface. Label one slide as calcite and the other as dolomite.2. Sample Placement: Using a spatula, take equal small amounts of calcite powder and dolomite powder and place them separately at the center of the corresponding slides.3. Reagent Addition: Use a dropper to add exactly one drop of alizarin red solution onto each powder sample.4. Standing: Allow the slides to stand undisturbed for approximately 2 seconds.5. Observation: Observe and compare the color changes of the two powder samples immediately after standing.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Calcite powder rapidly develops a distinct red or pink-red coloration after contact with alizarin red.2. Dolomite powder shows very weak staining or remains nearly unchanged in color within the 2-second period.3. The contrast in coloration between the two slides is clear and visually distinguishable.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAlizarin red selectively reacts with calcium carbonate. Calcite (CaCO3) contains readily available calcium ions that rapidly complex with alizarin red, producing a red stain. Dolomite (CaMg(CO3)2) contains magnesium, which inhibits rapid complexation, resulting in weak or delayed staining. Therefore, the difference in staining intensity within a short time allows rapid differentiation between calcite and dolomite.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: rapid mineral identification of calcite versus dolomite using selective staining. Minimum assumptions: two separate white glass slides, equal powder amounts, one visible drop of alizarin red, and a brief standing period. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) initial state shows two pale powders on slides; (2) reagent drop contacts each powder; (3) within a short pause, calcite transitions to clear red coloration while dolomite remains pale; (4) final comparison frame highlights the color contrast. Visibility requirements: close-up view of slides, clear color contrast, stable perspective to verify sequence and causality.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Water Levels Equalizing Between Two Connected ContainersI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Water Levels Equalizing Between Two Connected Containers2. Subject: Engineering – Systems Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that when two containers are connected at their bases, liquid will flow until the water levels equalize, illustrating pressure balance and system equilibrium.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo transparent containers of different shapes (e.g., one cylindrical, one conical), clear flexible tube, clamp or valve for the tube, colored water, stable flat surface, camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse photography.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place both empty transparent containers on a flat surface at the same base height. Ensure the camera is fixed, focused on both containers, and will not move during recording.2. Connection Setup: Connect the bases of the two containers with the clear tube. Keep the clamp or valve closed to prevent flow.3. Filling: Pour colored water into one container until its water level is noticeably higher than the other container, which remains lower or empty.4. Start Recording: Begin time-lapse recording with the camera focus fixed.5. Core Operation: Open the clamp or valve to allow water to flow through the tube between the containers.6. Observation Period: Allow the system to evolve until the water levels in both containers stop changing.7. End: Stop recording once the levels are clearly equal and stable. Close the valve and clean up equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: One container has a higher colored water level; the other has a lower level. No flow is observed while the tube is closed.2. During Connection Opening: Once the valve is opened, colored water flows through the clear tube from the container with the higher level to the lower one.3. Final State: The flow gradually slows and stops when both containers reach the same water level, despite their different shapes.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates the principle of hydrostatic pressure balance. The pressure at the base of each container depends on the height of the liquid column. When the containers are connected, a pressure difference caused by unequal water heights drives flow from higher pressure to lower pressure. Flow continues until pressures equalize, which occurs when the water levels are the same in both containers, illustrating equilibrium in a connected system.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Hydrostatic equilibrium in connected systems. Minimum assumptions: containers share the same base height, are rigid and open to the atmosphere, and are connected by a clear tube allowing free flow.Expected Phenomena Storyline: Phase 1 – Static setup with unequal colored water levels and no flow while the connection is closed. Phase 2 – Opening the base connection causes visible flow through the tube from higher to lower level due to pressure difference. Phase 3 – Water levels change smoothly over time and stabilize at equal heights, after which flow ceases. Visibility constraints: both containers and the connecting tube must remain in frame, with fixed camera focus to verify gradual, causal level changes.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Exothermic Temperature Rise When Mixing Ethanol and WaterI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Exothermic Effect of Mixing Ethanol and Water Visualized by Thermochromic SheetSubject: Engineering – Materials Science & EngineeringExperiment Objective: To demonstrate that mixing ethanol and water releases heat at constant pressure, and to visualize the temperature rise using a thermochromic sheet without external heating.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass beaker (250 mL), thermochromic temperature-sensitive sheet (wrapped around beaker), distilled water, ethanol (95%), graduated cylinder, glass stirring rod, camera with fixed focus for time-lapse recording, laboratory bench at room temperature.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Wrap the outside of the clean, dry glass beaker uniformly with the thermochromic sheet. Place the beaker on a stable bench and fix the camera position and focus for time-lapse photography.Initial State: Pour a measured volume of water (about 100 mL) into the beaker. Wait briefly to ensure the thermochromic sheet shows a uniform initial color corresponding to room temperature.Core Operation: Slowly add a measured volume of ethanol (about 50 mL) into the water at constant pressure. Gently stir the mixture with a glass rod to ensure uniform mixing. Do not apply any external heating.Observation and Recording: Continue stirring briefly, then stop and allow the mixture to stand. Record the color change of the thermochromic sheet over time using the fixed camera.Completion: After observation, stop recording, dispose of the mixture according to laboratory safety rules, and clean all equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The thermochromic sheet displays a uniform baseline color indicating room temperature.During Mixing: Shortly after ethanol is added and stirred, the thermochromic sheet begins to change color locally and then uniformly around the beaker.Final State: The color change indicates a temperature rise compared with the initial state, then gradually stabilizes as heat dissipates to the surroundings.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWhen ethanol and water are mixed, strong intermolecular interactions (especially hydrogen bonding) form between ethanol and water molecules. The formation of these interactions releases energy, making the mixing process exothermic. At constant pressure and without external heating, this released heat raises the temperature of the solution, which is visualized by the color change of the thermochromic sheet.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment RC Low-Pass Filter Smoothing a Flickering LEDI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: RC Low-Pass Filter Smoothing a Flickering LED Driven by a Square-Wave Signal2. Subject: Engineering – Communications Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how an RC low-pass filter smooths a rapidly switching electrical signal by visual comparison of two LEDs, and to understand the basic signal-smoothing principle of RC networks.II. Experimental EquipmentBattery-powered square-wave signal source (fast on–off switching), two identical LEDs, current-limiting resistors (for LEDs), one resistor and one capacitor forming an RC series network, connecting wires, breadboard or small prototyping board, battery, smartphone or camera with fixed focus and time-lapse function.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place all components on a tabletop. Ensure both LEDs are identical and oriented correctly. Fix the camera position above or in front of the setup and lock the focus to avoid refocusing during recording.2. Direct-Drive LED Setup: Connect the first LED in series with its current-limiting resistor directly to the square-wave source and battery.3. RC-Filtered LED Setup: Connect the second LED to the same square-wave source, but route the signal through a resistor–capacitor series network to ground before driving the LED.4. Power-On Operation: Switch on the battery-powered square-wave source so that both LEDs receive the same fast on–off signal.5. Recording: Start time-lapse or short video recording with the camera focus fixed, capturing both LEDs side by side during operation.6. Completion: After sufficient observation, switch off the power source and stop recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: When powered, both LEDs are off before the signal starts switching.2. During Operation: The directly driven LED appears to flicker rapidly or shows visible brightness changes corresponding to the square-wave switching. The LED connected through the RC network appears much steadier, with reduced flicker and smoother brightness.3. Comparative Effect: The difference in visual stability between the two LEDs becomes clear when observed side by side in the same frame.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAn RC low-pass filter allows low-frequency components of a signal to pass while attenuating high-frequency components. The square-wave signal contains rapid transitions (high-frequency components). In the RC network, the capacitor charges and discharges through the resistor, smoothing these rapid changes. As a result, the LED driven through the RC network receives a more averaged voltage and appears steady, while the directly driven LED reflects the fast on–off behavior of the original signal.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use proper current-limiting resistors to prevent LED damage.2. Ensure secure connections to avoid intermittent behavior unrelated to the RC effect.3. Keep camera focus fixed to ensure a fair visual comparison.4. Disconnect power after the experiment to avoid battery drain.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: RC low-pass filtering of a fast square-wave signal as visualized by LED brightness. Minimum assumptions: two identical LEDs, same square-wave source, one direct path and one RC-filtered path, fixed camera perspective. Expected phenomena storyline: Phase 1 – static tabletop setup with two LEDs visible side by side; Phase 2 – power applied and square-wave switching begins; Phase 3 – direct LED shows rapid flicker or brightness modulation while RC-filtered LED appears smoother and steadier; Phase 4 – sustained comparison clearly showing reduced flicker due to RC smoothing. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Drainage Speed Comparison in Gravel, Sand, and Silt LayersI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Drainage Speed Comparison in Gravel, Sand, and Silt Layers2. Subject: Engineering – Geotechnical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To compare drainage speeds of soils with different particle sizes through visual observation, and understand the influence of permeability and pore size on water flow in soil layers.II. Experimental EquipmentThree identical transparent columns; coarse gravel, medium sand, fine silt; measuring cup; water; collection tray; camera with fixed focus (for time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the three transparent columns side by side on a level surface. Fill the left column with coarse gravel, the middle column with sand, and the right column with fine silt, keeping equal heights and similar compaction.2. Setup: Position a collection tray beneath the columns. Fix the camera directly in front of the columns, lock focus and framing, and start time-lapse recording.3. Core Operation: Measure equal volumes of water. Pour the water simultaneously onto the top surface of each column.4. Observation: Continue recording as water infiltrates and drains through each soil layer.5. Completion: Stop recording after clear drainage differences are observed. Clean and store equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: All soil layers are dry or uniformly moist, with no free water at the bottom.2. During Drainage: Water passes rapidly through the gravel, moderately through the sand, and very slowly through the silt, with temporary ponding on the silt surface.3. Final State: The gravel column drains first, sand drains later, and silt retains water for the longest time.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesDrainage speed depends on soil permeability, which is controlled by particle size and pore connectivity. Coarse gravel has large, well-connected pores, allowing rapid water flow. Sand has smaller pores, slowing drainage. Fine silt has very small pores and higher capillary forces, greatly reducing permeability and drainage speed.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Composition of a Zinc–Copper Galvanic CellI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Zinc–Copper Galvanic Cell in Dilute Sulfuric Acid2. Subject: Engineering – Chemical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the basic composition and working principle of a galvanic cell by observing electric current generation when zinc and copper electrodes are immersed in dilute sulfuric acid and connected to an external circuit.II. Experimental EquipmentZinc plate (clean surface), copper plate (clean surface), beaker, dilute sulfuric acid (about 0.5–1.0 mol/L), connecting wires with clips, ammeter (zero-adjusted), support stand (optional), safety goggles and gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear safety goggles and gloves. Pour an appropriate amount of dilute sulfuric acid into a beaker so that both metal plates can be immersed.2. Electrode Setup: Clean the surfaces of the zinc and copper plates. Place them vertically and parallel to each other in the beaker, ensuring they do not touch.3. Circuit Connection: Use wires to connect the zinc plate and copper plate to the two terminals of the ammeter, forming a closed external circuit.4. Core Operation: Ensure both electrodes are simultaneously immersed in the dilute sulfuric acid, then observe the ammeter pointer.5. Observation and Recording: Keep the setup stable and focused. Observe and record the direction and magnitude of the ammeter deflection over time (time-lapsed observation).6. Completion: Disconnect the circuit, remove the electrodes, dispose of the solution properly, and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before connection, the ammeter pointer remains at zero.2. After Connection: Once the zinc and copper plates are connected through the ammeter and immersed in dilute sulfuric acid, the ammeter pointer deflects, indicating an electric current.3. Sustained Observation: Over time, the pointer remains deflected, showing continuous current generation while the circuit is closed.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates the principle of a galvanic cell. Zinc acts as the anode and undergoes oxidation (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻). Copper acts as the cathode, where hydrogen ions in dilute sulfuric acid gain electrons and are reduced (2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂). The flow of electrons from zinc to copper through the external circuit produces an electric current, which is detected by the ammeter.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure electrodes do not touch; use dilute sulfuric acid only; avoid skin contact with acid; disconnect the circuit after observation to prevent unnecessary electrode consumption.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Zinc–copper galvanic cell generating electric current via redox reactions in dilute sulfuric acid. Minimum assumptions: zinc is the anode, copper is the cathode, dilute sulfuric acid provides ions, and a closed external circuit allows electron flow.Phased Storyline: (1) Clear setup phase showing zinc and copper plates separately and the ammeter at zero; (2) Immersion and connection phase where both electrodes are placed in dilute sulfuric acid and connected by wires; (3) Causal transition where circuit completion leads to electron flow; (4) Observable outcome phase where the ammeter pointer deflects and remains stable. Visibility requirements: close-up, clear focus on electrode materials, wire connections, and ammeter pointer movement; time-lapse allowed to compress observation while preserving correct order.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Increasing Distance Between Transmitter and Receiver Causes LED Dimming2. Subject: Engineering – Communications Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that as the distance between a radio frequency (RF) transmitter and an LED-based receiver increases, the received signal strength decreases, resulting in visible dimming of the LED. Students observe the relationship between transmission distance, signal attenuation, and received power.II. Experimental Equipment1. Handheld radio frequency transmitter (battery-powered, continuously transmitting)2. LED receiver module (with antenna, signal detector, and LED indicator)3. Stable table (for placing the LED receiver)4. Indoor room with clear line-of-sight (one room, no walls in between)5. Measuring reference (floor tiles or approximate step distance, optional)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the LED receiver flat on a table in the room and ensure it is powered on. Confirm that the LED is functioning by briefly bringing the transmitter close to the receiver.2. Initial Positioning: Hold the powered handheld transmitter approximately 0.5–1 meter away from the LED receiver. Keep the transmitter orientation roughly constant and directed toward the receiver.3. Initial Observation: Observe and record the LED brightness when the transmitter is nearby. The LED should appear bright and stable.4. Core Operation: Slowly walk away from the table while continuously transmitting, increasing the distance between the transmitter and the receiver in a straight line.5. Distance Increase: Pause briefly at several distances (for example, 2 m, 4 m, and 6 m) while keeping the transmitter powered and oriented toward the receiver.6. Final Observation: Continue increasing distance until the LED becomes noticeably dim or nearly turns off.7. Conclusion and Reset: Stop moving, turn off the transmitter, and power down the receiver after observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: When the transmitter is close to the receiver, the LED on the receiver is bright and clearly visible.2. During Distance Increase: As the transmitter is carried farther away, the LED brightness gradually decreases.3. Long Distance State: At sufficiently large separation, the LED becomes very dim or turns off, indicating weak or insufficient received signal.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Core Principle: In wireless communication, signal strength decreases as transmission distance increases due to free-space path loss.2. Principle Explanation: The RF power emitted by the transmitter spreads out as it propagates through space. As distance increases, the power density at the receiver antenna decreases, resulting in a weaker received signal.3. LED Indication Logic: The LED brightness is proportional to the received signal power. Therefore, increasing distance leads to reduced received power and visible LED dimming.4. Engineering Significance: This experiment visually demonstrates attenuation, link budget concepts, and the importance of distance in communication system design.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the transmitter battery is sufficiently charged to avoid brightness changes unrelated to distance.2. Maintain similar transmitter orientation during movement to reduce directional effects.3. Avoid obstacles or human blocking between transmitter and receiver during the experiment.4. Conduct the experiment in one room to maintain a controlled environment.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Demonstrate free-space path loss in wireless communication, assuming a powered RF transmitter, a stationary LED-based receiver, line-of-sight indoor propagation, and LED brightness proportional to received signal strength.Phased Storyline: Phase 1 – Setup: Camera shows one room with an LED receiver resting on a table and a handheld transmitter nearby, LED brightly lit. Phase 2 – Separation Increase: The transmitter is carried steadily away while remaining powered and oriented toward the receiver; the LED brightness begins to decrease. Phase 3 – Attenuation Outcome: At larger separation, the LED appears dim or nearly off, visually confirming reduced received power. Visibility Requirements: Both transmitter movement and LED brightness must remain in frame or be clearly intercut to verify causal linkage between distance increase and LED dimming.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Nitrite Detection in Food (Colorimetric Method)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Nitrite Detection in Food by Colorimetric MethodSubject: Engineering – Food and Bioprocess EngineeringObjective: To detect nitrite in ham sausage extract using the Griess colorimetric reaction and understand the principle of azo dye formation.II. Experimental Reagents and EquipmentTest tube (1), test tube rack, dropper, prepared ham sausage extract, p-aminobenzenesulfonic acid solution, N-(1-naphthyl)ethylenediamine solution.III. Experimental Procedure1. Place a clean test tube on the rack and add 2 mL of ham sausage extract into the test tube.2. Using a dropper, add 1 drop of p-aminobenzenesulfonic acid solution to the extract.3. Add 1 drop of N-(1-naphthyl)ethylenediamine solution to the same test tube.4. Gently shake the test tube to mix the reagents thoroughly.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial state: The ham sausage extract is colorless or light yellow and transparent.After reaction: The solution gradually develops a pink to red coloration. The color intensity correlates with the nitrite content.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleNitrite in the sample reacts with p-aminobenzenesulfonic acid under acidic conditions to form a diazonium salt. This intermediate then couples with N-(1-naphthyl)ethylenediamine to form a pink or red azo dye. The appearance and intensity of the color indicate the presence and relative amount of nitrite in the food sample.

(3) Mixing phase – the test tube is shaken to ensure uniform reaction. (4) Result phase – the solution changes from colorless/light yellow to pink or red. Visibility constraints: the test tube contents and color change must be clearly visible, with a stable viewpoint allowing verification of sequence and causality.

manual: Instructions for the Demonstration: Snowflakes Falling and Accumulating on a Cold Metal Park BenchI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Snowflakes Falling and Accumulating on a Cold Metal Park BenchSubject: Engineering – Civil & Environmental EngineeringObjective: To observe and record the process of snowfall and accumulation on a cold metal surface using fixed-focus time-lapse photography, and to understand surface temperature effects on snow accumulation.II. Experimental EquipmentOutdoor metal park bench; natural snowfall environment (winter conditions); tripod-mounted camera or smartphone; weather-appropriate protection for equipment.III. Experimental Procedure1. Site Preparation: Select an outdoor metal park bench exposed to open air during active snowfall. Confirm ambient temperature is below freezing so the bench surface is cold.2. Camera Setup: Mount the camera on a tripod facing the bench. Fix the focus manually on the bench surface and lock exposure if possible. Do not adjust the camera after setup.3. Recording: Start time-lapse recording as snow begins falling steadily. Ensure the bench remains centered in the frame.4. Observation Period: Allow snow to fall and accumulate on the bench for a continuous period. Do not disturb the bench or remove snow.5. Completion: Stop recording after visible accumulation is formed. Power off and retrieve equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The metal bench surface is exposed, dark, and free of snow.During Snowfall: Snowflakes fall vertically under gravity and land on the bench. Individual flakes become visible against the metal surface.Accumulation Stage: With continued snowfall, snow layers gradually thicken and spread across the bench, reducing visible metal areas.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSnowflakes fall due to gravity. When they contact a cold metal surface with temperature below freezing, they do not melt immediately and can remain in place. Continuous snowfall leads to accumulation as deposition exceeds melting or sublimation. Metal, with high thermal conductivity, quickly equilibrates with cold air, supporting snow retention under freezing conditions.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Sedimentation of Sandy Soil in WaterI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Sedimentation of Sandy Soil in Clear Water2. Subject: Engineering – Agricultural Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe the sedimentation behavior of sandy soil in water and verify that sand settles quickly, forming a clear stratification boundary between clear water and sand.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent container (beaker or glass cup), clear water, sandy soil, stirring rod.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the transparent container on a stable surface and fill it with clear water.2. Adding Soil: Add an appropriate amount of sandy soil into the container.3. Stirring: Use a stirring rod to stir the mixture evenly so that the sand is fully suspended in the water.4. Standing: Stop stirring and leave the container standing undisturbed for about 10 seconds.5. Observation: Observe the changes in the mixture from the side of the transparent container.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial state: After stirring, the water appears turbid with sand particles suspended throughout.2. Standing process: Within a short time after stopping stirring, sand particles rapidly settle downward.3. manual: Experiment Title: Melting Ice in an Insulated Bowl Under Continuous HeatingSubject: Engineering – Chemical Engineering (Thermodynamics)I. Experiment ObjectiveTo demonstrate the relationship between energy input and phase change by observing the melting of ice in an insulated bowl under a continuously operating heat lamp, and to understand that added heat during melting is used for phase change rather than temperature rise.II. Experimental EquipmentInsulated bowl (1); ice cubes (several, similar size); water (small amount); heat lamp with stand; thermometer (optional); camera or smartphone with tripod; timer.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place several ice cubes into the insulated bowl and add a small amount of water so ice and liquid water coexist. Position the bowl on a stable surface.2. Camera Setup: Mount the camera on a tripod facing the bowl. Fix focus, exposure, and framing. Enable time-lapse or continuous recording.3. Heating Setup: Position the heat lamp above the bowl at a fixed distance. Ensure the lamp remains on continuously throughout the experiment.4. Core Operation: Turn on the heat lamp and start recording. Do not move the bowl, lamp, or camera during observation.5. Observation Period: Allow the system to run until most or all ice has melted. Stop recording and turn off the lamp.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Distinct solid ice cubes coexist with liquid water in the insulated bowl.2. During Heating: Ice cubes gradually shrink while remaining surrounded by water; both solid and liquid phases coexist for an extended period.3. Final State: Ice disappears, leaving only liquid water; no boiling occurs under typical lamp heating.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe heat lamp supplies continuous energy to the system. During melting, the absorbed energy is used as latent heat of fusion to break the solid ice structure rather than increasing temperature. Therefore, ice and water coexist until the phase change is complete, illustrating the relationship between energy input and phase change in thermodynamics.VI. PrecautionsKeep camera focus fixed; avoid splashing water near electrical equipment; do not touch the heat lamp during operation.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Comparative Experiment of Impact Compaction and Static Compaction EffectsI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Comparative Experiment of Impact Compaction and Static Compaction EffectsSubject: Engineering – Geotechnical EngineeringObjective: To compare the effects of static compaction and impact compaction on loose sand by observing changes in sand height and density under the same applied weight X.II. EquipmentTwo identical sand trays (A and B), dry loose sand, weight X (same mass for both trays), static loading plate, impact hammer or drop weight device, ruler or scale, camera.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fill sand trays A and B with the same mass of dry loose sand. Level the surface without compaction and record initial sand height.2. Static Compaction (Tray A): Place the loading plate on tray A and slowly apply weight X, keeping it stationary for a short time, then remove it.3. Impact Compaction (Tray B): Lift the same weight X to a fixed height and apply it vertically onto tray B once or several times in quick succession.4. Observation and Recording: Measure and record the final sand height in both trays. Observe surface settlement and relative compactness. Take a focused demonstration photograph showing both trays side by side.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial state: Both trays have loose sand with similar height and appearance.After compaction: Tray A shows slight settlement; Tray B shows明显 larger settlement and denser surface. Final sand height in tray B is lower than in tray A.V. Experimental Principle SummaryStatic compaction applies load slowly, allowing limited particle rearrangement. Impact compaction applies dynamic energy, overcoming inter-particle friction more effectively and causing sand particles to rearrange into a denser configuration. Therefore, under the same weight X, impact compaction results in greater densification and settlement than static compaction.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Comparison of static vs impact compaction effects on loose sand under equal weight. Minimum assumptions: sand is dry and loose; weight X is identical; trays are identical. Expected phased storyline: (1) Two identical trays with loose sand are shown side by side; (2) Static load is slowly applied to tray A with minimal settlement; (3) Impact load is applied to tray B causing visible sudden settlement; (4) Final comparison shows tray B with lower sand height and denser appearance. Visibility constraints: camera remains fixed and focused to clearly show height differences and loading actions.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Diode Envelope Detector Driving LED Brightness from an AM SignalI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Diode Envelope Detector Driving LED Brightness from an AM Signal2. Subject: Engineering - Communications Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the working principle of a diode-RC envelope detector by visually comparing LED brightness driven directly by an AM signal and by the detected envelope, and to understand how amplitude modulation conveys information.II. Experimental EquipmentAM signal generator (with adjustable carrier frequency and audio modulation), diode (e.g., 1N4148), resistor (e.g., 10 kΩ), capacitor (e.g., 10 µF), two LEDs (same color recommended), current-limiting resistors for LEDs, breadboard and connecting wires, DC bias or suitable output level from generator, camera or smartphone with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the breadboard and components on a stable surface. Fix the camera position and focus so that the entire circuit and both LEDs are clearly visible.2. Circuit Assembly: Connect the AM signal generator output to two paths. Path A connects directly to LED1 through a current-limiting resistor. Path B feeds a diode followed by an RC network (diode anode to signal, cathode to RC), and LED2 is connected across the RC output through its resistor.3. Parameter Setup: Set the carrier frequency to a high frequency (e.g., tens to hundreds of kHz) and enable audio-frequency amplitude modulation. Start with a low modulation depth.4. Core Operation: Power on the signal generator. Slowly and continuously vary the audio modulation amplitude or frequency over time.5. Observation and Recording: Keep the camera fixed and record the gradual changes in LED brightness as the modulation varies.6. Completion: After observation, turn off the signal generator and disconnect the circuit.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: LED1 (direct connection) may appear dim or show rapid flicker, while LED2 (after detector) shows steady or slowly varying brightness.2. During Modulation Variation: As the audio modulation increases or decreases, LED2 brightness smoothly follows the modulation envelope, becoming brighter or dimmer accordingly. LED1 shows less smooth changes due to the high-frequency carrier.3. Comparative Effect: The difference in visual behavior between the two LEDs becomes more obvious as modulation depth increases.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on amplitude modulation and diode envelope detection. An AM signal consists of a high-frequency carrier whose amplitude varies according to a low-frequency information signal. The diode-RC envelope detector rectifies the AM signal and filters out the carrier, leaving the modulation envelope. LED1 responds directly to the rapidly varying AM waveform, while LED2 responds to the detected envelope, visually demonstrating how information is recovered from an AM signal.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure correct diode polarity and proper RC values to avoid signal distortion.2. Use current-limiting resistors to protect LEDs.3. Fix camera focus and avoid moving the setup during recording.4. Do not exceed the voltage and current ratings of components.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Visual demonstration of AM envelope detection using a diode-RC circuit driving LED brightness. Minimum assumptions: an AM source with adjustable modulation, a correctly wired diode-RC detector, and two LEDs connected before and after detection. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Metal Reactivity with Acid Producing Gas Bubbles (Zinc vs Copper in Vinegar)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Reactivity of Zinc and Copper with Vinegar2. Subject: Engineering - Mechanical Engineering (Materials and Chemical Behavior)3. Experiment Objective: To observe and compare the reactivity of different metals with a weak acid by visualizing gas bubble formation, and to understand how metal activity affects corrosion and gas generation.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo clear glass beakers (same size), white vinegar (acetic acid solution), zinc strip (1 piece), copper strip (1 piece), tweezers or tongs, camera or smartphone with tripod (for time-lapse), label or marker (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, transparent beakers side by side on a stable surface. Pour equal volumes of vinegar into each beaker (about half full). Ensure the liquids are clear and free of bubbles.2. Setup for Recording: Position the camera directly in front of the beakers, adjust framing so both beakers are fully visible, and fix the focus and exposure. Do not move the camera afterward.3. Core Operation: Using tweezers, gently drop the zinc strip into the left beaker. Then drop the copper strip into the right beaker. Avoid splashing and do not stir.4. Observation Stage: Leave both beakers undisturbed. Record continuously or use time-lapse mode to capture changes over time.5. Completion: After sufficient observation, stop recording and safely dispose of the solution according to laboratory guidelines. Clean and store the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both beakers contain clear, colorless vinegar; metal strips are solid and shiny.2. Zinc in Vinegar (Left Beaker): Small gas bubbles gradually appear on the surface of the zinc strip and rise through the liquid; bubbling may increase over time.3. Copper in Vinegar (Right Beaker): Little to no visible gas bubbles form; the copper strip shows no obvious change during the observation period.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates metal reactivity with acids. Zinc, being more chemically active, reacts with acetic acid in vinegar to produce hydrogen gas, observed as bubbles on the metal surface. Copper is less reactive and does not readily react with weak acids like vinegar, so no significant gas production is observed.Core Reaction (simplified): Zn + 2H+ → Zn2+ + H2↑The difference in observable phenomena reflects the relative positions of zinc and copper in the metal activity series.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Water Surface Ripples Generated by a Fast VibratorI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Water Surface Ripples Generated by a Fast Vibrator2. Subject: Engineering - Communications Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how mechanical vibration strength affects wave generation and propagation on a water surface, and to visually observe ripple evolution using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentShallow water tray (transparent, flat bottom), clean water (depth 3–5 mm), small fast vibrating motor (variable strength or speed), power supply or controller, vibration isolation pad (optional), camera with tripod, lighting source, operator hand for manual adjustment.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the shallow tray on a stable table. Pour clean water into the tray to form a uniform shallow layer. Ensure the water surface is initially still.2. Equipment Setup: Fix the vibrating motor securely beneath the center of the tray so vibrations transmit upward through the tray bottom. Connect the motor to the power supply or controller.3. Camera Setup: Mount the camera on a tripod above the tray. Fix focus and framing so the entire water surface is visible. Enable time-lapse or accelerated recording; do not change focus during recording.4. Core Operation: Turn on the vibrator at low strength. Using one hand, slowly and continuously increase the motor strength by hand control, keeping the tray and camera untouched.5. Observation and Recording: Continuously record the water surface as ripple patterns emerge, intensify, and change with vibration strength.6. Completion: After clear ripple evolution is recorded, slowly reduce motor strength to zero, stop recording, and turn off equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Water surface is flat and mirror-like with no visible waves.2. Low Strength Vibration: Small, regular circular ripples appear near the center above the vibrator.3. Increasing Strength: Ripple amplitude increases, wave fronts become more pronounced, and interference patterns may appear across the tray.4. High Strength (brief): Ripples become dense and energetic, covering most of the water surface.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe experiment demonstrates mechanical wave generation on a liquid surface. A fast vibrator transfers periodic mechanical energy through the tray to the water, disturbing equilibrium and generating surface waves. As vibration strength increases, more energy is transmitted, leading to larger wave amplitudes and altered wavelengths. This visualizes fundamental wave concepts such as energy transmission, superposition, and dispersion, which are relevant to signal propagation principles in communications engineering.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the tray is stable to avoid water spillage. Keep electrical components dry. Adjust motor strength gradually to avoid sudden splashing. Maintain fixed camera focus for valid time-lapse comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Quick Sort Principle DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Quick Sort Principle Demonstration (Visual Animation)2. Subject: Engineering - Computer Science - Algorithms3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the working principle of the Quick Sort algorithm by animating the step-by-step sorting process on a simple horizontal array of numbered bars, helping learners understand partitioning, pivot selection, and recursive sorting.II. Experimental Materials (Virtual)1. A clean white background.2. A horizontal array of vertical bars labeled with numbers, e.g., [5, 3, 4, 1, 2].3. Visual highlights (colors) to distinguish pivot, elements being compared, and sorted elements.III. Experimental Procedure1. Initial Setup: Display a clean white background with a single horizontal row of numbered bars representing the unsorted array [5, 3, 4, 1, 2]. All bars are uniform in width, aligned at the bottom, and differ only in height and number label.2. Pivot Selection: Select the first (or last) element as the pivot and highlight it with a distinct color (e.g., red).3. Partitioning Process: Sequentially compare other bars with the pivot. Bars smaller than the pivot move to the left side; bars larger move to the right side. Use smooth horizontal animations to show swaps or movements.4. Pivot Placement: Place the pivot into its correct sorted position between the left and right partitions, visually fixing its position.5. Recursive Sorting: Repeat the above steps for the left and right sub-arrays. Each recursion step is shown clearly but accelerated to fit time constraints.6. Completion: End with all bars sorted in ascending order, uniformly colored to indicate completion.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Bars appear unordered, with random heights corresponding to their values.2. During Sorting: One bar is repeatedly highlighted as the pivot; other bars move left or right based on comparisons. The array gradually becomes more ordered.3. Final State: All bars are arranged from smallest to largest, with no further movement.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesQuick Sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm. It selects a pivot element, partitions the array into elements smaller and larger than the pivot, and then recursively applies the same process to each partition. The visual movement of bars directly represents comparisons, swaps, and recursive subdivision, illustrating the algorithm’s average-case efficiency and core logic.VI. Experimental Notes1. The animation should emphasize order and causality rather than speed.2. Colors must be used consistently to represent pivots and active comparisons.3. Only the core steps are retained to fit within a short demonstration time.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Visually demonstrate the Quick Sort algorithm using a simple array of numbered bars. Minimum assumptions: a fixed white background, a horizontal bar array, and color-coded pivots and comparisons. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) Unsorted array appears; (2) a pivot is highlighted; (3) other bars move left or right based on comparison; (4) pivot settles into final position; (5) recursive repetitions occur on sub-arrays; (6) final fully sorted array is shown. Visibility constraints: all bars must remain in view, movements must be horizontal and sequential, and causal links between comparison and movement must be visually explicit for verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Colored Dye Diffusion in Coarse Sand versus Fine SiltI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Colored Dye Diffusion in Coarse Sand versus Fine Silt2. Subject: Engineering - Geotechnical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To visually compare fluid diffusion behavior in coarse sand and fine silt, and to understand the influence of pore size and permeability on seepage and diffusion in soils.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical clear vertical containers, coarse sand, fine silt, clear water, colored dye (single color), droppers (2), tray or base for stability, camera or smartphone with tripod (for fixed-focus time-lapse recording).III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place the two clear containers side by side on a stable surface. Fill one container with coarse sand and the other with fine silt to the same height. Slowly add clear water to each until fully saturated, ensuring no visible air bubbles remain.Setup: Adjust the camera so both containers are fully in frame. Fix the focus, angle, and distance. Start time-lapse or continuous recording.Core Operation: Using two droppers, simultaneously add one drop of the same colored dye to the water surface at the center of each container.Observation: Allow the dye to diffuse naturally without disturbance. Continue recording for a short period, using time-lapse to accelerate the process.Conclusion: Stop recording after clear diffusion patterns are visible. Dispose of materials properly and clean equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both containers are clear, with colorless water and visible soil structure.During Diffusion: In coarse sand, the dye penetrates downward quickly along visible pore paths, spreading faster and more vertically. In fine silt, the dye spreads more slowly, diffusing laterally and remaining concentrated near the top for a longer time.Final State: A clear contrast in diffusion speed and pattern between the two soils is observed.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe experiment demonstrates that soil permeability and pore size control fluid diffusion behavior. Coarse sand has larger pores and higher permeability, allowing faster and more direct dye movement. Fine silt has smaller pores and lower permeability, restricting flow and slowing diffusion. This reflects fundamental seepage and transport principles in geotechnical engineering.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure both soils are fully saturated to avoid air interference. Setup: Place fresh spinach leaves into the transparent container. Put a small beaker containing clear limewater beside the leaves, ensuring it does not spill.3. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Stretching and Recovery of a Rubber Band Under Repeated PullingSubject: Engineering – Structural EngineeringExperiment Objective: To demonstrate elastic deformation and recovery under repeated tensile loading, and to understand the basic concept of elasticity through visual observation using time-lapse photography.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentRubber band (1, uniform and undamaged), one participant, camera or smartphone with tripod, stable background, adequate lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Initial State: The participant holds the rubber band horizontally between both hands at rest, with no visible stretching.3. Stretching Operation: Slowly pull both hands apart to stretch the rubber band to a clearly elongated length.4. Recovery Operation: Gradually move both hands back to the original position, allowing the rubber band to recover.5. Repetition: Repeat the stretch–relax cycle several times at a steady rhythm while the camera records continuously.6. Completion: Stop recording after multiple complete cycles are captured.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The rubber band has its original length and uniform thickness.2. During Stretching: As hands move apart, the rubber band elongates and becomes thinner.3. During Relaxation: When hands return, the rubber band shortens and largely recovers its original length.4. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe experiment demonstrates elastic deformation. When tensile force is applied, the rubber band stretches; when the force is removed, stored elastic energy allows it to return to its original shape. PrecautionsAvoid overstretching to prevent permanent deformation or breakage. Keep camera position and focus fixed to ensure consistent observation.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Steel Ball Falling Through Water vs Glycerin ColumnI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Steel Ball Falling in Water and Glycerin2. Subject: Engineering – Nuclear Engineering (Fluid Mechanics Fundamentals)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the effect of fluid viscosity on the falling speed of a solid sphere, understand drag force and terminal velocity, and visually compare low-viscosity and high-viscosity fluids.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo clear vertical cylinders of equal height; blue-tinted water; amber glycerin; two identical steel balls (same diameter and mass); release holder or ruler for height alignment; tray for catching balls.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the two clear cylinders vertically side by side on a level surface. Fill one cylinder with blue-tinted water and the other with amber glycerin to the same height, ensuring no bubbles.2. Alignment: Hold one identical steel ball above each cylinder opening at the same height, centered to avoid wall contact.3. Core Operation: Release both steel balls simultaneously so they begin falling at the same time.4. Observation: Observe and compare the falling speeds and trajectories of the two balls as they move downward through the liquids.5. Completion: Allow both balls to reach the bottom, then retrieve and clean equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both steel balls start from rest at the same height above the liquid surfaces.2. During Falling: The steel ball in blue-tinted water falls rapidly, while the steel ball in amber glycerin descends much more slowly and smoothly.3. Final State: The water ball reaches the bottom significantly earlier than the glycerin ball.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleWhen a sphere falls through a fluid, it is acted upon by gravity, buoyancy, and viscous drag. Water has low viscosity, producing smaller drag, so the steel ball quickly reaches a higher terminal velocity. Glycerin has much higher viscosity, generating a larger resistive force that greatly reduces the ball’s terminal velocity. This experiment visually demonstrates the relationship between viscosity and drag force, a key concept in fluid mechanics relevant to nuclear engineering systems involving coolant flow.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure identical balls and equal release height; avoid bubbles and wall contact; keep cylinders vertical for accurate comparison.
