Experiment Title: Comparison of Glider Winch Launches with Strong and Weak Pull2. Subject: Engineering – Aerospace Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how winch pull strength affects glider acceleration, climb angle, and initial altitude gain by comparing two winch launches of the same single-seat glider on the same runway using time-lapse photography.II. Experimental Equipment and ConditionsSingle-seat glider (same aircraft for both launches); winch system A with thick red cable (powerful winch); winch system B with thin blue cable (weaker winch); standard grass or paved glider runway; ground crew and pilot; fixed-position camera on tripod capable of time-lapse recording; calm or similar wind conditions for both launches.III. Observe the glider accelerating rapidly, lifting off early, and climbing steeply. End recording after cable release.3. Second Launch (Weak Pull): Reset the glider to the same start point. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Salt Solution Crystallization under Slow Cooling vs Rapid CoolingI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Salt Crystallization under Slow and Rapid Cooling2. Subject: Engineering - Materials Science & Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how cooling rate affects nucleation and crystal growth by comparing crystallization behavior of the same hot saturated salt solution cooled under different conditions, and to visually record the process using time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentSodium chloride (table salt), distilled water, beaker (for preparing solution), heating plate or hot water bath, thermometer, two identical shallow glass dishes, ice bath (ice and tray), bare laboratory countertop, camera or smartphone with tripod, timer, heat-resistant gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation of Saturated Solution: Heat distilled water in a beaker and gradually add sodium chloride while stirring until no more salt dissolves, forming a hot saturated solution. Maintain the solution near boiling to ensure saturation.2. Setup: Place two identical shallow glass dishes side by side. Prepare an ice bath next to the countertop. Fix the camera on a tripod facing both dishes and lock focus and exposure for time-lapse recording.3. Pouring Operation: Carefully and simultaneously pour equal volumes of the hot saturated salt solution into each shallow dish, ensuring similar liquid depth.4. Cooling Conditions: Immediately place one dish onto the ice bath (rapid cooling) and leave the other dish on the bare countertop (slow cooling).5. Recording: Start time-lapse photography and allow both dishes to cool undisturbed until crystallization is clearly observed.6. Completion: Stop recording after clear crystal patterns form. Dispose of solutions properly and clean equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both dishes contain clear, colorless hot salt solution with no visible crystals.2. Rapid Cooling (Ice Bath): Crystallization begins quickly; many small, fine crystals appear almost simultaneously, forming a dense crystalline layer.3. Slow Cooling (Countertop): Crystallization begins later; fewer nuclei form, allowing larger, well-defined crystals to grow gradually.4. Final State: The rapidly cooled dish shows fine-grained crystals, while the slowly cooled dish shows coarser, larger crystals.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesCooling rate strongly influences crystallization behavior. Rapid cooling creates high supersaturation, leading to a high nucleation rate and many small crystals. Slow cooling produces lower supersaturation, fewer nuclei, and allows more time for crystal growth, resulting in larger crystals. This principle is fundamental in materials processing and crystal engineering.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use identical dishes and equal solution volumes to ensure fair comparison.2. Handle hot solutions carefully to avoid burns.3. Do not disturb dishes during cooling, as vibration can affect nucleation.4. Ensure camera focus remains fixed throughout recording.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Cooling rate controls nucleation density and crystal size in salt crystallization. Minimum assumptions: same solute, same concentration, identical containers, and only cooling rate differs. Phased storyline: (1) Hot saturated salt solution poured into two identical shallow dishes; (2) one dish experiences rapid cooling on ice, the other slow cooling on a countertop; (3) supersaturation develops, triggering crystallization; (4) rapid cooling yields many small crystals, slow cooling yields fewer larger crystals. Visibility constraints: both dishes must remain in frame with fixed focus, and time-lapse acceleration should clearly show the chronological progression and contrast in crystal morphology.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment "Water Pump Flow Rate Controlled by PWM Output"I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Water Pump Flow Rate Controlled by PWM Output2. Subject: Engineering – Mechatronics & Robotics3. Knowledge Point: Water pump flow rate controlled by PWM output4. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) controls the rotational speed and flow rate of a small DC water pump; to visually observe the relationship between PWM duty cycle and water flow through a transparent tube while adjusting a rotary knob, and to record the process using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental Equipment- Small DC water pump (low-voltage)- PWM controller module with rotary knob (potentiometer)- DC power supply (matching pump rated voltage)- Transparent silicone or PVC tube- Clear water- Water container (inlet reservoir)- Receiving container (outlet container)- Camera or smartphone with tripod (focus fixed)- Connecting wiresIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   - Place the water pump near the inlet container filled with clear water.   - Connect the transparent tube to the pump outlet and lead the other end into the receiving container.   - Ensure the tube is free of air bubbles as much as possible.   - Mount the camera on a tripod, frame the pump, tube, rotary knob, and receiving container in one view, and fix the focus.2. Circuit Connection:   - Connect the DC power supply to the PWM controller input terminals.   - Connect the PWM controller output terminals to the DC water pump.   - Set the rotary knob to the minimum position (lowest duty cycle) before powering on.3. Core Operation:   - Turn on the power supply.   - Slowly rotate the knob clockwise to increase the PWM duty cycle.   - Observe the pump operation and water flow in the transparent tube.   - Turn the knob back and forth within a moderate range to show continuous changes in flow rate.   - Keep all components stationary except the rotary knob during operation.4. Recording:   - Maintain fixed camera focus and position throughout the experiment.   - Record or capture the process for time-lapse photography, emphasizing gradual changes in water flow.5. Shutdown:   - Rotate the knob back to the minimum position.   - Turn off the power supply.   - Stop recording and safely disconnect the circuit.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State:   - At minimum PWM duty cycle, the pump is stationary or rotates very slowly, and little to no water flows through the tube.2. Increasing PWM Output:   - As the knob is turned clockwise, the pump speed increases.   - Water begins to flow steadily through the transparent tube, with visibly increasing flow rate.3. Dynamic Adjustment:   - Turning the knob back and forth causes corresponding smooth increases and decreases in water flow.   - The water stream into the container becomes stronger or weaker in real time.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Core Principle:   - PWM controls the average voltage applied to the DC pump by adjusting the duty cycle of a high-frequency switching signal.2. Principle Analysis:   - A higher PWM duty cycle increases the effective voltage and current supplied to the motor, increasing its rotational speed.   - The pump speed directly affects the water flow rate, resulting in a proportional visual change in water movement through the tube.3. Control Characteristics:   - PWM provides efficient speed control with minimal energy loss, commonly used in mechatronic systems for actuators such as motors and pumps.VI. Experimental Precautions- Ensure the power supply voltage matches the pump rating.- Do not run the pump dry for extended periods.- Avoid water contact with electrical connections.- Keep the camera focus fixed to ensure consistent visual comparison.

manual: Experiment Title: Bootstrap Mean Confidence Interval VisualizationI. Basic Experiment InformationSubject: Engineering – Scientific ComputingObjective: To understand and visualize the bootstrap method for estimating the sampling distribution of the mean and constructing a 95% confidence interval through resampling and graphical analysis.II. Experimental Data and ToolsData: One original numerical sample of size n=20Tools: Scientific computing environment (e.g., Python with NumPy/Matplotlib or equivalent), display screen for dynamic visualizationIII. Experimental Procedure1. Original Sample Display: Load the original dataset (n=20). Display the data as blue scatter points along a numerical axis to represent the raw sample distribution.2. Bootstrap Resampling: Randomly resample with replacement from the original sample to generate one bootstrap sample of size 20. Repeat this process dynamically until 1000 bootstrap samples are generated.3. Mean Calculation: For each bootstrap sample, calculate its sample mean and store the result.4. Histogram Plotting: Plot a histogram of the 1000 bootstrap means using red bars, showing the empirical sampling distribution of the mean.5. Confidence Interval Annotation: Compute the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the bootstrap mean distribution. Annotate the histogram with the 95% confidence interval, labeled as (2.1, 3.8).6. Visualization Check: Observe that the histogram of bootstrap means is approximately normal in shape.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The original sample appears as 20 distinct blue scatter points.2. As resampling proceeds, the number of bootstrap samples increases to 1000.3. The histogram of bootstrap means forms a smooth, approximately normal red distribution.4. The 95% confidence interval (2.1, 3.8) is clearly marked on the histogram.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe bootstrap method is a resampling-based statistical technique. By repeatedly sampling with replacement from the original data, it approximates the sampling distribution of a statistic (here, the mean) without relying on strict parametric assumptions. The confidence interval is derived from percentiles of the bootstrap distribution, and by the Central Limit Theorem, the distribution of the sample mean tends to be approximately normal even if the original data are not.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Bootstrap estimation of the sampling distribution of the mean and construction of a 95% confidence interval using resampling.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: The original sample contains 20 numerical values; resampling is done with replacement; each bootstrap sample produces one mean; percentile bounds define the confidence interval.Expected Phenomena Storyline: Phase 1 shows the original data as blue scatter points. Phase 2 demonstrates repeated resampling until 1000 bootstrap samples are accumulated. Phase 3 visualizes the resulting red histogram of bootstrap means, which becomes smooth and approximately normal. Phase 4 highlights the causal result by annotating the 95% confidence interval (2.1, 3.8). All phases must follow this order and remain visible on screen for verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Condensation of Vapor Effluent in a Cooling Coil Before CollectionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Condensation of Vapor Effluent in a Cooling Coil Before Collection2. Subject: Engineering – Nuclear Engineering (Thermal-Hydraulics Demonstration)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that warm vapor can be condensed by heat removal in a coolant-chilled helical coil prior to collection, and to visually observe condensation, droplet coalescence, and continuous liquid flow using time-lapse imaging.II. Experimental EquipmentSealed vapor generator or vapor source (low-pressure, non-radioactive); transparent helical condenser coil; coolant circulation system (chiller, pump, inlet/outlet hoses); transparent collection vessel with drain; temperature indicators (optional); mounting frame; clear tubing and sealed fittings; camera with tripod and fixed-focus capability; safety gloves and goggles.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Assemble the sealed test rig. Connect the vapor source to the inlet of the transparent helical coil. Connect the coil outlet to the clear collection vessel. Ensure all joints are sealed. Mount the coil so its turns are fully visible.Cooling Setup: Connect the coolant chiller to the coil jacket or surrounding bath. Start coolant circulation and set it to a temperature below the vapor saturation temperature.Camera Setup: Position the camera facing the coil and collection vessel. Fix focus, exposure, and framing. Enable time-lapse or continuous recording.Core Operation: Start generating warm vapor and route it through the coil at a steady flow rate. Maintain continuous coolant flow.Observation Period: Allow the system to run as vapor cools in the coil, condenses, and drains into the collection vessel. Record continuously.Shutdown: Stop vapor generation, then coolant flow. Allow system to equilibrate before disassembly.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Coil is clear and dry; collection vessel empty or contains minimal liquid.During Operation: As warm vapor enters the chilled coil, fine droplets form on the inner wall, grow, and coalesce. Liquid films or droplets move downward along the helical path.Collection: Condensed liquid exits the coil outlet and accumulates steadily in the clear collection vessel, demonstrating continuous flow.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates heat transfer and phase change principles. When warm vapor contacts a surface cooled below its saturation temperature, latent heat is removed by the coolant, causing vapor to condense into liquid. The transparent helical coil increases surface area and residence time, enhancing condensation efficiency. Gravity and flow drive the condensed liquid into the collection vessel.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the system is sealed to prevent leaks. Use non-hazardous vapor only. Avoid thermal shock to glass components. Fix camera focus before operation to ensure consistent time-lapse observation.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Hydrogen Peroxide Decomposition with Varying Peroxide ConcentrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Hydrogen Peroxide Decomposition with Different Concentrations2. Subject: Engineering - Chemical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To compare the effect of hydrogen peroxide concentration on the rate of oxygen generation during catalytic decomposition, and to visually demonstrate reaction rate differences through balloon inflation.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo clear conical flasks (250 mL), one with a blue band and one with a red band; hydrogen peroxide solutions of different concentrations (e.g., low concentration in blue-banded flask, high concentration in red-banded flask); manganese dioxide catalyst (solid); two balloons; measuring cylinder; spatula; rubber stoppers or balloon necks; safety goggles; camera fixed on a tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear safety goggles. Place the two clear flasks side by side on a flat surface within the camera frame. Ensure the camera focus is fixed and will not change during recording.2. Solution Addition: Pour equal volumes of hydrogen peroxide into each flask. The blue-banded flask contains the lower concentration, and the red-banded flask contains the higher concentration.3. Balloon Setup: Stretch a balloon over the mouth of each flask, ensuring an airtight seal and that the balloons are initially deflated.4. Catalyst Addition: Simultaneously add an equal mass of manganese dioxide catalyst into each flask. Immediately reseal with the balloons if temporarily removed.5. Observation: Start time-lapse recording and observe the balloons inflating over time. Do not move the flasks or camera during the reaction.6. Completion: After balloon inflation stabilizes, stop recording. Dispose of reaction residues according to laboratory safety rules and clean equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both flasks contain clear, colorless hydrogen peroxide solutions with deflated balloons.2. After Catalyst Addition: Bubbles rapidly form in both flasks as oxygen gas is released.3. Comparative Observation: The balloon on the red-banded (higher concentration) flask inflates faster and to a larger volume than the balloon on the blue-banded (lower concentration) flask.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesHydrogen peroxide decomposes into water and oxygen gas in the presence of a catalyst such as manganese dioxide. The reaction rate depends on peroxide concentration. A higher concentration results in more frequent effective molecular collisions, increasing the rate of oxygen generation. The released oxygen inflates the balloons, visually demonstrating reaction rate differences.Core Reaction Equation: 2 H2O2 → 2 H2O + O2↑ (catalyzed by MnO2)

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Calling a Variable After Assignment Outputs Its ValueI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Calling a Variable After Assignment Outputs Its Value2. Subject: Engineering - Software Engineering (Python Programming Basics)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that in Python, calling or printing a variable after assignment outputs its current stored value, and that reassignment overwrites the previous value.II. Experimental EnvironmentComputer with Python installed, Python interactive terminal or command-line interface, keyboard, display screen.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Open the Python terminal or command prompt and ensure the Python interpreter is running.2. Code Input: In the terminal, type the following code line by line in order:   a = 20   b = 10   a = 1   print(a)3. Execution: Press Enter after each line; after entering print(a), allow the interpreter to execute the command.4. Completion: Observe the output displayed directly below the executed command in the terminal.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. After entering the assignment statements, no output is shown immediately.2. After executing print(a), the terminal outputs the number 1 on a new line.3. The displayed value corresponds to the most recent assignment of variable a.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesIn Python, variables store values through assignment statements. When a variable is reassigned, the new value replaces the old one in memory. The print() function outputs the current value bound to the variable at the time of execution. Therefore, although a was first assigned 20, the later assignment a = 1 overwrites it, and print(a) outputs 1.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Speaker Vibrating a Metal Plate with Sand under Pure Tone and White NoiseI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Observation of Sand Patterns on a Vibrating Metal Plate under Pure Tone and White Noise2. Subject: Engineering – Communications Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the difference between single-frequency (pure tone) excitation and broadband (white noise) excitation by observing sand motion and pattern formation on a metal plate driven by a speaker; to understand frequency selectivity and energy distribution in vibration systems.II. Experimental EquipmentSpeaker (capable of producing pure tone and white noise), rigid metal plate (thin, circular or square), fine dry sand (light-colored), signal generator or audio source, amplifier (if needed), camera with fixed focus, tripod, computer or controller for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Mount the metal plate firmly on top of the speaker so it can vibrate freely. Spread a thin, uniform layer of dry sand over the plate surface. Fix the camera on a tripod facing the plate, lock focus and exposure, and enable time-lapse recording.2. Pure Tone Excitation: Play a stable pure tone at a fixed frequency and moderate volume through the speaker. Maintain this state for several seconds while recording.3. Switching to White Noise: Without moving the camera or plate, switch the audio source from pure tone to white noise at similar overall loudness. Continue recording for several seconds.4. Completion: Stop the audio, end recording, and save the time-lapse video for observation and analysis.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Sand is evenly distributed on the stationary plate.2. Under Pure Tone: As the plate vibrates at a single frequency, sand gradually migrates away from regions of large vibration amplitude and accumulates along nodal lines, forming stable and regular patterns.3. Under White Noise: After switching to white noise, the previously stable patterns break down; sand becomes agitated and redistributes randomly, with no persistent nodal structures.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleA pure tone excites the plate at a single frequency, leading to standing wave modes with fixed nodes and antinodes. Sand accumulates at nodes where vibration amplitude is minimal, forming ordered patterns. White noise contains many frequencies simultaneously, exciting multiple modes at once. This prevents stable standing waves, resulting in irregular vibration and random sand motion. The experiment illustrates frequency selectivity, resonance, and the difference between narrowband and broadband signals in communications engineering.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure sand is dry and evenly spread; avoid excessive volume that may displace the plate; keep camera focus fixed; do not touch the apparatus during recording to maintain spatiotemporal consistency.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Demonstrate how different signal types (pure tone vs white noise) affect vibration patterns and energy distribution on a mechanical system.Minimum Assumptions: A speaker can reliably vibrate a metal plate; sand responds visibly to vibration amplitude; pure tones create standing waves while white noise excites multiple modes.Phased Storyline: (1) Static setup with sand-covered plate and fixed camera; (2) Pure tone causes gradual emergence of stable sand patterns (cause: single-frequency excitation); (3) Switch to white noise causes immediate loss of order and random sand motion (cause: broadband excitation); visibility must clearly show sand redistribution and the unchanged camera perspective for verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: DAC Feeding RC Filter to Drive LED with Gradual Brightness ChangeI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: DAC Feeding RC Filter to Drive LED with Gradual Rise/Fall2. Subject: Engineering – Mechatronics & Robotics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how a microcontroller digital-to-analog converter (DAC) output, when passed through an RC low-pass filter, produces a smooth analog voltage that drives an LED with gradual brightness changes; to understand the role of RC filtering in signal smoothing and observe time-domain behavior via time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentMicrocontroller with DAC output (e.g., Arduino/STM32), USB cable and computer, resistor (e.g., 1–10 kΩ), capacitor (e.g., 10–100 µF), LED (any visible color), breadboard and jumper wires, current-limiting resistor for LED, power supply (from microcontroller), fixed camera or smartphone on tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the microcontroller, breadboard, resistor, capacitor, and LED on the workbench. Fix the camera position and focus on the LED and circuit; ensure focus will not change during recording.2. Circuit Connection: Connect the DAC output pin of the microcontroller to the resistor. Connect the other end of the resistor to one terminal of the capacitor. Connect the other terminal of the capacitor to ground, forming an RC low-pass filter. Connect the filtered output node to the LED (with a current-limiting resistor) and then to ground.3. Program Setup: Write and upload a program that continuously updates the DAC value in a ramp or sinusoidal pattern (increasing and decreasing over time).4. Core Operation: Power the microcontroller and start the program. Begin time-lapse recording with the camera, keeping the scene unchanged.5. Completion: Allow the program to run long enough to capture several full cycles of LED brightening and dimming, then stop recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The LED is off or at a low, steady brightness when the DAC output is minimal.2. During Operation: As the DAC value increases, the LED brightness gradually increases rather than changing abruptly. When the DAC value decreases, the LED brightness gradually fades.3. Continuous Behavior: The LED repeatedly shows smooth rise and fall in brightness, clearly visible in the time-lapse recording.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. DAC Principle: The microcontroller DAC converts digital values into corresponding analog voltages.2. RC Filter Principle: The resistor and capacitor form a low-pass filter that smooths rapid voltage changes, characterized by the RC time constant.3. LED Driving Principle: LED brightness depends on the current through it, which is controlled by the filtered analog voltage. Therefore, a smoothly changing voltage results in gradual LED brightness changes.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure correct polarity of the LED and capacitor.2. Use an appropriate current-limiting resistor to prevent LED damage.3. Fix the camera focus and position before starting to avoid changes during time-lapse recording.4. Verify wiring before powering the circuit to prevent short circuits.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstrate DAC-to-analog conversion and RC low-pass filtering driving an LED with smooth brightness transitions. Minimum assumptions: a microcontroller with a working DAC, a correctly connected RC filter, and an LED whose brightness reflects analog voltage changes. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) Static workbench setup with fixed camera and visible circuit; (2) program starts updating DAC values; (3) RC filter smooths voltage changes; (4) LED brightness gradually increases and decreases in clear cycles. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Strength Comparison Experiment of Lime-Modified ClayI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Strength Comparison Experiment of Lime-Modified Clay2. Subject: Engineering – Geotechnical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To compare the strength and impact resistance of pure clay and lime-modified clay through a drop test, and to understand the strengthening effect of lime on clay soil.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentPure clay soil (for clod A), lime-modified clay soil (for clod B, pre-mixed with appropriate lime content), water (for molding), balance (optional), mold or hand-forming tools, flat hard ground or concrete slab, ruler or measuring tape (to ensure equal drop height).III. Experimental Procedure1. Sample Preparation: Add appropriate water to pure clay and to lime-modified clay separately. Knead each soil until uniform, then form two clods of similar size and shape. Label them as clod A (pure clay) and clod B (lime-modified clay).2. Conditioning: Allow both clods to rest for the same period so that moisture conditions are comparable.3. Drop Setup: Measure a fixed height (e.g., 1.0 m) above the ground. Ensure the ground surface is flat and hard.4. Core Operation: Hold clod A and clod B at the same height. Drop them vertically onto the ground, either simultaneously or one after the other from the same height.5. Observation and Recording: Observe the degree of cracking, fragmentation, and overall integrity of each clod after impact.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Clod A (Pure Clay): After impact, the clod shows obvious cracking, fragmentation, or even collapse into smaller pieces.2. Clod B (Lime-Modified Clay): After impact, the clod remains relatively intact, with fewer cracks and less fragmentation compared to clod A.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleLime reacts with clay minerals and pore water, causing ion exchange and pozzolanic reactions that form cementitious compounds. These reactions reduce plasticity and increase bonding between soil particles, significantly improving strength and impact resistance. Therefore, under the same impact conditions, lime-modified clay suffers less damage than pure clay.VI. PrecautionsEnsure both clods have similar size and moisture content; keep the drop height identical; conduct the experiment on a safe, clear ground surface.

Camera should maintain a stable perspective to clearly compare damage states.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Merge Sort Divide and Conquer Process DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Merge Sort Divide and Conquer Process Demonstration2. Subject: Engineering - Computer Science3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the divide-and-conquer mechanism of the Merge Sort algorithm using a simple horizontal array of numbered bars, helping learners understand recursive division, comparison, and merging of subarrays.II. Experimental Materials and Environment1. Display environment: Clean white background (digital canvas or slide).2. Visual elements: Horizontal array of vertical bars labeled with numbers (example array: [5, 3, 4, 1, 2]).3. Animation tool: Any software capable of simple step-by-step animation (e.g., presentation software or algorithm visualization tool).III. Experimental Operation Procedure1. Initial Setup: Display the unsorted array [5, 3, 4, 1, 2] as evenly spaced vertical bars arranged horizontally on a white background. Each bar’s height corresponds to its number value.2. Divide Phase: Visually split the array into two halves. Continue dividing each subarray into smaller subarrays until each subarray contains only one bar.3. Merge Phase: Begin merging adjacent subarrays. During each merge, compare bars pairwise and reorder them into ascending order.4. Step-by-Step Animation: Clearly animate each comparison and movement of bars during merging, ensuring only adjacent subarrays are merged at a time.5. Completion: Continue merging until a single sorted array [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] is formed and displayed horizontally.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial Phenomenon: Bars appear unordered, with varying heights representing unsorted values.2. Division Phenomenon: The array is repeatedly split into smaller groups, visually separated but maintaining order within groups.3. Merging Phenomenon: Bars move and reorder during merging; smaller bars consistently move before larger bars within each merge.4. Final Phenomenon: All bars form a single horizontal array in ascending order, with smooth transitions and no overlap.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesMerge Sort is a classic divide-and-conquer algorithm. The core principle is to divide a large problem (sorting an array) into smaller subproblems (sorting subarrays), solve each subproblem recursively, and then merge the solutions. The merge operation ensures global order by repeatedly comparing the smallest elements of sorted subarrays. This guarantees a time complexity of O(n log n) and stable, deterministic sorting behavior.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Visual understanding of the Merge Sort divide-and-conquer algorithm. Minimum assumptions: a static white background, a horizontal array of numbered bars, and stepwise animation showing division and merging. Expected phenomena storyline: Phase 1 shows an unsorted array; Phase 2 recursively divides the array into single-element subarrays; Phase 3 merges subarrays with visible comparisons and ordered movement; Phase 4 ends with a fully sorted array. Key causal transitions include division preceding merging and comparisons causing bar reordering. Visibility constraints: all bars and groupings must remain on screen, with clear separation and smooth transitions for verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Vitamin A Detection by Antimony Trichloride Colorimetric MethodI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Vitamin A Detection (Antimony Trichloride Colorimetric Method)Subject: Engineering – Food and Bioprocess EngineeringExperiment Objective: To qualitatively detect vitamin A in cod liver oil extract by observing the characteristic color reaction with antimony trichloride, and to understand the principle of colorimetric analysis of fat‑soluble vitamins.II. Experimental Reagents and EquipmentDry test tube (1), test tube rack, graduated pipette or dropper, cod liver oil extract, antimony trichloride chloroform solution (SbCl3 in chloroform), protective gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ensure the test tube is clean and completely dry, then place it upright on the test tube rack.2. Sample Addition: Using a pipette, accurately measure 2 mL of cod liver oil extract and transfer it into the dry test tube.3. Reagent Addition: Measure 3 mL of antimony trichloride chloroform solution and quickly add it to the same test tube.4. Mixing and Observation: Gently swirl the test tube to mix the contents and immediately observe the color change.5. Completion: Record the observed color, then place the test tube back on the rack for comparison or disposal according to waste regulations.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The cod liver oil extract appears light yellow to pale and transparent in the dry test tube.After Reagent Addition: Upon adding antimony trichloride solution and mixing, a rapid blue to blue‑green coloration develops.Color Stability: The blue coloration may gradually fade with time due to instability of the colored complex.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleVitamin A (retinol and related compounds) contains a conjugated polyene structure. In chloroform medium, antimony trichloride reacts with this conjugated system to form an unstable blue or blue‑green colored complex. The appearance and intensity of the color indicate the presence of vitamin A. Subject: Engineering – Mechatronics & Robotics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how a Passive Infrared (PIR) motion sensor detects human movement and automatically controls a table lamp, and to understand the basic working principle of PIR-based automatic lighting control systems.II. Experimental Equipment1. PIR motion sensor module (with adjustable sensitivity and delay, if available)2. Table lamp (AC powered or low-voltage lamp compatible with the sensor)3. Power supply (according to sensor and lamp requirements)4. Connecting wires or plug-in control socket5. Doorway and dimly lit room6. Mounting tape or bracket (to fix the PIR sensor near the door)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   - Ensure the room lighting is dim so that the lamp’s on/off state is clearly visible.   - Power off all equipment before connection.2. Equipment Setup:   - Mount the PIR motion sensor near the door at about chest height, facing the entrance area.   - Connect the PIR sensor output to the control input of the table lamp (or to a relay controlling the lamp).   - Connect the PIR sensor and lamp to the power supply.3. Initial Check:   - Turn on the power and confirm the lamp is initially off when no one is in the room.   - Allow the PIR sensor to stabilize for several seconds if required.4. Core Operation:   - A person opens the door and enters the room.   - The person pauses briefly, then stands still near the door.   - After a short time, the person turns around and leaves the room.5. Subject: Engineering – Communications Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe the constellation diagram of a live 16-QAM signal using an oscilloscope in XY mode, understand the effect of additive noise on digital modulation signals, and visually relate noise power to symbol dispersion.II. Experimental EquipmentDigital signal generator (capable of 16-QAM modulation), noise source or adjustable AWGN module, oscilloscope with XY display mode, two coaxial cables, computer or signal source controller, camera mounted on tripod (focus fixed for time-lapse photography).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Power on the signal generator and oscilloscope. Set the generator to output a baseband or IF 16-QAM signal with I and Q outputs. Ensure all equipment is warmed up and stable.2. Connection: Connect the I-channel output to the oscilloscope X input and the Q-channel output to the Y input. Use equal cable lengths to avoid delay mismatch.3. Oscilloscope Setup: Set the oscilloscope to XY mode. Adjust vertical and horizontal scales so that the full constellation fits clearly on the screen. Disable time-based triggering.4. Initial Observation (Low Noise): Set the noise source to minimum or off. Observe and confirm 16 distinct, tightly clustered constellation points arranged in a 4×4 grid.5. Core Operation (Noise Increase): Gradually increase the noise level during continuous operation. Do not change signal amplitude or oscilloscope scaling. Keep the camera focus fixed and record continuously.6. Completion: Increase noise until constellation points become significantly spread and partially overlapping, then stop recording. Power down equipment after observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: With little or no noise, the XY display shows 16 clear, stationary point clusters corresponding to ideal 16-QAM symbols.2. During Noise Increase: As noise power increases, each point cluster expands into a cloud. The centers remain approximately fixed, while dispersion increases.3. High Noise State: At high noise levels, clusters may overlap, making symbol decision boundaries visually ambiguous.V. Summary of Experimental Principles16-QAM modulation maps digital symbols onto 16 discrete I-Q coordinate points. In an ideal channel, these appear as fixed points on an XY plot. Additive white Gaussian noise introduces random perturbations to the I and Q components, causing received symbols to deviate from ideal locations. As noise power increases, variance of these deviations increases, visually observed as constellation spreading. This experiment directly demonstrates the relationship between noise, signal-to-noise ratio, and symbol reliability.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure oscilloscope is in true XY mode, not time-interleaved display.2. Increase noise gradually to preserve observable causality.3. Do not adjust scaling during recording, as this affects comparability.4. Fix camera focus and position to ensure valid time-lapse comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Single-Transistor NOT Gate Inverting an LEDI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: NOT Gate Built with a Single NPN Transistor Inverting an LED State2. Subject: Engineering – Electrical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the logical inversion (NOT operation) using a single NPN transistor on a breadboard; to understand how a transistor works as an electronic switch and how the input signal at the base controls the output state of an LED.II. Experimental EquipmentBreadboard (1); NPN transistor (e.g., 2N3904 or 2N2222, 1); LED (1, red preferred); resistor for LED current limiting (220–1kΩ, 1); base resistor (4.7kΩ–10kΩ, 1); battery or DC power supply (3–9V, 1); slide switch or push-button switch (1); jumper wires; optional multimeter.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the breadboard on a flat surface. Ensure the power supply is turned off. Identify the transistor pins (collector, base, emitter) according to its datasheet.2. Circuit Assembly:(1) Insert the NPN transistor into the breadboard with emitter connected to the ground (negative terminal of the battery).(2) Connect the LED in series with the current-limiting resistor between the positive terminal of the battery and the collector of the transistor (LED anode toward the positive supply, cathode toward the collector).(3) Connect one end of the base resistor to the transistor base.(4) Connect the other end of the base resistor to one terminal of the switch.(5) Connect the other terminal of the switch to the positive terminal of the battery.(6) Connect the negative terminal of the battery to the ground rail of the breadboard.3. Power-On and Operation:(1) Turn on the power supply.(2) Observe the LED when the switch is open (no base current).(3) Press or toggle the switch to apply voltage to the transistor base.(4) Release the switch and observe the LED state again.4. Shutdown: Turn off the power supply and disconnect the battery. Remove components if required.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State (Switch Open): No current flows into the transistor base; the transistor is in cutoff. The LED is ON (current flows from the battery through the LED and resistor to the collector-emitter path).2. Switch Pressed (Input High): Base current flows through the base resistor; the transistor turns ON (saturation). The collector is pulled toward ground, and the LED turns OFF.3. Switch Released: Base current stops; the transistor turns OFF again, and the LED turns ON.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates a NOT logic function using a single NPN transistor. The transistor operates as an electronic switch. When the input at the base is LOW (switch open, no base current), the transistor is OFF, allowing the LED to remain ON. When the input at the base is HIGH (switch closed, base current flows), the transistor turns ON and pulls the collector to ground, causing the LED to turn OFF. Thus, the output (LED state) is the logical inversion of the input, realizing a NOT gate.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Always use a current-limiting resistor with the LED to prevent damage.2. Verify transistor pin configuration before wiring to avoid incorrect connections.3. Do not exceed the rated voltage of the LED and transistor.4. Power off the circuit before modifying connections.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: a NOT logic gate implemented with a single NPN transistor acting as a switch. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Iron Detection in Spinach Extract by o-Phenanthroline Colorimetric MethodI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Iron Detection in Spinach Extract (o-Phenanthroline Colorimetric Method)2. Subject: Engineering – Food and Bioprocess Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the qualitative detection of iron in food using the o-phenanthroline colorimetric method; to understand the reduction of Fe3+ to Fe2+ and the formation of a colored complex; to master the basic operation of adding reagents to a food extract and observing color changes.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (1 tube, clean and dry), test tube rack, graduated pipette or dropper, spinach extract (prepared by crushing spinach with water and filtering, greenish liquid), hydroxylamine hydrochloride solution, o-phenanthroline solution, distilled water (optional for rinsing), safety gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube vertically on a test tube rack. Wear safety goggles and gloves. Ensure the spinach extract is well mixed and free of large solid residues.2. Sample Addition: Use a graduated pipette to accurately measure 2 mL of spinach extract and transfer it into the test tube. Observe and record the initial color of the extract.3. Reduction Step: Add several drops (about 3–5 drops) of hydroxylamine hydrochloride solution into the test tube. Gently shake the test tube to mix. This step reduces any Fe3+ present to Fe2+.4. Color Development: Add several drops (about 3–5 drops) of o-phenanthroline solution into the same test tube. Gently shake or swirl to ensure thorough mixing.5. Observation: Allow the test tube to stand for a short time (seconds to 1 minute) and observe the color change of the solution.6. Completion: After observation, place the test tube back on the rack. Dispose of the solution according to laboratory waste regulations and clean the equipment.IV. After Adding Hydroxylamine Hydrochloride: No obvious color change is observed; the solution remains green, indicating the reduction reaction occurs without visible change.3. After Adding o-Phenanthroline: If iron is present, the solution gradually develops an orange-red to reddish-orange color, indicating the formation of the iron–o-phenanthroline complex. The intensity of the color reflects the relative iron content.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe o-phenanthroline colorimetric method is based on the specific complexation reaction between ferrous iron (Fe2+) and o-phenanthroline. In food samples, iron may exist as Fe3+. Hydroxylamine hydrochloride acts as a reducing agent, converting Fe3+ into Fe2+. The Fe2+ ions then react with o-phenanthroline to form a stable orange-red tris(o-phenanthroline) iron(II) complex. The appearance of the characteristic color confirms the presence of iron in the spinach extract and forms the basis for qualitative or quantitative iron analysis.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation of Salt Solution: Pour a small amount of water into the clear glass dish to form a shallow layer (approximately 2–3 mm deep). manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Wind Tunnel Smoke Visualization Forming Parallel Streaklines2. Subject: Engineering – Aerospace Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To visualize airflow patterns in a closed-loop wind tunnel by injecting thin smoke streams, observe the formation of parallel streaklines under steady uniform flow, and understand the relationship between flow uniformity and streakline behavior.II. Experimental EquipmentClosed-loop low-speed wind tunnel with transparent test section; axial or centrifugal fan with speed control; smoke generator (oil-based or glycol-based); multiple evenly spaced upstream smoke injection nozzles; flow straighteners/honeycomb (pre-installed); camera with tripod; lighting system; control panel for fan and smoke; safety gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ensure the wind tunnel test section is clean and transparent. Check that smoke nozzles are evenly spaced upstream of the test section centerline. Mount the camera perpendicular to the test section and fix focus and exposure.2. System Startup: Turn on the wind tunnel fan and gradually increase speed until a steady operating condition is reached. Wait until vibrations and speed fluctuations disappear.3. Smoke Injection: Activate the smoke generator and inject thin white smoke streams simultaneously through all upstream nozzles. Adjust smoke flow so each stream is continuous and narrow.4. Observation and Recording: Observe the smoke behavior in the test section. Start time-lapse or continuous recording while keeping the camera fixed. Maintain steady fan speed during observation.5. Shutdown: Stop smoke injection first, then gradually reduce fan speed to zero. Turn off power and allow residual smoke to dissipate.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before smoke injection, the test section appears clear with no visible flow structures.2. During Injection: Thin white smoke streams enter the test section from evenly spaced nozzles.3. Steady State: Under steady fan speed, the smoke streams remain smooth, continuous, and form nearly parallel streaklines downstream, indicating uniform flow.4. Disturbance (if any): Minor spreading or waviness may appear near walls, while the core flow remains parallel.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSmoke visualization uses smoke as a passive tracer that follows local airflow velocity. In a closed-loop wind tunnel with flow straighteners and steady fan speed, the velocity field in the test section is approximately uniform. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Motion Comparison of Identical Markers on a Rotating Turntable2. Subject: Engineering – Mechanical Engineering (Dynamics)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that identical markers placed at different radial positions on a rotating turntable have the same angular motion but different linear speeds, thereby understanding the relationship between angular velocity, radius, and tangential velocity.II. Experimental Equipment1. Motorized turntable capable of steady rotation about a vertical central axis2. Two identical visual markers (same size, shape, color, and mass)3. Adhesive or mounting clips for attaching markers4. Power supply and speed control for the motor5. Overhead camera or observer positioned above the turntableIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ensure the turntable is powered off and placed on a stable horizontal surface. Verify that the turntable rotates smoothly about its central axis.2. Marker Installation: Attach one identical marker near the center of the turntable (small radius). Attach the second identical marker near the outer edge of the turntable (large radius). Ensure both markers are firmly fixed and lie flat on the turntable surface.3. Initial Observation: From an overhead view, confirm that both markers are stationary and clearly visible before rotation begins.4. Core Operation: Turn on the motor and set the turntable to rotate at a constant speed. Maintain steady rotation for several seconds.5. Observation Phase: Observe the motion of both markers during rotation, focusing on their paths, speeds, and relative movement with respect to the center.6. Shutdown: Turn off the motor and allow the turntable to come to a complete stop. Remove the markers if necessary.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both markers are stationary at different distances from the center of the turntable.2. During Rotation: Both markers rotate around the central axis together and complete each full revolution in the same amount of time.3. Comparative Motion: The marker near the outer edge travels a longer circular path and appears to move faster along its path than the marker near the center.4. End State: When the motor is turned off, both markers slow down and stop simultaneously.V. Summary of Experimental Principle1. Angular Motion Principle: All points on a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis share the same angular velocity and angular acceleration.2. Linear Speed Relationship: The linear (tangential) speed v of a point on a rotating body is given by v = ωr, where ω is the angular velocity and r is the distance from the axis of rotation.3. Principle Explanation: Although the two markers are identical and rotate together, the marker farther from the center has a larger radius r, resulting in a higher linear speed. This explains why the outer marker covers more distance in the same time.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure markers are identical to avoid visual or inertial bias.2. Secure markers firmly to prevent detachment during rotation.3. Maintain a constant rotational speed for clear comparison.4. Observe from directly above to avoid perspective distortion.

Phase 2 (Action) – motor starts and the turntable rotates steadily about its center. Visibility Constraint: an overhead or near-overhead perspective is required to clearly verify circular paths, relative speeds, and shared angular motion.

manual: Experiment Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Gaussian Blur and Bilateral Filter on a Noisy Color Photograph2. Subject: Engineering – Mechatronics & Robotics (Image Processing and Machine Vision)3. Experiment Objective: To visually compare the effects of Gaussian blur and bilateral filtering on a noisy color photograph, understand their different smoothing characteristics, and observe how increasing filter strength affects noise reduction and edge preservation through a split-screen time-lapse demonstration with fixed camera focus.II. Experimental Equipment and Software1. Digital camera or virtual camera module (focus locked, fixed position)2. Tripod or rigid mount (to ensure no camera movement during time-lapse)3. Computer with image processing environment (e.g., MATLAB, Python + OpenCV)4. Noisy color photograph (single image used for both filters)5. Display or monitor capable of split-screen visualization6. Image processing software capable of Gaussian blur and bilateral filter parameter adjustmentIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   (1) Select a single noisy color photograph and load it into the image processing software.   (2) Fix the camera or virtual viewpoint; ensure no zoom, focus, or angle changes throughout the experiment.   (3) Create a split-screen layout: left panel for Gaussian blur, right panel for bilateral filter.2. Initial Setup:   (1) Apply no filtering initially; display the original noisy image on both sides for baseline comparison.   (2) Add a blue rectangular frame around the left image to indicate Gaussian blur.   (3) Add a green rectangular frame around the right image to indicate bilateral filter.3. Core Operation (Time-lapse Filtering):   (1) Gradually increase the Gaussian blur strength on the left image by increasing the kernel size or standard deviation.   (2) Simultaneously, gradually increase the bilateral filter strength on the right image by increasing spatial and range parameters.   (3) Capture frames continuously or at fixed intervals to form a time-lapse sequence, ensuring both sides update synchronously.4. Observation and Recording:   (1) Observe changes in noise level, edge sharpness, and color transitions on both sides.   (2) Ensure the camera focus and viewpoint remain unchanged during the entire process.5. Completion:   (1) Stop parameter adjustment once strong smoothing is achieved.   (2) Save the final split-screen output and time-lapse sequence.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both left and right images show identical noisy color photographs with visible grain and color fluctuations.2. During Filtering:   (1) Gaussian blur (left, blue frame): Noise gradually reduces, but edges and fine details become increasingly blurred.   (2) Bilateral filter (right, green frame): Noise reduces while major edges and object boundaries remain relatively sharp.3. High Filter Strength:   (1) Gaussian blur produces a smooth but noticeably smeared image.   (2) Bilateral filter produces a smoother image that still preserves edge contrast.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Gaussian Blur Principle:   Gaussian blur performs linear smoothing by convolving the image with a Gaussian kernel, averaging pixel values based solely on spatial distance. This reduces noise but also blurs edges.2. Bilateral Filter Principle:   The bilateral filter performs non-linear smoothing by considering both spatial distance and pixel intensity differences. Pixels with similar colors contribute more strongly, allowing noise reduction while preserving edges.3. Comparative Insight:   The experiment demonstrates that Gaussian blur prioritizes overall smoothness, whereas bilateral filtering balances noise reduction and edge preservation, which is critical in machine vision and robotics perception tasks.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both filters use the same original image for fair comparison.2. Keep camera focus and viewpoint fixed to maintain spatiotemporal consistency.3. Adjust parameters gradually to clearly observe progressive changes.4. Avoid asynchronous updates between left and right images.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Visual comparison of Gaussian blur and bilateral filtering on a noisy image under controlled, fixed-view conditions. Minimum assumptions: a single noisy color photo, two standard image filters, and synchronized parameter increase. Expected storyline: (1) identical noisy images appear side-by-side; (2) left image with blue frame gradually smooths and loses edge sharpness as Gaussian blur strength increases; (3) right image with green frame smooths while retaining clearer edges as bilateral filter strength increases; (4) both reach strong smoothing with distinct visual characteristics. Visibility constraints: split-screen must remain stable, frames and colors must be clearly visible, and no camera movement or focus change should occur.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic InformationTitle: Demonstration of Battery Internal Resistance via Bulb Voltage SagSubject: Engineering – Energy EngineeringObjective: To demonstrate how increased internal resistance in a worn battery causes voltage sag under load, observed as reduced bulb brightness.II. EquipmentTwo identical incandescent bulbs with holders; two identical switches; one new battery (left); one worn battery (right); connecting wires; workbench.III. Procedure1. Setup: On a workbench, connect the left bulb and switch to the new battery, and the right bulb and switch to the worn battery. Ensure both circuits are otherwise identical.2. Initial State Check: Confirm both switches are OFF and bulbs are unlit.3. Simultaneous ON: Toggle both switches ON at the same time.4. Waiting: Observe both bulbs for a short period.5. OFF–ON Retoggle: Turn both switches OFF together, then immediately turn them ON again.6. End: Leave switches ON briefly for observation, then turn OFF.IV. Observations1. Upon initial switching ON, both bulbs light, appearing similar at first.2. After a short time, the right bulb (worn battery) becomes noticeably dimmer than the left.3. Principle SummaryA real battery has internal resistance. Under load, a worn battery has higher internal resistance, causing a larger internal voltage drop and reduced terminal voltage. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Quenching vs Air-Cooling of Steel Wire and Bending BehaviorI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Quenching vs Air-Cooling of Steel Wire2. Subject: Engineering – Structural Engineering / Materials Behavior3. Experiment Objective: To compare the mechanical behavior of steel after rapid quenching and slow air-cooling by observing differences in bending, and to understand the effect of cooling rate on steel microstructure and ductility.II. Experimental EquipmentSteel wire (2 identical pieces, same diameter and length), gas torch or alcohol torch, clear water in a beaker, pliers (or gloved hands), heat-resistant surface, safety goggles, heat-resistant gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Put on safety goggles and heat-resistant gloves. Place the two identical steel wires on a heat-resistant surface.2. Heating: Use the torch to heat both steel wires evenly until they glow red along the same length, indicating similar temperature.3. Cooling Treatment:   a. Quenching: Immediately place one glowing wire into the beaker of clear water until fully cooled.   b. Air-Cooling: Place the second glowing wire on the heat-resistant surface and allow it to cool naturally in air.4. Bending Test: After both wires are cool to touch, hold them side by side using pliers or hands and apply similar bending force to each.5. Observation and Cleanup: Observe bending behavior, then store equipment safely after cooling.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Quenched Wire: Resists bending strongly; may spring back or fracture with limited deformation.2. Air-Cooled Wire: Bends more easily and smoothly, showing greater plastic deformation without breaking.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSteel heated to a red glow forms austenite. Rapid quenching in water prevents carbon diffusion, forming hard and brittle martensite, increasing strength but reducing ductility. Slow air-cooling allows formation of ferrite and pearlite, which are softer and more ductile. Therefore, cooling rate directly affects steel’s microstructure and bending behavior.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Avoid touching hot steel directly; ensure complete cooling before bending.2. Quench carefully to prevent water splashing.3. Ensure both wires are identical and heated to similar temperatures for fair comparison.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Cooling rate affects steel microstructure and mechanical behavior. Minimum assumptions: two identical steel wires, heated to red glow, cooled by water quench vs air, then bent with similar force.Phased storyline: (1) Heating phase—both wires visibly glow red; (2) Cooling divergence—one wire rapidly quenched in clear water, the other left to cool in air; (3) Mechanical test—both wires bent side by side; (4) Outcome contrast—quenched wire shows higher stiffness/brittleness, air-cooled wire shows greater ductility. Visibility constraints: clear view of glow, cooling method, and simultaneous bending for direct comparison.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Pyrolytic Graphite Hovering Above a Neodymium Magnet ArrayI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Diamagnetic Levitation of Pyrolytic Graphite2. Subject: Engineering – Electrical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate diamagnetic levitation by observing a thin sheet of pyrolytic graphite hovering above a checkerboard array of neodymium magnets with alternating poles, and to record the stable hovering state using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental Equipment1. Small neodymium cube magnets (multiple units, identical size)2. Non-magnetic base plate or tabletop3. Pyrolytic graphite sheet (thin, square, approximately 10–20 mm per side)4. Plastic tweezers (non-magnetic)5. Camera or smartphone with tripod (time-lapse capable)6. Ruler or spacer (optional, for alignment)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Clean the tabletop and ensure no ferromagnetic debris is present. Place the camera on a tripod above the tabletop and fix the focus and framing so the entire magnet array area is visible.2. Magnet Arrangement: Arrange the neodymium cube magnets on the tabletop in a checkerboard pattern. Adjacent magnets must have alternating north and south poles facing upward. Ensure magnets are tightly packed and level.3. System Check: Verify the array is stable and does not move when lightly tapped. Do not adjust the camera focus after this step.4. Core Operation: Using plastic tweezers, hold the thin square of pyrolytic graphite a few millimeters above the center of the magnet array. Gently release it without imparting horizontal motion.5. Recording: Start time-lapse or continuous recording immediately after release, keeping the environment free from air currents or vibration.6. Completion: After sufficient observation time, stop recording. Carefully remove the graphite and magnets and store them safely.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The graphite is held above the magnet array and released.2. During Release: Instead of falling onto the magnets, the graphite descends slightly and then stabilizes.3. Stable State: The pyrolytic graphite hovers a small but visible distance above the magnet array, remaining laterally stable above specific positions corresponding to the magnetic field pattern.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplePyrolytic graphite is a strongly diamagnetic material, meaning it develops an induced magnetic moment opposite to an applied magnetic field. The checkerboard arrangement of neodymium magnets with alternating poles creates a magnetic field with strong gradients. The diamagnetic repulsive force acting on the graphite balances gravitational force, resulting in stable levitation above points of minimum magnetic field strength. This experiment visually demonstrates magnetic field interaction, field gradients, and diamagnetism within the context of electrical engineering and applied physics.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Handle neodymium magnets carefully to avoid pinching fingers.2. Use only non-magnetic tools near the array.3. Avoid air currents, as the graphite sheet is very light.4. Keep electronic devices and magnetic storage media away from strong magnets.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Diamagnetic levitation of pyrolytic graphite in a non-uniform magnetic field created by an alternating-pole neodymium magnet array. Minimum assumptions: pyrolytic graphite is diamagnetic; neodymium magnets provide strong, static magnetic fields; gravity acts downward; camera viewpoint is fixed. Phased storyline: (1) Static setup phase showing a checkerboard magnet array on a tabletop from a fixed overhead or angled view; (2) Release phase where a thin square graphite sheet is lowered and released above the array; (3) Transition phase where the graphite briefly descends then stops; (4) Stable phase where the graphite hovers steadily above the array. Visibility constraints: the gap between graphite and magnets must be discernible; no camera refocusing or viewpoint change should occur; hovering stability over time confirms the causal mechanism.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Radial Heat Spreading on a Uniform Aluminum Plate2. Subject: Engineering – Energy Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that heat introduced at a point on a uniform metal plate spreads radially outward through thermal conduction, and to visualize this process using wax melting under time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentUniform aluminum plate (flat, clean), opaque wax (thin, even coating), small electric heater or soldering-iron-type heater, heat-resistant support, power supply, fixed-position camera (tripod-mounted), timer or time-lapse recording device, safety gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the aluminum plate horizontally on a heat-resistant support. Ensure the plate is uniform in thickness and free of debris. Evenly coat the surface with a thin layer of opaque wax and allow it to solidify completely.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera directly above the plate, centered on the plate’s midpoint. Fix focus, zoom, and exposure. Do not adjust the camera during the experiment.3. Heater Placement: Gently place the small heater so that it touches the exact center of the aluminum plate from below or above (as designed), ensuring stable contact.4. Heating and Recording: Turn on the heater and simultaneously start time-lapse recording. Maintain constant heating power throughout the experiment.5. Completion: After a clear radial melting pattern is observed, turn off the heater. Stop recording and allow the plate to cool before cleanup.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The wax-coated aluminum plate appears uniformly opaque, with no melted regions.2. Early Heating: Wax at the center begins to melt first, forming a small circular transparent or glossy region.3. Intermediate Stage: The melted region expands outward evenly in all directions, forming concentric circular boundaries.4. Later Stage: A clearly visible radial melting pattern is formed, with the largest melted area at the center and decreasing temperature effects outward.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates heat conduction in a uniform metal plate. When heat is applied at a single point, thermal energy spreads through the aluminum by conduction. Because the plate is uniform and isotropic, heat flows equally in all directions, producing a radially symmetric temperature distribution. The wax serves as a visual indicator: it melts where the local temperature exceeds its melting point, thereby mapping the heat distribution over time.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure even wax coating to avoid misleading melting patterns.2. Keep the heater power constant during observation.3. Do not move the camera or plate during recording.4. Handle the heated plate with gloves to avoid burns.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Lifting Strength of Identical Electromagnets with Different Core MaterialsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Lifting Strength of Identical Electromagnets with Iron and Aluminum Cores2. Subject: Engineering – Electrical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To compare the lifting strength of two identical electromagnets using different core materials (iron and aluminum) through direct observation, and to understand the influence of core material on magnetic field strength.II. Experimental EquipmentIdentical electromagnet coils (2); iron core (1); aluminum core (1); DC power supply with switch; connecting wires; steel washers (two identical piles); insulating stand or holder; tabletop surface.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the two electromagnets side by side on the tabletop. Insert an iron core into the left coil and an aluminum core into the right coil. Ensure the coils, windings, and dimensions are identical.2. Setup of Test Objects: Place two identical piles of steel washers directly below the two electromagnets, ensuring equal distance and alignment.3. Power Connection: Connect both electromagnets to the same DC power supply so they are energized simultaneously. Keep the power switched off initially.4. Core Operation: Switch on the power supply. Slowly and steadily lower both electromagnets toward the washer piles at the same time, keeping their heights equal.5. Observation and Completion: Hold the position briefly to allow washers to be attracted. Then lift the electromagnets vertically and observe the number of washers lifted by each. Switch off the power and return equipment to the initial state.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both washer piles remain stationary on the tabletop when the electromagnets are unpowered.2. During Energizing and Lowering: After powering, the left electromagnet with the iron core attracts washers strongly, lifting a large number. The right electromagnet with the aluminum core attracts few or no washers.3. Final State: When lifted, the iron-core electromagnet holds significantly more washers than the aluminum-core electromagnet.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWhen current flows through a coil, a magnetic field is produced. A ferromagnetic core such as iron has high magnetic permeability, which concentrates and strengthens the magnetic field, greatly increasing lifting force. Aluminum is not ferromagnetic and does not significantly enhance the magnetic field. Therefore, under identical electrical conditions, an iron-core electromagnet has much greater lifting strength than an aluminum-core electromagnet.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both coils are identical and powered by the same supply to guarantee a fair comparison.2. Keep hands clear of washers during energizing to avoid pinching.3. Do not overheat the coils; limit the duration of power-on time.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Differential Settlement Using Two Columns on Uneven Soil CompactionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Differential Settlement of Two Columns on Unevenly Compacted Soil2. Subject: Engineering – Structural Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how differences in soil compaction lead to differential settlement under identical structural loads, and to visually observe beam deformation caused by uneven foundation settlement.II. Experimental EquipmentRigid base platform; two transparent soil boxes of equal size; granular soil material; tamping tool; two identical model columns; rigid beam (model girder); standardized weight block; ruler or scale markers; fixed camera or tripod for time-lapse photography.III. Experimental Procedure1. Soil Preparation: Fill the left soil box with soil and tamp it densely in layers to achieve high compaction. Fill the right soil box with the same soil but place it loosely with minimal compaction.2. Column Installation: Place one identical model column vertically at the center of each soil box, ensuring equal initial height and alignment.3. Beam Placement: Carefully place the rigid beam horizontally across the tops of the two columns, ensuring initial level alignment.4. Load Application: Place a standardized weight at the midpoint of the rigid beam so that the load is equally distributed to both columns.5. Observation Setup: Fix the camera position and focus; begin time-lapse recording without moving the camera.6. Observation Period: Allow settlement to occur; no further manual intervention is applied during recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Beam is level; both columns have equal height; no visible settlement.2. During Loading: The column on the loose soil gradually settles more than the column on the dense soil.3. Final State: The rigid beam tilts toward the loose-soil side, indicating differential settlement; the dense-soil side shows minimal settlement.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on the principle of soil compressibility and foundation settlement. Under identical loads, loosely compacted soil undergoes greater compression than densely compacted soil. Because the two columns experience different foundation stiffness, unequal vertical displacement occurs, producing differential settlement and rotation of the rigid beam. This demonstrates a key structural engineering concept explaining uneven deformation and potential structural damage in real foundations.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure columns are identical and initially vertical; apply load centrally; avoid disturbing soil during observation; keep camera fixed to ensure reliable time-lapse comparison.

Minimum assumptions: identical columns and beam rigidity, same applied load, different soil stiffness (dense vs loose), gravity-driven settlement.Phased Storyline: (1) Initial setup shows level beam on two identical columns over visually distinct soil boxes; (2) centered load is applied; (3) over time, loose-soil side settles more, dense side remains relatively stable; (4) beam rotates/tilts toward the loose side. Visibility constraints: fixed camera, clear left–right distinction, settlement and beam rotation must be observable without cuts.

manual: Experiment Title: Cantilever Beam with Tip Load DemonstrationI. Basic InformationSubject: Engineering – Structural EngineeringObjective: To observe the bending deformation, smooth curvature, and rotation of cross-sections of a cantilever beam under an increasing tip load, and to understand the basic mechanical principle of cantilever beam bending.II. EquipmentThin striped plastic ruler (beam), rigid clamp or vise, table or stand, small hook or tape, several small weights (coins or washers), camera or smartphone with tripod, ruler or scale (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Clamp one end of the plastic ruler firmly to the table so that the ruler extends horizontally, forming a cantilever. Ensure the striped face is visible.2. Adjust the camera on a tripod facing the side of the ruler; fix focus and framing so the entire beam is visible. Do not move the camera afterward.3. Ensure the free end of the ruler is unloaded and horizontal; this is the initial state.4. Attach a small hook or tape at the free tip of the ruler.5. Start time-lapse or continuous recording.6. Add small weights one by one to the free tip at short, regular intervals. After each addition, briefly pause to allow the ruler to settle.7. Continue until a clear downward bending is observed, then stop adding weights and end recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The ruler is straight and horizontal.2. During Loading: As each weight is added, the free end deflects downward. The beam forms a smooth, continuous curve rather than sharp angles.3. Progressive Change: Increased load leads to larger deflection and more pronounced curvature; the stripes indicate gradual rotation of cross-sections along the beam.V. Experimental Principle SummaryA cantilever beam fixed at one end bends under a load applied at its free end due to bending moments. According to beam theory, the bending moment is maximum at the fixed end and decreases toward the free end, producing a smooth curvature. The deformation remains elastic for small loads, and cross-sections rotate progressively while remaining approximately plane.VI. PrecautionsEnsure the clamp is secure; add weights gradually to avoid sudden large deformation; keep the camera fixed throughout the experiment.

Experiment Title: Comparison of Water Absorption in Wheat Seedlings With and Without Root Hairs2. Subject: Engineering – Agricultural Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the role of root hairs in water absorption by comparing the rate of red ink movement in wheat seedlings with intact root hairs and with root hairs removed.II. Experimental MaterialsTwo similar wheat seedlings, red ink solution (diluted with water), two transparent containers or beakers, tweezers or soft cloth (for removing root hairs), stand or support to keep seedlings upright.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Select two wheat seedlings of similar height and thickness. Keep one seedling intact. Gently rub or wash the roots of the other seedling to remove most root hairs without damaging the main root.2. Setup: Place the two seedlings side by side. Pour equal amounts of red ink solution into two separate transparent containers.3. Core Operation: At the same time, immerse the roots of each seedling into separate containers of red ink solution. Ensure only the roots are submerged and the seedlings remain upright and still.4. Observation: Observe the movement of red ink along the stalks over a short period (several minutes), focusing on the speed and height of color change.5. Completion: After clear differences are observed, remove the seedlings and clean the materials.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Summary of Experimental PrincipleRoot hairs greatly increase the surface area of roots in contact with water.
