manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Effect of Diagonal Bracing on Tower Stability Under Wind LoadI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Effect of Diagonal Bracing on Tall Model Towers Under Wind2. Subject: Engineering – Structural Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how diagonal bracing increases the lateral stability and stiffness of tall structures by comparing the wind-induced response of two model towers, one with diagonal bracing and one without.II. Experimental EquipmentTabletop or flat platform; two tall model towers of identical height and material (one with diagonal bracing, one without); electric fan with steady wind setting; camera or smartphone with tripod; ruler or reference scale (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the tabletop in a stable indoor environment free from external drafts. Position the two model towers upright on the tabletop, side by side, with equal spacing and identical base conditions.2. Setup: Ensure one tower includes clear diagonal bracing on its faces, while the other tower has only vertical members. Place the electric fan directly in front of the towers at the same distance from both.3. Camera Arrangement: Fix the camera on a tripod facing the towers. Lock focus and exposure to avoid changes during recording. Set to time-lapse or continuous recording.4. Core Operation: Turn on the fan to a steady, constant wind speed. Allow wind to blow continuously toward both towers for the duration of recording.5. Completion: After sufficient observation time, turn off the fan and stop recording. Reset equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both towers stand vertically with no visible movement when the fan is off.2. During Wind Loading: When the fan operates, the unbraced tower exhibits noticeable lateral sway or vibration. The braced tower shows significantly reduced movement.3. Over Time: The difference in deformation becomes more apparent; the unbraced tower may lean or oscillate more, while the braced tower remains relatively stable.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesDiagonal bracing increases a structure’s lateral stiffness by forming triangular load paths that efficiently resist shear and bending. Under wind load, unbraced frames rely mainly on bending of vertical members, leading to larger deflections. Braced frames transfer wind forces through axial tension and compression in the braces, reducing deformation and improving overall stability.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure both towers are securely placed to prevent sliding; use the same wind setting throughout; keep camera position fixed; avoid touching the table during operation.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Biuret Reagent Reaction with Egg White ProteinsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Biuret Reagent Reaction with Egg White Proteins2. Subject: Engineering – Biomedical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To detect proteins using the Biuret reaction by comparing the color change of Biuret reagent in egg white solution and water, and to understand the principle of protein identification based on peptide bonds.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tubes (2 identical tubes), test tube rack, dropper or pipette, Biuret reagent (blue), egg white solution (diluted with water), distilled water (control), safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, identical test tubes on a test tube rack on the lab bench and wear safety goggles.2. Sample Addition: Add an equal volume (about 2–3 mL) of egg white solution into the left test tube; add the same volume of distilled water into the right test tube as a control.3. Reagent Addition: Using a dropper, add several drops of blue Biuret reagent into each test tube.4. Mixing: Gently swirl both test tubes to mix the contents evenly, avoiding vigorous shaking.5. Observation: Place the test tubes back on the rack and observe the color changes.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both test tubes contain colorless liquids; Biuret reagent is blue before reaction.2. After Mixing: The left test tube containing egg white gradually turns violet or purple; the right test tube containing water remains blue with no obvious color change.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe Biuret reaction is a qualitative test for proteins. Biuret reagent contains copper(II) ions in an alkaline solution. When proteins with peptide bonds are present, the copper(II) ions form a coordination complex with the peptide bonds, producing a violet or purple color. Egg white is rich in protein (albumin), so a positive violet reaction occurs. Water contains no protein, so no color change is observed, serving as a negative control.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Visualization of the Biuret protein test demonstrating selective color change due to peptide bonds in proteins. Minimum assumptions: two identical test tubes on a lab bench, one with egg white protein solution and one with water, blue Biuret reagent added and gently swirled.Phased storyline: (1) Static setup showing left/right test tubes with different contents; (2) Addition of blue Biuret reagent to both tubes; (3) Gentle swirling motion; (4) Causal transition where the egg white tube changes to violet/purple while the water tube remains blue. Visibility constraints: clear view of liquid color and gradual change, stable perspective to compare left and right tubes simultaneously.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Water Heavy Metal Lead Detection (Dithizone Colorimetric Method)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Water Heavy Metal Lead Detection by Dithizone Colorimetric MethodSubject: Engineering - Civil & Environmental EngineeringExperiment Objective: To demonstrate the extraction and visual detection of lead ions in water by forming a colored complex with dithizone and observing phase separation after shaking.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (clean and dry), test tube rack, two droppers or pipettes, lead-containing water sample, dithizone chloroform solution, protective gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube on the rack. Wear gloves and goggles to ensure safety.2. Sample Addition: Using a dropper, measure and add 2 mL of the lead-containing water sample into the test tube.3. Reagent Addition: Using another dropper, add 2 mL of dithizone chloroform solution into the same test tube.4. Mixing: Seal the test tube opening with a stopper or finger and gently shake the test tube for several seconds to ensure thorough contact between the aqueous and organic phases.5. Standing and Separation: Place the test tube back on the rack and allow it to stand until the mixture separates clearly into two layers.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Two immiscible liquids are present; the aqueous layer is colorless, and the chloroform layer containing dithizone is typically green.After Shaking: The liquids mix temporarily, appearing cloudy.After Standing: The mixture separates into two clear layers. The chloroform (organic) layer shows a distinct red or reddish-purple color, while the aqueous layer remains nearly colorless.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleDithizone is an organic chelating agent that reacts with lead ions (Pb2+) in water to form a colored lead-dithizonate complex. When shaken with chloroform, this complex preferentially dissolves in the organic phase. Due to the immiscibility and density difference between water and chloroform, the system separates into two layers upon standing, with the colored organic layer indicating the presence of lead in the water sample.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstrate lead detection via dithizone extraction using minimal assumptions that two immiscible liquids, correct reagents, and gravity-driven separation are visible. Expected storyline: (1) aqueous sample placed in test tube, (2) dithizone chloroform added forming two initial layers, (3) shaking causes temporary mixing enabling complex formation, (4) standing leads to clear phase separation, (5) colored organic layer appears indicating lead presence. Visibility constraints: camera must clearly show liquid volumes, shaking action, and final two-layer color contrast for verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Vitamin B2 Detection in Milk (Fluorescence Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Vitamin B2 Detection in Milk by Fluorescence Method2. Subject: Engineering – Food and Bioprocess Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To understand the fluorescence detection principle of vitamin B2 (riboflavin) in food systems and to observe the fluorescence signal of vitamin B2 in milk using an ultraviolet spectrophotometer.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsUltraviolet–visible spectrophotometer with fluorescence observation capability, quartz cuvette (path length 1 cm), micropipette or graduated pipette, milk sample, laboratory tissue, gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Turn on the ultraviolet spectrophotometer and allow it to warm up. Set the detection wavelength to 445 nm. Ensure the quartz cuvette is clean, dry, and free of fingerprints.2. Sample Loading: Use a pipette to accurately measure 2 mL of milk sample. Slowly transfer the milk into the quartz cuvette, avoiding bubbles.3. Placement: Wipe the outer surface of the cuvette with laboratory tissue. Place the cuvette into the sample holder of the spectrophotometer, aligning the transparent faces with the light path.4. Measurement: Close the instrument lid and initiate measurement or observation under ultraviolet excitation at 445 nm.5. Completion: After observation, remove the cuvette, dispose of the sample according to laboratory rules, and clean the cuvette.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The milk sample appears as an opaque white liquid under normal light.2. Under UV Excitation: When irradiated at 445 nm, the milk sample exhibits a visible fluorescence signal due to the presence of vitamin B2; the fluorescence intensity is observable relative to background.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleVitamin B2 (riboflavin) is a naturally fluorescent compound. When excited by ultraviolet or blue light at an appropriate wavelength (around 445 nm), riboflavin molecules absorb energy and transition to an excited state. Upon returning to the ground state, part of the absorbed energy is emitted as fluorescence. By placing a milk sample in a quartz cuvette and irradiating it at 445 nm, the fluorescence signal can be observed, providing qualitative evidence of vitamin B2 in milk.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Quartz cuvettes must be used because ordinary glass absorbs ultraviolet light.2. Avoid bubbles or fingerprints, as they interfere with optical measurements.3. Handle ultraviolet light sources carefully and avoid direct eye exposure.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstration of vitamin B2 fluorescence detection in milk using UV spectrophotometry. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: riboflavin in milk fluoresces when excited at 445 nm; quartz cuvette allows UV transmission; correct sample volume ensures standard observation. Phased storyline: (1) preparation and wavelength setting on spectrophotometer; (2) accurate measurement and transfer of 2 mL milk into a quartz cuvette; (3) insertion of cuvette into instrument; (4) UV excitation and visible fluorescence observation. Key causal transition: UV excitation leads to fluorescence emission. Visibility constraints: clear view of cuvette, instrument setting (445 nm), and fluorescence response within a short, accelerated sequence suitable for a 10-second video.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Saltwater vs Distilled Water Conductivity Comparison Using a Small MotorI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Electrical Conductivity of Saltwater and Distilled Water Using a DC Motor2. Subject: Engineering – Chemical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To visually compare the electrical conductivity of saltwater and distilled water by observing the operating state of a small DC motor in a battery-powered circuit, and to understand the role of ions in electrical conduction of aqueous solutions.II. Experimental EquipmentSmall DC motor (low-voltage), battery (AA or 9V) with holder, connecting wires with clips, metal electrodes (2 identical pairs, e.g., copper or graphite rods), two identical clear beakers, saltwater solution (prepared by dissolving sodium chloride in water), distilled water, insulating support, camera or smartphone with fixed mount for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear beakers side by side on a stable surface. Label the left beaker as saltwater and the right beaker as distilled water. Pour equal volumes of saltwater into the left beaker and distilled water into the right beaker.2. Electrode Placement: Insert a pair of identical metal electrodes into each beaker, ensuring the electrodes in each beaker do not touch each other and are immersed to the same depth.3. Circuit Connection: Connect the battery, DC motor, and the electrodes to form a complete circuit so that current must pass through the solution in the beaker before reaching the motor. Ensure both beaker circuits are wired in the same configuration (tested one after the other or via a switch).4. Recording Setup: Fix the camera position and focus so that both beakers and the motor are clearly visible. Do not adjust focus during recording.5. Core Operation: Power the circuit connected to the saltwater beaker and observe the motor. Then power the circuit connected to the distilled water beaker under the same conditions.6. Completion: Turn off the power, disconnect the circuit, dispose of solutions properly, and clean electrodes and beakers.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The motor is stationary when the circuit is not powered.2. Saltwater Beaker: When powered, the motor rotates noticeably and steadily, indicating sufficient current flow through the saltwater.3. Distilled Water Beaker: When powered, the motor rotates very slowly or not at all, indicating minimal current flow.4. Comparison: The motor performance with saltwater is clearly stronger than with distilled water.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSaltwater contains dissolved sodium and chloride ions that move freely in solution, allowing electric current to pass easily. Distilled water has very few ions, so its electrical conductivity is extremely low. When the circuit is completed through saltwater, higher current flows and the motor operates effectively. When the circuit is completed through distilled water, insufficient current flows to drive the motor. This demonstrates the relationship between ionic concentration and electrical conductivity in aqueous solutions.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use low-voltage batteries to ensure safety.2. Ensure electrodes do not touch directly in the solution.3. Keep electrode material and immersion depth consistent between beakers.4. Fix camera focus and position to ensure valid time-lapse comparison.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Demonstrate that aqueous electrical conductivity depends on ionic concentration, using motor speed as a visible indicator. Minimum assumptions: saltwater contains mobile ions; distilled water contains negligible ions; higher current leads to stronger motor rotation.Expected Phenomena Storyline: Phase 1 – Static setup with two identical beakers and a visible motor circuit. Phase 2 – Circuit powered through saltwater, causing clear and sustained motor rotation. Phase 3 – Circuit powered through distilled water, showing weak or absent motor motion. Phase 4 – Stable comparison under fixed camera perspective, enabling verification of causal differences. Visibility constraints: both beakers, electrodes, wiring, and motor must remain in frame with fixed focus to confirm temporal and causal consistency.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Comparing Slope Stability of Dry Sand vs Moist SandI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Comparison of Slope Stability of Dry Sand and Moist SandSubject: Engineering – Structural Engineering (Geotechnical Basics)Objective: To visually compare the slope stability of dry sand and moist sand under increasing inclination, and understand the role of moisture-induced cohesion in slope stability.II. Equipment and MaterialsTwo identical flat trays; dry sand (uniform grain size); moist sand (same sand with small amount of water, evenly mixed); adjustable tilting platform or manual tilt mechanism; camera or smartphone with tripod; ruler or angle indicator (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the two trays side by side on the same tilting platform. Fill one tray with dry sand and level its surface. Fill the other tray with moist sand of the same volume and level its surface similarly.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera to view the trays from the side. Fix focus, framing, and exposure. Ensure both trays are fully visible. Start time-lapse or continuous recording.3. Core Operation: Slowly tilt the platform upward at a steady, uniform rate so that both trays experience the same increase in angle.4. Observation Phase: Continue tilting until clear sand movement or collapse occurs in both trays.5. End: Stop tilting after both sands have shown failure or sliding. Stop recording.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both dry and moist sand surfaces are stable and level.During Tilting: As the angle increases, dry sand begins to slide and collapse at a relatively low angle, forming a gentle slope. Moist sand remains stable for a longer time and can maintain a steeper slope.Final State: Moist sand collapses at a higher tilt angle than dry sand.V. Experimental Principle SummaryDry sand has little to no cohesion between particles, so stability relies mainly on friction. Moist sand contains small amounts of water that create capillary forces between grains, increasing apparent cohesion. This added cohesion allows moist sand to resist sliding and maintain steeper slopes, resulting in higher slope stability compared with dry sand.VI. PrecautionsEnsure both trays are identical and sand volumes are equal; moisture should be limited to avoid slurry; tilt rate must be steady and the same for both trays; keep camera fixed throughout recording.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Crumpled Paper vs Flat Paper Falling Through AirI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Crumpled Paper vs Flat Paper Falling Through Air2. Subject: Engineering - Energy Engineering (Fluid Resistance)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the effect of air resistance on falling objects by comparing the falling motion of two identical paper sheets, one tightly crumpled and one flat, released simultaneously from the same height in still indoor air.II. Experimental Equipment1. Two identical paper sheets (same size, material, and color)2. Indoor space with still air (classroom or hallway)3. Step stool or table (optional, to ensure sufficient height)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Select two identical paper sheets. Tightly crumple one sheet into a compact ball, and keep the other sheet completely flat and unfolded.2. Positioning: Stand indoors in a location without airflow. Hold the crumpled paper in one hand and the flat paper in the other hand, ensuring both papers are at the same height and positioned side by side.3. Core Operation: Simultaneously release both papers at the same moment without pushing them downward.4. Observation: Watch both papers as they fall through the air until they reach the ground.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The crumpled paper falls relatively quickly and reaches the ground first.2. The flat paper falls more slowly, often fluttering or swaying as it descends.3. The difference in falling time and motion between the two papers is clearly observable.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesAlthough both papers have the same mass and are acted on by gravity, they experience different air resistance. The flat paper has a larger surface area in contact with air, producing greater drag force, which reduces its downward acceleration. The crumpled paper has a smaller effective surface area, experiences less air resistance, and therefore falls faster. This experiment demonstrates the role of air resistance in energy dissipation and motion through fluids.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the air is still; avoid fans, air conditioners, or open windows.2. Release both papers simultaneously from the same height to ensure a fair comparison.3. Do not throw or push the papers downward during release.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Detection of Tea Polyphenols by Folin–Ciocalteu Colorimetric MethodSubject: Engineering – Food and Bioprocess EngineeringExperiment Objective: To qualitatively detect tea polyphenols in green tea extract through a colorimetric reaction, observe the color change process under alkaline conditions, and understand the basic principle of polyphenol determination.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (clean and dry), test tube rack, micropipette or graduated dropper, green tea extract, Folin–Ciocalteu (Folin-phenol) reagent, sodium carbonate solution, camera or imaging device for close-up and time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube on the rack and ensure the camera is focused on the test tube area for clear close-up recording.2. Sample Addition: Use a pipette to add 1 ml of green tea extract into the test tube.3. Reagent Addition: Add 0.5 ml of Folin–Ciocalteu reagent into the test tube, then gently shake the test tube to mix evenly.4. Alkalization: Add 1 ml of sodium carbonate solution into the mixture and shake gently again to ensure uniform mixing.5. Standing and Recording: Keep the test tube standing at room temperature for 5 minutes. Maintain focus on the test tube and perform time-lapse photography to record the gradual color change.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The green tea extract appears light yellow or pale green.2. After Folin Reagent Addition: The solution may become slightly darker.3. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe Folin–Ciocalteu colorimetric method is based on the redox reaction between phenolic compounds and the Folin reagent under alkaline conditions. Tea polyphenols reduce phosphomolybdic–phosphotungstic acid complexes in the Folin reagent to form blue-colored compounds. Sodium carbonate provides an alkaline environment that enables the reaction. The intensity of the blue color correlates with the amount of polyphenols present in the sample.VI. Experimental NotesEnsure correct order of reagent addition; mix gently to avoid splashing; maintain stable camera focus throughout the standing period to clearly capture the color development.

Filtration: Assemble a funnel with filter paper. Filter the mixture to remove solid residues. Collect the clear filtrate in a clean container.4. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Single Linked List Head Insertion Node Insertion Operation DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Single Linked List Head Insertion Demonstration2. Subject: Engineering - Computer Science - Data Structures3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the head insertion operation in a singly linked list, understand how a new node is inserted at the head, and observe how the head pointer is redirected to the new node.II. Experimental Materials (Virtual/Animation Elements)1. Visual representation of singly linked list nodes (rectangles with data and next fields).2. Labels for node values (e.g. 2, 3, 4, 5, and new node 1).3. Arrows representing next pointers and the head pointer.III. Experimental Procedure1. Initial State Setup: Display a singly linked list with nodes in order [2] -> [3] -> [4] -> [5]. The head pointer points to node [2].2. New Node Creation: Create a new node with data value [1], shown separately, with its next pointer initially empty.3. Pointer Assignment: Set the next pointer of node [1] to point to the original head node [2].4. Head Redirection: Redirect the head pointer from node [2] to node [1].5. Final State Display: Show the updated list as [1] -> [2] -> [3] -> [4] -> [5], with the head pointer clearly pointing to node [1].IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initially, the head pointer points to the first node with value [2].2. After creating node [1], it is not yet part of the list.3. When node [1].next points to node [2], the list structure begins to change logically.4. After redirecting the head pointer, node [1] becomes the new first node, and the list order updates accordingly.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesA singly linked list head insertion works by changing pointer references rather than moving data. The core principle is that the new node"s next pointer must reference the original head, and then the head pointer is updated to reference the new node. This operation has constant time complexity O(1) and does not depend on the length of the list.VI. Experimental Notes1. The order of pointer operations is critical to avoid losing access to the original list.2. Clear labeling of pointers helps in understanding the causal relationship between steps.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Head insertion in a singly linked list, assuming basic knowledge of nodes, next pointers, and a head pointer. Minimum assumptions include that each node has a data field and a single next pointer. Expected phenomena should be presented as a short phased storyline: (1) show the initial list with head pointing to [2]; (2) introduce a new node [1]; (3) connect new node next to old head; (4) redirect head to new node; (5) display the final list. Key causal transition is that pointer reassignment, not data movement, causes the structural change. The animation should maintain a fixed viewpoint so pointer redirection and list order changes are clearly visible for verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Beam Bridge Model Progressively Loaded with Small WeightsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Progressive Central Loading of a Simply Supported Beam Bridge Model2. Subject: Engineering – Structural Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe the deformation behavior of a simply supported beam under progressively increasing central load, understand the relationship between load and deflection, and demonstrate basic principles of beam bending through time-lapse observation.II. Experimental EquipmentBeam bridge model (straight beam with uniform cross-section), two rigid piers/supports of equal height, flat tabletop, identical small weights (multiple pieces), ruler or scale (optional), camera or smartphone with tripod, adequate lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Setup Preparation: Place the two rigid piers on the tabletop with a fixed span. Lay the beam horizontally on the piers to form a simply supported beam. Ensure the beam is initially level and stable.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera facing the side of the beam so that the entire span and midspan are visible. Fix focus, framing, and exposure. Start time-lapse recording.3. Initial State Recording: Record the unloaded state of the beam for a short duration to establish the reference position.4. Progressive Loading: Place one identical small weight gently at the center of the beam deck. After the beam stabilizes, place the next identical weight at the same central position. Repeat until a clear deflection trend is observed, avoiding damage or collapse.5. Completion: Stop adding weights, end the time-lapse recording, and carefully remove the weights. Dismantle the setup.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: With no load, the beam remains straight or nearly straight between the two supports.2. During Loading: After each additional weight is placed at the center, the beam exhibits an increased downward deflection at midspan.3. Progressive Trend: The midspan deflection increases monotonically as more identical weights are added, while the supports remain stationary.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesA simply supported beam subjected to a central concentrated load experiences bending, producing maximum bending moment and maximum deflection at midspan. Within the elastic range, beam deflection increases with applied load. This experiment visually demonstrates the load–deflection relationship and the fundamental principle of elastic bending in structural engineering.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure supports are rigid and do not move; use identical weights; place weights gently at the exact center; do not exceed the beam’s safe load capacity; keep the camera fixed throughout recording.

manual: Experimental Instruction ManualI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Same Binary Bit Stream Encoded as Unipolar NRZ vs Polar NRZSubject: Engineering – Communications EngineeringExperiment Objective: To observe and compare unipolar NRZ and polar NRZ line coding schemes by displaying the same binary bit stream simultaneously on a dual-channel oscilloscope, and to understand their voltage characteristics and encoding principles.II. Experimental EquipmentSignal generator with digital output or pattern generator (1 unit); dual-channel oscilloscope (1 unit); BNC signal cables (2); power supply and probes as required.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Power on the signal generator and oscilloscope. Set the oscilloscope to dual-channel display and time-domain mode.2. Signal Configuration: Configure the signal generator to output a continuous binary bit stream (e.g., 10110010…) with a fixed bit rate.3. Encoding Setup: Set one output of the generator (or encoding module) to unipolar NRZ (logic 1 = +V, logic 0 = 0 V) and the other to polar NRZ (logic 1 = +V, logic 0 = −V), ensuring both use the same clock and bit stream.4. Connection: Connect the unipolar NRZ output to Channel 1 (left) of the oscilloscope and the polar NRZ output to Channel 2 (right).5. Observation Adjustment: Adjust the oscilloscope time base and voltage scale so several bits are clearly visible on both channels.6. Continuous Observation: Allow the system to run continuously and observe the waveform correspondence between the two channels.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Channel 1 (Unipolar NRZ): The waveform switches between 0 V and a positive voltage level, remaining constant during each bit interval.2. Channel 2 (Polar NRZ): The waveform switches between equal positive and negative voltage levels, centered around 0 V, remaining constant during each bit interval.3. Comparison: Bit transitions on both channels occur at the same time, confirming that both signals represent the same binary bit stream with different encoding schemes.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesNRZ (Non-Return-to-Zero) line coding represents binary data by holding a constant voltage level throughout each bit period. In unipolar NRZ, bits are represented using 0 V and +V, resulting in a DC component. In polar NRZ, bits are represented using −V and +V, producing a zero-mean signal with improved spectral properties. This experiment demonstrates how different line coding schemes encode identical binary information while exhibiting distinct voltage characteristics.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure common grounding between instruments; avoid exceeding oscilloscope voltage limits; verify synchronization so both channels display the same bit timing.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Pre-charged vs Uncharged Capacitor Driving an LEDI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of LED Response Driven by Pre-charged and Uncharged Capacitors2. Subject: Engineering – Electrical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that a pre-charged capacitor can temporarily drive an LED when connected in a circuit, while an uncharged capacitor cannot, and to understand capacitor discharge behavior in an RC circuit through visual comparison.II. Experimental EquipmentDC power supply (for pre-charging), two identical capacitors (one with red sleeve, one with blue sleeve), two identical LEDs, two identical resistors, connecting wires, single-pole single-throw switch (one switch controlling both branches), mounting board, camera with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Circuit Setup: Construct two identical LED–resistor–capacitor branches side by side on a board. Ensure component values and wiring orientation are the same. Mark the left capacitor with a red sleeve and the right capacitor with a blue sleeve.2. Pre-charging: Disconnect both branches from the LEDs using the switch in the open position. Use the DC power supply to pre-charge only the left (red-sleeved) capacitor to a specified voltage. After charging, disconnect it from the power supply. Leave the right (blue-sleeved) capacitor uncharged.3. Camera Preparation: Position the camera facing both branches. Fix the focus, exposure, and framing to ensure both LEDs are clearly visible throughout the experiment.4. Core Operation: Close the single switch so that both capacitor branches are simultaneously connected to their respective LEDs and resistors.5. Observation and Recording: Allow the camera to record the LED behavior continuously for a short period, suitable for time-lapse playback.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before the switch is closed, both LEDs are off.2. Immediately After Switching: The LED connected to the pre-charged red-sleeved capacitor lights up briefly, showing a visible flash or glow that quickly fades. The LED connected to the uncharged blue-sleeved capacitor remains off or shows no noticeable light.3. After a Short Time: Both LEDs are off, indicating that the stored energy in the pre-charged capacitor has been released.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesA capacitor stores electrical energy when charged. When the switch is closed, the pre-charged capacitor discharges through the resistor and LED, producing a transient current that causes the LED to emit light briefly. The current decays exponentially as the capacitor voltage decreases. An uncharged capacitor has no stored energy, so it cannot initially drive current through the LED. This experiment visually demonstrates capacitor discharge behavior and energy storage in RC circuits.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure correct polarity of LEDs and capacitors to avoid damage.2. Use identical components in both branches to ensure fair comparison.3. Fix camera focus and avoid moving the setup during recording.4. Do not exceed the rated voltage of the capacitors during pre-charging.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstrate the causal difference between a pre-charged and an uncharged capacitor in driving an LED within identical RC circuits. Minimum assumptions: identical components, one capacitor initially charged, one uncharged, and a single switch simultaneously connecting both to their LEDs.Phased storyline: (1) Static setup with two side-by-side branches, LEDs off; (2) clear switch-closing action; (3) immediate visible flash and decay of the LED on the pre-charged (red-sleeved) branch; (4) absence of light on the uncharged (blue-sleeved) branch; (5) final state with both LEDs off. Visibility constraints: fixed camera focus, both LEDs and capacitor colors clearly visible to verify sequence and causal relationship.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Iodine Test on Albino Corn Seedling LeavesI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Iodine Test of Albino Corn Seedling Leaves2. Subject: Engineering – Agricultural Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To verify that albino corn seedling leaves do not produce starch due to lack of chlorophyll by decolorizing the leaves and testing with iodine solution, and to understand the relationship between photosynthesis and starch formation.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentAlbino corn seedling leaves, beaker with hot water, ethanol (95%), beaker for ethanol, forceps, dropper, iodine solution, Petri dish or white porcelain dish, distilled water.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Select fresh albino corn seedling leaves and rinse them briefly with water to remove surface impurities.2. Killing and Softening: Use forceps to place the leaves into hot water for a short time (about 30 seconds) to kill the cells and soften the tissue.3. Decolorization: Transfer the leaves into a beaker containing ethanol. Place the beaker in a hot water bath if needed until the leaves become yellowish white, indicating chlorophyll removal.4. Rinsing: Remove the decolorized leaves with forceps and rinse them with clean water to remove residual ethanol and soften the leaves.5. Iodine Test: Lay the leaf flat on a Petri dish. Using a dropper, add iodine solution dropwise onto the leaf surface, ensuring even coverage.6. Observation: Observe the color change of the leaf surface carefully.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before iodine addition: The albino leaf appears yellowish white after ethanol decolorization.2. After iodine addition: The leaf remains yellowish white or light brown, with no blue-black color appearing.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplePhotosynthesis in green plants requires chlorophyll to synthesize starch. Albino corn seedling leaves lack chlorophyll and therefore cannot carry out normal photosynthesis or produce starch. Iodine solution turns blue-black in the presence of starch. Since no starch is present in albino leaves, no blue-black color appears after iodine treatment, confirming the absence of starch.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Handle hot water and ethanol carefully to avoid burns or fire hazards.2. Ensure complete decolorization before adding iodine solution.3. Use a white dish to make color observation clear.4. Dispose of ethanol and iodine waste according to laboratory safety rules.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Albino corn leaves lack chlorophyll and therefore do not form starch, resulting in no blue-black reaction with iodine after decolorization. Minimum assumptions: albino leaves are visually pale; ethanol removes pigments; iodine indicates starch presence by color change.Phased storyline: (1) Introduction of pale albino corn leaves and clear tools; (2) brief immersion in hot water to prepare tissue; (3) transfer to ethanol causing visible decolorization; (4) rinsing and flattening the leaf on a dish; (5) iodine applied dropwise; (6) final observation where the leaf remains yellowish white with no blue change. Key causal transition: lack of chlorophyll leads to no starch, which leads to no iodine color reaction. Visibility constraints: close-up views of leaf color before and after iodine, and clear perspective on each tool during stepwise operations.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: DNA Gel Electrophoresis Demonstrating Intact vs Degraded DNAI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: DNA Gel Electrophoresis Showing Clear Bands vs Smeared Bands from Degraded DNA2. Subject: Engineering – Biomedical Engineering (Molecular Biology Techniques)3. Experiment Objective: To compare the electrophoretic patterns of fresh (intact) DNA and degraded DNA using agarose gel electrophoresis; to understand how DNA integrity affects band patterns under UV illumination; to demonstrate correct loading, running, and imaging of a DNA gel suitable for time-lapse photography with fixed camera focus.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsAgarose powder, electrophoresis buffer (1× TAE or TBE), microwave or hot plate, gel casting tray and comb, electrophoresis chamber and power supply, DNA loading dye, DNA ladder (marker), fresh intact DNA sample (tube color A, e.g., blue), degraded DNA sample (tube color B, e.g., red), micropipettes and tips, UV transilluminator or gel documentation system, DNA stain (e.g., ethidium bromide or safe alternative), protective gloves and goggles, camera mounted above the gel with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Gel Preparation: Weigh agarose (e.g., 1 g per 100 mL buffer) and dissolve it in electrophoresis buffer by heating until fully clear. Allow the solution to cool slightly, add DNA stain if required, pour into the casting tray with comb in place, and let it solidify.2. Sample Preparation: Add loading dye to both fresh DNA and degraded DNA samples. Gently mix without creating bubbles. Place samples in clearly distinguishable colored tubes.3. Gel Setup: Remove the comb, place the gel into the electrophoresis chamber, and add buffer until the gel is fully submerged. Ensure wells are near the negative (cathode) end.4. Loading Samples: Using a micropipette, load DNA ladder into the first lane. Load fresh DNA from the blue tube into one lane and degraded DNA from the red tube into a separate lane. Avoid puncturing the wells or cross-contamination.5. Electrophoresis Run: Connect the electrodes correctly (DNA migrates toward the positive electrode). Set the power supply (e.g., 80–120 V) and start electrophoresis.6. Imaging and Time-Lapse Setup: Place the gel on the UV transilluminator or within a gel documentation system. Fix the camera position and focus before starting the run or before imaging to ensure consistent time-lapse recording. Do not adjust focus during recording.7. Completion and Shutdown: After sufficient separation, turn off the power supply. Observe and record the gel image under UV illumination. Dispose of waste according to safety regulations.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Wells are clearly visible; no bands are present before electrophoresis.2. During Electrophoresis: DNA migrates from wells toward the positive electrode, with smaller fragments moving faster.3. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Binary Tree Level-order Traversal DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Binary Tree Level-order Traversal Demonstration2. Subject: Engineering - Computer Science - Data Structures3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the concept and execution process of binary tree level-order traversal, helping learners understand how nodes are visited level by level from top to bottom and left to right.II. Experimental Materials (Visual Elements)1. A simple binary tree with 7 nodes labeled 1–7.2. Light-colored background to ensure visual clarity.3. Bright highlight color (e.g., red) for visited nodes.4. Horizontal output list area at the bottom of the screen.III. Experimental Operation Process1. Initialization: Display a simple binary tree on a light background. Node 1 is the root, nodes 2 and 3 are its children, and nodes 4–7 form the next level.2. Traversal Start: Begin level-order traversal from the root (node 1).3. Level-by-Level Highlighting: Highlight nodes level by level from top to bottom. Within each level, visit nodes from left to right.4. Node Visit Action: When a node is visited, briefly apply a bright glowing highlight to the node.5. Output Update: Immediately append the value of the visited node to the horizontal output list at the bottom of the screen.6. Completion: Continue until all nodes (1–7) have been visited and added to the output list.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: All nodes are visible with no highlights; the output list is empty.2. During Traversal: Nodes glow one by one in level-order sequence (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7). Each glow is followed by the appearance of the node value in the output list.3. Final State: All nodes have been highlighted once, and the output list shows the complete traversal order in a single horizontal line.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesLevel-order traversal is a breadth-first traversal method for binary trees. It visits nodes level by level, starting from the root and proceeding from left to right within each level. The core principle relies on a queue data structure: nodes are dequeued for visiting and their child nodes are enqueued in order. This experiment visualizes the algorithmic logic by directly linking node visitation (highlighting) with output generation (list appending).VI. NotesThis demonstration simplifies timing to fit short video constraints while preserving the correct traversal order and causal relationships.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Sandbox Model Demonstration of Pile Spacing EffectI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Sandbox Model of Pile Spacing Effect (Closely Spaced vs Widely Spaced Piles)2. Subject: Engineering – Structural Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the influence of pile spacing on load-sharing efficiency and settlement behavior of pile groups using a simple sandbox model and time-lapse observation.II. Experimental Equipment1. Clear sand trays (2 identical trays)2. Uniform dry sand (same type and density for both trays)3. Vertical wooden dowels (8 total, identical size)4. Square rigid plates (2, identical size and thickness)5. Identical weights or load blocks (2 sets with equal mass)6. Ruler or spacing jig (for consistent dowel placement)7. Camera with tripod and time-lapse functionIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clear sand trays side by side on a level surface. Fill both trays with sand to the same height and lightly level the surface.2. Pile Installation: Insert four vertical dowels into each tray. In the left tray, place dowels closely spaced beneath the footprint of the square plate. In the right tray, place dowels with wider spacing while keeping the same number and depth.3. Plate Placement: Position one square plate on top of the dowels in each tray, ensuring full contact and alignment.4. Camera Setup: Fix the camera on a tripod facing both trays. Lock focus, exposure, and framing. Activate time-lapse mode.5. Loading Operation: Add identical weights simultaneously onto both square plates in a smooth and controlled manner.6. Observation Period: Allow the system to deform under load while recording with time-lapse.7. Completion: Stop recording after settlement stabilizes. Remove loads and document final states.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both trays appear identical in sand level and plate elevation.2. During Loading: After weights are applied, sand around dowels begins to compress and plates start to settle.3. Comparative Outcome: The closely spaced dowel group shows larger and faster settlement, while the widely spaced group exhibits smaller settlement and better load distribution.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates the pile group effect in structural engineering. Closely spaced piles interact strongly, causing overlapping stress zones in the soil, reducing efficiency and increasing settlement. Widely spaced piles mobilize soil resistance more effectively, leading to improved load-sharing and reduced settlement. The sandbox model provides a qualitative visualization of this principle.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure identical sand conditions and dowel properties in both trays.2. Apply loads simultaneously and evenly to avoid bias.3. Keep camera settings fixed to ensure valid time-lapse comparison.

Experiment Title: Observation of Alpha Particle Tracks in a Cloud Chamber2. Subject: Engineering – Nuclear Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To visually observe alpha particle tracks using a tabletop cloud chamber, understand the interaction between ionizing radiation and supersaturated vapor, and recognize basic radiation detection principles.II. Experimental EquipmentTabletop diffusion cloud chamber with transparent walls; absorbent felt lining; high-purity isopropyl alcohol (or ethanol) vapor; cold plate or dry ice base; small weak sealed alpha radioactive source; tweezers; flashlight or LED side light; darkened room; protective gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the cloud chamber on a stable table in a dim room. Line the chamber base with felt and saturate it evenly with alcohol. Put on protective gloves.2. Cooling: Place the chamber on the cold plate or dry ice base and wait 2–3 minutes until a supersaturated alcohol vapor layer forms near the bottom.3. Source Placement: Using tweezers, place the small sealed alpha source just above the chamber floor, near the center.4. Illumination: Shine a low-angle flashlight or LED light across the chamber to illuminate the vapor layer.5. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Malachite Copper Ion Detection by Ammonia Water Color Development MethodSubject: Engineering – Geotechnical Engineering (Applied Chemistry)Experiment Objective: To identify copper ions released from malachite through dissolution in dilute hydrochloric acid and confirm their presence by forming a blue copper–ammonia complex with ammonia water.II. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube on the rack and wear safety goggles.2. Sample Addition: Add a small amount of malachite powder into the test tube.3. Acid Dissolution: Using a dropper, add 2 drops of dilute hydrochloric acid into the test tube. Gently shake the test tube to promote dissolution until the green solid largely disappears and a blue-green solution forms.4. Color Development: Add 3 drops of ammonia water into the solution. Gently mix and observe the color change.5. Completion: Place the test tube back on the rack for observation, then dispose of waste solution properly and clean the apparatus.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Malachite appears as a green solid powder at the bottom of the test tube.2. Summary of Experimental PrincipleMalachite reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to release copper(II) ions into solution:Cu2CO3(OH)2 + 4HCl → 2CuCl2 + CO2↑ + 3H2O.When ammonia water is added, ammonia molecules coordinate with Cu2+ ions to form the stable deep-blue tetraamminecopper(II) complex [Cu(NH3)4]2+. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Rubbery Creep of a Heated Acrylic Rod Under a Hanging WeightI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Rubbery Creep of Heated Acrylic Rod Under Constant Load2. Subject: Engineering – Materials Science & Engineering (Polymer Mechanics)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the time-dependent creep behavior of acrylic (PMMA) in the rubbery state by comparing deformation of a heated rod with an unheated control rod under identical constant loads.II. Experimental Equipment- Clear acrylic rods (2, identical dimensions)- Metal weights (2, identical mass)- Rigid support frame with hooks or clamps- Heat source (heat gun or infrared lamp)- Thermally safe stand or shield- Camera with tripod (fixed focus, time-lapse mode)- Ruler or scale marker (for visual reference)III. Experimental Procedure1. Setup: Suspend two identical clear acrylic rods vertically from a rigid support. Attach equal metal weights to the lower end of each rod, ensuring both rods are straight and freely hanging.2. Camera Fixation: Position the camera directly in front of the rods. Fix focus, framing, and exposure. Include a ruler or scale marker in the frame. Start time-lapse recording.3. Control Condition: Keep the left acrylic rod at room temperature throughout the experiment. Do not apply any heat to it.4. Heating Operation: Apply heat evenly to the right acrylic rod using a heat gun or infrared lamp, maintaining a safe distance to avoid melting or discoloration.5. Observation Period: Continue heating while recording. Allow sufficient time for visible deformation to occur in the heated rod.6. Completion: Stop heating and recording once a clear difference in elongation between the two rods is observed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both acrylic rods are the same length, clear, and undeformed under identical weights.2. During Heating: The right rod gradually elongates over time while supporting the same weight; the left rod remains nearly unchanged.3. Final State: A clear length difference is observed, with the heated right rod longer than the unheated left rod.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAcrylic is a thermoplastic polymer. When heated toward or above its glass transition temperature, polymer chain mobility increases, and the material enters a rubbery state. Under constant stress (from the hanging weight), the heated rod exhibits time-dependent viscoelastic deformation known as creep. The unheated rod remains in the glassy state, showing minimal deformation. This comparison directly illustrates the temperature dependence of polymer mechanical behavior.VI. Experimental Precautions- Do not overheat the acrylic to avoid melting or bubbling.- Ensure equal weights and identical rod dimensions.- Keep the camera fixed to allow reliable time-lapse comparison.- Use heat-resistant gloves and maintain safe distances during heating.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Gram Staining of Bacterial Smear on Glass SlideI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Gram Staining of Bacterial Smear on Glass SlideSubject: Engineering – Biomedical EngineeringExperiment Objective: To master the standard Gram staining procedure used in clinical laboratories, distinguish Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria by color under a light microscope, and understand the staining principle based on bacterial cell wall structure.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsClean glass slides; inoculating loop; bacterial culture; Bunsen burner or alcohol lamp; staining rack; crystal violet solution; Gram’s iodine solution; 95% ethanol or alcohol decolorizer; safranin solution; distilled water wash bottle; absorbent paper; light microscope; immersion oil (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Smear Preparation: Place a drop of distilled water on a clean glass slide. Using a sterile inoculating loop, transfer a small amount of bacterial culture into the water and spread evenly to form a thin smear.2. Air Drying and Heat Fixation: Allow the smear to air dry completely. Pass the slide quickly through the flame 2–3 times with the smear side up to heat-fix the bacteria.3. Primary Staining: Place the slide on a staining rack and flood the smear with crystal violet for about 1 minute. Rinse gently with distilled water.4. Mordant Treatment: Cover the smear with Gram’s iodine for about 1 minute. Rinse gently with distilled water.5. Decolorization: Hold the slide at an angle and apply alcohol dropwise for 10–20 seconds until runoff is nearly colorless. Immediately rinse with water to stop decolorization.6. Counterstaining: Flood the smear with safranin for about 30–60 seconds. Rinse gently with water and blot dry with absorbent paper.7. Microscopic Observation: Place the slide on the microscope stage. Observe first under low power, then under oil immersion if available.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitially, the smear appears colorless. After crystal violet and iodine, all bacteria appear purple. After alcohol decolorization, Gram-positive bacteria remain purple while Gram-negative bacteria become colorless. After safranin counterstaining, Gram-positive bacteria appear purple, and Gram-negative bacteria appear pink/red under the microscope.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleGram staining differentiates bacteria based on differences in cell wall structure. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan layer that retains the crystal violet–iodine complex during alcohol decolorization, remaining purple. Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane; alcohol removes the crystal violet–iodine complex, and they are subsequently counterstained red or pink by safranin.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Gram staining as a differential staining technique distinguishing Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria based on cell wall structure. Key causal transitions must be visible in correct order, with close-up views of staining steps and a final microscopic perspective to verify outcomes.

Experiment Title: Crystal Nucleation in Supersaturated Sodium Acetate Solution (Hot Ice)2. Subject: Engineering – Materials Science & Engineering3. Camera Setup: Mount the camera on a tripod facing the dish. Adjust the framing so that both the dish and the pouring path are clearly visible. Core Operation: Slowly and steadily pour the supersaturated sodium acetate solution from the clear container onto the solid sodium acetate crystal in the shallow dish. Avoid shaking or splashing during pouring.5. Observation and Recording: Continue recording as the solution contacts the crystal and crystallization occurs. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Flashlight Transmission Through Clear Quartz, Milky Quartz, and GalenaI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Light Transmission Through Quartz and Galena Samples2. Subject: Engineering – Geotechnical Engineering (Engineering Geology)3. Experiment Objective: To visually compare the light transmission and opacity characteristics of clear quartz, milky quartz, and galena by observing their interaction with a moving light source, and to understand how mineral composition and internal structure affect optical properties relevant to geological identification.II. Experimental Equipment1. Mineral samples: clear quartz (transparent), milky quartz (translucent), galena (opaque metallic luster)2. Handheld flashlight (white light, continuous beam)3. Dark tabletop or dark background surface4. Low-light indoor environment (lights dimmed or off)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the experiment on a dark tabletop in a dim room to enhance contrast. Arrange three mineral samples in a straight horizontal line: clear quartz on the left, milky quartz in the center, and galena on the right. Ensure the samples are upright and stable.2. Initial Observation: With the flashlight turned off, observe and confirm the natural appearance of the samples under ambient low light: clear quartz appears transparent, milky quartz cloudy white, and galena dark gray with metallic sheen.3. Core Operation: Turn on the handheld flashlight and position it behind the clear quartz sample at a low height, aligned with the samples. Slowly sweep the flashlight from left to right behind the three samples, keeping the distance between flashlight and samples approximately constant.4. Observation Process: Carefully observe the amount of light passing through or being blocked by each sample as the flashlight moves behind them.5. Completion: After the flashlight passes behind the galena sample, turn off the flashlight and end the experiment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Clear Quartz (Left): When the flashlight is behind clear quartz, light passes through strongly, and the sample appears bright and transparent with clear illumination on its front side.2. Milky Quartz (Center): When the flashlight moves behind milky quartz, light partially passes through. The sample glows softly but appears cloudy, with reduced brightness compared to clear quartz.3. Galena (Right): When the flashlight is behind galena, almost no light passes through. The sample appears dark, blocking the beam completely, possibly reflecting a small amount of light from its surface.4. Sequence Consistency: The changes in brightness occur sequentially from left to right, matching the flashlight movement.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the relationship between mineral internal structure and optical properties. Clear quartz has a well-ordered crystal lattice that allows light to transmit with minimal scattering, making it transparent. Milky quartz contains numerous fluid inclusions and microfractures that scatter light, resulting in translucency. Galena, composed of lead sulfide with a dense metallic crystal structure, absorbs and reflects light rather than transmitting it, making it opaque. These optical differences are important in engineering geology for mineral identification and material assessment.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Handle mineral samples carefully to avoid dropping or chipping.2. Do not shine the flashlight directly into eyes.3. Maintain a stable flashlight speed to ensure clear comparison of phenomena.

Visibility constraints: camera must clearly show front faces of samples and relative brightness changes; perspective should remain fixed to verify sequential causal transitions.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Graph Depth-First Search (DFS) DemonstrationSubject: Engineering - Computer ScienceExperiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the working process of the Depth-First Search algorithm on a simple graph, helping learners understand node visitation order, stack behavior, and the core principles of DFS through animation.II. Experimental Equipment and Environment1. Computer with animation or visualization software2. White digital canvas/background3. Predefined simple graph with 6 labeled nodes (A, B, C, D, E, F) connected by lines4. Color scheme: red (current node), blue (discovered but unprocessed nodes), gray (visited/processed nodes)5. Side panel for stack (DFS auxiliary structure) visualizationIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Open the visualization environment and display a white background. Draw a simple connected graph with 6 labeled nodes and visible edges. Place a stack visualization panel on the side.2. Initialization: Select node A as the starting node. All nodes are initially uncolored (default black outline).3. Start DFS: Highlight node A in red to indicate the start. Push node A onto the stack.4. Traversal Process: Repeatedly perform DFS steps:   a. From the current node, select an unvisited neighbor.   b. Change the neighbor node to blue to indicate discovery.   c. Push the neighbor onto the stack and move to it, changing it to red as the current node.5. Backtracking: When a node has no unvisited neighbors, mark it as visited by fading it to gray and pop it from the stack.6. Continuation: Continue the process until the stack is empty and all nodes are visited.7. Completion: All nodes should appear gray, and the stack visualization should be empty.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Six labeled nodes are visible on a white background with clear edges and no color highlighting.2. During DFS: Node A turns red first. Neighboring nodes are discovered one by one, turning blue, then red as they become the current node. The stack visualization updates synchronously.3. After Processing: Nodes with all neighbors explored gradually fade to gray, indicating completion.4. Final State: All nodes are gray, and the stack is empty, showing DFS has finished.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesDepth-First Search is a graph traversal algorithm that explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking. It uses a stack (explicit or implicit via recursion) to manage traversal order. The color changes represent node states: unvisited, discovered, currently being explored, and fully visited. This experiment visually maps algorithmic steps to observable state changes, reinforcing understanding of DFS logic and execution flow.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Depth-First Search traversal on a simple graph using visual state changes and a stack. Minimum assumptions: a static 6-node graph, DFS starting from node A, and a clear color-state mapping. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) static graph displayed; (2) node A highlighted as start; (3) neighbors discovered sequentially with stack updates; (4) backtracking with nodes fading to gray; (5) traversal ends with all nodes visited. Visibility constraints: fixed camera, clear labels, and simultaneous view of graph and stack to verify causal relationships.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Cobalt(II) Chloride Hydration Equilibrium (Pink–Blue Color Shift)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Temperature-Dependent Color Change of Cobalt(II) Chloride Solution2. Subject: Engineering – Chemical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the hydration–dehydration equilibrium of cobalt(II) chloride through reversible color changes under heating and cooling, and to visually observe the effect of temperature on chemical equilibrium.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass test tube (1), test tube rack, aqueous cobalt(II) chloride solution (moderate concentration), hot water bath (≈70–80°C), ice water bath (0–5°C), beakers for baths, lab bench, camera on tripod (fixed focus) for time-lapse recording, safety goggles and gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the camera on a tripod facing the lab bench and fix the focus and framing. Put on safety goggles and gloves. Pour cobalt(II) chloride solution into the clear test tube to about one-third of its volume and place it in the test tube rack.2. Initial Observation: Observe and record the initial color of the solution at room temperature.3. Heating Step: Place the test tube into the hot water bath, ensuring the solution level is below the bath water level. Keep it in the bath until the color change is明显.4. Cooling Step: Transfer the same test tube directly into the ice water bath and allow the solution to cool until the color change is明显.5. Alternation (Optional): Repeat the heating and cooling cycle once more to show reversibility.6. Completion: Return the test tube to the rack, stop recording, and dispose of or store the solution according to safety regulations.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The cobalt(II) chloride solution appears pink at room temperature, indicating a hydrated state.2. In Hot Water Bath: The solution gradually changes from pink to blue as temperature increases.3. In Ice Water Bath: The blue solution gradually returns to pink upon cooling.4. Reversibility: Repeated alternation between hot and ice baths results in repeatable pink–blue color shifts.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesCobalt(II) chloride exists in equilibrium between hydrated and less-hydrated forms. The pink color corresponds mainly to the hydrated complex [Co(H2O)6]2+, while the blue color corresponds to the less-hydrated or chloride-coordinated form. Heating shifts the equilibrium toward dehydration (blue), while cooling shifts it toward hydration (pink), in accordance with Le Chatelier’s principle.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Avoid direct contact with hot water and ice to prevent burns.2. Ensure the test tube is heat-resistant and handled with care.3. Do not ingest or spill cobalt(II) chloride solution; dispose of it properly after the experiment.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Water Flow Through a Tube with One Pump vs Two Identical Pumps in Series2. Subject: Engineering – Control & Automation3. Experiment Objective: To visually compare the flow characteristics and transport speed of fluid in a tube driven by one pump versus two identical pumps connected in series, and to understand how pump configuration affects pressure head and flow rate using dye tracing and time-lapse observation.II. Experimental Equipment1. Transparent flexible tubes (2 identical tubes, same length and inner diameter)2. Identical water pumps (3 units total; left branch uses 1 pump, right branch uses 2 pumps in series)3. Clear containers or reservoirs (2 identical containers for outlet collection)4. Water supply (clean, clear water)5. Liquid dye (food coloring or tracer dye, clearly visible in water)6. Syringes or droppers (for injecting dye pulses)7. Power supply and switches (to start pumps simultaneously)8. Fixed-position camera or smartphone with tripod (capable of time-lapse recording)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   a. Place two identical transparent tubes side by side, ensuring they are straight, level, and clearly visible.   b. Connect the left tube to a single pump and the right tube to two identical pumps connected in series.   c. Ensure both tubes draw water from the same type of inlet reservoir and discharge into identical clear containers.2. Camera Setup:   a. Fix the camera on a tripod directly facing both tubes and containers.   b. Adjust focus, exposure, and framing so that the entire tube length and outlets are visible.   c. Lock focus and do not change camera position during the experiment.3. System Check:   a. Fill both systems with clear water, removing air bubbles from the tubes.   b. Briefly test pumps individually to confirm normal operation, then turn them off.4. Core Operation:   a. Prepare equal volumes of dye in two syringes or droppers.   b. Start all pumps simultaneously using the same timing reference.   c. Immediately inject a short, sharp dye pulse into the inlet of each tube at the same time.5. Observation and Recording:   a. Record the experiment using time-lapse or continuous video.   b. Observe the movement of dye fronts along each tube and into the containers.6. Experiment Completion:   a. Stop the pumps after the dye reaches the outlet containers.   b. Save and label the recorded footage for comparison.   c. Drain water if necessary and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both tubes are filled with clear, colorless water; no dye is present.2. After Injection:   a. Dye pulses appear simultaneously at both inlets.   b. In the tube with two pumps in series, the dye front travels faster and reaches the outlet container earlier.   c. In the single-pump tube, the dye front moves more slowly and arrives later.3. Final State: The container fed by two pumps shows earlier and stronger coloration compared to the container fed by one pump.V. Summary of Experimental Principle1. Identical pumps connected in series increase the total pressure head applied to the fluid while maintaining similar flow path geometry.2. Higher pressure head results in greater flow velocity in the tube under comparable resistance conditions.3. The dye acts as a tracer, making differences in flow speed and transport time directly observable.4. This experiment demonstrates a core principle of fluid control systems: pump configuration directly affects system performance.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure pumps are identical and correctly oriented.2. Remove air bubbles to avoid flow disturbances.3. Inject dye pulses as simultaneously as possible.4. Keep camera focus and position fixed throughout the experiment.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Binary Tree In-order Traversal Operation DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Binary Tree In-order Traversal Operation Demonstration2. Subject: Engineering - Computer Science - Data Structures3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the in-order traversal (left-root-right) of a binary tree, helping learners understand traversal order and its correspondence to output sequences.II. Experimental Materials and EnvironmentA simple binary tree diagram with seven nodes labeled 1–7; light-colored background; animation or visualization tool capable of highlighting nodes in a bright color (e.g., red) and displaying a horizontal output list at the bottom of the screen.III. Experimental Procedure1. Initialization: Display a simple binary tree with labeled nodes (1–7) on a light background. Ensure all nodes are in a neutral color and the output list at the bottom is empty.2. Start Traversal: Begin the in-order traversal from the root node, following the rule: traverse the left subtree, visit the root, then traverse the right subtree.3. Node Visiting: Each time a node is visited, highlight it briefly using a bright color (such as a red glow).4. Output Update: Immediately after highlighting a node, append its label value to the horizontal output list at the bottom of the screen, from left to right.5. Continuation: Repeat the highlight-and-append process until all nodes have been visited according to in-order traversal.6. Completion: End the demonstration when the output list contains all node values in the correct in-order sequence.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The binary tree is static, all nodes unhighlighted, and the output list is empty.2. During Traversal: Nodes are highlighted one by one in in-order sequence; after each highlight, the corresponding value appears appended to the output list.3. Final State: All nodes have been highlighted exactly once, and the output list shows the complete in-order traversal result from left to right.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleIn-order traversal is a fundamental binary tree traversal method in computer science. Its principle is to recursively access the left subtree, then process the current node, and finally access the right subtree. This demonstration visualizes the traversal process, linking each node visit to a sequential output, thereby clarifying how tree structure determines traversal order.VI. NotesEnsure the highlighting order strictly follows left-root-right logic. The glow and output update should be synchronized to reinforce causal understanding.

Visibility Constraints: Tree structure, node labels, highlight color, and output list must remain clearly visible and stable throughout for verification.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visualization of Global and Local Extrema of a Univariate Function2. Subject: Engineering – Scientific Computing3. Knowledge Point: Visualization of Global and Local Extrema for Univariate Functions4. Experiment Objective: Through graphical visualization, understand the concepts of global minimum and local maximum of a univariate function, master the method of using coordinate systems to analyze function behavior, and visually identify extrema based on calculus principles.II. Experimental Environment and Tools1. Computer with scientific computing or plotting software (e.g., MATLAB, Python with Matplotlib, or equivalent visualization tool)2. Display screen with white background3. Coordinate plotting module supporting custom axis ranges and point annotationsIII. Experimental Procedure1. Coordinate System Setup: Open the plotting software and create a two-dimensional Cartesian coordinate system. Set the x-axis range to [-3, 3] and the y-axis range to [-5, 5]. Ensure the background is white and axes are clearly labeled.2. Function Definition: Define the univariate function y = x^3 - 3x + 1 within the software.3. Curve Plotting: Plot the function over the interval x ∈ [-3, 3]. Adjust resolution to ensure the curve is smooth with no jagged edges. Set the curve color to blue.4. Extrema Calculation: Compute the derivative y" = 3x^2 - 3 and solve y" = 0 to obtain critical points x = -1 and x = 1. Evaluate the function values at these points.5. Marking Extrema: Identify x = -1 as the local maximum and x = 1 as the global minimum within the displayed interval. Mark the local maximum with an orange solid dot and label its coordinates. Mark the global minimum with a red solid dot and label its coordinates.6. Final Display Check: Ensure all elements (axes, curve, colored markers, coordinate labels) are clearly visible and correctly positioned.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The coordinate system appears on a white background with x-axis ranging from -3 to 3 and y-axis ranging from -5 to 5.2. A smooth blue cubic curve representing y = x^3 - 3x + 1 is displayed without jagged edges.3. The curve rises to a peak at x = -1, where an orange solid dot marks the local maximum with its coordinates.4. The curve descends to a valley at x = 1, where a red solid dot marks the global minimum with its coordinates.5. The relative positions of the extrema visually match the analytical results.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Mathematical Principle: For a univariate differentiable function, extrema occur at critical points where the first derivative equals zero or is undefined.2. Calculus Basis: By computing the first derivative of y = x^3 - 3x + 1 and solving y" = 0, the critical points x = -1 and x = 1 are obtained.3. Extrema Identification: The nature of extrema is determined by the function behavior around critical points. Within the given interval, x = -1 corresponds to a local maximum, while x = 1 corresponds to a global minimum.4. Visualization Significance: Graphical visualization provides an intuitive and reliable way to verify analytical results and understand global versus local behavior of functions.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Comparison of Insulated vs Uninsulated Hot Side in Identical Stirling EnginesSubject: Engineering – Energy EngineeringObjective: To demonstrate how thermal insulation on the hot side of a Stirling engine affects start-up time and operating speed by reducing heat loss and increasing effective temperature difference.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical tabletop Stirling engines; thermal insulation sleeve or wrap (heat-resistant) for one hot cylinder; two identical alcohol or gas burners; ignition source; heat-resistant base; camera on tripod with fixed focus (time-lapse capable).III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place the two identical Stirling engines side by side on a heat-resistant surface. Install insulation only on the left engine’s hot cylinder; keep the right engine’s hot cylinder bare. Ensure both engines are initially at rest.Camera Setup: Position the camera facing both engines, frame them symmetrically, fix focus and exposure, and enable time-lapse or continuous recording.Heating Operation: Place identical burners beneath the hot side of each engine at equal distances.
