manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Water Flow over Sand in a Shallow Clear Flume Forming Asymmetric RipplesI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Formation of Asymmetric Sand Ripples under Unidirectional Flow2. Subject: Engineering – Geotechnical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the formation and migration of asymmetric sand ripples caused by steady unidirectional water flow over a loose sand bed, and to relate the observed bedforms to sediment transport mechanisms.II. Experimental EquipmentShallow clear flume (transparent sides and base), fine uniform sand (dry, loose), water supply with flow control valve, flow straightener (optional), leveling tools, ruler or scale, camera with tripod (fixed focus), lighting source (uniform), stopwatch or timer.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Level the flume horizontally. Spread a uniform layer of loose sand on the flume bottom and carefully level it to form a flat bed without pre-existing ripples.2. Initial Setup: Fill the flume slowly with clear water to a shallow depth, ensuring the sand bed is not disturbed. Allow water to become still.3. Camera Setup: Position the camera perpendicular to the flume side, fix focus and framing to include the entire sand bed region of interest, and set time-lapse or continuous recording.4. Flow Initiation: Gradually start the water flow and adjust the valve to obtain a steady, uniform, unidirectional flow over the sand bed.5. Core Observation Stage: Maintain constant flow conditions. Allow water to flow continuously while recording. Do not disturb the flume during the experiment.6. Completion: After clear ripple patterns have formed and migrated, stop the flow gradually. Save the recorded footage for analysis.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The sand bed is flat and smooth, with no visible bedforms.2. Early Stage: Individual sand grains begin to move intermittently; small undulations appear on the bed surface.3. Development Stage: Undulations grow into distinct asymmetric ripples with a gentle upstream slope (stoss side) and a steeper downstream slope (lee side).4. Migration Stage: Ripples migrate slowly in the downstream direction while maintaining their asymmetric shape.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates sediment transport and bedform development under flowing water. When unidirectional flow exerts shear stress on a loose sand bed, sand grains are entrained and transported. Deposition and erosion occur unevenly, leading to the growth of asymmetric ripples. The gentle stoss slope forms where particles are pushed upward by flow, while the steep lee slope forms due to grain avalanching. Ripple migration occurs as erosion on the upstream side and deposition on the downstream side continue under steady flow conditions.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure flow is increased gradually to avoid scouring the bed. Maintain constant discharge during observation. Avoid vibrations or disturbances to the flume and camera. Ensure clear water and uniform lighting for accurate visual recording.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Iodine Solution Partitioning into Oil versus WaterI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Partitioning of Iodine between Oil and Water2. Subject: Engineering - Biomedical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the differential solubility and partitioning behavior of iodine between polar (water) and nonpolar (oil) phases, and to demonstrate how shaking affects solute distribution and phase separation, with emphasis on visual observation suitable for time-lapse photography.II. Experimental Equipment1. Transparent glass vial with a screw cap (1 vial, approximately 10–20 mL volume)2. Distilled water (colorless, transparent)3. Vegetable oil or mineral oil (colorless to pale yellow, immiscible with water)4. Iodine solution (aqueous iodine-potassium iodide solution, brown in color)5. Dropper or pipette6. Camera or smartphone mounted on a stable tripod (for time-lapse recording)7. Lab bench or flat surface with uniform lightingIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   a. Place the clean, dry glass vial upright on the lab bench.   b. Add distilled water to the vial until it fills approximately half of the vial volume.   c. Slowly add oil along the inner wall of the vial until a clear oil layer forms above the water layer. Do not shake; allow the two layers to stabilize.2. Addition of Iodine Solution:   a. Using a dropper, add 2–3 drops of brown iodine solution into the vial.   b. Observe briefly as the iodine initially enters the water layer, giving it a light brown coloration.3. Shaking Operation:   a. Tightly cap the vial to prevent leakage.   b. Gently but thoroughly shake the vial for 5–10 seconds to allow iodine to contact both oil and water phases.4. Phase Separation and Recording:   a. Place the vial upright on a stable, flat surface.   b. Fix the camera focus and position; ensure the entire vial is clearly visible.   c. Start time-lapse photography or continuous recording.   d. Allow the vial to stand undisturbed while the oil and water layers gradually separate.5. Completion:   a. After clear separation is observed, stop recording.   b. Dispose of the solution according to laboratory safety guidelines and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Two distinct, colorless layers are visible, with oil on top and water at the bottom.2. After Adding Iodine (Before Shaking): The water layer becomes light brown, while the oil layer remains nearly colorless.3. Immediately After Shaking: The entire liquid appears uniformly brown and cloudy due to dispersion of iodine between phases.4. During Standing and Separation: Two layers reappear; the upper oil layer gradually turns a deeper brown or purple-brown, while the lower water layer becomes lighter in color.5. Final State: A clear phase boundary is visible, with iodine predominantly concentrated in the oil layer.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Core Principle: Iodine is a nonpolar or weakly polar substance that preferentially dissolves in nonpolar solvents (oil) rather than polar solvents (water).2. Partitioning Mechanism: When shaken, iodine temporarily distributes between both phases. Upon standing, thermodynamic equilibrium drives iodine to partition preferentially into the oil phase.3. Biomedical Engineering Relevance: This experiment models liquid–liquid extraction and partition coefficients, which are fundamental concepts in drug delivery, pharmacokinetics, and biomedical separation processes.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the vial is tightly capped before shaking to prevent leakage.2. Shake gently to avoid forming persistent emulsions.3. Maintain consistent lighting and fixed camera focus to ensure clear time-lapse observation.4. Handle iodine solution carefully, as it can stain skin and surfaces.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Liquid–liquid partitioning of iodine between polar water and nonpolar oil. Minimum assumptions: oil and water are immiscible, iodine preferentially dissolves in oil, shaking increases contact, and standing allows gravity-driven phase separation.Phased storyline: (1) Initial setup shows a transparent vial with oil clearly layered above water. (2) Brown iodine solution is added, initially coloring the water. (3) The vial is capped and shaken, causing temporary uniform coloration. (4) The vial is set down; over time, layers re-form. (5) Final state shows a darker brown oil layer above a lighter water layer. Visibility constraints: the camera must remain fixed, the entire vial must stay in frame, and the phase boundary and color changes must be clearly visible for verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Selection Sort Algorithm Execution Process DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Selection Sort Algorithm Execution Process DemonstrationSubject: Engineering - Computer ScienceExperiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the execution process of the Selection Sort algorithm, helping learners understand how the algorithm repeatedly selects the minimum element from the unsorted portion of an array and places it in the correct position.II. Experimental MaterialsWhite background canvas; a horizontal array of numbered bars representing integers (example array: [5, 3, 4, 1, 2]); visual markers such as color highlights for current index, minimum value, and sorted portion.III. Experimental Procedure1. Initial Setup: Display a clean white background with a horizontal array of vertical bars labeled [5, 3, 4, 1, 2]. All bars start in a neutral color.2. First Pass: Highlight the first bar as the current position. Scan the remaining bars to the right, highlighting the currently compared bar and updating the highlighted minimum when a smaller value is found.3. First Swap: After reaching the end of the array, swap the minimum bar found with the bar at the current position. Mark the first position as sorted.4. Subsequent Passes: Move the current position one step to the right and repeat the process on the remaining unsorted portion: scan, identify the minimum, and swap.5. Completion: Continue until all bars are sorted in ascending order. Display the final sorted array.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Bars appear unsorted in a horizontal line on a white background.During Sorting: One bar is fixed as the current position, another indicates the current minimum, and comparisons proceed left to right; swaps occur after each scan.Final State: Bars are arranged in ascending order, and all are marked as sorted.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSelection Sort works by dividing the array into a sorted and an unsorted region. In each iteration, the algorithm selects the minimum element from the unsorted region and swaps it with the first element of that region. This process repeats until the entire array is sorted. The algorithm emphasizes comparison-based sorting and has a time complexity of O(n^2).VI. NotesFor short demonstration videos (around 10 seconds), scanning and swapping actions should be visually accelerated while maintaining correct order and logic.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Milling a Metal Block with a Rotating Cutter (Time-Lapse Demonstration)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Milling a Metal Block with a Rotating Cutter2. Subject: Engineering – Mechanical Engineering (Manufacturing Processes)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the basic milling process in which a rotating milling cutter removes chips from a metal block clamped on a milling table, and to observe material removal through repeated lateral passes using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentVertical milling machine, end mill or face mill, metal block (e.g., aluminum or mild steel), machine vise or clamps, milling table with feed control, cutting fluid (optional), safety goggles, fixed camera mounted on tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear safety goggles. Clean the milling table and metal block. Securely clamp the metal block in a vise on the milling table, ensuring it is rigid and level.2. Tool Setup: Install the milling cutter in the spindle and check that it is properly tightened. Set an appropriate spindle speed for the material.3. Camera Setup: Position the camera to clearly view the cutter, metal block, and table motion. Fix focus, exposure, and framing. Start time-lapse recording.4. Initial Positioning: Lower the rotating cutter to lightly touch the top surface of the metal block, then set the cutting depth.5. Core Operation: Start the spindle. Engage the table feed so the milling table moves laterally, allowing the rotating cutter to remove material and generate chips.6. Repeated Passes: After one pass, retract slightly, return the table, adjust depth if needed, and perform additional lateral passes across the surface.7. Completion: Stop the feed and spindle. Stop the camera recording. Remove chips and power down the machine.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The metal block has a rough, unmachined surface; the cutter is stationary.2. During Milling: As the cutter rotates and moves laterally, metallic chips are produced and ejected; a clear cutting sound is heard; the surface behind the cutter appears smoother.3. After Repeated Passes: The top surface becomes progressively flatter and more uniform, with visible tool marks aligned with the feed direction.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesMilling is a machining process in which a multi-edge rotating cutter removes material from a stationary workpiece through relative motion. The cutter rotation provides cutting speed, while the lateral movement of the table provides feed. Material is removed in the form of chips due to shear deformation when cutting edges exceed the material’s shear strength. Repeated passes improve dimensional accuracy and surface finish.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the workpiece is firmly clamped. Do not change camera focus during recording. Keep hands away from rotating parts. Remove chips only after the machine stops.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Paper Airplane Gliding vs Stalling at Different Launch AnglesI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Paper Airplane Gliding vs Stalling at Different Launch Angles2. Subject: Engineering – Aerospace Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe how launch angle affects the flight distance of a paper airplane, and to understand the aerodynamic principles of lift, glide, and stall by comparing flights at small and large launch angles.II. Experimental Equipment1. Two identical paper airplanes (same paper, same fold design)2. Open indoor space or calm outdoor area3. Marked launch point and level ground4. Fixed camera or smartphone on tripod (time-lapse mode)5. Measuring tape or floor markers (optional)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fold two identical paper airplanes. Choose a launch point at a fixed height (e.g., shoulder height). Set the camera on a tripod facing the flight area and fix the focus and framing.2. Camera Setup: Enable time-lapse or continuous shooting. Ensure the entire flight path and landing area are within the frame.3. Small-Angle Launch: Hold the first airplane at the launch point. Throw it forward with a small upward angle relative to the horizontal, using moderate and steady force.4. Observation: Allow the airplane to complete its flight and land. Do not move the camera.5. Large-Angle Launch: From the same position and height, throw the second identical airplane with a much larger upward angle, using similar force.6. Completion: Let the airplane land. Stop the camera recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Small-Angle Launch: The paper airplane travels forward smoothly, maintains a stable glide, descends gradually, and covers a longer horizontal distance.2. Large-Angle Launch: The paper airplane climbs steeply, slows down, then pitches downward abruptly, showing a stall, and lands after a shorter horizontal distance.3. Time-Lapse Result: The flight paths clearly differ in shape and length when viewed in the time-lapse images.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Lift and Glide: At a small launch angle, airflow over the wings produces sufficient lift with low drag, allowing a long, stable glide.2. Stall at Large Angle: At a large launch angle, the angle of attack becomes too high, airflow separates from the wing surface, lift decreases sharply, and the airplane stalls.3. Conclusion: For identical paper airplanes launched with similar force from the same height, a smaller launch angle generally produces a longer flight distance than a larger launch angle due to more efficient aerodynamic lift and reduced stall.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both airplanes are identical to control variables.2. Use similar throwing force for both launches.3. Perform the experiment in still air to reduce environmental interference.4. Keep the camera fixed to ensure valid visual comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Ripple Marks Forming in a Shallow Sand Tray Under Flowing WaterI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Ripple Marks Forming in a Shallow Sand Tray Under Flowing Water2. Subject: Engineering – Geotechnical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how flowing water over loose sediment generates ripple marks, and to understand the relationship between flow, shear stress, and sediment transport through visual time-lapse observation.II. Experimental EquipmentShallow rectangular tray; fine, uniform sand; clean water supply; water inlet device (hose, tube, or small channel); outlet or overflow control; stable support table; camera or smartphone with tripod; adequate lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the shallow tray on a level table. Spread fine sand evenly across the bottom to form a flat sand bed with uniform thickness. Slowly add water until the sand is just submerged, avoiding disturbance of the surface.2. Setup: Position the water inlet at one end of the tray so water can enter smoothly and flow across the sand surface toward the opposite end. Adjust the outlet or tray tilt so excess water can exit without raising the water level significantly.3. Camera Arrangement: Fix the camera directly above or at a low oblique angle to clearly capture the sand surface. Lock focus, exposure, and framing for time-lapse recording.4. Core Operation: Start a steady, continuous flow of water from the inlet. Maintain a constant flow rate for several minutes so that water moves uniformly across the sand surface.5. Observation and Recording: Record the process using time-lapse or accelerated video, capturing gradual changes in the sand bed.6. Completion: Stop the water flow after clear ripple marks have formed. Save the recorded video and drain the tray if required.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The sand surface is smooth and flat beneath shallow, clear water.2. Early Stage: Small irregular disturbances appear on the sand surface as water begins to flow.3. Development Stage: Disturbances organize into regular ripple marks, typically oriented perpendicular to the flow direction.4. Stabilization Stage: Ripple spacing and height become relatively uniform, and ripples may slowly migrate downstream.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesFlowing water exerts shear stress on the sand bed. When this stress exceeds the critical threshold for particle movement, sand grains are entrained and redeposited. Small perturbations grow due to feedback between flow velocity and sediment transport, forming ripple marks. This process illustrates fundamental sediment transport and bedform development principles in geotechnical and hydraulic engineering.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure uniform sand grain size; maintain a steady flow rate; avoid disturbing the tray during recording; keep camera settings fixed for clear time-lapse comparison.

Minimum assumptions include a shallow tray, fine loose sand, and a steady unidirectional water flow sufficient to mobilize grains.Phased storyline: (1) Setup phase shows a flat sand bed under shallow water with a fixed camera view. (2) Flow initiation introduces steady water from one end, with no abrupt level changes. (3) Early interaction phase shows subtle sand movement. (4) Formation phase reveals organized ripple marks emerging perpendicular to flow. (5) Stabilization phase shows mature ripples with slight downstream migration. Visibility constraints: camera must continuously capture the same sand surface area; time-lapse acceleration is acceptable as long as causal order is preserved.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Metal Spring Stretched by Sequentially Added Identical WeightsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Metal Spring Stretched by Sequentially Added Identical Weights2. Subject: Engineering – Structural Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe the elastic deformation of a metal spring under gradually applied and removed loads, verify the relationship between load and extension, and demonstrate basic elastic behavior relevant to structural engineering.II. Experimental EquipmentMetal helical spring (elastic, undeformed initially), fixed rigid support or stand, identical weights (multiple, same mass and shape), hook or hanger for weights, ruler or scale (optional, for reference), camera on tripod with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Secure the rigid support on a stable surface. Hang the metal spring vertically from the support, ensuring it is free to extend downward. Position the camera facing the spring and lock focus and framing.2. Initial State Recording: Record the spring without any added weight, showing its natural length.3. Stepwise Loading: Add one identical weight to the bottom of the spring. Pause briefly to allow the spring to come to rest. Continue adding identical weights one by one, each time pausing after addition.4. Maximum Load State: After the final weight is added, record the fully extended but elastic state of the spring.5. Stepwise Unloading: Remove the weights one by one in the reverse order, pausing after each removal to observe the spring shortening.6. End State: Record the spring after all weights are removed, returning close to its original length.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The spring hangs vertically with minimal extension.2. During Loading: With each added identical weight, the spring extends downward by an additional amount. The extension increases stepwise and remains stable during pauses.3. Maximum Load: The spring reaches its greatest extension while remaining intact and elastic.4. During Unloading: As weights are removed one by one, the spring shortens stepwise.5. Final State: After all weights are removed, the spring approximately returns to its original length.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates elastic deformation and Hooke’s law. Within the elastic limit of the metal spring, the extension of the spring is proportional to the applied force (weight). Adding identical weights increases the force in equal increments, resulting in approximately equal increments of extension. Removing the weights reverses the process, showing elastic recovery. This principle underlies load–deformation analysis in structural engineering.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Elastic deformation of a metal spring under incremental loading, assuming a vertical setup, identical discrete loads, and elastic behavior within limits. Minimum assumptions include gravity acting downward, a fixed support, and a spring obeying Hooke’s law qualitatively. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) initial unstressed spring at rest; (2) sequential addition of identical weights causes stepwise downward extension, each followed by a brief static pause; (3) maximum extension under full load; (4) sequential removal of weights causes stepwise shortening; (5) near-return to original length. Visibility constraints: the entire spring, weights, and support must remain in frame with a fixed camera perspective to verify order, proportional extension, and causal relationships.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Simulation Experiment of Sand Slope Reinforcement with GeogridsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Simulation Experiment of Sand Slope Reinforcement with Geogrids2. Subject: Engineering - Geotechnical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the reinforcement effect of geogrids on sand slopes by comparing the stability and collapse behavior of a reinforced and an unreinforced sand slope under water infiltration.II. Experimental EquipmentSand platforms (2, identical size), dry sand, geogrid material (plastic mesh or similar), water container or watering can, ruler or scraper (for shaping slopes), collection tray (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two sand platforms side by side on a flat surface. Pour dry sand onto each platform and shape it into two identical sand slopes with similar height and inclination.2. Reinforcement Setup: Cover the surface of one sand slope evenly with a geogrid, ensuring close contact between the geogrid and the sand surface. Leave the other sand slope uncovered as a control.3. Initial Observation: Observe and record the initial shape and stability of both slopes before water application.4. Core Operation: Simultaneously pour water slowly and evenly from the top of both sand slopes, keeping the water flow rate approximately the same.5. Observation: Continuously observe the deformation, erosion, and collapse process of both slopes during water infiltration.6. Completion: Stop pouring water after clear differences in slope behavior are observed. Record final states of both slopes.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both sand slopes maintain stable shapes with clear slope surfaces.2. During Water Pouring: The unreinforced sand slope shows rapid surface erosion, sand sliding, and partial or complete collapse. The reinforced slope shows limited deformation, with sand largely retained by the geogrid.3. Final State: The unreinforced slope is significantly flattened or collapsed, while the geogrid-reinforced slope remains relatively intact with minor erosion.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the principle of soil reinforcement in geotechnical engineering. Water infiltration reduces the shear strength of sand by increasing pore water pressure and decreasing inter-particle friction. In the unreinforced slope, this leads to rapid instability and collapse. The geogrid in the reinforced slope provides tensile resistance and interlocking with sand particles, redistributing stresses and restricting deformation, thereby significantly improving slope stability.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both slopes have similar geometry and sand quantity for fair comparison.2. Pour water evenly and simultaneously to maintain consistent experimental conditions.3. Avoid excessive water flow that may obscure the observation of gradual collapse behavior.

Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how axial compression reduces the stability of a slender member and how a steady lateral force can induce bending and buckling-like deformation in a foam or rubber beam; to visually observe deformation evolution using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental Equipment1. Foam or rubber beam (uniform cross-section, straight, elastic)2. Two rigid flat plates (metal or thick acrylic) for axial compression3. Support frame or table7. Camera or smartphone with tripod (time-lapse capable)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the foam or rubber beam horizontally between two parallel flat plates on a stable table. Align the beam so its longitudinal axis is straight.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera perpendicular to the beam’s side, ensuring the full length and midspan are visible. Fix the focus and exposure; enable time-lapse mode.3. Axial Compression: Gradually move the plates toward each other using clamps or a screw press, applying a small but visible lengthwise compressive force to the beam. Do not release this compression during the experiment.4. Lateral Force Setup: Tie the cord around the beam at midspan. Route the cord perpendicular to the beam axis.5. Core Operation: Apply a steady sideways force by gently pulling the cord or attaching a small constant weight. Maintain constant compression and lateral force.6. Observation Phase: Allow the beam to deform while the camera records. Do not change camera focus or viewpoint.7. Completion: After sufficient deformation is observed, stop recording, slowly release the lateral force, then release the axial compression.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Deformation Development: Under combined compression and lateral force, bending becomes more pronounced, often forming a smooth curved shape; deformation increases gradually over time.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates a fundamental concept in structural engineering: axial compression reduces the stability of slender members. When a compressed beam is subjected to a lateral force, even a small sideways load can cause significant bending or buckling-like deformation. Foam or rubber is used because its low stiffness allows large, visible deformations at low forces, making the instability process easy to observe.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Apply compression gradually to avoid sudden collapse.2. Ensure the lateral force is steady and constant.3. Keep camera focus fixed to ensure reliable time-lapse comparison.4. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Ripple Marks Forming in Sand under Unidirectional Water FlowI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Ripple Marks Forming in Sand under Unidirectional Water Flow2. Subject: Engineering - Geotechnical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the formation of ripple marks on a fine-sand bed under steady unidirectional water flow, and to relate bedform geometry to flow-induced sediment transport mechanisms.II. Experimental EquipmentClear flume tank with adjustable inlet and outlet, water circulation pump or constant-head tank, fine uniform sand (light-colored, grain size ~0.1–0.3 mm), leveling spatula or straightedge, flow control valve, ruler or scale (optional), lighting for clear observation.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Clean the flume tank. Evenly spread a thin layer (5–10 mm) of fine sand along the flume bottom and level it carefully to create a flat initial bed.2. Filling: Slowly introduce water into the flume from downstream to upstream to avoid disturbing the sand bed until the bed is fully submerged.3. Flow Setup: Start the pump or open the inlet valve gradually. Adjust the valve to establish a steady, unidirectional current along the flume length.4. Core Operation: Maintain a constant flow rate. Do not touch or disturb the sand bed during the run.5. Observation: Observe the sand surface continuously as the flow persists, focusing on the initiation of grain motion and the emergence of bedforms.6. Termination: After clear ripple marks have formed, slowly reduce the flow and stop the pump. Drain water carefully if needed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The sand bed is flat and smooth under still water.2. Early Stage: With flow initiation, individual sand grains begin to move, and small irregular undulations appear on the bed.3. Development Stage: Undulations grow into regular ripple marks with asymmetric shapes: a gentle upstream (stoss) slope and a steeper downstream (lee) slope.4. Mature Stage: Ripple marks become evenly spaced and may slowly migrate downstream with continued flow.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesUnder steady unidirectional flow, shear stress exerted by moving water mobilizes sand grains once a critical threshold is exceeded. Small perturbations on the bed grow due to feedback between flow velocity and sediment transport. Erosion occurs on the stoss side, while deposition occurs on the lee side, producing asymmetric ripple marks that migrate in the flow direction. This demonstrates fundamental sediment transport and bedform development principles in fluvial environments.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure flow is increased gradually to avoid washing out the sand bed; maintain constant discharge during observation; use uniform fine sand for clear ripple formation; avoid vibrations or disturbances to the flume during the experiment.

Visibility should focus on a side or top-oblique view of the sand bed to verify ripple geometry and causal progression.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Two Different-Sized Syringes Connected by a Fluid-Filled Tube Lifting a WeightI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Demonstration of Hydraulic Pressure Transmission Using Two Syringes2. Subject: Engineering – Aerospace Engineering (Fluid Mechanics Fundamentals)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate Pascal’s principle by observing how pressure applied to a small syringe is transmitted through an incompressible fluid to a larger syringe, enabling it to lift a weight.II. Experimental EquipmentSmall syringe (without needle), large syringe (without needle), transparent flexible tube (filled completely with water or hydraulic oil), clamp or stand (optional), small weight (e.g., metal block), flat support surface, camera with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fill both syringes and the connecting tube completely with fluid, ensuring no air bubbles remain. Connect the small and large syringes firmly with the tube.2. Setup: Place the large syringe vertically with its plunger facing upward. Carefully place the weight on top of the large syringe plunger so it rests stably.3. Camera Setup: Position the camera facing the syringes. Fix the focus and keep the framing unchanged to allow time-lapse photography.4. Core Operation: Use a hand to slowly press down the plunger of the smaller syringe. Maintain steady pressure for a moment, then gradually release the plunger.5. Repeatability: Press and release the smaller syringe once or twice to clearly show the lifting and lowering motion of the weighted plunger.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both plungers are stationary; the weight rests on the large plunger.2. During Pressing: As the small syringe plunger is pressed, the plunger of the large syringe moves upward, lifting the weight.3. During Releasing: When the small syringe plunger is released, the large plunger moves downward and the weight descends smoothly.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on Pascal’s principle, which states that pressure applied to a confined incompressible fluid is transmitted equally in all directions. When force is applied to the small syringe, it creates pressure in the fluid. The same pressure acts on the larger syringe plunger. Because the larger plunger has a greater cross-sectional area, it produces a larger output force, allowing it to lift a weight even though the input force is applied by hand on the smaller syringe.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure there are no air bubbles in the system, as air will reduce pressure transmission efficiency.2. Press the syringe slowly to avoid sudden fluid leakage or tube detachment.3. Secure the weight to prevent slipping during lifting.4. Keep the camera fixed to maintain consistent visual reference.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Second-Order Tensor Field Ellipsoid Visualization (Stress Field)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Second-Order Tensor Field Ellipsoid Visualization of a Stress Field2. Subject: Engineering – Scientific Computing3. Experiment Objective: To visualize a 3D spatial stress tensor field using ellipsoids, understand how second-order tensors are represented by eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and interpret stress state, principal directions, and magnitude through shape and color mapping.II. Experimental Environment and Tools1. Computer with GPU support2. Scientific visualization software or programming environment (e.g., Python with NumPy and VTK/Matplotlib, or MATLAB)3. Predefined 3D stress tensor field dataset or analytical stress field function4. 3D rendering window with camera controlIII. Experimental Procedure1. Data Preparation: Load or define a 3D spatial grid and assign a symmetric second-order stress tensor to each grid point.2. Tensor Decomposition: For each tensor, compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors to obtain principal stresses and directions.3. Ellipsoid Construction: At each grid point, generate an ellipsoid whose three principal axes align with eigenvectors; scale axis lengths proportionally to the absolute values of eigenvalues.4. Color Mapping: Assign red color to ellipsoids dominated by tensile (positive) principal stress and blue color to ellipsoids dominated by compressive (negative) principal stress.5. Spatial Arrangement: Place ellipsoids evenly throughout the 3D domain, adjusting sampling density to avoid overlap.6. Rendering and Annotation: Render the 3D scene; add a visible text annotation Ellipsoid: Tensor Feature Visualization; enable basic lighting and a fixed or slowly rotating camera.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The screen displays a 3D spatial field filled with ellipsoids.2. Red ellipsoids indicate tensile stress regions, while blue ellipsoids indicate compressive stress regions.3. The long axis of each ellipsoid aligns with the principal stress direction.4. The ratio of long to short axes varies, reflecting differences in principal stress magnitude.5. Ellipsoids are evenly distributed in space and do not overlap.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on the mathematical representation of a second-order stress tensor. A symmetric tensor can be diagonalized into principal stresses (eigenvalues) and principal directions (eigenvectors). By mapping eigenvectors to ellipsoid orientations and eigenvalues to axis lengths, tensor properties become visually interpretable. Color encoding further distinguishes tensile and compressive stress states, enabling intuitive analysis of complex 3D stress fields.VI. Notes and Precautions1. Ensure tensors are symmetric to allow physical interpretation.2. Control ellipsoid scaling to prevent overlap.3. Maintain consistent color mapping for correct stress sign interpretation.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Water Droplet on Increasingly Hot Metal Surface Showing Nucleate to Film BoilingI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Water Droplet on Increasingly Hot Metal Surface Showing Nucleate to Film Boiling2. Subject: Engineering – Nuclear Engineering (Heat Transfer)3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the change of boiling regimes of water on a heated metal surface as temperature increases, and to understand nucleate boiling, transition boiling, and film boiling (Leidenfrost effect).II. Experimental EquipmentMetal plate with smooth surface (stainless steel or aluminum), electric heating element or hot plate with adjustable power, thermometer or thermocouple (optional), dropper or pipette, distilled water, heat-resistant gloves, camera with tripod (fixed focus), safety goggles.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Clean and dry the metal plate to remove oil and dust. Place the plate flat on the heating element. Set up the camera on a tripod above or at an angle to the plate, fix the focus and framing for time-lapse recording.Heating: Turn on the heating element and gradually increase the temperature at a steady rate. Allow the plate to cool before cleaning and storing equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaLow temperature: Droplets spread slightly and evaporate slowly, with small bubbles forming at the contact surface (nucleate boiling).Medium temperature: Droplets evaporate rapidly with vigorous bubbling and audible sizzling (transition boiling).High temperature: Droplets bead up, levitate, and move on a vapor layer, lasting longer before evaporating (film boiling or Leidenfrost effect).V. Experiment Objective: To understand the basic principle of an array deduplication algorithm by visually demonstrating how duplicate elements are detected, marked, removed, and how the array is compacted step by step.II. The final displayed array contains only unique elements, with no red slashes remaining.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the core principle of an array deduplication algorithm. By sequentially traversing the array and comparing each element with previously retained elements, duplicates can be identified. Marking highlights redundant data, while removal and left-shifting illustrate in-place compaction. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Pendulum Motion in Air and in Viscous Fluid2. Subject: Engineering – Structural Engineering (Dynamics)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the effect of damping on oscillatory motion by comparing two identical pendulums released simultaneously from the same angle, one swinging freely in air and the other submerged in a viscous fluid (thick oil). Through visual comparison, understand how viscous resistance dissipates mechanical energy and reduces oscillation amplitude over time.II. Experimental Equipment- Identical pendulum bobs (2) with equal mass and shape- Identical strings or rods of equal length (2)- Rigid support frame or stand allowing side-by-side suspension- Transparent container (1), large enough to fully submerge a pendulum- Thick, transparent oil (e.g., glycerin or mineral oil)- Angle marker or protractor (optional, for consistent release angle)- Clamp or holder for fixing the containerIII. Experimental Procedure1. Setup: Secure the support frame on a stable surface. Suspend two identical pendulums side by side from the same height using strings of equal length. Ensure both pendulums can swing freely without interference.2. Fluid Preparation: Place the transparent container beneath one pendulum and fill it with thick oil until the pendulum bob is fully submerged when at rest. Ensure the oil is still, without visible flow.3. Initial Positioning: Pull both pendulums to the same initial angle relative to the vertical (using an angle marker if available). Hold them steady so that both are aligned and at rest.4. Simultaneous Release: Release both pendulums at the same time without giving any additional push.5. Observation Period: Allow both pendulums to swing freely while observing their motion side by side for several oscillations.6. Completion: Continue observation until the pendulum in oil shows明显 reduction in amplitude or nearly comes to rest, then stop the experiment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: At the moment of release, both pendulums start swinging from the same angle with similar initial motion.2. Early Motion: The pendulum in air continues oscillating with relatively large amplitude, while the pendulum in oil immediately shows slower motion.3. Over Time: The amplitude of the pendulum in oil decreases rapidly with each swing, and its motion becomes heavily damped. The pendulum in air also loses amplitude but at a much slower rate.4. Final State: After a short time, the pendulum in oil nearly stops oscillating, while the pendulum in air continues swinging for a longer duration.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates damping in oscillatory systems. A pendulum swinging in air experiences small resistive forces (air resistance), so its mechanical energy is lost slowly. When the pendulum is submerged in a viscous fluid, it experiences a much larger resistive (viscous damping) force proportional to its velocity. This force converts mechanical energy into thermal energy within the fluid, causing rapid energy dissipation. As a result, the amplitude of oscillation decreases more quickly in the viscous fluid than in air. This principle is fundamental in structural engineering for understanding vibration control and energy dissipation mechanisms in structures.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both pendulums are identical in length and mass to guarantee a fair comparison.2. Release both pendulums simultaneously without extra force.3. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Edge-Triggered D Flip-Flop Driving an LEDI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Edge-Triggered D Flip-Flop Driving an LED2. Subject: Engineering – Electrical Engineering (Digital Electronics)3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the working principle of an edge-triggered D flip-flop by using a pulse generator as the clock source and an LED as the output indicator; to verify that the output updates only on the active clock edge and follows the D input; to observe the effect of changing clock frequency on output behavior.II. Experimental EquipmentEdge-triggered D flip-flop IC (e.g., 74HC74 or equivalent), breadboard, LED (with current-limiting resistor), pulse/signal generator, DC power supply (5 V), toggle switch or jumper for D input, connecting wires, oscilloscope (optional), lab bench, camera with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the breadboard on the lab bench. Power off all equipment. Fix the camera position and focus to cover the entire setup for time-lapse photography.2. Circuit Setup: Insert the D flip-flop IC into the breadboard. Connect VCC and GND to the power supply. Connect the Q output to an LED in series with a resistor to ground. Connect the clock input (CLK) to the output of the pulse generator. Connect the D input to a toggle switch or jumper that can be manually flipped between logic 0 and logic 1. Tie unused inputs (e.g., preset/clear) to their inactive logic levels.3. Initial Power-On: Set the pulse generator to a low-frequency square wave (e.g., 1 Hz). Turn on the power supply and pulse generator. Confirm that the LED is initially stable.4. Core Operation – D Input Change: Manually flip the D toggle switch to logic 1 or logic 0 while observing the LED. Note that the LED does not change immediately but updates on the next active clock edge.5. Core Operation – Clock Frequency Change: After observing correct edge-trigger behavior, slowly turn the frequency knob of the pulse generator to increase the clock frequency. Observe changes in the LED’s blinking or update speed.6. Completion: Return the frequency to a low value, turn off the power supply and generator, and disconnect the circuit.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The LED reflects the stored state of the D flip-flop and remains stable between clock edges.2. D Input Change: When the D toggle switch is flipped, the LED does not change immediately; it changes state only at the next active clock edge.3. Frequency Adjustment: As the clock frequency increases, the LED updates more rapidly, eventually appearing to blink faster or appear continuously on/off due to persistence of vision.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesAn edge-triggered D flip-flop samples the logic level at its D input only at a specific clock edge (rising or falling). The sampled value is stored internally and appears at the Q output until the next triggering edge. The LED serves as a visual indicator of the Q output. Changing the clock frequency does not alter the logical behavior but affects how often the output is updated, demonstrating the relationship between clock rate and observable output changes.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure correct power supply voltage to avoid damaging the IC. Always use a current-limiting resistor with the LED. Avoid changing wiring while the circuit is powered. Keep the camera focus fixed throughout recording to maintain consistent observation.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: LED Shift Register Driven by a Visible Clock PulseI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: LED Shift Register Driven by a Visible Clock Pulse2. Subject: Engineering – Control & Automation3. Experiment Objective: To understand the working principle of a digital shift register by observing how a fixed data input is transferred step by step through a row of LEDs under manual clock pulses, and to recognize the role of clock signals in sequential logic circuits.II. Experimental Equipment1. Shift register IC (e.g., 74HC595 or 74HC164)2. LED array (8 LEDs) with current-limiting resistors3. Manual clock source (push button or rotary pulse knob)4. Fixed data source (logic HIGH connected to data input)5. Power supply (5 V DC)6. Breadboard and connecting wiresIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Power off the circuit. Insert the shift register IC into the breadboard. Connect the power and ground pins correctly. Connect each output pin of the shift register to an LED with a series resistor.2. Data Setup: Connect the data input pin of the shift register to a fixed logic HIGH (Vcc) so that a constant ‘1’ is shifted into the register.3. Clock Setup: Connect the clock input of the shift register to a visible manual clock device (push button or knob). Ensure each press or step generates one clear clock pulse.4. Initial State: Power on the circuit. Observe that all LEDs are initially off or in a known reset state.5. Core Operation: Use your hand to press the clock button (or turn the knob) repeatedly, generating one pulse at a time.6. Observation: After each clock pulse, observe the LEDs. A lit LED appears at the first position and then moves step by step along the row with each subsequent pulse.7. Completion: After several pulses, observe the LED reaching the last position. Stop pressing the clock and power off the circuit.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: All LEDs are off (or only the first LED state is defined after reset).2. After First Pulse: The first LED in the row lights up.3. Subsequent Pulses: With each manual clock trigger, the lit state shifts sequentially from one LED to the next.4. Final State: The lit LED reaches the last position; earlier LEDs remain off, showing clear one-directional shifting.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesA shift register is a sequential digital circuit composed of cascaded flip-flops. The clock signal controls when data is transferred. Each clock pulse causes the data at the input to be loaded into the first flip-flop, while the previous contents of each flip-flop move to the next stage. Because the data input is fixed at logic HIGH, each pulse inserts a ‘1’ that propagates along the register. The LEDs connected to the outputs visually represent the internal states of the flip-flops, making the clock-driven shifting process observable.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure correct power polarity to avoid damaging the IC.2. Use current-limiting resistors to protect the LEDs.3. Press the clock button slowly and distinctly to avoid multiple unintended pulses.4. Power off the circuit before modifying connections.

Experiment Title: RC Circuit Charging a Capacitor Causing an LED to Gradually Brighten2. Subject: Engineering – Systems Engineering (Basic Electronics)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the charging process of a capacitor in a series RC circuit and observe how the increasing capacitor voltage causes an LED to gradually brighten; to understand the time-dependent behavior of RC circuits.II. Experimental EquipmentBattery (DC power supply, 3–9 V), switch (single-pole), resistor (e.g., 330–1k ohm), capacitor (electrolytic, e.g., 100–1000 µF, rated above battery voltage), LED (any visible color), connecting wires, tabletop or breadboard (optional).III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Place all components on a tabletop. Ensure the battery is disconnected and the switch is in the open (off) position. Identify the polarity of the LED and the capacitor.Circuit Connection: Connect the battery, switch, resistor, capacitor, and LED in series. Ensure correct polarity for the LED (anode toward the positive side) and capacitor (positive terminal toward the battery).Core Operation: With the circuit fully connected and visible, use a hand to close the switch, allowing current to flow through the circuit.Observation Stage: Keep the switch closed and observe the LED carefully for changes in brightness over time.Conclusion and Reset: After observation, open the switch to disconnect the power. Allow the capacitor to discharge before repeating the experiment if needed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before the switch is closed, the LED is off and the capacitor is uncharged.2. After Closing the Switch: The LED does not reach full brightness immediately; instead, it gradually becomes brighter over a short period.3. Final State: After sufficient time, the LED reaches a steady maximum brightness as the capacitor becomes nearly fully charged.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesIn a series RC circuit, when the switch is closed, current flows from the battery through the resistor and into the capacitor, charging it gradually. The voltage across the capacitor increases exponentially with time according to the RC time constant. As the capacitor charges, the voltage available across the LED increases, causing the LED current and brightness to rise gradually rather than instantly. This demonstrates the time-dependent response of RC circuits and the role of the resistor in controlling charging speed.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure correct polarity of the LED and capacitor to avoid damage.2. Use an appropriate resistor value to limit current through the LED.3. Do not exceed the voltage rating of the capacitor.4. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Scalar vs Vector Data Visualization ComparisonI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Scalar vs Vector Data Visualization Comparison2. Subject: Engineering – Scientific Computing3. Experiment Objective: To understand the fundamental differences between scalar field and vector field data through visualization, and to learn how different visual encodings (color grids and arrows) represent physical quantities over the same spatial region.II. Experimental Equipment and SoftwareComputer with scientific computing software (e.g., Python with Matplotlib/NumPy, MATLAB, or equivalent), pre-prepared spatial grid data, scalar dataset (temperature field), vector dataset (wind velocity field), display screen capable of split-screen visualization.III. Experimental Procedure1. Data Preparation: Load a 2D spatial grid representing a fixed geographic or computational region. Import the scalar data (temperature values) and vector data (wind velocity components) defined on the same grid.2. Scalar Field Visualization (Left Panel): Plot the temperature data using a color grid or heatmap. Apply a continuous color map where color intensity represents temperature magnitude. Add a color bar legend.3. Vector Field Visualization (Right Panel): Plot the wind data using arrows. Set arrow direction to represent wind direction and arrow length to represent wind speed magnitude. Use black arrows for clarity.4. Split-Screen Layout: Arrange the display so that the scalar field is shown on the left and the vector field on the right, ensuring both panels share the same spatial extent and orientation.5. Final Check: Verify alignment of the two panels, consistency of spatial axes, and clarity of legends. Render the final visualization.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Left Panel Phenomenon: A continuous color grid is observed, with different colors indicating variations in temperature across the region.2. Right Panel Phenomenon: Black arrows are observed at grid points, where arrow direction shows wind flow direction and arrow length increases with wind speed.3. Comparative Observation: Both panels depict the same spatial region, allowing direct comparison between temperature distribution and wind behavior.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Scalar Field Principle: A scalar field assigns a single magnitude value (e.g., temperature) to every point in space, which is effectively visualized using color intensity.2. Vector Field Principle: A vector field assigns both magnitude and direction (e.g., wind velocity) to every point, requiring arrows or glyphs for visualization.3. Visualization Principle: Using split-screen visualization over the same spatial region highlights the conceptual and practical differences between scalar and vector data representations in scientific computing.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure consistent spatial grids for both datasets; choose appropriate color maps and arrow scaling to avoid misinterpretation; maintain clear legends and labels for accurate reading.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Hand-Crank Generator Lighting a BulbI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Hand-Crank Generator Lighting a Bulb Through Manual Motion2. Subject: Engineering – Energy Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the conversion of mechanical energy into electrical energy and then into light energy by manually turning a hand-crank generator, and to understand the relationship between cranking speed and electrical output through direct visual observation of bulb brightness.II. Experimental Equipment1. Hand-crank generator (manual generator with rotating handle)2. Small clear incandescent light bulb (low-voltage)3. Connecting wires (pre-attached or clip wires)4. Stable tabletop5. Camera or smartphone mounted on a fixed stand (focus locked for time-lapse photography)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the hand-crank generator on a stable tabletop. Ensure the generator is firmly positioned so it does not slide during operation. Connect the output terminals of the generator to the small clear light bulb using wires. Check that all connections are secure.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera so that the generator, the operator’s hand, and the clear light bulb are all visible in the frame. Fix the camera focus and exposure to prevent automatic changes during recording. Start time-lapse or continuous recording.3. Initial State Observation: Keep the hand-crank stationary. Observe and record that the light bulb is off when the generator is not being turned.4. Core Operation – Slow Cranking: Slowly turn the hand-crank using one hand. Maintain a steady, low speed for several seconds. Observe the light bulb.5. Core Operation – Faster Cranking: Increase the cranking speed gradually. Continue turning at a higher speed for several seconds. Observe changes in the brightness of the bulb.6. Intermittent Stopping: Stop turning the hand-crank completely for a short moment, then resume turning again at a moderate or high speed. Repeat this stop–start process once or twice.7. Completion: Gradually slow down the cranking until it stops. Turn off the camera and disconnect the equipment after recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: When the hand-crank is not moving, the clear light bulb remains completely off.2. Slow Cranking: When the hand-crank is turned slowly, the bulb lights up dimly, emitting weak light.3. Faster Cranking: As the cranking speed increases, the bulb becomes noticeably brighter.4. Stopping: When the cranking stops, the bulb immediately goes out. When cranking resumes, the bulb lights up again.5. Overall Pattern: The brightness of the bulb changes synchronously with the speed of the hand-crank rotation.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates energy conversion in energy engineering. Mechanical energy provided by the human hand is converted into electrical energy by the hand-crank generator through electromagnetic induction. Inside the generator, rotating coils or magnets change the magnetic flux, inducing an electric current in the circuit. The generated electrical energy is then converted into light energy by the bulb. A higher cranking speed increases the rate of magnetic flux change, producing a higher voltage and current, which results in a brighter bulb. When cranking stops, energy input ceases, no current is generated, and the bulb turns off.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure all electrical connections are secure to avoid intermittent contact.2. Do not crank excessively fast to prevent damage to the generator or bulb.3. Keep the tabletop stable and dry.4. Fix the camera focus and avoid touching the camera during recording to ensure clear time-lapse results.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Sudden Thermal Contact Between a Hot Plate and a Cool Metal Slab (Thermal Camera Observation)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Thermal Front Formation During Sudden Contact Between Hot Plate and Cool Metal Slab2. Subject: Engineering – Energy Engineering (Heat Transfer)3. Experiment Objective: To visually observe transient heat conduction when a cool flat metal slab suddenly contacts a powered hot plate, using a thermal camera to record the moment of contact and the subsequent seconds; to understand transient heat transfer, temperature gradients, and thermal diffusion at a solid–solid interface.II. Experimental EquipmentPowered electric hot plate with flat surface (temperature preset and stabilized), flat metal slab (e.g., aluminum or steel, room temperature), thermal infrared camera (top-down view, fixed focus), tripod or fixed mount for camera, heat-resistant gloves, insulating mat or bench surface, timer or camera time-lapse function.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the hot plate on a stable bench and power it on. Set it to a constant temperature (e.g., 120–150 °C) and allow it to reach steady state. Ensure the metal slab remains at room temperature. Mount the thermal camera directly above the hot plate, fix the focus, lock exposure and color scale, and start continuous or time-lapse recording.2. Initial Observation: Record several seconds of the hot plate alone to establish a uniform high-temperature thermal image (warm colors such as yellow–red).3. Core Operation (Sudden Contact): Wearing heat-resistant gloves, quickly and smoothly place the cool flat metal slab onto the hot plate surface in full contact, without sliding.4. Continuous Recording: Continue recording for several seconds after contact, ensuring the camera remains fixed and focused, capturing the evolving thermal pattern.5. Completion: Stop recording, remove the metal slab safely after sufficient cooling, and turn off the hot plate.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before Contact: The thermal image shows a uniformly hot region corresponding to the hot plate, with stable warm colors.2. At the Moment of Contact: Immediately upon contact, a sharp thermal contrast appears at the interface; the metal slab initially appears cool (blue–purple) while the contact region on the slab rapidly changes color.3. After Contact (Next Seconds): A visible thermal front propagates across the metal slab from the contact area, with colors transitioning smoothly from cool to warm. Simultaneously, the hot plate surface beneath the slab shows localized cooling near the interface.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates transient heat conduction governed by the temperature difference between two solids. When the cool metal slab contacts the hot plate, heat flows from the hot plate (high temperature) to the slab (low temperature) according to Fourier’s law. The initially steep temperature gradient at the interface produces a rapid heat flux, visualized by the thermal camera as a moving color front. Over time, thermal diffusion reduces the gradient, and the temperature distribution becomes more uniform. The experiment highlights contact heat transfer, transient conduction, and thermal diffusivity of metals.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the camera focus and color scale are fixed before contact to allow accurate comparison over time.2. Avoid sliding the slab to prevent frictional heating artifacts.3. Use gloves and follow heat safety procedures.4. Ensure stable mounting to avoid camera motion during recording.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: transient heat conduction during sudden solid–solid contact, visualized by infrared thermography. Minimum assumptions: a powered hot plate at steady high temperature, a cool flat metal slab at room temperature, instantaneous full contact, and a fixed top-down thermal camera with locked focus and color scale. Expected phased storyline: (1) Pre-contact phase—uniform hot plate thermal field recorded from above; (2) Contact phase—instant appearance of sharp thermal contrast at the interface as the cool slab touches the hot plate; (3) Post-contact phase—over the next seconds, a smooth thermal front propagates across the slab while the underlying hot plate shows localized cooling. Visibility constraints: the entire contact area must remain within the camera frame, with no camera movement, enabling clear verification of causal heat-flow-driven color changes over time.

Final State: Traversal stops at the last element, and the bar representing the maximum value is emphasized in red.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe experiment demonstrates the principle of the maximum value search algorithm. By sequentially traversing an array and comparing each element with a stored maximum, the algorithm ensures that after the final comparison, the stored value represents the maximum of the entire array. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Corn Seedling Xylem Transport DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Observation of Xylem Transport in Corn Seedlings Using Red Dye2. Subject: Engineering – Agricultural Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that water and dissolved substances are transported upward in plants through xylem vessels by observing red dye movement in corn seedlings, and to distinguish xylem from phloem in a stem cross-section.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentCorn seedlings with intact root systems (2–3 plants), transparent container or beaker, red dye solution (red ink diluted with water), blade or scalpel, white background or paper, camera for time-lapse recording (optional), paper towels.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Select healthy corn seedlings with intact roots. Rinse roots gently to remove soil without damaging them.2. Dye Immersion: Pour red dye solution into a transparent container. Place the corn seedlings into the container so that only the roots are immersed in the solution.3. Dye Uptake: Allow the seedlings to stand in the dye solution for about 5 seconds. A brief time-lapse recording can be used to emphasize the uptake process.4. Sampling: Remove one seedling from the container and gently blot excess dye from the surface.5. Cutting Operation: Using a clean blade, cut the stem horizontally at a position above the root–stem junction.6. Display: Place the cut surface against a white background and observe the cross-section carefully.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before immersion, the stem interior is not visibly colored.2. After immersion and cutting, red coloration is observed in discrete vascular bundles arranged in a ring.3. The xylem vessels appear red due to dye transport, while the phloem tissue remains colorless or lightly colored.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on the principle of plant water transport. Water and dissolved substances are absorbed by roots and transported upward mainly through xylem vessels driven by transpiration pull and capillary action. When corn seedling roots are immersed in red dye, the dye moves with water through the xylem. After cutting the stem, the red-stained xylem vessels can be clearly observed, while the phloem, responsible for organic nutrient transport, does not carry the dye and remains colorless. This visual contrast verifies the functional difference between xylem and phloem.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure roots remain intact to maintain normal transport pathways.2. Use a sharp blade carefully to obtain a clean cross-section and avoid injury.3. Observe promptly after cutting to prevent diffusion artifacts.

Experiment Title: Formation of Milk Protein Film on a Heated Stainless Steel Surface2. Subject: Engineering – Nuclear Engineering (Heat Transfer and Fouling Phenomena)3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the formation of a milk protein fouling film on a stainless steel surface under constant heating and flow conditions, and to understand heat-induced protein denaturation and surface deposition.II. Experimental EquipmentStainless steel plate (polished, flat), electric heating plate or cartridge heater (mounted below), transparent tray or channel, peristaltic pump or circulation pump, milk (fresh whole milk), tubing, thermometer or temperature controller, camera with fixed focus (for time-lapse), support stand, power supply.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Clean and dry the stainless steel plate to remove grease and residues. Place it horizontally at the bottom of the transparent tray. Mount the heating device directly beneath the plate.2. System Setup: Connect the pump and tubing to form a closed loop, allowing milk to circulate uniformly across the upper surface of the stainless steel plate. Ensure no air bubbles remain in the system.3. Camera Setup: Position the camera above or at an angle to clearly capture the plate surface through the transparent tray. Fix the focus and frame to cover the entire plate area for time-lapse recording.4. Operation: Start milk circulation at a constant flow rate. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Carotene Detection (Simplified Paper Chromatography Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Detection of Carotene in Carrot by Simplified Paper Chromatography2. Subject: Engineering – Food and Bioprocess Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To detect and visually observe carotene in carrot extract using paper chromatography, understand the basic separation principle of pigments based on polarity and solubility, and master simple chromatographic operation and observation methods.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsChromatographic filter paper (rectangular strip), fresh carrot extract (prepared by grinding carrot with a small amount of solvent and filtering), capillary tube or micropipette, developing chamber or beaker with lid, petroleum ether–acetone developing solvent (mixed solvent), pencil, ruler, tweezers, camera or imaging device.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Cut a strip of chromatographic filter paper. Draw a light pencil line about 1.5–2 cm from the bottom as the origin line.2. Sample Spotting: Use a capillary tube to take carrot extract and gently spot it at the center of the origin line. Allow the spot to air-dry; repeat spotting 2–3 times to concentrate the pigment, drying between each spotting.3. Developing Setup: Pour a small amount of petroleum ether–acetone developing solvent into the developing chamber so that the solvent level is below the origin line.4. Chromatographic Development: Using tweezers, place the filter paper vertically into the chamber, ensuring the spotted end is at the bottom and does not touch the chamber wall. Cover the chamber.5. Development and Observation: Allow chromatographic separation to proceed for about 5 minutes. Observe the solvent front rising and pigment bands separating.6. Termination and Imaging: Remove the paper when clear separation appears, immediately mark the solvent front with a pencil, and place the paper on a flat surface. Focus the camera on the paper and perform time-lapse or focused photography to record the separation result.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The carrot extract spot appears as a small orange dot at the origin line.2. During Development: As the solvent rises, an orange pigment band migrates upward from the origin, separating from the initial spot.3. Final Result: A distinct orange band corresponding to carotene is visible above the origin, with the solvent front near the top of the paper.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplePaper chromatography separates substances based on differences in solubility and adsorption between the stationary phase (filter paper) and the mobile phase (petroleum ether–acetone solvent). Carotene is a nonpolar pigment, which has higher solubility in the nonpolar developing solvent and weaker adsorption to the paper. Therefore, carotene migrates upward with the solvent, forming a visible orange band, enabling its detection and identification.VI. Experimental Precautions1. The solvent level must remain below the origin line to prevent sample dissolution.2. Handle organic solvents in a well-ventilated area and avoid open flames.3. Do not touch the paper surface with bare hands to avoid contamination.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Simplified paper chromatography for carotene detection in food engineering. Minimum assumptions: carrot extract contains carotene; filter paper acts as stationary phase; petroleum ether–acetone acts as mobile phase; pigment migration is visible and accelerable via time-lapse.Phased storyline: (1) Static setup showing filter paper with orange spot at bottom; (2) Paper placed into solvent with spot above solvent level; (3) Solvent front rises and orange carotene band migrates upward, separating from origin; (4) Development stops with clear band pattern; (5) Camera focuses and time-lapse emphasizes separation progression. Visibility constraints: camera must clearly capture paper surface, solvent front position, and color band movement from a fixed perspective.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Observation of Binary FSK Signal on an OscilloscopeI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Oscilloscope Observation of Binary Frequency Shift Keying (FSK) Signal2. Subject: Engineering – Communications Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the basic characteristics of a binary FSK signal by using an oscilloscope to simultaneously display a digital square-wave control signal and a sine-wave carrier whose frequency switches between two discrete values according to the digital signal state. Students will master basic signal connection, oscilloscope triggering and scaling, and visual analysis of modulation phenomena.II. Experimental Equipment1. Dual-channel oscilloscope (with adjustable time base, voltage scale, and trigger)2. Function generator or FSK signal source (capable of generating square-wave data and FSK-modulated sine wave)3. Two BNC signal cables4. Power supply (if required by the signal source)5. Camera or recording device (fixed focus, suitable for time-lapse or continuous recording)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   a. Power on the oscilloscope and signal source, and allow them to warm up for stable operation.   b. Set the camera on a fixed tripod facing the oscilloscope screen, and fix the focus to avoid focus hunting during recording.2. Signal Connection:   a. Connect Channel 1 (CH1) of the oscilloscope to the digital square-wave data signal output.   b. Connect Channel 2 (CH2) of the oscilloscope to the FSK-modulated sine-wave carrier output.3. Oscilloscope Setup:   a. Set both channels to voltage-time (time-domain) display mode.   b. Adjust CH1 vertical scale so the square wave is clearly visible with distinct high and low levels.   c. Adjust CH2 vertical scale to clearly display the sine wave without clipping.   d. Adjust the time base so that several periods of the square wave and corresponding sine-wave cycles are visible.   e. Set the trigger source to CH1 and trigger on the rising edge to stabilize the waveform display.4. Core Operation:   a. Enable the binary FSK signal generation.   b. Observe the oscilloscope screen while the square-wave digital signal toggles between logic high and logic low states.   c. Record the oscilloscope display using the camera, ensuring the screen remains stable and in focus.5. Completion:   a. Stop recording after several switching cycles are clearly observed.   b. Turn off the signal source and oscilloscope.   c. Disconnect all cables and restore equipment to its original state.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The oscilloscope displays two stable traces simultaneously.2. CH1 shows a square-wave digital signal alternating between high and low voltage levels.3. CH2 shows a continuous sine-wave carrier.4. When the square-wave signal is at logic high, the sine wave on CH2 has one fixed frequency (f1).5. When the square-wave signal switches to logic low, the sine wave frequency switches to a different fixed frequency (f2).6. The frequency changes of the sine wave are synchronized in time with the transitions of the square-wave signal.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesBinary Frequency Shift Keying (FSK) is a digital modulation technique in which digital information is transmitted by shifting the frequency of a carrier wave between two discrete values. Observing both signals on the oscilloscope directly demonstrates the time-domain relationship between digital data and frequency modulation.VI. Experimental Precautions1. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Comparative Experiment of Bearing Capacity between Pile Foundation and Non-Pile Foundation under Seismic LoadI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparative Experiment of Bearing Capacity between Pile Foundation and Non-Pile Foundation under Seismic Load2. Subject: Engineering – Geotechnical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To compare the bearing capacity and seismic performance of pile foundations and non-pile foundations by observing settlement differences under simulated seismic vibration.II. Experimental EquipmentVibration table (1), sand tables (2, identical size), model piles (3, for sand table A), dry sand (uniform), equal weights (2), fixing clamps or bolts, ruler or scale marker, camera (for focused and time-lapsed recording).III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Place two empty sand tables side by side. Install three model piles vertically and evenly spaced in sand table A; leave sand table B without piles. Fill both tables with the same type and amount of sand, keeping surface level consistent.Loading Stage: Place equal weights at the center of each sand table surface. Ensure the weights are identical in mass, shape, and contact area.Fixation Stage: Secure both sand tables firmly onto the vibration table to prevent sliding during vibration.Core Operation: Start the vibration table to simulate seismic loading. Maintain the same vibration intensity and duration for both sand tables. Record the process using a fixed camera with time-lapse or accelerated mode.Observation and Termination: Observe and record the settlement of the weights during vibration. After sufficient visible settlement difference appears, stop vibration and end recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both sand tables have level surfaces; weights remain stable with no visible settlement.2. During Vibration: Sand in both tables rearranges and densifies. The weight on sand table B (non-pile foundation) gradually sinks more明显 and faster.3. Final State: Sand table A shows smaller settlement due to load transfer through piles, while sand table B shows larger settlement due to lower bearing capacity.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesUnder seismic load, vibration causes sand particles to rearrange and compact, leading to foundation settlement. Pile foundations transfer part of the load to deeper, more stable layers through piles, reducing surface settlement and improving bearing capacity. Non-pile foundations rely only on shallow soil resistance and therefore experience larger settlement under the same seismic conditions.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure equal sand properties and loading conditions for both sand tables.2. Fix sand tables securely to avoid lateral movement.3. Keep vibration parameters consistent throughout the experiment.4. Use time-lapse recording to clearly present settlement differences within a short duration.
