manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Lycopene Detection in Tomato by Acetone Extraction-Colorimetric MethodI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Lycopene Detection in Tomato (Acetone Extraction-Colorimetric Method)2. Subject: Engineering - Food and Bioprocess Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To extract lycopene from tomato homogenate using acetone and determine its presence by measuring absorbance at 503nm with a spectrophotometer, understanding the basic principle of solvent extraction and colorimetric analysis.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsBeaker (50mL), electronic balance, glass rod, filter paper and funnel, cuvette, spectrophotometer, tomato homogenate, acetone (analytical grade), gloves and safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Put on safety goggles and gloves. Turn on the spectrophotometer to warm up and set the wavelength to 503nm.2. Weighing: Use an electronic balance to accurately weigh 5g of tomato homogenate and transfer it into a clean beaker.3. Extraction: Add 10mL of acetone into the beaker containing the tomato homogenate. Stir thoroughly with a glass rod for uniform extraction until the mixture appears evenly colored.4. Filtration: Place filter paper in a funnel and filter the mixture into another clean container. Collect the clear filtrate.5. Measurement: Pour an appropriate amount of the filtrate into a clean cuvette, wipe the outside of the cuvette dry, and place it into the spectrophotometer. Measure the absorbance at 503nm.6. Completion: Record the absorbance value. Dispose of waste solvent according to laboratory regulations and clean all glassware.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The tomato homogenate is red and opaque; acetone is colorless and transparent.2. During Extraction: After adding acetone and stirring, the liquid phase gradually turns red as lycopene dissolves into acetone.3. After Filtration: The filtrate is a clear red solution without solid particles.4. Measurement: The spectrophotometer displays an absorbance value at 503nm, indicating the presence of lycopene.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleLycopene is a fat-soluble carotenoid pigment in tomatoes that is readily soluble in organic solvents such as acetone. During extraction, lycopene dissolves into acetone, forming a red solution. Lycopene has a characteristic maximum absorbance around 503nm. According to the Beer-Lambert law, the absorbance measured at this wavelength is proportional to the lycopene concentration in the extract, allowing qualitative or quantitative detection.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Avoid strong light exposure to prevent lycopene degradation.2. Ensure accurate weighing and volume measurement for reliable results.3. Keep the cuvette clean and properly oriented during spectrophotometric measurement.4. Handle acetone in a well-ventilated area and dispose of waste properly.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: U-shaped Iron Core Electromagnet Attracting Iron FilingsSubject: Engineering – Energy EngineeringExperiment Objective: To demonstrate how an energized coil on an iron core produces a magnetic field that attracts iron filings, and to visually observe magnetic field distribution at the poles and air gap.II. Experimental EquipmentU-shaped soft iron core; insulated copper coil wound on one leg of the core; low-voltage DC power supply or battery with switch; connecting wires; iron filings; flat tabletop; insulating mat; camera or smartphone with fixed focus (for time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the U-shaped iron core flat on the tabletop with a visible air gap between the two ends. Camera Setup: Position the camera above or at an angle to clearly capture the core and air gap. Fix the focus and keep the camera stationary.3. Energizing the Coil: Close the switch to energize the coil, allowing current to flow through the copper wire.4. Sprinkling Iron Filings: While the coil is energized, gently sprinkle iron filings evenly over the iron core ends and across the air gap.5. Observation: Observe the distribution and alignment of the iron filings while the current flows.6. Power Off: Open the switch to cut off the current and continue observing the changes in the iron filings.7. Cleanup: After observation, remove filings, disconnect the power supply, and store equipment properly.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Iron filings lie loosely and randomly on the tabletop and core surface.When Energized: Iron filings are rapidly attracted to the iron core, concentrating at the two ends (magnetic poles) and forming visible patterns bridging the air gap.After Power Off: The attraction weakens; some filings fall away, while a small amount may remain temporarily due to residual magnetism.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWhen electric current flows through the copper coil, a magnetic field is generated around the coil. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Pressure-Induced Deformation of a Thin-Walled Metal Canister2. Subject: Engineering – Nuclear Engineering (Structural Mechanics / Containment Integrity)3. Demonstration Objective: To visually demonstrate how external pressure causes deformation and collapse of a thin-walled metal canister when the surrounding pressure is reduced in a controlled environment, illustrating pressure differential and structural stability concepts relevant to nuclear containment systems.II. Experimental Equipment1. Thin-walled metal canister (e.g., aluminum beverage can, intact, empty, dry)2. Transparent pressure chamber (acrylic or glass, sealed)3. Vacuum pump with pressure control valve4. Pressure gauge (connected to the chamber, displaying internal pressure)5. Stable base or stand for the canister6. Safety goggles and gloves7. Camera or direct visual access through the transparent chamberIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:- Inspect the metal canister to ensure it is empty, sealed, and free of visible dents.- Place the canister upright on the base inside the transparent pressure chamber.- Close and seal the chamber lid securely.2. System Setup:- Connect the vacuum pump to the chamber outlet.- Ensure the pressure gauge is functioning and initially reads approximately atmospheric pressure.- Verify all connections are airtight.3. Core Operation (Demonstration Phase):- Start the vacuum pump slowly.- Gradually evacuate air from the pressure chamber, steadily reducing the surrounding pressure.- Maintain a continuous and smooth pumping rate to avoid sudden pressure shocks.4. Observation and Recording:- Observe the canister continuously through the transparent chamber.- Note any changes in shape, surface curvature, or structural stability as pressure decreases.- Continue evacuation until clear deformation or collapse occurs.5. Termination and Reset:- Stop the vacuum pump once the core phenomenon is observed.- Slowly reintroduce air into the chamber to return it to atmospheric pressure.- Open the chamber only after pressure is fully equalized.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State:- The canister maintains its original cylindrical shape under atmospheric pressure.2. During Pressure Reduction:- As external pressure decreases, the canister walls begin to show slight inward curvature.- Subtle creasing or buckling appears on the canister surface.3. Final State:- At a critical pressure differential, the canister undergoes rapid inward collapse or significant deformation.- The collapse occurs suddenly after gradual deformation.V. Summary of Experimental Principle1. Core Principle:- The experiment demonstrates pressure-induced structural instability due to pressure differential.2. Principle Analysis:- The canister initially contains air at near-atmospheric pressure.- As the surrounding pressure is reduced, the internal pressure becomes relatively higher than the external pressure.- This pressure differential generates compressive stress on the thin canister walls.- When the stress exceeds the material’s critical buckling limit, structural instability occurs, leading to sudden deformation or collapse.3. Engineering Relevance:- This principle is directly applicable to nuclear engineering, particularly in the design of containment vessels, fuel cladding, and storage canisters, where resistance to external pressure and buckling is critical.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the pressure chamber is rated for vacuum operation.2. Reduce pressure gradually to prevent damage to equipment.3. Do not touch the chamber during evacuation.4. Always wear safety goggles during operation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Pressure-induced deformation and buckling of a thin-walled metal structure under external pressure reduction.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions:- The canister is thin-walled, sealed, and initially at atmospheric internal pressure.- The surrounding pressure is reduced steadily using a vacuum pump.- Material behavior follows basic elastic–buckling principles.Expected Phenomena (Phased Storyline):Phase 1 (Initial Equilibrium): Canister remains cylindrical and stable inside a transparent chamber at normal pressure.Phase 2 (Pressure Reduction): Pump evacuates air; pressure gauge drops; canister walls show gradual inward curvature.Phase 3 (Critical Transition): Once a critical pressure differential is reached, visible buckling initiates.Phase 4 (Final Outcome): Sudden inward collapse or severe deformation occurs, clearly linked to pressure reduction.Visibility Constraints:- Transparent chamber and clear side view are required.- Deformation and collapse must be directly observable without camera cuts.- Chronological order must be preserved, though the process may be accelerated to fit a 10-second video.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Binary Tree Pre-order Traversal Operation DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Binary Tree Pre-order Traversal Operation Demonstration2. Subject: Engineering - Computer Science3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the pre-order traversal process of a binary tree, understand the visiting order of nodes (root-left-right), and observe how traversal results are generated sequentially.II. Experimental Materials and Environment1. A simple binary tree diagram with 7 nodes labeled 1–7.2. Light-colored background for clear visual contrast.3. Highlight color (bright red) and glow effect for visited nodes.4. A horizontal output list area at the bottom of the screen.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Display a simple binary tree with node 1 as the root, nodes 2 and 3 as its children, and nodes 4–7 forming the lower level, all on a light background.2. Initialization: Ensure all nodes are in a neutral color and the output list at the bottom is empty.3. Core Operation: Begin pre-order traversal.   (1) Visit the root node first, highlight it in red with a brief glow, and append its value to the output list.   (2) Recursively traverse the left subtree, repeating the highlight-and-append operation for each node.   (3) After finishing the left subtree, traverse the right subtree using the same method.4. Completion: Stop the traversal when all nodes (1–7) have been visited and displayed in the output list.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The binary tree is static, with all nodes unhighlighted and the output list empty.2. During Traversal: Each node glows red briefly when visited, and its value appears sequentially in the bottom output list from left to right.3. Final State: All nodes have been visited once, and the output list shows the complete pre-order traversal sequence.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesPre-order traversal is a fundamental binary tree traversal method in computer science. The principle is to visit the root node first, then recursively traverse the left subtree, followed by the right subtree. This experiment visualizes the algorithmic logic by linking each visit action to a visible node highlight and an immediate update of the traversal result list, reinforcing the causal relationship between algorithm steps and output.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Binary tree pre-order traversal (root-left-right). Minimum assumptions: a fixed binary tree with labeled nodes, a light background, a visible highlight effect, and an output list area. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) Static tree initialization with empty output list; (2) Root node is highlighted and added to the list; (3) Left subtree nodes are highlighted and appended in order; (4) Right subtree nodes follow; (5) The output list grows left-to-right in exact pre-order sequence. Visibility constraints: the entire tree and output list must remain on screen, with clear color contrast and smooth sequential transitions for verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: VTK Tensor Field Ellipsoid DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: VTK Tensor Field Ellipsoid Visualization Demonstration2. Subject: Engineering – Scientific Computing (Visualization)3. Experiment Objective: To understand how tensor field data can be visualized using ellipsoids in VTK, master the basic workflow of writing and running C++ programs with the VTK library, and observe how tensor eigenvalues and eigenvectors are mapped to ellipsoid shape, size, and orientation in a 3D interactive window.II. Experimental Environment and Equipment1. Hardware: Desktop or laptop computer with mouse and display.2. Software Environment:   - C++ compiler (e.g., GCC, Clang, or MSVC).   - VTK library installed and correctly configured.   - Development environment or text editor (e.g., Visual Studio, VS Code).3. Data: Sample tensor field dataset supported by VTK (e.g., .vtk or .vti file containing tensor attributes).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   - Ensure the VTK library is installed and environment variables are configured.   - Prepare a tensor field dataset with valid tensor attributes.   - Create a new C++ source file for the experiment.2. Code Writing Stage:   - Include necessary VTK header files (such as vtkSmartPointer, vtkTensorGlyph, vtkSphereSource, vtkPolyDataMapper, vtkActor, vtkRenderer, vtkRenderWindow, vtkRenderWindowInteractor).   - Load the tensor field data using an appropriate VTK reader.   - Set up a vtkTensorGlyph object and choose ellipsoid glyphs.   - Configure glyph parameters so that the long axis corresponds to the principal eigenvector direction and the ellipsoid size corresponds to tensor eigenvalues.   - Set the color mapping to a green gradient.   - Create renderer, render window, and interactor, and set the background color to black.3. Compilation and Execution:   - Compile the C++ program and resolve any compilation errors.   - Run the executable file.4. Visualization and Interaction:   - Observe the pop-up 3D visualization window.   - Use the mouse wheel or drag operations to zoom and rotate the scene.   - Verify that ellipsoids respond correctly to interaction and remain stable during zooming and rotation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State:   - After execution, a black-background 3D render window appears on the screen.2. Visualization State:   - The tensor field is represented by multiple ellipsoids distributed in 3D space.   - Ellipsoids show a green color gradient.   - The long axis of each ellipsoid aligns with the principal eigenvector direction of the tensor.   - The overall size of each ellipsoid varies according to the tensor eigenvalues.3. Interactive Phenomena:   - Zooming and rotating with the mouse changes the viewpoint smoothly.   - The ellipsoids maintain correct orientation and relative size during interaction.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Tensor Visualization Principle:   - A second-order tensor can be decomposed into eigenvalues and eigenvectors.   - Eigenvectors define the principal directions, and eigenvalues define the magnitude along those directions.2. Ellipsoid Mapping:   - In VTK, tensor glyphs map eigenvectors to the axes of ellipsoids and eigenvalues to their lengths, forming an intuitive geometric representation of tensor data.3. Visualization Pipeline:   - VTK follows a pipeline model: data input → processing (glyph generation) → mapping → rendering → interaction.   - The renderer and interactor enable real-time visualization and user interaction, facilitating analysis of tensor fields.VI. manual: Binary Search Algorithm Execution Process Demonstration Experimental Instruction ManualI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Binary Search Algorithm Execution Process Demonstration2. Subject: Engineering – Computer Science – Algorithms3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the execution process of the binary search algorithm by comparing a target value (e.g., 11) with elements in an ordered array, helping learners understand the idea of halving the search range and improving search efficiency.II. Experimental Materials and Environment1. Visual interface or animation canvas.2. Pure white background.3. A horizontal array of 15 identical squares, evenly spaced.4. Numbers 1 to 15 displayed clearly inside the squares in ascending order.5. A highlighted target value label: Target = 11.III. Experimental Procedure1. Initialization: Display a pure white background. Place 15 squares horizontally in the center, numbered 1 to 15 from left to right. Show the target value 11 above or beside the array.2. First Comparison: Highlight the middle square (position 8, value 8). Compare 8 with target 11. Indicate result: 8 < 11.3. Range Reduction: Visually dim or mark squares 1–8 as excluded, keeping squares 9–15 active.4. Second Comparison: Highlight the new middle of the remaining range (position 12, value 12). Compare 12 with 11. Indicate result: 12 > 11.5. Range Reduction: Dim or exclude squares 12–15, keeping squares 9–11 active.6. Third Comparison: Highlight the middle of the remaining range (position 10 or 11 depending on convention; demonstrate clearly). Compare with target.7. Result Confirmation: Highlight square numbered 11 distinctly and indicate that the target has been found. End the demonstration.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: All 15 squares are equally visible on a white background, with no emphasis.2. During Search: At each step, one square is highlighted as the comparison point, and part of the array is visually excluded based on comparison results.3. Final State: Only the square numbered 11 remains highlighted, confirming successful search.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Core Principle: Binary search operates on an ordered dataset by repeatedly comparing the target value with the middle element and halving the search range.2. Algorithm Logic: If the middle value is less than the target, search continues in the right half; if greater, in the left half.3. Efficiency Explanation: By discarding half of the remaining elements at each step, binary search achieves logarithmic time complexity O(log n), making it much faster than linear search for large datasets.

Phase 2 – Iterative Comparison: The midpoint square is highlighted, compared to the target, and a clear visual cue shows exclusion of half the array; this repeats with a reduced range. Phase 3 – Termination: The square containing the target value is highlighted as the final result. Visibility must remain centered on the array, with clear highlighting and dimming to verify causal transitions between steps.

manual: Sequential Search Algorithm Execution Process DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Sequential Search Algorithm Execution Process Demonstration2. Subject: Engineering - Computer Science3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate how a sequential (linear) search algorithm works by scanning an array from left to right, comparing each element with a target value, and understanding the basic idea, execution steps, and characteristics of sequential search.II. Experimental Equipment (Virtual/Animation)1. A clean 2D animation environment.2. A horizontal array of numbered boxes, for example: [5, 1, 2, 4, 3].3. A clearly marked target value, for example: 4.4. A highlighted pointer or indicator representing the current index being checked.III. Experimental Procedure1. Initialization: Display the array of numbered boxes laid out horizontally on the screen. Clearly show the target value to be searched.2. Starting Position: Place the highlighted pointer at the leftmost box of the array (index 0).3. Sequential Comparison: Move the pointer step by step from left to right. At each position, visually compare the number in the current box with the target value.4. Match Judgment: If the current number is not equal to the target, keep the pointer moving to the next box. If the number equals the target, stop the pointer and highlight the matched box.5. Result Display: Indicate that the target value has been found and optionally show its position (index) in the array.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: All array elements are visible, evenly spaced, and unhighlighted; the pointer is at the first element.2. During Search: The pointer moves one box at a time from left to right. Each visited box is briefly highlighted to show comparison.3. When Target Is Found: The pointer stops at the box containing the target value, and this box is distinctly highlighted to indicate success.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSequential search is a basic searching algorithm that checks each element in a list one by one from the beginning until the target value is found or the list ends. Its core principle is straightforward comparison: each element is compared with the target in order, without using any prior ordering information. The algorithm is simple to implement and works for both ordered and unordered arrays, but its efficiency decreases as the array size increases, with a time complexity of O(n).VI. Experimental Notes1. The pointer must always move in a left-to-right order without skipping elements.2. Visual highlighting should clearly distinguish the current element being compared.3. For demonstration purposes, the process can be accelerated, but the comparison order must remain correct.

No sorting or advanced data structures are assumed.Phased storyline: (1) Setup phase showing the full array and target value; (2) search phase where the pointer moves step by step from left to right, with each movement causing a comparison; (3) termination phase where the pointer stops upon finding the target and highlights the result. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Damped and Undamped Vertical Mass–Spring Systems2. Subject: Engineering – Structural Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the effect of a viscous dashpot on the dynamic response of a mass–spring system by comparing damped and undamped oscillations.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical vertical mass–spring systems (same spring constant and mass); one viscous dashpot (transparent oil-filled cylinder) attached in parallel to the left system; rigid support frame; displacement reference scale (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Mount the two mass–spring systems vertically on the same support frame, ensuring identical geometry and mass. Attach the viscous dashpot securely to the left system only. Ensure both systems are at rest.2. Initial Displacement: Using both hands, pull the two masses downward to the same vertical displacement, keeping springs aligned and motionless before release.3. Simultaneous Release: Release both masses at the same time without adding extra force.4. Observation: Observe and compare the subsequent vertical motions of the two masses until both systems come to rest.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both masses start from the same displaced position.2. Undamped System (Right): The mass oscillates up and down repeatedly with nearly constant or slowly decreasing amplitude.3. Damped System (Left): The mass oscillates with rapidly decreasing amplitude and returns to equilibrium much faster.4. Final State: The damped system comes to rest earlier, while the undamped system continues oscillating for a longer time.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleA mass–spring system without damping conserves mechanical energy aside from minor losses, resulting in sustained oscillations. When a viscous dashpot is added, a damping force proportional to velocity is generated, converting mechanical energy into heat within the fluid. This energy dissipation reduces oscillation amplitude over time and shortens the settling duration. The experiment demonstrates the role of viscous damping in controlling structural vibrations.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both springs and masses are identical to allow fair comparison.2. Release both masses simultaneously to avoid initial condition errors.3. Secure the dashpot firmly to prevent lateral motion or detachment.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Viscous damping in a mass–spring system, assuming linear springs, identical masses, vertical motion under gravity, and velocity-proportional damping from a fluid-filled dashpot.Phased Storyline: (1) Static setup with two identical vertical systems, dashpot visible only on the left; (2) equal downward displacement applied to both masses; (3) simultaneous release; (4) immediate divergence in motion where the right system oscillates repeatedly while the left system shows shrinking oscillations; (5) left system settles first, right system continues oscillating. The camera should maintain a fixed side-by-side view to verify simultaneous action, relative amplitudes, and settling behavior.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Thermal Insulation Reducing Heat Loss in a Small Building Wall (Infrared Observation)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Thermal Insulation Reducing Heat Loss in a Small Building Wall Observed by Infrared Imaging2. Subject: Engineering – Civil & Environmental Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how thermal insulation reduces heat loss through building walls by comparing infrared surface temperatures of an insulated wall section and an uninsulated wall section under identical indoor heating conditions, and to understand the principle of heat transfer through building envelopes.II. Experimental EquipmentSmall test building model or test box with two adjacent exterior wall sections; thermal insulation material (installed on one wall section); bare wall section of the same material and thickness (without insulation); internal electric heater or heating lamp; power supply; infrared (thermal) camera with time-lapse function; tripod or fixed mount for infrared camera; thermometer or temperature controller (optional); timer or clock.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the small test building in a stable indoor environment with minimal air drafts. Ensure the two wall sections are adjacent, one insulated and one bare, with identical orientation and exposure conditions.2. Heating Setup: Install the heater inside the test building, centered to provide uniform internal heating. Set the heater to a constant power level. Close the building to minimize air leakage.3. Camera Setup: Position the infrared camera outside the building, facing both wall sections simultaneously. Fix the camera on a tripod, ensure both walls are fully in frame, and lock the focus, angle, and distance. Select an appropriate temperature color scale and enable time-lapse recording.4. Initial Recording: Start infrared recording before turning on the heater to capture the initial temperature distribution of both wall surfaces.5. Core Operation: Turn on the internal heater and maintain constant heating. Allow the system to run while the infrared camera records exterior surface temperatures continuously or at fixed intervals.6. Completion: After a sufficient observation period, stop heating and recording. Save and review the infrared images or video sequence.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: At the beginning, both the insulated wall and bare wall show similar infrared colors, indicating similar surface temperatures.2. During Heating: As heating continues, the exterior surface of the bare wall gradually shows warmer infrared colors (higher apparent temperature), while the insulated wall remains cooler, showing darker or cooler colors.3. Later Stage: A clear temperature contrast appears between the two wall sections, with the bare wall consistently hotter than the insulated wall under the same internal heating conditions.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on the principle of heat transfer in building envelopes, including conduction through solid materials. Thermal insulation increases the thermal resistance (R-value) of the wall, reducing heat flow from the warm interior to the cooler exterior. As a result, less heat reaches the exterior surface of the insulated wall, leading to a lower exterior surface temperature compared to the bare wall. Infrared imaging visualizes this difference by converting surface temperature into color-coded thermal images.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both wall sections experience the same environmental conditions (wind, radiation, orientation).2. Keep the camera position and focus fixed throughout the experiment to ensure valid time-lapse comparison.3. Avoid touching wall surfaces during the experiment to prevent disturbance of heat transfer.4. Follow electrical safety procedures when using heaters and power supplies.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Thermal insulation reduces heat loss through building walls by increasing thermal resistance, observable as lower exterior surface temperatures under identical internal heating. Minimum assumptions: two adjacent wall sections with identical base materials, one with added insulation; constant internal heat source; fixed-position infrared camera. Expected phenomena storyline: Phase 1 – initial state with similar exterior temperatures; Phase 2 – internal heating begins, heat conducts outward; Phase 3 – bare wall exterior warms faster and appears hotter in infrared, while insulated wall remains cooler; verification requires a stable external viewpoint capturing both walls simultaneously with consistent color scale and time progression.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Airfoil in a Wind Tunnel with Smoke StreamlinesI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visualization of Airflow over an Airfoil Using Smoke in a Wind Tunnel2. Subject: Engineering – Aerospace Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe airflow behavior around a fixed airfoil at a slight angle of attack, visualize streamline acceleration and downward deflection using smoke, and understand the aerodynamic principle of lift generation.II. Experimental EquipmentLow-speed wind tunnel with transparent test section, airfoil model (2D section), adjustable mounting mechanism, smoke generator or smoke wire system, uniform airflow source, fixed-focus camera (tripod-mounted, time-lapse capable), lighting system.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Secure the airfoil model rigidly in the center of the wind tunnel test section and set a slight positive angle of attack (approximately 3–6 degrees). Ensure the test section is clean and transparent.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera perpendicular to the test section, ensuring the entire airfoil and upstream/downstream region are in frame. Fix the focus and exposure, and enable time-lapse recording.3. Smoke Introduction: Activate the smoke generator upstream of the airfoil to produce thin, evenly spaced smoke streams aligned with the incoming airflow.4. Core Operation: Start the wind tunnel at a steady low speed. Maintain constant airflow while smoke streams pass over and under the airfoil.5. Observation and Recording: Record the steady-state flow for several seconds, ensuring smoke streamlines clearly show acceleration over the upper surface and downward bending downstream.6. Shutdown: Stop airflow, turn off smoke generation, save the recorded footage, and power down equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before airflow, smoke streams are straight and parallel in the upstream region.2. During Airflow: As air passes the airfoil, smoke above the airfoil accelerates and curves closer together; downstream streamlines bend downward relative to the freestream direction.3. Steady State: A stable pattern of downward-deflected streamlines is observed, indicating momentum change of the airflow.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the aerodynamic principle of lift. A slight angle of attack causes the airfoil to deflect airflow downward, producing a change in momentum. According to Newton’s third law and conservation of momentum, the downward deflection of air results in an upward force (lift) on the airfoil. The accelerated flow over the upper surface is associated with pressure differences explained by Bernoulli’s principle, while the overall lift is best understood through momentum balance.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the airfoil is firmly fixed; keep airflow speed constant; use uniform smoke density; avoid refocusing the camera during recording; follow safety procedures for smoke generation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Visualization of lift generation by observing smoke streamlines around a fixed airfoil at slight angle of attack in a wind tunnel. Minimum assumptions include steady low-speed airflow, visible smoke as passive tracers, and a rigidly mounted airfoil.Phased Storyline: (1) Establishment of a stable wind tunnel scene with straight upstream smoke streams; (2) Introduction of airflow past the fixed airfoil, showing acceleration over the upper surface; (3) Clear downstream downward bending of smoke streamlines indicating momentum change; (4) Stable time-lapse view with fixed camera focus and consistent perspective for verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Incandescent Bulb Brightness Change When a Resistor Is Added in SeriesI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Incandescent Bulb Brightness Change When a Resistor Is Added in Series2. Subject: Engineering - Electrical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe and compare the brightness of two identical incandescent bulbs when one is directly connected to a DC power source and the other is connected in series with a resistor, and to understand the relationship between current, resistance, and power dissipation.II. Experimental EquipmentDC power supply (low-voltage, adjustable), two identical incandescent bulbs with holders, one visible fixed resistor (rated for safe power dissipation), connecting wires, switch (optional), stable mounting board, camera on tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Mount two identical bulbs side by side on the board. Ensure both bulbs are off. Fix the camera position and focus so both bulbs and the resistor are clearly visible.Circuit Connection: Connect the left bulb directly to the DC power source. Connect the right bulb in series with the visible resistor, then to the same DC power source. Verify correct polarity and secure connections.Core Operation: Turn on the DC power source and adjust to the rated voltage of the bulbs. Do not change the camera focus or circuit configuration during recording.Recording: Record the brightness change using time-lapse photography for several seconds after power-on.Shutdown: Turn off the power supply and allow components to cool.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both bulbs are off before power is applied.2. After Power-On: The left bulb (direct connection) lights up brighter, while the right bulb (with series resistor) lights up noticeably dimmer.3. Steady State: After a short time, both bulbs reach stable brightness levels, maintaining the brightness difference.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesAdding a resistor in series increases the total circuit resistance, reducing the current according to Ohm’s law (I = V/R). The reduced current lowers the electrical power dissipated by the bulb (P = I²R), resulting in lower filament temperature and reduced brightness. The directly connected bulb receives higher current and therefore dissipates more power, appearing brighter.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Series resistance reduces current and power in an incandescent bulb circuit. Minimum assumptions include identical bulbs, a stable DC source, and a visible series resistor.Phased Storyline: (1) Initial setup with both bulbs off and clearly wired; (2) Power-on event initiating current flow; (3) Immediate brightness contrast with direct bulb brighter; (4) Short stabilization period showing persistent brightness difference. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Cholesterol Detection by Liebermann-Burchard MethodI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Cholesterol Detection by Liebermann-Burchard Method2. Subject: Engineering – Food and Bioprocess Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To qualitatively detect cholesterol in egg yolk extract through color reaction observation, and to understand the reaction principle of sterols with strong acids.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsDry test tube (15×150 mm), test tube rack, measuring pipette or graduated dropper, egg yolk extract, glacial acetic acid, concentrated sulfuric acid, protective gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ensure the test tube is clean and completely dry, and place it on the test tube rack. Wear protective goggles and gloves.2. Sample Addition: Use a pipette to transfer 1 mL of egg yolk extract into the dry test tube.3. Dissolution: Add 5 mL of glacial acetic acid into the test tube. Gently swirl until the egg yolk extract is fully dissolved, forming a clear or slightly yellow solution.4. Reaction Initiation: Carefully add 1 mL of concentrated sulfuric acid along the inner wall of the test tube.5. Mixing: Immediately shake the test tube gently to mix the contents evenly.IV. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Air Quality O₃ Detection (Indigo Disulfonate Fading Method)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Air Quality O₃ Detection by Indigo Disulfonate Fading MethodSubject: Engineering - Civil & Environmental EngineeringObjective: To demonstrate the qualitative detection of ozone (O₃) in air by observing the fading of indigo disulfonate solution when exposed to an ozone-containing air sample.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (clean, dry), test tube rack, graduated dropper or pipette, gas delivery tube, ozone-containing air sample (from ozone generator or prepared source), indigo disulfonate solution (blue), safety gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube on the rack. Wear safety goggles and gloves.2. Solution Addition: Use a pipette to accurately add 2 mL of blue indigo disulfonate solution into the test tube.3. Gas Introduction: Insert the gas delivery tube slightly into the test tube without touching the liquid surface excessively.4. Core Operation: Pass the ozone-containing air sample through the test tube for approximately 2 seconds at a steady flow rate.5. Completion: Remove the gas tube, stop the gas flow, and keep the test tube stationary for observation.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The indigo disulfonate solution is uniformly blue and transparent.During Gas Introduction: Upon passing ozone-containing air, the blue color begins to fade.Final State: After about 2 seconds of exposure, the solution becomes significantly lighter or nearly colorless.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleIndigo disulfonate is a blue dye that can be oxidized by ozone, a strong oxidizing agent present in polluted air. When ozone passes through the solution, it oxidizes the conjugated structure of indigo disulfonate, breaking the chromophore and causing the blue color to fade. The degree of fading is qualitatively related to the presence of ozone, forming the basis of this air quality detection method.VI. PrecautionsEnsure accurate measurement of 2 mL solution; avoid prolonged ozone exposure; dispose of used solutions according to laboratory waste regulations.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Analog Voltmeter Needle Swing for One Battery vs Two Batteries in SeriesI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Analog Voltmeter Shows Larger Needle Swing for Two Batteries in SeriesSubject: Engineering – Electrical EngineeringObjective: To observe that an analog voltmeter shows a larger needle deflection when connected across two identical batteries in series compared with one battery, and to understand the relationship between voltage and meter deflection.II. Experimental EquipmentAnalog voltmeter (DC range), two identical cylindrical dry batteries (e.g., AA or D cells), insulating tape, red and black voltmeter probes, flat tabletop, camera fixed on a tripod or stand.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the analog voltmeter on a tabletop. Set it to an appropriate DC voltage range. Fix the camera focus and position so the meter scale is clearly visible.2. Single-Battery Test: Connect the red probe to the positive terminal and the black probe to the negative terminal of one cylindrical battery. Keep the connection steady and observe the needle position.3. Series-Battery Setup: Tape two identical batteries together in series, ensuring the positive terminal of one contacts the negative terminal of the other.4. Series-Battery Test: Connect the red probe to the free positive terminal and the black probe to the free negative terminal of the battery pair. Observe the new needle position.5. Completion: Disconnect the probes and turn off or reset the voltmeter.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. With one battery, the voltmeter needle deflects to a certain position on the scale.2. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesAn analog voltmeter measures voltage by needle deflection proportional to the applied potential difference. When two identical batteries are connected in series, their voltages add. Therefore, the total voltage across the meter is higher than that of a single battery, causing a larger current through the meter mechanism and a greater needle deflection.

Preparation: Ensure the power supply is turned off. Check that the two light bulbs are identical and the ammeter is functioning properly.2. Circuit Connection: Connect the two identical light bulbs in series with the power supply and switch. Leave three accessible points (A, B, and C) in the circuit: A before the first bulb, B between the two bulbs, and C after the second bulb.3. Measurement at Point A: Insert the ammeter in series at point A. Close the switch to energize the circuit and record the ammeter reading.4. Measurement at Point B: Open the switch. Move the ammeter to point B, ensuring correct series connection. Close the switch and record the ammeter reading.5. Measurement at Point C: Open the switch again. Move the ammeter to point C. Close the switch and record the ammeter reading.6. End of Experiment: Open the switch, disconnect the power supply, and restore the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. After closing the switch, both light bulbs light up with the same brightness.2. The ammeter readings at points A, B, and C are equal or nearly equal.3. Changing the ammeter position does not affect the brightness of the bulbs.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesIn a series circuit, electric current has only one path to flow. According to the current law of series circuits, the current is the same at all points in the circuit. Therefore, when the ammeter is connected at different positions (A, B, and C), the measured current values are equal. This demonstrates that current does not get consumed by circuit elements; it remains constant throughout a series circuit.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Faraday Ice Pail with Gold-Leaf ElectroscopeI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Faraday Ice Pail DemonstrationSubject: Engineering – Electrical EngineeringObjective: To demonstrate electrostatic induction and charge redistribution using a neutral metal can connected to a gold-leaf electroscope when a charged object is inserted without contact.II. Experimental EquipmentMetal can (conductive, open top), insulating stand, connecting wire, gold-leaf electroscope, charged rod (glass or plastic) with insulating handle, charging material (silk or wool).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the metal can on the insulating stand. Connect the can to the terminal of the gold-leaf electroscope using a conducting wire. Ensure the can and electroscope are initially neutral; the gold leaves should hang together.2. Charging the Rod: Rub the rod with the appropriate material to give it a static charge. Hold the rod only by its insulating handle.3. Core Operation: Slowly lower the charged rod vertically into the metal can without touching the can or the wire. Keep the rod suspended inside the can for a short moment.4. Withdrawal: Slowly withdraw the charged rod from the can, again without making contact.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The gold leaves are not diverged, indicating no net charge.Rod Lowered In: As the charged rod enters the can, the gold leaves diverge, indicating induced charge separation and a net charge appearing on the electroscope.Rod Withdrawn: When the rod is removed, the gold leaves gradually collapse back together, showing the induced effect disappears when the external charge is removed.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates electrostatic induction. When a charged object is brought inside a neutral conductor without contact, charges within the conductor redistribute: opposite charges are attracted toward the inner surface and like charges move to the outer surface, flowing to the electroscope and causing leaf divergence. No net charge is transferred because there is no contact. When the charged object is withdrawn, charges redistribute uniformly again, and the electroscope returns to its neutral state.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Faraday ice pail electrostatic induction. Minimum assumptions: a neutral conducting can on an insulating stand, electrically connected to a gold-leaf electroscope; a charged rod held by an insulating handle; no physical contact during insertion.Phased Storyline: (1) Neutral setup verification with collapsed leaves; (2) Charged rod lowered into can causing immediate leaf divergence due to induced charge redistribution; (3) Rod held briefly with sustained divergence; (4) Rod withdrawn leading to gradual collapse of leaves. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Starch Gelatinization Degree Detection (Iodine Colorimetric Method)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Starch Gelatinization Degree Detection by Iodine Colorimetric MethodSubject: Engineering – Food and Bioprocess EngineeringObjective: To distinguish ungelatinized and gelatinized starch by observing their color reactions with iodine solution and to understand the relationship between starch structure and gelatinization degree.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentTest tubes (2, identical size), test tube rack, dropper, iodine solution (I2-KI), ungelatinized starch suspension (room temperature, opaque), gelatinized starch solution (heated in water bath until transparent or semi-transparent), safety gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean test tubes on a rack and label them A and B.2. Sample Addition: Add an equal volume (about 2–3 mL) of ungelatinized starch suspension into tube A; add the same volume of gelatinized starch solution into tube B.3. Iodine Addition: Using a dropper, add exactly one drop of iodine solution into tube A, then one drop into tube B.4. Mixing and Observation: Gently shake each tube to mix and immediately observe the color changes.5. Completion: Place the test tubes back on the rack and record observations; dispose of solutions properly after the experiment.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial state: Tube A contains a milky, opaque starch suspension; tube B contains a clearer, viscous starch solution.After iodine addition: Tube A rapidly turns blue–black, indicating a strong iodine–starch complex; tube B shows a much lighter blue, reddish-brown, or nearly unchanged color.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleIodine molecules can insert into the helical structure of amylose in starch, forming a blue–black complex. In ungelatinized starch, the granular and ordered helical structure remains intact, producing a strong blue–black color. During gelatinization, heating disrupts hydrogen bonds and destroys the ordered helical structure of starch, reducing iodine binding. Therefore, gelatinized starch shows a weaker or no blue coloration. The color intensity reflects the degree of starch gelatinization.

Experimental EnvironmentComputer with Python installed, code editor (such as VS Code or IDLE), terminal or integrated console, screen recording software (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Open a code editor on the computer.2. Create a new Python file.3. Define a list variable with values [1,2,3,4].4. Write a for loop that iterates through the list.5. Inside the loop, use the print function to output each element.6. Save the file.7. Run the Python program using the terminal or run button in the editor.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before running, the code editor displays the defined list and for loop.2. After running the program, the terminal prints the numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4.3. Each number appears on a new line, in the same order as in the list.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesIn Python, a for loop is used to iterate over each element of an iterable object such as a list. The loop assigns each list element to a loop variable in sequence. When the print statement is executed inside the loop, the current element is output to the terminal. Therefore, the terminal displays each list element one by one in the original order of the list.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstrate the basic mechanism of a Python for loop iterating over a list. Minimum assumptions: a visible code editor, a Python list [1,2,3,4], a for loop, and a terminal output. Expected phased storyline: (1) screen shows code editor with list and for loop; (2) user runs the program; (3) terminal displays outputs 1, then 2, then 3, then 4 in order. Key causal transition: executing the for loop causes sequential print outputs. Visibility constraints: code text and terminal output must be clearly readable, and the chronological order of actions must be preserved.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Tourmaline Pyroelectricity Detection (Paper Scrap Adsorption Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Tourmaline Pyroelectricity Detection Experiment (Paper Scrap Adsorption Method)2. Subject: Engineering - Geotechnical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the pyroelectric property of tourmaline by heating one end of a tourmaline crystal and observing its ability to attract light paper scraps.II. Experimental EquipmentTourmaline crystal (one piece, with clear crystal ends), alcohol lamp, matches or lighter, small dry paper scraps (confetti-sized), tweezers (optional), heat-resistant mat.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the alcohol lamp on a stable surface and scatter a small pile of dry paper scraps on the table. Ensure the tourmaline crystal is dry and clean.2. Heating Operation: Light the alcohol lamp. Hold the tourmaline crystal with your hand or tweezers and heat only one end of the crystal evenly in the flame for several seconds.3. Core Demonstration: Immediately after heating, move the heated end of the tourmaline crystal close to the paper scraps without touching them.4. Completion: Observe the phenomenon, then extinguish the alcohol lamp and place the tourmaline on a heat-resistant surface to cool.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before heating, the paper scraps remain still and are not attracted to the tourmaline crystal.2. After Heating: When the heated end of the tourmaline approaches the paper scraps, the scraps are attracted and jump toward or stick to the crystal.3. Cooling Effect: As the crystal cools, the attraction gradually weakens and disappears.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleTourmaline is a typical pyroelectric crystal. When its temperature changes due to heating, internal electric polarization occurs, generating opposite electric charges at the two ends of the crystal. The charged end creates an electric field that attracts nearby light neutral objects such as paper scraps through electrostatic induction, demonstrating the pyroelectric effect.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Do not touch the flame directly; avoid overheating the crystal.2. Keep paper scraps dry to ensure clear adsorption.3. Extinguish the alcohol lamp promptly after the experiment to ensure safety.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Pyroelectricity of tourmaline, defined as temperature-change-induced electric polarization producing surface charges. Minimum assumptions: a real crystal with polar axis, visible heating source, and lightweight neutral paper scraps susceptible to electrostatic attraction.Phased Storyline: (1) Setup phase: tourmaline crystal, alcohol lamp, and scattered paper scraps are visible and stationary. (2) Cause phase: one end of the crystal is heated by a visible flame. (3) Transition phase: immediately after heating, the crystal is moved toward the paper scraps. (4) Effect phase: paper scraps jump up or adhere to the crystal. Visibility constraints: close-up framing to clearly see flame contact, crystal end, and motion of paper scraps; continuous shot to verify causal order.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Effervescent Tablet Dissolving in Cold vs Hot WaterI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Effervescent Tablet Dissolving in Cold vs Hot Water (Bubble Rate Comparison)Subject: Engineering – Chemical EngineeringObjective: To compare the dissolution rate and gas release of identical effervescent tablets in cold and hot water, and to understand the effect of temperature on reaction kinetics and mass transfer.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical clear glass cups; ice water (0–5°C); hot water (70–90°C, visibly steaming); two identical effervescent tablets; thermometer (optional); heat-resistant gloves; camera on tripod (front view, fixed focus).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear glasses side by side on a flat surface. Fill one with ice water and the other with hot water. Ensure equal water volumes.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera directly in front of the glasses. Fix focus and exposure. Start recording or time-lapse mode.3. Core Operation: Simultaneously drop one effervescent tablet into each glass without splashing.4. Observation: Continue recording until bubbling largely subsides in both glasses.5. Completion: Stop recording, allow water to cool, and dispose of solutions safely.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both tablets sink and begin producing bubbles.2. During Reaction: The tablet in hot water releases bubbles much faster and dissolves more quickly; vigorous bubbling is observed. The tablet in cold water produces fewer bubbles and dissolves more slowly.3. Final State: The hot-water tablet dissolves completely earlier than the cold-water tablet.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleEffervescent tablets react with water to produce carbon dioxide gas. Increasing temperature increases molecular motion, reaction rate, and gas diffusion, leading to faster dissolution and more rapid bubble release in hot water compared with cold water.VI. Experimental PrecautionsUse heat-resistant gloves when handling hot water; ensure glasses are identical and water volumes equal; drop tablets simultaneously; keep camera fixed for valid comparison.

Phase 2 simultaneous tablet drop. Phase 3 immediate bubbling in both glasses, with hot water showing faster and denser bubbles. Phase 4 rapid completion in hot water while cold water continues slower bubbling. Visibility constraints: steady front view, fixed focus, clear bubbles, visible ice and steam for temperature verification.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Three Bulbs in Series and the Effect of Adding an Extra Bulb2. Subject: Engineering – Electrical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe that in a series circuit, adding an additional bulb causes all bulbs to become dimmer, and to understand the relationship between total resistance and current in a series circuit.II. Experimental EquipmentBattery (1, appropriate voltage), small identical bulbs (4), bulb holders (4), connecting wires (with clips), switch or manual wire disconnection point, flat tabletop.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the battery, three bulb holders, and wires neatly on a tabletop. Ensure all bulbs are identical and functional.2. Initial Circuit Setup: Connect three bulbs in series with the battery to form a closed loop. Ensure all connections are secure.3. Initial Observation: Close the circuit. Observe that the three bulbs glow steadily with similar brightness.4. Circuit Opening: Briefly open the circuit by disconnecting one wire so that current stops flowing.5. Inserting the Fourth Bulb: Insert a fourth identical bulb into the same series loop, extending the circuit while keeping all bulbs in series.6. Reconnection: Reconnect the circuit to close the loop.7. Final Observation: Observe the brightness of all four bulbs after reconnection.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. With three bulbs in series, all bulbs glow steadily at a certain brightness.2. When the circuit is opened, all bulbs go out.3. After inserting the fourth bulb and reconnecting the circuit, all four bulbs glow, but each bulb is noticeably dimmer than before.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleIn a series circuit, the same current flows through all components. Adding an extra bulb increases the total resistance of the circuit. According to Ohm’s law (I = V/R), when the total resistance increases while the battery voltage remains constant, the current decreases. As a result, each bulb receives less current and power, causing all bulbs to glow dimmer.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use identical bulbs to ensure a fair comparison of brightness.2. Open the circuit before inserting or removing bulbs to avoid short circuits.3. Ensure all connections are firm to prevent flickering or incorrect observations.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Series circuit behavior—adding a load (bulb) in series increases total resistance and reduces current, causing all bulbs to dim.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: A simple DC battery, identical bulbs, ideal series connections, and visible bulb brightness as an indicator of current.Phased Storyline:Phase 1 (Setup): On a tabletop, a battery and three identical bulbs are connected in series; camera shows a clear overview of the circuit.Phase 2 (Initial State): Circuit is closed; three bulbs glow steadily with equal brightness.Phase 3 (Intervention): A hand opens the circuit, inserts a fourth bulb into the same series loop, then reconnects the circuit.Phase 4 (Outcome): All four bulbs glow simultaneously but are visibly dimmer than before, clearly linking the action (adding a bulb) to the effect (reduced brightness).Visibility Constraints: The tabletop layout, wiring path, and bulb brightness before and after insertion must remain in view to verify causal transitions.

Basic InformationExperiment Title: Dissection and Observation of Pumpkin Male Flower (Incomplete Flower)Subject: Engineering – Agricultural EngineeringObjective: To dissect and observe a pumpkin male flower, verify that it is an incomplete flower by confirming the absence of pistil and the presence of calyx, corolla, and stamens.II. Preparation: Place the fresh male pumpkin flower flat on the dissection tray with the flower opening facing upward. Observe its external shape.2. Petal Removal: Use tweezers to gently remove the corolla (petals), exposing the internal reproductive structures. Avoid damaging internal organs.3. Longitudinal Dissection: Hold the flower steady and use a scalpel to cut the flower longitudinally from top to base, dividing it into two symmetrical halves.4. Internal Observation: Spread the cut halves slightly and observe the internal structures, focusing on the presence or absence of reproductive organs.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The male flower is an incomplete flower because it lacks a pistil. Through dissection, the internal structure reveals only male reproductive organs (stamens) along with accessory structures (calyx and corolla), confirming its classification as an incomplete male flower.

Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the flat table on stable ground. Ensure the table surface is clean and level.2. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates structural buckling under vertical compression. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Array Deduplication (Two-Pointer Method) Principle DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Array Deduplication Using the Two-Pointer Method2. Subject: Engineering - Computer Science - Data Structures and Algorithms3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate how the two-pointer method removes duplicate elements from a sorted array by observing pointer movement and array state changes.II. Experimental Materials1. A simple animation interface or presentation canvas2. A horizontally arranged sorted array of integers with duplicates, e.g., [1,1,2,2,3,3,4]3. Two visual pointers: slow pointer (blue) and fast pointer (red)4. Light, neutral background for clear contrastIII. Experimental Procedure1. Initialization: Display the array horizontally on a light background. Place both slow (blue) and fast (red) pointers at the first element of the array.2. Fast Pointer Movement: Move the fast pointer one step to the right to scan the array from left to right.3. Comparison Operation: At each step, compare the value at the fast pointer with the value at the slow pointer.4. Update Rule:   - If the values are the same, keep the slow pointer stationary and move the fast pointer right.   - If the values are different, move the slow pointer one step to the right and update its value to match the fast pointer value.5. Iteration: Repeat the comparison and update steps until the fast pointer reaches the end of the array.6. Result Display: Highlight the portion of the array up to the slow pointer to indicate the deduplicated result.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The array shows repeated numbers; both pointers start at the first element.2. During the Process: The red fast pointer moves through every element, while the blue slow pointer moves only when a new unique value is found.3. Final State: The left portion of the array (from index 0 to slow pointer) contains unique elements in sorted order.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe two-pointer method relies on the sorted property of the array. The fast pointer scans each element to detect changes, while the slow pointer tracks the position of the last unique element. When a new value is found, it is placed at the next position after the last unique value. This achieves in-place deduplication with O(n) time complexity and O(1) extra space.VI. Experimental Notes1. The array must be sorted for the method to work correctly.2. Pointer colors and labels should remain consistent throughout the demonstration.3. The animation should maintain clear left-to-right motion to reflect algorithm logic.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Demonstrate array deduplication using the two-pointer algorithm on a sorted array. Minimum assumptions: the array is sorted, duplicates exist, and two pointers operate with distinct roles.Phased Storyline: (1) Setup phase shows a horizontal duplicated array with labeled blue slow and red fast pointers at the start. (2) Scanning phase shows the fast pointer moving right and triggering comparisons. (3) Update phase shows the slow pointer advancing only when a new value is detected. (4) Result phase highlights the deduplicated prefix. Visibility requirements: clear pointer colors, labels, and consistent left-to-right motion to verify causal logic.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Magnetic Field Around a Straight Vertical Current-Carrying Wire2. Subject: Engineering - Electrical Engineering (Electromagnetism)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the magnetic field distribution around a straight vertical wire carrying DC current by the deflection of surrounding compasses; to understand the direction relationship between current and magnetic field; to verify that reversing the current reverses the magnetic field direction.II. Experimental EquipmentStraight copper wire (vertical, insulated except at ends), non-magnetic table with central hole, DC power supply or battery pack, switch, connecting wires, 6–8 identical magnetic compasses, camera or smartphone with fixed focus (for time-lapse), tape or markers for positioning compasses.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Insert the straight wire vertically through the hole at the center of the table, ensuring it is perpendicular to the tabletop. Connect the wire to the DC power supply through a switch, but keep the switch open.2. Compass Arrangement: Evenly place multiple compasses on the tabletop around the wire at the same radial distance, ensuring all compass needles initially point to geographic north when no current flows.3. Camera Setup: Fix the camera above the table, lock focus and exposure, and ensure all compasses and the central wire are clearly visible for time-lapse recording.4. Initial Observation (No Current): Record the initial state with the switch off; compass needles remain aligned north–south.5. Current On: Close the switch to allow DC current to flow through the vertical wire. Continue recording.6. Observation of Deflection: Observe and record the simultaneous deflection of all compass needles, forming a circular pattern around the wire.7. Current Reversal: Open the switch, reverse the battery connections to change current direction, then close the switch again.8. Observation After Reversal: Observe and record that all compass needles deflect in the opposite direction compared with the previous current direction.9. Completion: Open the switch, stop recording, disconnect the power supply, and restore equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. With no current, all compass needles point uniformly north–south.2. When current flows upward or downward through the wire, each compass needle deflects tangentially to an imaginary circle centered on the wire.3. All compasses show consistent clockwise or counterclockwise deflection depending on current direction.4. After reversing the battery connections, the deflection direction of every compass reverses.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesA straight current-carrying conductor generates a magnetic field in the surrounding space. The magnetic field lines form concentric circles around the wire, lying in planes perpendicular to the wire. The direction of the magnetic field is determined by the right-hand rule: when the thumb points in the direction of conventional current, the curled fingers indicate the magnetic field direction. Reversing the current reverses the magnetic field, causing opposite compass deflections.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use a non-magnetic table and supports to avoid interference.2. Ensure compasses are identical and placed at equal distances from the wire.3. Avoid large currents to prevent heating of the wire.4. Fix camera focus and position to ensure reliable time-lapse comparison.

manual: Experiment Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Packing Behavior of Coarse Sand and Mixed-Size Sand Under Tapping2. Subject: Engineering – Materials Science & Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how particle size distribution affects packing density and void ratio in granular materials by comparing uniform coarse sand and mixed-size sand in identical cylinders under repeated tapping.II. Experimental Equipment1. Two identical transparent cylinders (same diameter and height, with flat bottoms)2. Uniform coarse sand (single particle size, dry)3. Mixed-size sand (wide particle size distribution, dry)4. Flat, rigid solid surface (e.g., lab bench)5. Ruler or scale (for observing height changes, optional)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   a. Ensure both cylinders are clean, dry, and identical.   b. Place the two empty cylinders side by side on the solid surface.2. Filling Stage:   a. Pour uniform coarse sand into the first cylinder until it reaches a marked initial height.   b. Pour mixed-size sand into the second cylinder until it reaches the same initial height as the first cylinder.   c. Do not compact the sand during pouring; allow it to settle naturally under gravity.3. Initial Observation:   a. Observe and record that both sand columns have equal heights before tapping.4. Core Operation (Tapping):   a. Hold both cylinders upright and tap them simultaneously on the solid surface.   b. Apply the same tapping force and frequency to both cylinders.   c. Repeat tapping several times (e.g., 5–10 taps), keeping the cylinders vertical.5. Final Observation:   a. Place the cylinders back on the surface side by side.   b. Observe and compare the final sand heights in the two cylinders.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both cylinders show sand at the same height; sand appears loosely packed with visible voids.2. During Tapping: Sand particles rearrange and settle downward due to vibration.3. Final State:   a. The uniform coarse sand shows a small decrease in height.   b. The mixed-size sand shows a noticeably larger decrease in height and becomes more compact.   c. After tapping, the mixed-size sand column is lower than the coarse sand column.V. Summary of Experimental Principle1. Granular Packing Principle: The packing density of granular materials depends strongly on particle size distribution.2. Uniform Coarse Sand: Particles of similar size create larger voids that cannot be efficiently filled, limiting compaction even under vibration.3. Mixed-Size Sand: Smaller particles fill the voids between larger particles during tapping, reducing the overall void ratio and increasing packing density.4. Engineering Significance: Materials with well-graded (mixed-size) particle distributions achieve higher density and stability, which is critical in soil mechanics, concrete aggregates, and foundation engineering.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both sands are dry to avoid cohesion effects.2. Use identical tapping strength for both cylinders to ensure fair comparison.3. Keep cylinders vertical to avoid uneven settling.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Effect of particle size distribution on packing density of granular materials. Minimum assumptions: sand is dry, non-cohesive; cylinders are identical; tapping provides vibration energy enabling particle rearrangement.Phased storyline: (1) Setup phase – two identical transparent cylinders with equal-height sand, one coarse and one mixed-size, placed side by side. (2) Action phase – repeated tapping on a rigid surface, applied equally to both cylinders. (3) Result phase – visible settling of sand; mixed-size sand column becomes lower than coarse sand. Key causal transition: vibration allows particles to rearrange, smaller grains filling voids between larger ones. Visibility constraints: camera must clearly show cylinder height comparison before and after tapping from a fixed perspective.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Deck of Cards Sheared Sideways as an Edge-Dislocation AnalogueSubject: Engineering – Materials Science & EngineeringObjective: To use a stacked deck of playing cards as a physical analogue to visualize edge dislocation motion and shear deformation in crystalline materials through direct observation and time-lapse recording.II. Experimental EquipmentPlaying cards (1 full deck, 40–60 cards stacked neatly), flat table or desk, human hand (operator), camera or smartphone with tripod, time-lapse or fixed-focus recording mode.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the deck of cards neatly stacked on a flat table. Align edges so layers are parallel. Set the camera facing the side of the deck at table height. Fix focus and framing; do not adjust during recording.2. Initial State Recording: Start recording (or time-lapse). Ensure the deck remains stationary for a short moment to capture the initial undeformed state.3. Shearing Operation: Using one hand, gently push the middle region of the deck sideways, parallel to the table surface, while keeping the bottom cards in contact with the table.4. Holding and Release: Hold the sideways displacement briefly, then release the hand smoothly without disturbing the camera.5. End State Recording: Continue recording to capture partial recovery or relaxation of the deck. Stop recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The deck appears as a uniform rectangular stack with aligned edges.2. During Shear: Cards slide relative to each other, producing a stepped or offset profile; maximum displacement occurs near the pushed region.3. After Release: The deck partially returns toward its original shape, though some offset may remain due to friction.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment models an edge dislocation in crystalline materials. Each card represents an atomic plane. The sideways push introduces localized shear, analogous to the movement of an edge dislocation under applied stress. Friction between cards represents lattice resistance, and partial recovery after release reflects elastic deformation combined with irreversible slip. The demonstration visually explains how macroscopic shear can arise from layer-by-layer motion at the microscopic scale.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the table is level to avoid gravity-induced sliding. Apply force gently to prevent the deck from toppling. Keep the camera fixed to maintain consistent observation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Edge dislocation analogue using a sheared deck of cards. Minimum assumptions: cards act as discrete layers with friction; sideways force causes relative slip; camera view remains fixed.Phased Storyline: (1) Static, aligned deck on table (baseline). (2) Hand applies sideways force at the middle, causing progressive layer-by-layer slip and visible shear offset. (3) Hand releases; deck shows partial elastic recovery and residual offset. Visibility constraints: side view preferred to observe layer offsets; fixed focus required to verify temporal causality and continuity.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Phosphorus Detection in Egg Yolk by Molybdenum Blue MethodSubject: Engineering – Food and Bioprocess EngineeringExperiment Objective: To qualitatively detect phosphorus (phosphate) in egg yolk by forming molybdenum blue, and to understand the basic detection principle of phosphorus in food samples.II. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube on the rack. Ensure the egg yolk extract is uniformly mixed.2. Sampling: Use a pipette to accurately take 2 mL of egg yolk extract and add it into the test tube.3. Heating: Place the test tube into a boiling water bath and heat for about 2 minutes.5. Completion: Remove the test tube carefully from the water bath and place it back on the rack for observation.IV.
