manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Rotating Spoked Wheel under Adjustable Strobe Light (Wagon-Wheel Effect)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Rotating Spoked Wheel under Adjustable Strobe Light2. Subject: Engineering – Communications Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the wagon-wheel effect caused by temporal sampling, and to relate apparent motion to strobe flash frequency and sampling theory.II. Experimental EquipmentSpoked wheel mounted on a motor with adjustable steady rotation speed; adjustable strobe light with controllable flash frequency; dark room or light-shielded enclosure; camera on tripod with fixed focus and fixed position for time-lapse photography; power supplies.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the spoked wheel on a stable mount in a dark room. Fix the camera on a tripod facing the wheel and lock focus and exposure. Ensure ambient light is off.2. Initial Setup: Set the wheel to rotate at a constant, steady angular speed. Turn on the strobe light at a low flash rate.3. Core Operation: While the wheel continues rotating, gradually increase the strobe flash frequency in small steps without stopping the wheel.4. Recording: Use the fixed camera to record the wheel continuously (time-lapse or continuous video) as the flash rate changes.5. Completion: After observing several distinct apparent motion states, stop the strobe and motor, then save the recorded footage.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. At low flash rates, the wheel appears to rotate normally but with jerky, discrete positions.2. At specific flash rates, the wheel appears stationary, with spokes seemingly frozen in place.3. At slightly higher flash rates, the wheel appears to rotate slowly forward or backward, despite the actual rotation direction remaining unchanged.4. As the flash rate continues to increase, these apparent motion states repeat periodically.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe wagon-wheel effect is a temporal aliasing phenomenon. The strobe light samples the continuously rotating wheel at discrete time intervals. When the sampling frequency matches or is close to an integer multiple of the wheel’s rotation frequency, successive images align, producing apparent standstill or reversed motion. This demonstrates key principles of sampling, aliasing, and signal interpretation in communications engineering.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the wheel rotation speed is constant throughout the experiment.2. Keep the camera fixed; do not refocus or move it during recording.3. Change the strobe frequency gradually to clearly observe transitions between apparent motion states.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: the wagon-wheel effect as an aliasing phenomenon caused by discrete temporal sampling of periodic motion. Minimum assumptions: a rigid spoked wheel rotates at constant speed; illumination is provided only by an adjustable strobe; observation is from a fixed viewpoint. Expected phased storyline: (1) initial normal-looking but segmented rotation at low flash rate; (2) transition to apparent standstill when flash rate synchronizes with rotation; (3) emergence of slow forward or reverse apparent motion as flash rate slightly deviates; (4) repetition of these states as frequency increases. Visibility constraints: dark background, clearly visible spokes, stable camera perspective to verify apparent motion changes.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: AM Radio Transmission: Microphone Modulating Carrier Amplitude Observed on OscilloscopeSubject: Engineering – Communications EngineeringObjective: To demonstrate amplitude modulation (AM) by observing how a microphone signal varies the amplitude envelope of a high-frequency carrier on an oscilloscope as a person speaks softly and then loudly.II. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place all equipment on the lab bench. Power off the transmitter and oscilloscope. Fix the camera focus toward the oscilloscope screen.2. Connections: Connect the microphone to the audio input of the AM transmitter. Connect the transmitter output to the antenna. Connect the oscilloscope probe to the transmitter RF output or a monitoring test point.3. Instrument Setup: Power on the oscilloscope. Set time base to clearly display the RF carrier and its envelope. Set voltage scale to avoid clipping.4. Baseline Observation: Power on the transmitter with no speech input. Observe a steady carrier waveform with constant amplitude.5. Core Operation: Speak softly into the microphone for several seconds, then speak loudly. Maintain the same distance from the microphone.6. Recording and End: Observe and record the oscilloscope display. Power off all equipment after observation.IV. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAmplitude modulation (AM) encodes audio information by varying the amplitude of a high-frequency carrier in proportion to the instantaneous audio signal from the microphone. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Zinc Detection in Food (Dithizone Colorimetric Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Zinc Detection in Oyster Extract by Dithizone Colorimetric Method2. Subject: Engineering – Food and Bioprocess Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the qualitative detection of zinc ions in food samples by observing the color reaction between zinc ions and dithizone. Through adding dithizone solution and acetic acid buffer to oyster extract and shaking, students understand the basic operation of colorimetric analysis and the principle of metal ion detection.II. Experimental Reagents and Equipment1. Test tube (clean and dry, 10–15 mL capacity)2. Test tube rack3. Graduated dropper or pipette4. Oyster extract (pre-treated and filtered food sample)5. Dithizone solution (prepared in organic solvent, green in color)6. Acetic acid–sodium acetate buffer solution (pH about 4–5)7. Protective gloves and safety gogglesIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube on the test tube rack and wear safety goggles. Ensure the oyster extract is clear and free of suspended solids.2. Sample Addition: Use a pipette to accurately transfer 2 mL of oyster extract into the test tube.3. Reagent Addition: Add an appropriate amount of acetic acid buffer solution to the test tube to adjust the reaction environment.4. Color Reagent Addition: Add several drops of dithizone solution into the same test tube.5. Core Operation: Hold the test tube with fingers or a test tube holder and gently shake it for several seconds to ensure thorough mixing of the oyster extract, buffer, and dithizone solution.6. Observation: Place the test tube back on the rack and immediately observe the color change of the solution.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The oyster extract appears light-colored or nearly colorless; the dithizone solution is green before reaction.2. After Shaking: If zinc ions are present in the oyster extract, the solution changes from green to red or reddish-purple due to the formation of a zinc–dithizone complex.3. Result Judgment: The appearance of a stable red or purplish-red color indicates the presence of zinc; little or no color change indicates low or no zinc content.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe dithizone colorimetric method is based on the selective complexation reaction between zinc ions (Zn2+) and dithizone under weakly acidic conditions. In the presence of acetic acid buffer, zinc ions in the oyster extract react with dithizone to form a colored zinc–dithizone chelate. This complex exhibits a characteristic red or reddish-purple color, which can be visually observed or further quantified by colorimetric measurement. The color intensity is related to the zinc concentration, forming the basis for qualitative or quantitative zinc analysis in food samples.VI. Experimental Precautions1. The pH must be controlled using acetic acid buffer; improper pH may affect color development.2. Shake gently to avoid solution splashing or loss.3. Dithizone solution should be freshly prepared and protected from strong light.4. Dispose of waste solutions according to laboratory safety regulations.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Qualitative zinc detection in food using the dithizone colorimetric method under weakly acidic conditions. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: zinc ions are present in oyster extract; acetic acid buffer provides suitable pH; dithizone forms a colored chelate with zinc upon mixing. Phased storyline: (1) setup phase showing a test tube with 2 mL oyster extract; (2) reagent addition phase where acetic acid buffer and dithizone solution are added; (3) mixing phase with gentle shaking as the causal trigger; (4) result phase where a red or purplish-red color appears and stabilizes. Visibility constraints: the camera should clearly capture the liquid color inside the test tube before and after shaking to allow verification of the colorimetric change.

manual: Simulation Experiment Instruction Manual: Seismic Response Comparison between Soft and Hard Soil LayersI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Simulation Experiment of Seismic Response Comparison between Soft and Hard Soil Layers2. Subject: Engineering – Geotechnical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To visually compare the seismic response characteristics of soft soil and hard soil under the same vibration input, and to understand the amplification effect of soft soil during seismic loading.II. Experimental Equipment1. Vibration table (with adjustable and uniform vibration output)2. Two identical transparent containers (same size and shape)3. Soft clay (uniformly mixed, high water content)4. Dense gravel (well-graded, compacted)5. Fixing devices or clamps (to secure containers to the vibration table)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the vibration table on a stable surface and ensure it is powered off. Prepare two identical transparent containers.2. Soil Filling: Fill container A with soft clay, ensuring uniform consistency and no large air gaps. Fill container B with dense gravel and lightly compact it to represent hard soil.3. Installation: Fix the bottoms of both containers firmly onto the same vibration table, ensuring identical boundary conditions and vertical alignment.4. Initial Observation: Observe and record the initial static state of the soils in both containers.5. Vibration Operation: Turn on the vibration table and apply the same vibration intensity and frequency to both containers simultaneously.6. Observation Process: Continuously observe and compare the amplitude and deformation of the soil in container A and container B during vibration.7. Shutdown: Turn off the vibration table after clear differences are observed and allow the soil to return to rest.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before vibration: Both soft clay and dense gravel remain stable with no visible movement.2. During vibration: The soft clay in container A shows明显 larger amplitude deformation, surface waving, and overall stronger motion. The dense gravel in container B exhibits smaller amplitude movement and remains relatively stable.3. Comparison result: Under the same vibration input, the motion amplitude of soft clay is significantly greater than that of dense gravel.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on the seismic response characteristics of different soil types. Soft clay has lower stiffness and shear wave velocity, which leads to seismic wave amplification and larger deformation under vibration. Dense gravel has higher stiffness and energy dissipation capacity, resulting in smaller vibration amplitude. Therefore, under identical seismic excitation, soft soil layers amplify ground motion more than hard soil layers.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both containers are identical and firmly fixed to avoid boundary condition differences.2. Keep vibration parameters consistent throughout the experiment.3. Observe from the side to clearly compare soil deformation amplitudes.4. Avoid excessive vibration intensity that may cause soil spillage or container instability.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Comparison of seismic response between soft clay and dense gravel under identical vibration input, assuming linear vibration input, identical container geometry, and fixed boundary conditions. Minimum assumptions include uniform soil filling, simultaneous excitation, and visual access to soil deformation. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) Setup phase with two identical transparent containers fixed on a vibration table; (2) Activation phase where vibration starts uniformly; (3) Response phase where soft clay exhibits larger, more visible deformation while dense gravel shows restrained motion; (4) Comparison phase highlighting amplitude contrast. Visibility requirements: side view of containers, clear distinction of soil textures, and continuous view during vibration to verify causal and temporal relationships.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: LED Diode Allows Current in One Direction (Battery Polarity Flip)2. Subject: Engineering – Materials Science & Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the one-way conduction property of an LED diode by reversing the polarity of a coin-cell battery and observing changes in illumination.II. Experimental EquipmentLED (standard 3–5 mm, any visible color), coin-cell battery (e.g., CR2032), two short insulated wires with stripped ends, flat tabletop, fixed camera or tripod (focus locked for time-lapse), clean and dimly lit room (optional for visibility).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the coin-cell battery flat on the tabletop. Identify the positive (+) and negative (−) sides. Fix the camera position and lock focus.2. Wiring: Connect one wire from the positive side of the battery to the anode (long leg) of the LED. Connect the second wire from the cathode (short leg) of the LED to the negative side of the battery, forming a series circuit.3. Observation 1 (Forward Bias): Observe the LED. If correctly oriented, the LED lights up steadily.4. Polarity Reversal: Without changing the LED or wires, use hands to flip the battery so that the polarity is reversed relative to the LED.5. Observation 2 (Reverse Bias): Observe the LED again. The LED should turn off and emit no light.6. Optional Repeat: Flip the battery back to the original orientation to confirm repeatability.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: LED is unlit before completing the circuit.2. Forward Bias: When the battery polarity forward-biases the LED, the LED emits visible light.3. Reverse Bias: After flipping the battery, the LED does not emit light.4. Repeatability: Re-flipping restores illumination, showing consistent one-way conduction.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAn LED is a semiconductor diode that allows current to flow primarily in one direction. When forward-biased, charge carriers cross the p–n junction and recombine, releasing energy as visible light. When reverse-biased, the junction blocks current, preventing light emission. Reversing battery polarity switches between these two states, directly demonstrating diode one-way conductivity.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Avoid short-circuiting the battery without the LED in the loop.2. Do not apply excessive force to LED leads or battery.3. Maintain fixed camera focus and framing to ensure clear comparison of states.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Rotary Dimmer Knob Controlling Incandescent Lamp BrightnessI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Rotary Dimmer Control of Incandescent Lamp Brightness2. Subject: Engineering – Electrical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how a rotary dimmer knob adjusts the brightness of an incandescent lamp, understand the relationship between control input and electrical power delivery, and observe corresponding changes in light intensity.II. Experimental EquipmentWall-mounted rotary dimmer switch, incandescent bulb with lamp holder, household AC power supply, insulated electrical wiring (pre-installed), wall plate, camera fixed on tripod (focus locked), safety gloves (optional).III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Ensure the dimmer switch is correctly wired to the incandescent bulb and securely mounted on the wall. Confirm the bulb is intact and off. Fix the camera on a tripod, frame both the dimmer knob and bulb, and lock focus for time-lapse recording.Initial State: Set the dimmer knob to the minimum position; the bulb should be off or very dim.Core Operation: A hand slowly rotates the dimmer knob clockwise toward the maximum position. Pause briefly, then rotate the knob counterclockwise back toward the minimum position. Repeat once if needed for clarity.Observation and Completion: Observe brightness changes during rotation. After demonstration, return the knob to a low setting and stop recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The incandescent bulb is dark or faintly glowing.2. During Rotation Up: As the knob is rotated toward higher settings, the bulb gradually becomes brighter, with a warmer glow intensifying.3. During Rotation Down: As the knob is rotated back, the bulb’s brightness gradually decreases until it dims or turns off.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesA rotary dimmer controls the effective voltage and power delivered to an incandescent bulb, commonly using phase-angle control with a triac. Adjusting the knob changes the conduction angle of the AC waveform, altering the RMS voltage across the filament. Higher RMS voltage increases filament temperature and light output; lower RMS voltage reduces temperature and brightness. The smooth filament response produces continuous brightness variation.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use only incandescent bulbs; LEDs or CFLs may behave differently.2. Do not touch live wiring during operation.3. Rotate the knob slowly to clearly observe brightness changes.4. Ensure camera focus remains fixed to avoid visual inconsistency.

Experimental EquipmentTransparent Galton board with evenly spaced pegs; single top funnel; identical metal balls; vertical collection bins at the bottom; stable stand.III. Experimental Procedure1. Setup: Place the transparent Galton board upright on a stable surface, ensuring a front-on view with all pegs and bins visible.2. Loading: Put a batch of identical metal balls into the single top funnel.3. Release: Open the funnel or release balls one by one so they fall under gravity.4. Falling Process: Allow balls to collide with pegs, randomly deflecting left or right at each peg.5. Collection: Let all balls settle into the vertical bins at the bottom.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial: Bins are empty; balls begin falling from the top funnel.During: Balls bounce off successive pegs, creating zigzag paths with left-right randomness.Final: More balls accumulate in central bins, fewer in outer bins, forming a bell-shaped distribution.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleEach peg collision represents an independent random binary decision (left or right). With many identical trials, the sum of these random events produces a normal distribution. This demonstrates how stochastic processes in systems engineering can yield predictable aggregate behavior.VI. PrecautionsEnsure pegs are evenly spaced; use identical balls; keep the board vertical and unobstructed for clear observation.

Minimum assumptions: gravity-driven motion, identical balls, symmetric left-right deflection at evenly spaced pegs, and fixed vertical bins.Phased storyline: (1) Static setup—front-on transparent board with visible pegs and empty bins. (2) Action—balls released from a single top funnel, falling and deflecting at each peg. (3) Transition—paths diverge left and right while remaining downward under gravity. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Electrolysis Cell Showing Faster Gas Bubble Formation After Adding Supporting ElectrolyteI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Electrolysis Cell Showing Faster Gas Bubble Formation After Adding Supporting Electrolyte2. Subject: Engineering – Chemical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the role of a supporting electrolyte in increasing solution conductivity during electrolysis by visually comparing gas evolution rates in two identical electrolysis cells.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent electrolysis cells (2 identical), DC power supply (constant voltage), metal electrodes (same material and size, 2 pairs), connecting wires with clips, distilled water, potassium nitrate (KNO3) solid, balance or spatula, stirring rod, safety goggles, camera or smartphone fixed on tripod.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Put on safety goggles. Place two identical transparent electrolysis cells side by side. Add equal volumes of distilled water to each cell.2. Electrode Setup: Insert identical metal electrodes into each cell at the same spacing and depth. Connect both cells in parallel to the same DC power supply to ensure identical voltage.3. Initial Electrolysis: Turn on the power supply. Observe that both cells produce gas bubbles slowly at the electrodes.4. Addition of Supporting Electrolyte: Turn off the power briefly. Add a small, measured amount of potassium nitrate to the right-hand cell only. Stir gently until fully dissolved. Leave the left cell unchanged.5. Comparative Electrolysis: Turn the power supply back on. Fix the camera focus and start time-lapse recording. Allow electrolysis to proceed for a short, accelerated period.6. Completion: Turn off the power supply. Stop recording. Dispose of solutions according to laboratory waste rules and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both cells contain clear, colorless water with identical electrodes and minimal bubbling.2. After Adding Potassium Nitrate: The right cell shows a rapid increase in the number and size of gas bubbles at both electrodes.3. Comparison: Under the same voltage, gas bubble formation in the right cell is visibly faster and denser than in the left cell, which continues bubbling slowly.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplePure water has low electrical conductivity, so electrolysis proceeds slowly. Potassium nitrate acts as a supporting electrolyte, dissociating into ions (K+ and NO3−) that increase the solution’s ionic conductivity. Higher conductivity allows greater current to flow at the same voltage, accelerating the electrochemical reactions at the electrodes and resulting in faster gas evolution.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both cells and electrodes are identical to guarantee a fair comparison.2. Do not add excessive potassium nitrate; only enough to dissolve completely.3. Keep the camera fixed to ensure accurate visual comparison.4. Always turn off the power supply before adjusting electrodes or adding chemicals.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Supporting electrolytes increase electrical conductivity and electrolysis rate without being consumed. Minimum assumptions: two identical electrolysis setups share the same voltage source; potassium nitrate fully dissolves and does not participate in electrode reactions. Phased storyline: (1) establish identical initial electrolysis with slow bubbling in both cells; (2) add potassium nitrate only to the right cell; (3) resume electrolysis and show accelerated, denser bubble formation on the right while the left remains slow; (4) maintain fixed camera and time-lapse view to verify causal contrast. Visibility constraints: both cells must remain in the same frame, electrodes and bubbles clearly visible, with a stable viewpoint for direct comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Time-lapse Observation of Soybean Seed GerminationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Time-lapse Observation of Soybean Seed Germination2. Subject: Engineering – Agricultural Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe and verify the germination sequence of soybean seeds, demonstrating that the radicle breaks through the seed coat first and grows downward, followed by the plumule growing upward, using a simplified accelerated time-lapse method.II. Experimental EquipmentSoaked soybean seeds (5–10 seeds), transparent Petri dish or clear plastic dish, filter paper, clean water, dropper or spray bottle, fixed camera or smartphone with tripod, light source.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Soak soybean seeds in clean water for 6–8 hours to initiate germination. Cut filter paper to fit the dish and place it flat at the bottom.2. Setup: Moisten the filter paper evenly with water until fully damp but not flooded. Place soaked soybean seeds on the filter paper, spaced apart, with the hilum facing sideways if possible.3. Sealing and Positioning: Cover the dish with its transparent lid to reduce evaporation. Place the dish under a fixed camera in a well-lit environment, ensuring a close-up view.4. Time-lapse Recording: Keep the camera fixed. Record or simulate accelerated time-lapse to show sequential stages over a short duration.5. Observation Focus: Ensure the camera captures seed swelling, seed coat splitting, radicle emergence and downward growth, followed by plumule emergence and upward growth.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial Stage: Seeds absorb water and visibly swell.2. Middle Stage: The seed coat splits open.3. Early Germination: The radicle emerges first from the split seed coat and grows downward.4. Later Germination: The plumule emerges after the radicle and grows upward.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSoybean seed germination begins with water absorption (imbibition), activating metabolic processes. The radicle emerges first due to its role in anchoring the seedling and absorbing water and nutrients, exhibiting positive geotropism. The plumule subsequently grows upward, showing negative geotropism, developing into the shoot. This ordered emergence reflects the fundamental biological principle of seed germination.VI. Experimental PrecautionsMaintain moisture without flooding; keep the camera fixed; avoid disturbing seeds during observation; ensure sufficient light for clear imaging.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Cathodic Protection by Sacrificial AnodeI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Cathodic Protection by Sacrificial Anode (Zinc–Steel System)2. Subject: Engineering – Chemical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the principle of cathodic protection by sacrificial anode through visual observation of corrosion behavior in a simulated seawater environment, and to understand how a more active metal protects steel from corrosion.II. Experimental EquipmentBeaker (250–500 mL), sodium chloride solution (approximately 3.5% NaCl, simulating seawater), zinc block (sacrificial anode), steel component (steel strip or nail), conducting wire with clips, sandpaper (for surface cleaning), camera or recording device (for time-lapse observation), gloves and safety goggles.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Clean the surfaces of the zinc block and steel component with sandpaper to remove oxide layers; prepare sodium chloride solution and pour it into the beaker until it is about two-thirds full.Connection Stage: Use a conducting wire to firmly connect the zinc block to the steel component, ensuring good electrical contact.Immersion Stage: Place the connected zinc and steel together into the beaker so that both are fully immersed in the sodium chloride solution without touching the beaker walls.Observation Stage: Position the camera to focus on the beaker and metals; record the system using time-lapse photography to observe gradual changes.Completion Stage: After sufficient observation time, remove the metals, dispose of the solution properly, and clean all equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The sodium chloride solution is clear and colorless; zinc and steel surfaces appear metallic and shiny.2. During Immersion: Over time, the zinc surface gradually becomes dull, rough, or covered with whitish corrosion products, while the steel surface shows little or no rust formation.3. Final State: Zinc exhibits明显 corrosion, whereas the steel remains largely intact, indicating effective protection.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on electrochemical corrosion theory. Zinc is more electrochemically active than iron (steel). When electrically connected in an electrolyte, zinc acts as the anode and preferentially oxidizes, releasing electrons. Steel becomes the cathode, receiving electrons and thus being protected from oxidation. This process is known as cathodic protection by sacrificial anode and is widely used in marine and industrial corrosion prevention.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Cathodic protection by sacrificial anode, requiring the assumption of an electrolyte (saltwater), electrical connection between two dissimilar metals, and relative electrode activity (zinc more active than steel).Expected Phenomena Storyline: Phase 1 – Setup: A clear beaker of saltwater with zinc and steel electrically connected and immersed. Phase 2 – Initiation: After immersion, no immediate dramatic change, but system remains stable. Phase 3 – Progression (time-lapse): Zinc surface gradually dulls and corrodes, while steel maintains its appearance. Phase 4 – Outcome: Visible preferential corrosion of zinc confirms sacrificial protection of steel. The camera should remain fixed on the beaker, ensuring corrosion progression is visually verifiable.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Binary Tree Post-order Traversal Operation DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Binary Tree Post-order Traversal Operation Demonstration2. Subject: Engineering - Computer Science3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the post-order traversal process of a binary tree, understand the visiting order of nodes (left subtree, right subtree, root), and observe how traversal results are generated step by step.II. Experimental Materials and Environment1. A simple binary tree diagram with 7 nodes labeled 1–7.2. Light-colored background for clear visibility.3. Visual highlighting effect (bright color such as red) and brief glow animation.4. Horizontal output list displayed at the bottom of the screen.III. Experimental Operation Process1. Initialization: Display a simple binary tree with nodes labeled 1–7 on a light background. Ensure all nodes are in a neutral color and the output list is empty.2. Start Traversal: Begin post-order traversal from the root node.3. Left Subtree Traversal: Recursively visit the left child nodes. When a leaf node is reached, briefly highlight it in red with a glow effect.4. Output Update: After highlighting a node, append its label value to the horizontal output list at the bottom of the screen.5. Right Subtree Traversal: After completing the left subtree, traverse the right subtree using the same highlight-and-append process.6. Visit Root: Once both subtrees of a node are processed, highlight the parent node and append its value to the output list.7. Completion: Continue until all nodes are visited and the output list shows the complete post-order traversal sequence from left to right.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The binary tree is static; no nodes are highlighted, and the output list is empty.2. During Traversal: Nodes glow one by one in post-order sequence. Each glow is immediately followed by the appearance of the node’s value in the output list.3. Final State: All nodes have been highlighted exactly once, and the output list contains the full post-order traversal result.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Core Principle: Post-order traversal is a depth-first traversal method where each node is visited after its left and right subtrees.2. Logical Order: The visiting order strictly follows Left Subtree → Right Subtree → Root.3. Visual Mapping: Highlighting a node represents the moment it is visited; appending its value to the output list represents recording the traversal result.4. Educational Significance: This visual demonstration links abstract traversal algorithms with intuitive visual and sequential output, reinforcing understanding of binary tree operations.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Copper ElectroplatingI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Copper Electroplating on Iron Sheet2. Subject: Engineering - Chemical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To understand the basic process and principle of copper electroplating by observing copper deposition on an iron cathode and dissolution of a copper anode in copper sulfate solution under direct current.II. Experimental EquipmentDC power supply (low-voltage), iron sheet (to be plated), copper sheet (anode), copper sulfate solution (CuSO4, blue), beaker, connecting wires with clips, sandpaper, distilled water, support stand (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Polish the surface of the iron sheet with sandpaper, rinse with distilled water, and dry. Clean the copper sheet similarly.2. Setup: Pour an appropriate amount of copper sulfate solution into the beaker. Immerse both metal sheets vertically without touching each other.3. Connection: Connect the iron sheet to the negative terminal of the DC power supply (cathode). Connect the copper sheet to the positive terminal (anode).4. Energizing: Turn on the power supply to provide a steady low voltage current. Keep the setup stable.5. Observation and Recording: Focus the camera on the electrodes and solution. Use time-lapse photography to record changes after energizing.6. Completion: After sufficient time, turn off the power supply, remove the electrodes, rinse them with water, and dry.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Iron sheet is gray and clean; copper sheet is reddish-brown; solution is uniformly blue.2. Final State: The iron sheet is evenly coated with metallic copper.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesCopper electroplating is an electrolytic process. When direct current passes through CuSO4 solution, copper atoms at the anode lose electrons and enter the solution as Cu2+ ions. These ions migrate to the cathode and gain electrons, depositing as metallic copper on the iron surface.Anode reaction: Cu → Cu2+ + 2e-Cathode reaction: Cu2+ + 2e- → CuOverall principle: Electrical energy drives redox reactions to achieve metal coating.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Brownian Motion of Microspheres in Water as an Analog of Molecular Thermal MotionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Brownian Motion of Microspheres in Water as an Analog of Molecular Thermal Motion2. Subject: Engineering - Biomedical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe Brownian motion of micron-sized polystyrene microspheres under different temperature conditions using an optical microscope, and to understand the relationship between thermal energy and molecular-scale random motion.II. Experimental EquipmentOptical microscope with camera attachment, microscope slides or shallow glass dishes (2), cover slips (optional), aqueous suspension of micron-sized polystyrene microspheres, blue cooling pad, red warming pad, dropper or pipette, distilled water, camera control software for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Place two clean glass dishes on the laboratory bench. Add equal volumes of distilled water into each dish. Gently add a small drop of polystyrene microsphere suspension into each dish and mix lightly to ensure uniform dispersion.Temperature Setup: Place one glass dish onto the blue cooling pad and the other onto the red warming pad. Allow both dishes to equilibrate for a short time so that a stable temperature difference is established.Microscope Setup: Place the cooling-pad dish onto the microscope stage. Adjust illumination and focus until individual microspheres are clearly visible. Fix the microscope focus and camera position to prevent changes during recording.Recording: Start time-lapse photography or continuous video recording for a short period. After recording the cooling condition, carefully replace it with the warming-pad dish without changing the microscope focus. Record the microsphere motion under the warming condition using the same settings.Completion: Stop recording, save the image or video files, and remove the samples. Clean the glass dishes and return equipment to their proper places.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Microspheres appear as small, bright circular particles suspended in water, with no overall directional flow.2. Cooling Condition: In the dish on the blue cooling pad, microspheres exhibit slow, random, jittery motion with relatively small displacement over time.3. Warming Condition: In the dish on the red warming pad, microspheres show more vigorous random motion, with faster movement and larger displacement compared to the cooling condition.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesBrownian motion refers to the continuous, random motion of small particles suspended in a fluid, caused by collisions with thermally agitated molecules of the surrounding medium. Water molecules are in constant thermal motion, and their collisions with microspheres produce observable random trajectories. Increasing temperature raises the average kinetic energy of water molecules, leading to more frequent and forceful collisions. Therefore, microspheres at higher temperature (warming pad) display more intense Brownian motion than those at lower temperature (cooling pad). This experiment uses microspheres as a visible analog to illustrate molecular thermal motion.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure equal particle concentration and water volume in both dishes. Avoid convection currents caused by sudden temperature changes or mechanical disturbance. Keep microscope focus fixed during comparisons. Handle warming and cooling pads carefully to avoid burns or condensation effects.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Comparison of Slope Stability of Moist Clay Pile and Dry Sand PileI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Slope Stability: Moist Clay Pile vs Dry Sand Pile2. Subject: Engineering – Geotechnical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To visually compare slope stability of cohesive soil (moist clay) and non-cohesive soil (dry sand) under small external disturbance, and to understand the role of cohesion and internal friction in slope stability.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentFlat rigid table; moist clay (uniformly mixed, plastic state); dry sand (clean, loose); two identical measuring cups or scoops; optional ruler or scraper for shaping piles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Clean and level the table surface. Ensure moist clay is cohesive but not flowing, and sand is dry and free-flowing.2. Forming Piles: Use the same measuring cup to pour an equal volume of moist clay onto the left side of the table and shape it into a small conical pile. Pour an equal volume of dry sand onto the right side to form a similar pile.3. Initial Observation: Observe and note the initial slope angles and shapes of both piles before disturbance.4. Core Operation: Gently tap the table once or twice with your hand near the center, applying the same tapping strength for both piles.5. Final Observation: Observe the changes in shape, slope angle, and stability of each pile after tapping.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both piles stand stably on the flat table; the clay pile appears smoother and more cohesive, while the sand pile appears granular.2. After Tapping: The dry sand pile partially collapses, spreads outward, and its slope angle decreases noticeably. The moist clay pile shows little change, maintaining most of its original shape with only minor deformation.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleMoist clay contains water-induced cohesion between particles, providing shear strength even without confinement. Dry sand lacks cohesion and relies mainly on internal friction. When tapping introduces vibration, frictional resistance in sand is reduced, causing particles to rearrange and the slope to fail. Clay, due to cohesion, resists this disturbance and remains more stable. This demonstrates why cohesive soils generally exhibit higher slope stability than non-cohesive soils under small disturbances.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Simulation of Liquefiable Sand Reinforcement with Stone ColumnsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Simulation Experiment of Liquefiable Sand Reinforcement with Stone Columns2. Subject: Engineering – Geotechnical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the liquefaction-induced deformation of saturated loose sand under vibration and to compare the reinforcement effect of a stone column by observing differences between reinforced and unreinforced sand.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent container A (1), transparent container B (1); loose clean sand; water supply; stone column model (gravel-filled cylindrical column); vibration table; fixing clamps or frame; camera or observation window (for focused and time-lapse observation).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place containers A and B on a stable surface. Fill both containers with loose sand in layers and slowly add water until the sand is fully saturated, ensuring no trapped air.2. Reinforcement Setup: Insert the stone column vertically into the center of container A, extending from the base to near the sand surface. Container B remains without reinforcement.3. Fixation: Secure both containers firmly onto the vibration table to prevent sliding or overturning during vibration.4. Initial Observation: Observe and record the initial sand surface and internal structure through the transparent walls.5. Core Operation: Activate the vibration table at a fixed frequency and amplitude. Maintain vibration for a short, continuous period suitable for time-lapse presentation.6. Observation and Recording: Focus the camera on both containers simultaneously. Record the deformation process, including settlement, lateral spreading, and sand disturbance.7. Termination: Stop vibration, allow sand to stabilize, and record the final deformation state.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both containers show stable, saturated loose sand with flat surfaces; the stone column in A is clearly visible.2. During Vibration: Sand in container B shows rapid settlement, surface subsidence, and lateral deformation, simulating liquefaction behavior. Container A shows noticeably smaller deformation, with sand movement constrained around the stone column.3. Final State: After vibration stops, container B exhibits larger overall deformation, while container A maintains better structural integrity.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleLoose saturated sand is prone to liquefaction under cyclic loading due to excess pore water pressure buildup, leading to strength loss and large deformation. Stone columns reinforce liquefiable sand by increasing stiffness, providing drainage paths, and redistributing stress, thereby reducing deformation during vibration.VI. Experimental NotesEnsure full saturation of sand; keep vibration parameters consistent for both containers; focus observation on comparative deformation rather than exact time duration.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstrate liquefaction of saturated loose sand under vibration and the mitigating effect of stone column reinforcement. Minimum assumptions: loose sand fully saturated; vibration represents seismic loading; stone column acts as a stiffer, permeable inclusion. Phased storyline: (1) Static setup with two transparent containers on a vibration table, A reinforced and B unreinforced; (2) vibration starts, causing visible sand disturbance; (3) progressive deformation where B shows larger settlement and spreading while A remains relatively stable; (4) vibration stops with clear final contrast. Visibility requirements: side-by-side view, transparent walls, fixed camera, focused framing, and time-lapse acceleration to show deformation trends clearly.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Observation of Corn Grain StructureI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Observation of Corn Grain StructureSubject: Engineering – Agricultural EngineeringExperiment Objective: To observe the external shape and internal structure of corn grains, verify that the embryo is pale yellow and accounts for about one-third of the grain, and identify dent or hard kernel types through direct observation.II. Experimental Materials and ToolsCorn kernels (several, intact and mature), white tray or dish, small knife or scalpel, tweezers (optional), paper towel.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place several dry, intact corn kernels evenly on a white tray to ensure clear contrast for observation.2. External Observation: Select one kernel. Hold it between fingers and slowly rotate it to observe the front and side views, noting the overall shape and whether it appears dent-type or hard-type.3. Cutting Operation: Place the selected kernel flat on the tray with the embryo side facing upward. Using a small knife, carefully cut the kernel longitudinally along its long axis.4. Internal Observation: Gently separate the two halves. Observe the exposed internal structure, focusing on the embryo’s position, color, and proportion relative to the whole grain.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. External Phenomena: The corn kernel appears oval or wedge-shaped; dent-type kernels show a slight depression at the crown, while hard-type kernels have a smooth, rounded surface.2. Internal Phenomena: After longitudinal cutting, a pale yellow embryo is visible on one side of the kernel, occupying approximately one-third of the total grain volume. The remaining portion is mainly endosperm, appearing white or light yellow.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesCorn is a caryopsis, in which the seed coat is fused with the fruit wall. Its proportion (about one-third of the grain) and lateral position are stable biological characteristics. Kernel shape differences (dent or hard type) are mainly determined by the composition and arrangement of endosperm, which can be identified through external observation and rotation.VI. Experimental PrecautionsCut carefully to avoid injury; ensure the cutting direction is longitudinal to correctly expose the embryo; use mature, undamaged kernels for accurate observation.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Food Dye Diffusion Through Agar Gel with Pre-cut ChannelsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Food Dye Diffusion Through Agar Gel with Pre-cut Channels2. Subject: Engineering - Materials Science & Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe diffusion in a soft solid medium and understand how pre-cut channels influence mass transport pathways; to demonstrate time-lapse observation of diffusion phenomena.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentClear rectangular agar gel slab (approximately 10 x 5 x 1 cm) with visible pre-cut channels; food dye (water-soluble, high-contrast color such as blue or red); plastic dropper or pipette; flat table surface; absorbent paper; camera or smartphone with tripod; adequate lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clear rectangular agar gel slab flat on the table. Ensure the pre-cut channels are clearly visible on the surface. Adjust lighting to avoid glare.2. Camera Setup: Mount the camera on a tripod above or at an oblique angle to the agar slab. Fix the focus and exposure. Enable time-lapse or continuous recording.3. Core Operation: Using a dropper, place one small drop of food dye at a single edge of the agar slab where the channels open. Do not disturb the gel after placing the dye.4. Observation Period: Allow time to pass while recording. Do not add additional dye or move the setup.5. Completion: Stop recording after clear diffusion along the channels is observed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The agar gel is transparent or translucent, and channels are clearly visible; the dye is concentrated at the edge.2. Over Time: The dye gradually spreads into the agar from the point of contact, forming a color gradient.3. Channel Effect: Dye preferentially advances along the pre-cut channels, spreading faster within channels than through the bulk agar.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates diffusion in a gel, a soft solid with a porous network. Driven by concentration gradients, dye molecules move from regions of high concentration to low concentration. Pre-cut channels provide paths of lower resistance, increasing effective diffusivity along these routes. The process follows diffusion principles described by Fick’s laws, illustrating mass transport in materials with structured pathways.VI. PrecautionsUse a small amount of dye to avoid flooding channels; keep the agar surface intact; maintain fixed camera focus; clean the table after the experiment.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Diffusion-driven mass transport in a gel with engineered pathways (pre-cut channels). Minimum assumptions: agar is stationary, dye is water-soluble, diffusion dominates transport, and channels lower transport resistance.Phased storyline: (1) Static setup with clear agar and visible channels; (2) dye placement at one edge creates a concentration gradient; (3) time-lapse shows gradual, continuous dye spread; (4) dye advances preferentially along channels, forming smooth gradients. Visibility constraints: fixed camera, stable lighting, and clear view of channels and color front to verify causal diffusion behavior.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Chocolate Piece Softening and Liquefying When Gently HeatedI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Chocolate Piece Softening and Liquefying When Gently Heated2. Subject: Engineering - Energy Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe the physical process of heat transfer and phase change by demonstrating how a single piece of chocolate softens and liquefies when placed on a gently heated metal pan under steady heating conditions.II. Experimental EquipmentMetal pan (flat-bottomed), heat source (electric hot plate or alcohol burner with low flame), single piece of chocolate (uniform size), heat-resistant gloves or tongs, thermometer (optional), camera or recording device.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the metal pan on the heat source. Ensure the heat source is set to a low, steady output. Prepare the camera to record continuously.2. Placement: Put a single piece of chocolate at the center of the metal pan before heating begins.3. Heating Operation: Turn on the heat source to gently heat the pan. Maintain steady, low heat without direct flame contact with the chocolate.4. Continuous Observation: Record continuously for several minutes while keeping heating conditions unchanged.5. Completion: After the chocolate has clearly softened and liquefied, turn off the heat source and stop recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The chocolate maintains a solid shape with clear edges.2. Softening Stage: After heating, the chocolate surface becomes glossy and edges begin to round and slump.3. Liquefaction Stage: The chocolate gradually loses its solid form and spreads into a viscous liquid on the pan.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates heat transfer and phase change. Thermal energy is transferred from the heated metal pan to the chocolate by conduction. As the chocolate absorbs heat and reaches its melting temperature range, intermolecular forces weaken, causing the solid chocolate to soften and eventually liquefy. This is a physical change without chemical reaction, illustrating basic principles of energy transfer and material phase behavior.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use low, steady heat to avoid burning the chocolate.2. Avoid touching the hot pan directly; use protective equipment.3. Ensure continuous recording without interruption to capture the full process.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Curcumin Detection (Ethanol Extraction–Colorimetric Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Curcumin Detection in Chili by Ethanol Extraction–Vanillin–Sulfuric Acid Colorimetric Method2. Subject: Engineering – Food and Bioprocess Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To qualitatively detect curcumin in chili extract through a colorimetric reaction with vanillin–sulfuric acid reagent, master the basic color-developing operation of adding reagent and mixing, and understand the principle of acid-catalyzed color formation of curcuminoids.II. Experimental Reagents and Equipment1. Chili ethanol extract (prepared in advance, clear yellow to orange solution)2. Vanillin–sulfuric acid reagent (freshly prepared, colorless to pale yellow)3. Test tube (clean and dry, 10–15 mL capacity)4. Graduated pipette or micropipette (1 mL and 2 mL ranges)5. Test tube rack6. Protective gloves and safety gogglesIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube vertically on the test tube rack. Wear safety goggles and gloves to ensure safe operation.2. Sample Addition: Using a pipette, accurately transfer 1 mL of chili ethanol extract into the test tube. Observe that the solution is initially light yellow or orange and transparent.3. Reagent Addition (Core Demonstration Step): Using another pipette, add 2 mL of vanillin–sulfuric acid reagent slowly into the same test tube containing the chili extract.4. Mixing: Immediately hold the test tube and gently shake it back and forth or swirl it to mix the solutions evenly. Avoid splashing or spilling.5. Standing Observation: Place the test tube back onto the rack and observe the color change within a short time.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The chili extract appears light yellow to orange, transparent, with no precipitate.2. After Reagent Addition and Shaking: The solution rapidly develops a distinct red to reddish-brown coloration.3. Final State: The color becomes uniform throughout the solution, indicating successful color development.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCurcumin is a natural polyphenolic compound present in chili. In a strongly acidic environment provided by sulfuric acid, curcumin reacts with vanillin to form a stable colored complex. This acid-catalyzed condensation reaction produces a red or reddish-brown color, whose appearance indicates the presence of curcumin. The intensity of the color is related to the curcumin content and forms the basis of qualitative and quantitative colorimetric analysis in food engineering.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Vanillin–sulfuric acid reagent is strongly acidic; handle carefully and avoid skin contact.2. The reagent should be added slowly to prevent excessive heat release.3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how a capacitor connected across a DC motor can smooth voltage fluctuations from a pulsing power source, resulting in steadier motor operation, and to visually compare motor behavior with and without a capacitor.II. Experimental Equipment- DC motors (2 identical small DC motors)- Pulsing DC power source (e.g., rectified but unsmoothed supply)- Electrolytic cylindrical capacitor (appropriate voltage rating)- Connecting wires- Mounting base or bench- Camera or smartphone on tripod (fixed focus, time-lapse capable)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Secure the two identical DC motors side by side on the mounting base. Ensure both motor shafts are free to rotate without obstruction.2. Power Connection: Connect both motors to the same pulsing DC power source. One motor is connected directly to the source.3. Capacitor Installation: Connect the cylindrical capacitor in parallel across the terminals of the second motor, observing correct polarity.4. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesA pulsing DC power source provides voltage that rises and falls periodically. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Sine Wave Multiplied by Cosine Producing a Visible Beat EnvelopeI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Observation of Beat Envelope from Sine–Cosine MultiplicationSubject: Engineering – Electrical EngineeringExperiment Objective: To demonstrate that multiplying a low-frequency sine wave by a higher-frequency cosine wave using an analog multiplier produces an amplitude-modulated signal with a visible envelope on an oscilloscope; to understand the mathematical and physical principle of signal multiplication.II. Experimental EquipmentFunction generator A (low-frequency sine output); Function generator B (higher-frequency cosine or sine output with phase set to cosine); Analog multiplier module or IC (e.g., AD633); Dual-trace analog oscilloscope; BNC cables and probes; DC power supply for multiplier; Lab bench and fixed camera for time-lapse photography.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the analog multiplier and oscilloscope on the lab bench. Power off all instruments. Set the camera facing the oscilloscope screen and fix focus and position.2. Signal Setup: Configure function generator A to output a sine wave of low frequency (e.g., 10 Hz–50 Hz) and moderate amplitude. Configure function generator B to output a higher-frequency cosine wave (e.g., 500 Hz–2 kHz) with similar amplitude.3. Circuit Connection: Connect the sine wave to input X of the analog multiplier and the cosine wave to input Y. Supply the required DC power to the multiplier. Connect the multiplier output to Channel 2 of the oscilloscope.4. Reference Connection: Connect the original sine wave directly to Channel 1 of the oscilloscope as a reference.5. Observation Setup: Set the oscilloscope to dual-trace mode. Adjust time base and vertical scales so that both the sine wave and the multiplier output are clearly visible.6. Core Operation: Turn on both signal generators. Fine-tune frequencies so the sine varies slowly compared with the cosine.7. Recording: Observe the waveforms and record the oscilloscope display using the fixed camera.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Channel 1 shows a clean low-frequency sine wave.2. After Multiplication: Channel 2 shows a high-frequency waveform whose amplitude varies slowly over time.3. Key Phenomenon: The outline (envelope) of the Channel 2 waveform matches the shape and period of the original sine wave, forming a visible beat or amplitude modulation effect.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe analog multiplier outputs a signal proportional to the product of its two inputs. If the inputs are sin(ω1 t) and cos(ω2 t), the output is proportional to sin(ω1 t)cos(ω2 t) = 1/2[sin((ω1+ω2)t) + sin((ω1−ω2)t)]. When ω2 is much larger than ω1, the result appears as a high-frequency carrier with an envelope determined by the low-frequency sine. This experiment visually demonstrates signal multiplication and the origin of amplitude modulation and beat envelopes.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure correct power supply polarity for the multiplier; avoid overdriving inputs; keep probe grounds consistent; fix camera focus before recording to avoid visual artifacts.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Copper Pipe Joint Brazed with Silver Filler Flowing by Capillary ActionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Copper Pipe Sleeve Joint Silver Brazing by Capillary Action2. Subject: Engineering – Mechanical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how molten silver brazing filler flows into a copper sleeve joint by capillary action during brazing, and to observe the formation of a sound brazed joint.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo copper pipes (one sized to fit into the other as a sleeve joint), silver brazing rod, flux suitable for silver brazing (if required), gas torch, wire brush or abrasive cloth, heat-resistant gloves, fireproof work surface, camera with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Mechanically clean the outer surface of the inner pipe and the inner surface of the outer pipe using a wire brush or abrasive cloth until shiny. Wipe away debris. Apply a thin, even layer of flux to the joint surfaces if required.2. Assembly: Insert the smaller copper pipe into the larger pipe to form a sleeve joint with uniform overlap. Place the assembly horizontally on a fireproof surface.3. Camera Setup: Position the camera facing the joint seam. Fix the focus and framing to clearly show the joint area for time-lapse recording.4. Heating: Ignite the torch and heat the joint evenly, moving the flame around the circumference to raise the temperature uniformly. Do not directly melt the filler with the flame.5. Filler Application: When the joint reaches brazing temperature, gently touch the silver brazing rod to the seam. Allow the molten filler to be drawn into the joint by capillary action.6. Initial State: Copper pipes remain solid; silver filler does not melt when touched to a cold joint.2. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSilver brazing relies on capillary action, where molten filler metal is drawn into a narrow joint gap due to surface tension and wetting of the base metal. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Ensure the shake table is powered off and level. Inspect both building models to confirm the short model is rigid and the tall model is slender and flexible.Placement: Securely mount the short stiff model and the tall flexible model side by side on the shake table, ensuring both are firmly attached and aligned in the same shaking direction.Input Setting: Select or pre-program the same horizontal earthquake motion for the shake table. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Microcontroller Button Input Triggering LED Output in Real Time2. Subject: Engineering - Mechatronics & Robotics3. Experiment Objective: To understand how a microcontroller reads a digital input from a pushbutton and controls a digital output to drive an LED in real time; to observe the direct causal relationship between human input and electronic output.II. Experimental Equipment- Microcontroller board (e.g., Arduino Uno or equivalent, powered via USB)- Breadboard- Pushbutton (momentary switch)- LED (any visible color, e.g., red)- Current-limiting resistor for LED (220–330 ohms)- Jumper wires- USB power cableIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the microcontroller and breadboard on a tabletop. Ensure the microcontroller is powered and preloaded with a simple program that reads a digital input pin and sets a digital output pin accordingly.2. Wiring: Insert the pushbutton into the breadboard and connect it to a digital input pin and ground (or Vcc) using jumper wires. Connect the LED in series with a resistor to a digital output pin and ground.3. Initial Check: Power on the microcontroller. Do not press the button. Observe the initial LED state (typically OFF).4. Core Operation: Use a hand to press the pushbutton. Hold briefly, then release. Repeat pressing and releasing the button at varying rhythms (slow, fast, irregular).5. Observation Setup: Keep the camera fixed in position and focus throughout the experiment to allow clear time-lapse or continuous observation.6. Completion: After observation, stop pressing the button and power off the microcontroller if required.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: With no button press, the LED remains in a stable initial state (usually OFF).2. During Button Press: Each time the button is pressed, the LED immediately changes state (turns ON).3. During Button Release: When the button is released, the LED immediately returns to its original state (turns OFF).4. Rhythm Variation: As the pressing rhythm changes, the LED follows the same rhythm in real time, with no visible delay.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the basic principle of digital input-output control in mechatronics. The pushbutton acts as a digital input device, producing a HIGH or LOW electrical signal depending on its state. The microcontroller continuously reads this input and, according to its programmed logic, sets the output pin connected to the LED. The LED, as an output actuator, converts the electrical signal into visible light. This real-time response illustrates closed-loop human–machine interaction at a fundamental level.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure correct wiring to avoid short circuits.2. Always use a current-limiting resistor with the LED.3. Do not change wiring while the board is powered.4. Keep the tabletop and components stable to maintain clear observation.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Rapid Cooling of Molten Sugar to Form Candy Glass (Amorphous Solid)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Rapid Cooling of Molten Sugar to Form Clear Candy Glass2. Subject: Engineering – Materials Science & Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how rapid cooling inhibits crystallization and leads to the formation of an amorphous solid (candy glass) by comparing molten sugar cooled rapidly on an ice-cooled metal slab with molten sugar cooled slowly at room temperature; to observe differences in transparency, brittleness, and fracture behavior.II. Experimental EquipmentGranulated sugar (approximately 200 g), heat-resistant saucepan or beaker, hot plate or stove, thermometer (range up to 200 °C), two shallow trays (metal or silicone), one thick metal slab, ice bath (ice and water), heat-resistant gloves, spatula or spoon, camera mounted on tripod (fixed focus for time-lapse photography).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the metal slab on the bench and position it in an ice bath so that the slab is thoroughly cooled. Place one shallow tray directly on the ice-cooled metal slab. Place the second shallow tray on the bench at room temperature. Set up the camera on a tripod, framing both trays in view, and fix focus and exposure for time-lapse recording.2. Melting Sugar: Add granulated sugar to the saucepan or beaker and heat slowly on the hot plate. Stir gently as the sugar melts. Monitor the temperature; continue heating until the sugar becomes a clear, bubble-free molten liquid (approximately 160–170 °C).3. Pouring Operation: Carefully pour equal amounts of molten sugar into each shallow tray, one on the ice-cooled slab and one at room temperature. Do not disturb or move the trays after pouring.4. Cooling and Recording: Allow both samples to cool undisturbed while the camera records the cooling process. Observe the difference in cooling speed and appearance as the sugar solidifies.5. Mechanical Test: After complete cooling, gently flex or snap each sugar sample by hand (using gloves). Observe and compare the fracture behavior.6. Cleanup: Turn off heating equipment, allow remaining materials to cool, and clean utensils after the sugar has solidified.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Rapidly Cooled Sample (Ice-Cooled Slab): The sugar solidifies quickly into a clear, transparent, glass-like solid. The surface is smooth and shiny. When flexed or snapped, it breaks sharply with a brittle fracture, producing clean edges.2. Slowly Cooled Sample (Room Temperature): The sugar cools more slowly and appears cloudy or slightly opaque due to crystallization. The surface may show grainy texture. When snapped, it fractures less cleanly and may crumble along crystalline boundaries.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWhen molten sugar cools, its molecules may either arrange into an ordered crystalline structure or become frozen in a disordered arrangement. Rapid cooling on an ice-cooled metal slab removes heat quickly, preventing molecules from organizing into crystals. As a result, the sugar forms an amorphous solid known as candy glass, which is transparent and brittle. In contrast, slow cooling at room temperature allows time for crystallization, leading to a cloudy, polycrystalline solid. This experiment illustrates the relationship between cooling rate, molecular arrangement, and material properties, a core concept in materials science.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Molten sugar is extremely hot and can cause severe burns; always wear heat-resistant gloves.2. Do not stir or disturb the sugar after pouring, as this may induce crystallization.3. Ensure the camera focus and position are fixed before pouring to maintain consistent time-lapse recording.4. Handle hardened sugar carefully to avoid sharp fragments during snapping.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Rapid cooling suppresses crystallization, producing an amorphous solid (candy glass). Minimum mechanistic assumptions: molten sugar behaves as a viscous liquid; heat extraction rate controls molecular mobility and ordering. Expected phased storyline: Phase 1 – clear molten sugar poured equally into two trays; Phase 2 – rapid solidification on ice-cooled metal versus slower cooling at room temperature, visible as faster hardening and higher transparency; Phase 3 – mechanical test showing brittle, sharp fracture for rapidly cooled sample and less clean fracture for slowly cooled sample. Visibility constraints: both trays must remain in frame with fixed camera focus, allowing side-by-side temporal comparison and clear observation of transparency and fracture behavior.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Electromagnet with Iron Core vs Air Core Lifting Metal ObjectsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Iron-Core and Air-Core Electromagnets2. Subject: Engineering – Energy Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To compare the magnetic lifting ability of an iron-core electromagnet and an air-core electromagnet under the same power conditions, and to understand the role of an iron core in enhancing magnetic field strength.II. Experimental EquipmentDC power supply (one, adjustable low voltage), switch (one, controlling both coils simultaneously), insulated copper wire coils (two identical coils), soft iron core (one, inserted into one coil), connecting wires, steel washers (identical, multiple), non-magnetic tabletop, camera or smartphone on tripod (focus fixed for time-lapse).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place steel washers in two equal stacks on the tabletop. Position the two coils vertically above the stacks at the same height; insert the iron core into one coil and leave the other as air-core. Fix the camera focus and framing.2. Circuit Connection: Connect both coils in parallel to the same DC power supply through a single switch, ensuring identical voltage for both.3. Core Operation: Turn on the camera recording. Flip the switch to turn on the power to both coils simultaneously and keep it on briefly. Then turn the switch off to cut power to both coils together.4. Completion: Stop recording after observing the full on–off cycle. Disconnect the power supply.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Power Off (Initial): Both coils show no attraction; washers remain on the tabletop.2. Power On: Both coils attract washers upward. The iron-core electromagnet lifts more washers and/or lifts them faster and more stably than the air-core electromagnet.3. Power Off Again: Washers drop back to the tabletop as magnetism disappears.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleWhen electric current flows through a coil, it generates a magnetic field. Inserting an iron core greatly increases the magnetic field strength because the iron becomes magnetized and concentrates magnetic flux. Under the same power supply, an iron-core electromagnet therefore produces a stronger magnetic force than an air-core electromagnet, allowing it to lift more metal objects. When the current is switched off, the magnetic field collapses and the attraction disappears.VI. Precautions1. Use low voltage to avoid overheating the coils.2. Ensure both coils receive the same voltage for a fair comparison.3. Keep the camera fixed to clearly compare changes over time.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Pushbutton Switch Driving an LED Fully On or Fully OffI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Pushbutton Switch Driving an LED Fully On or Fully Off2. Subject: Engineering - Electrical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how a momentary pushbutton switch controls the on and off state of an LED in a simple series circuit, understand basic circuit switching principles, and observe direct cause-and-effect between human operation and electrical response.II. Experimental EquipmentBreadboard or tabletop circuit base, low-voltage DC power source (e.g., 3–5 V battery pack), momentary pushbutton switch, single LED, current-limiting resistor (e.g., 220–330 ohms), connecting wires, camera mounted above the tabletop (focus fixed for time-lapse), human hand for operation.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Place the breadboard or circuit base on a stable tabletop. Fix the camera above the circuit, adjust framing so all components are visible, and lock the focus to avoid refocusing during recording.Circuit Assembly: Connect the positive terminal of the power source to one terminal of the pushbutton. Connect the other pushbutton terminal to the resistor, then connect the resistor to the anode (long leg) of the LED. Connect the cathode (short leg) of the LED back to the negative terminal of the power source, forming a complete series circuit.Initial Check: Without pressing the pushbutton, observe the LED to confirm it is off, indicating the circuit is open.Core Operation: Using a hand, press and hold the pushbutton. After a short moment, release the pushbutton. Repeat this press-and-release action several times at a steady rhythm suitable for time-lapse capture.End of Experiment: Stop pressing the button, disconnect the power source, and end recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The LED remains completely off when the pushbutton is not pressed.2. During Button Press: Each time the pushbutton is pressed, the LED immediately lights up brightly.3. During Button Release: When the pushbutton is released, the LED immediately turns fully off.4. Repeated Operation: With repeated pressing and releasing, the LED correspondingly switches on and off in sync with the hand motion.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the basic principle of an electrical switch in a series circuit. A momentary pushbutton acts as a normally open switch. When pressed, it closes the circuit, allowing current to flow from the power source through the resistor and LED, causing the LED to emit light. The resistor limits current to protect the LED. When the button is released, the circuit opens, current stops, and the LED turns off. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Smoke Streaklines over an Airfoil in a Wind TunnelI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Observation of Smoke Streaklines over an Airfoil in a Wind TunnelSubject: Engineering – Aerospace EngineeringObjective: To visualize airflow patterns around a thin airfoil at different angles of attack using smoke streaklines, and to understand the aerodynamic principles of lift and flow separation under steady airflow conditions.II. Experimental EquipmentLow-speed wind tunnel with transparent test section; thin airfoil model with rotation mount; angle-of-attack adjustment mechanism with scale; smoke generator and injector nozzle; uniform lighting source; camera mounted on tripod with fixed focus for time-lapse photography.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ensure the wind tunnel is off. Mount the thin airfoil horizontally at zero angle of attack in the center of the test section. Check that the rotation mechanism moves smoothly.2. Smoke Setup: Position the smoke injector upstream of the airfoil so that multiple thin, continuous smoke lines enter the test section parallel to the airflow.3. Camera Setup: Place the camera perpendicular to the test section window. Fix focus, exposure, and framing. Do not change settings during the experiment.4. Start Airflow: Turn on the wind tunnel and adjust to a steady, uniform airflow speed. Confirm that smoke forms clear, straight streaklines upstream.5. Core Operation: Gradually rotate the airfoil to increase the angle of attack in small increments, holding each angle briefly. Maintain steady airflow and continuous smoke injection.6. Recording: Capture time-lapse images or continuous video during the entire rotation process.7. Shutdown: Return the airfoil to zero angle of attack, turn off smoke generation, then stop the wind tunnel.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: At zero angle of attack, smoke streaklines remain nearly straight and symmetric above and below the airfoil.Increasing Angle of Attack: Smoke lines curve over the upper surface and slightly compress below, indicating changes in airflow velocity and pressure.Higher Angle of Attack: Curvature increases; near the upper surface, smoke may thicken or become irregular, indicating flow separation.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates fundamental aerodynamic principles. According to fluid dynamics and Bernoulli’s principle, increasing angle of attack alters the pressure distribution around the airfoil. Air accelerates over the upper surface, creating lower pressure and lift. At high angles of attack, adverse pressure gradients cause boundary-layer separation, visible as disturbed smoke streaklines.VI. PrecautionsEnsure steady airflow before adjusting angle of attack; avoid sudden rotation; keep camera focus fixed; ensure adequate ventilation when using smoke.

Phase 3 – At higher angles, reveal visible disturbance or separation in smoke streaklines. Visibility Constraints: Camera remains fixed, side-on view of the transparent test section, ensuring continuous observation of airflow evolution without cuts.
