manual: Instructions for the Experiment Salt Dissolving in Water Enables Electrical ConductionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Salt Dissolving in Water Enables Electrical Conduction2. Subject: Engineering – Chemical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that pure water conducts electricity poorly, while salt dissolved in water forms ions that enable electrical conduction between electrodes, verified through a simple circuit with a bulb.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical clear glass beakers; distilled (pure) water; table salt (sodium chloride); two pairs of identical metal electrodes; two identical low-voltage batteries; two identical small bulbs; connecting wires; switch; camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Place two clean, clear beakers side by side on a stable table. Pour equal volumes of pure water into both beakers. Label one beaker Pure Water and the other Salt Solution.Solution Preparation: Add a small measured amount of salt into the Salt Solution beaker and stir until completely dissolved. Ensure the Pure Water beaker remains unchanged and clear.Circuit Setup: Insert identical metal electrodes into each beaker, ensuring equal immersion depth and no contact between electrodes. Connect each pair of electrodes to an identical circuit consisting of a battery, switch, and bulb.Camera Setup: Fix the camera focus and position so both beakers, electrodes, batteries, and bulbs are clearly visible in the same frame for time-lapse photography.Core Operation: Simultaneously close the switches of both circuits.Observation and Completion: Observe the bulbs for several seconds, then open the switches. End the recording and clean up the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before switching on, both bulbs are off; both liquids are colorless and transparent.2. Stable State: The brightness difference remains stable during the observation period.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesPure water contains very few free ions and therefore has very low electrical conductivity. When salt dissolves in water, it dissociates into sodium and chloride ions, which act as charge carriers. Under an applied voltage, these ions move between electrodes, allowing electric current to flow and lighting the bulb. The experiment visually demonstrates the relationship between ionic concentration and electrical conductivity.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use low-voltage batteries to ensure safety.2. Ensure electrodes are identical and inserted to the same depth to maintain fairness.3. Avoid touching electrodes while the circuit is closed.4. Keep the camera fixed to ensure clear comparison.

Experiment Title: Soil Phosphorus Content Detection by Molybdenum Blue Colorimetric Method2. Subject: Engineering – Civil & Environmental Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the color development reaction of phosphate in soil digestion solution using ammonium molybdate–ascorbic acid reagent, and to understand the principle of phosphorus determination by molybdenum blue colorimetry.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (clean and dry), test tube rack, graduated pipette or micropipette (2 ml), dropper, boiling water bath, phosphorus-containing soil digestion solution, ammonium molybdate–ascorbic acid reagent, test tube holder or clamp, protective gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube on the rack and ensure the water bath is heated to boiling. Wear protective equipment.2. Sampling: Use a pipette to accurately transfer 2 ml of the phosphorus-containing soil digestion solution into the test tube.3. Reagent Addition: Add 3 drops of ammonium molybdate–ascorbic acid reagent into the test tube using a dropper. Gently mix without splashing.4. Heating: Place the test tube into the boiling water bath and heat for approximately 1 minute.5. Observation and Recording: Keep the camera focused on the test tube and perform time-lapse photography to capture the color change process.6. Completion: Remove the test tube from the water bath and place it back on the rack for final observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesIn acidic conditions, phosphate ions in the soil digestion solution react with ammonium molybdate to form phosphomolybdic acid. Experiment Title: Simulation Experiment of Accelerating Soft Soil Consolidation with Vacuum Preloading2. Subject: Engineering – Geotechnical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the principle of vacuum preloading for accelerating soft soil consolidation by comparing the settlement behavior and surface smoothness of clay under atmospheric conditions and vacuum conditions.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo transparent containers of identical size; soft clay slurry (uniformly mixed); sealing lid with vacuum interface (for container B); vacuum pump with tubing; ruler or scale (optional, for reference); camera for fixed-point time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fill two identical transparent containers with the same amount and height of soft clay slurry, ensuring similar initial water content and surface level.2. Core Operation: Start the vacuum pump to evacuate air from container B, maintaining a stable negative pressure. Container A remains undisturbed and open.5. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Box-Muller Transform Normal Random Number Generation VisualizationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Box-Muller Transform Normal Random Number Generation Visualization2. Subject: Engineering – Scientific Computing3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate how two independent uniform random variables can be transformed into normally distributed random variables using the Box-Muller transform, and to understand the causal relationship between uniform and normal distributions.II. Experimental Environment and ToolsComputer with programming or visualization environment (e.g., Python/Matlab), random number generator capable of producing uniform random numbers, plotting tool supporting scatter plots and split-screen display.III. Experimental Procedure1. Initialization: Set up a split-screen display with two coordinate plots of equal size. Label the left plot as U1–U2 and the right plot as Z1–Z2.2. Uniform Random Number Generation: Continuously generate pairs of independent uniform random numbers U1 and U2 in the interval (0,1). Plot them as black scatter points in the left panel.3. Box-Muller Transformation: Apply the Box-Muller formulas Z1 = sqrt(-2 ln U1) cos(2πU2) and Z2 = sqrt(-2 ln U1) sin(2πU2) to each pair.4. Normal Scatter Plotting: Plot the resulting Z1 and Z2 as blue scatter points in the right panel.5. Annotation and Update: Add the text annotation ‘Box-Muller Transform: Uniform→Normal’ to the right panel. Update both panels synchronously as new points are generated.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The left panel shows uniformly scattered black points filling a square region; the right panel begins with sparse blue points.2. Dynamic Process: As points accumulate, the left panel remains uniformly filled, while the right panel gradually forms a dense center with fewer points outward.3. Final Observation: The right panel clearly exhibits a bell-shaped clustering characteristic of a two-dimensional normal distribution, contrasting with the uniform pattern on the left.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe Box-Muller transform is a mathematical method that converts two independent uniform(0,1) random variables into two independent standard normal random variables. By applying logarithmic and trigonometric operations, the uniform randomness is redistributed into a Gaussian form. This experiment visually confirms the principle that normal distributions can be generated from uniform random numbers through deterministic transformation.VI. Notes and PrecautionsEnsure U1 is never exactly zero to avoid logarithm errors; maintain consistent axis scales for both plots; focus on synchronous updates to clearly show causality.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Visual demonstration of the Box-Muller transform converting uniform random variables into normally distributed variables. Minimum assumptions: existence of independent uniform random number generator, correct mathematical transform, and 2D scatter visualization.Expected phased storyline: Phase 1 shows a stable split-screen layout. Phase 2 displays continuous generation of black uniform scatter on the left. Phase 3 introduces simultaneous blue scatter on the right after transformation. Phase 4 reveals causal contrast: left remains uniform while right forms a bell-shaped cluster. Visibility constraints: both panels must be visible at all times, colors and annotation must be readable, and updates must occur synchronously to verify causality.

Experiment Title: Effect of Airflow on the Melting Speed of Wax Droplets2. Subject: Engineering – Nuclear Engineering (Heat Transfer Demonstration)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how airflow enhances convective heat transfer by comparing the melting speed of two identical wax droplets on a heated metal surface, one in still air and one under steady airflow.II. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Heat Conduction Comparison of Metal, Wood, and Plastic RodsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Heat Conduction in Metal, Wood, and Plastic Rods2. Subject: Engineering – Nuclear Engineering (Heat Transfer Fundamentals)3. Experiment Objective: To compare the heat conduction ability of metal, wood, and plastic by observing the melting sequence of wax dots along rods heated at one end, and to understand the concept of thermal conductivity.II. Experimental EquipmentMetal rod, wooden rod, plastic rod (equal length and diameter); candle or alcohol lamp (heat source); wax (to form small dots); stand or heat-resistant support; ruler or marker; lighter or matches; camera with fixed focus (for time-lapse recording); heat-resistant gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the three rods horizontally on a heat-resistant support, parallel to each other. Ensure equal spacing and that one end of each rod is aligned.2. Wax Placement: Place small, evenly spaced wax dots along the length of each rod, starting near the heated end and extending toward the far end.3. Camera Setup: Position the camera facing the rods from the side or above. Fix the focus and framing so all rods and wax dots are clearly visible. Start time-lapse recording.4. Heating Operation: Simultaneously apply heat to one aligned end of all three rods using the candle or alcohol lamp. Maintain a constant flame position.5. Observation Period: Allow heating to continue while recording, until clear differences in wax melting are observed along the rods.6. Completion: Remove the heat source, stop recording, and allow rods to cool before handling.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: All wax dots are solid and intact on the three rods.2. During Heating: Wax on the metal rod near the heated end melts first and successively melts farther dots; wax on the wooden rod melts more slowly and over a shorter distance; wax on the plastic rod melts last or only near the heated end.3. Final State: The extent and speed of wax melting follow the order: metal > wood > plastic.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesHeat is transferred along a solid by conduction. Different materials have different thermal conductivities. Metal has high thermal conductivity, so heat travels quickly along it, melting wax dots in sequence. Wood and plastic are poor conductors (insulators), so heat spreads slowly, resulting in delayed or limited wax melting. This experiment visually demonstrates the relative heat conduction properties of materials.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure rods are of similar size to allow fair comparison.2. Apply heat simultaneously and at the same position on each rod.3. Avoid touching heated rods directly; use gloves.4. Keep the camera fixed to ensure accurate time-lapse comparison.

Expected phenomena storyline: (Phase 1) All rods with intact wax dots under fixed camera view; (Phase 2) Heating begins at one end, with no immediate change elsewhere; (Phase 3) Wax near the heated end of the metal rod melts first, followed by progressive melting along the metal, while wood shows slower, limited melting and plastic shows minimal delay-melting; (Phase 4) Clear material-dependent differences are visible before heating stops. Visibility constraints: all rods must remain in frame, wax dots clearly visible, fixed focus and stable perspective to verify temporal order and causal heat transfer.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Mass–Spring–Damper Struck Briefly with a MalletI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Transient Vibration Response of a Mass–Spring–Damper System Under Impulse Excitation2. Subject: Engineering – Mechanical Engineering (Dynamics and Vibrations)3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the transient vibration response of a mass–spring–damper system when subjected to a brief external impulse; to relate the observed oscillatory motion and decay characteristics to system parameters such as mass, stiffness, and damping; to visually record the process using fixed-focus time-lapse or accelerated photography.II. Experimental EquipmentMass–spring–damper assembly (one mass attached to a linear spring and viscous damper), rigid bench or support frame, rubber mallet (soft head), clamp or fixture for hanging the system from the bench edge or frame, high-speed or time-lapse capable camera with tripod, ruler or scale marker (optional, for displacement reference), adequate lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   Secure the mass–spring–damper system to the bench or support frame so that it hangs vertically and can move freely in one dimension. Ensure the spring and damper are aligned vertically and not touching surrounding objects. Place a visible scale or marker behind the mass if displacement estimation is desired.2. Camera Setup:   Position the camera on a tripod facing the system from the side. Adjust framing so that the entire range of motion of the mass is visible. Fix the camera focus and exposure settings to avoid automatic refocusing during motion. Start time-lapse or accelerated recording mode before excitation.3. Initial State Check:   Allow the mass to come to complete rest. Confirm that there is no residual motion and that the damper is not leaking or obstructed.4. Core Operation (Impulse Excitation):   Using one hand, deliver a single, brief strike to the mass with the rubber mallet in the direction of motion. Immediately withdraw the hand and mallet from the frame, leaving the system completely untouched after the strike.5. Observation Period:   Continue recording while the mass oscillates freely and gradually comes to rest due to damping. Do not apply any further external forces.6. Completion:   Stop recording after the vibration has clearly decayed. Turn off the camera and safely store the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The mass hangs motionless at its static equilibrium position under gravity.2. Immediately After Impact: The mass receives an impulse and is suddenly displaced, beginning oscillatory motion about the equilibrium position.3. During Free Vibration: The mass oscillates up and down with gradually decreasing amplitude. The period of oscillation remains approximately constant, while peak displacement reduces over time.4. Final State: After sufficient time, the oscillations decay and the mass returns to rest at the equilibrium position.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the transient response of a linear mass–spring–damper system subjected to an impulse input. The brief mallet strike approximates an impulse force, imparting an initial velocity to the mass. After the impulse, the system undergoes free vibration governed by Newton’s second law and the linear differential equation: m x¨ + c x˙ + k x = 0. The spring provides a restoring force proportional to displacement, while the damper dissipates mechanical energy, causing the vibration amplitude to decay. The observed motion reflects underdamped behavior, where oscillations occur with exponentially decreasing amplitude.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use a rubber mallet to avoid damaging the mass or introducing excessive force.2. Apply only one brief strike; do not push or hold the mass after impact.3. Ensure the camera focus is fixed to prevent visual artifacts during motion.4. Keep hands and tools out of the frame after excitation to maintain experimental validity.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: transient vibration of a linear mass–spring–damper system under impulse excitation. Minimum assumptions: a single-degree-of-freedom system hangs vertically, a brief external impulse is applied once, and no further forces act afterward except gravity, spring force, and damping. Expected phenomenon storyline: (1) system at rest at equilibrium; (2) brief mallet strike imparts impulse; (3) immediate onset of oscillatory motion; (4) amplitude decays over successive cycles due to damping; (5) motion ceases at equilibrium. Visibility constraints: full system must remain in frame, camera focus fixed, and hand/mallet must leave the scene immediately after impact to verify free vibration.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Measuring Soil pH Using a Handheld pH MeterI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Measurement of Acidic and Alkaline Soil pH Using a Handheld pH Meter2. Subject: Engineering - Agricultural Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To measure and compare the pH values of acidic soil and alkaline soil using a handheld pH meter, verify that acidic soil has pH < 7 and alkaline soil has pH > 7, and master the standard procedure for soil pH measurement.II. Experimental EquipmentHandheld soil pH meter (with probe), two soil samples (one acidic, one alkaline, clearly labeled), clean water (for moistening soil and rinsing probe), spray bottle or dropper, clean tissue or soft cloth, calibration solutions (pH 4.0 and pH 7.0, if required by the meter).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the two soil samples in separate containers and label them acidic soil and alkaline soil. Lightly moisten each soil sample with clean water so that it is damp but not muddy.2. Calibration: Turn on the handheld pH meter and calibrate it according to the manufacturer instructions using standard buffer solutions to ensure accurate readings.3. Measurement of Acidic Soil: Insert the clean probe vertically into the moist acidic soil to a suitable depth, ensuring good contact between the probe and soil. Keep the probe still and wait until the reading on the screen stabilizes. Record or observe the displayed pH value.4. Cleaning: Remove the probe from the soil, rinse it with clean water, and gently wipe it dry with tissue or a soft cloth.5. Measurement of Alkaline Soil: Insert the cleaned probe into the moist alkaline soil in the same manner. Wait for the reading to stabilize and observe the displayed pH value.6. Completion: Turn off the pH meter, clean the probe, and store the equipment properly.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. When the probe is inserted into the acidic soil, the pH meter displays a stable numerical value less than 7 (for example, around pH 5 to 6).2. After cleaning the probe and inserting it into the alkaline soil, the pH meter displays a stable numerical value greater than 7 (for example, around pH 8 to 9).3. The two pH readings are clearly different, reflecting the different chemical properties of the soils.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSoil pH is a measure of the acidity or alkalinity of soil, determined by the concentration of hydrogen ions in the soil solution. A pH meter measures the electrical potential difference generated by a sensitive electrode when it contacts the soil moisture. Acidic soils have higher hydrogen ion concentration and therefore pH values less than 7, while alkaline soils have lower hydrogen ion concentration and pH values greater than 7. Proper calibration and probe contact with moist soil ensure accurate and reliable pH measurements.VI. Experimental Precautions1. The soil must be moist to ensure good electrical contact between the probe and soil.2. Always calibrate the pH meter before use for accurate results.3. Clean the probe between measurements to avoid cross-contamination.4. Handle the probe gently to prevent damage.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: verification of soil acidity and alkalinity through direct pH measurement using a handheld meter. Minimum assumptions: two distinct soil samples (acidic and alkaline), a functional calibrated pH meter, and visible numerical display. Phased storyline: (1) setup with labeled soils and meter; (2) calibration establishes measurement validity; (3) insertion into moist acidic soil causes the meter reading to change and stabilize below 7; (4) probe cleaning as a transition preventing cross-contamination; (5) insertion into moist alkaline soil causes a new stabilization above 7. Visibility constraints: close-up view of probe insertion and meter screen to clearly verify numerical values and their causal relation to each operation.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Iodine Color Change Disappearing as Amylase Digests StarchI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Disappearance of Iodine Color During Amylase Digestion of Starch2. Subject: Engineering – Chemical Engineering (Biochemical Reaction Demonstration)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that amylase catalyzes the hydrolysis of starch, causing the iodine–starch blue-black color to disappear, and to understand enzymatic specificity using a control comparison.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsTwo identical fresh potato slices (same size and thickness), two clear glass dishes, iodine solution (dilute iodine–potassium iodide), amylase solution (e.g., salivary or commercial amylase), distilled water, dropper or pipette, camera or smartphone with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Quinine in Tonic Water Glowing Under UV LightI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Fluorescence of Quinine in Tonic Water Under UV Light2. Subject: Engineering - Biomedical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate fluorescence caused by quinine in tonic water under ultraviolet (UV) excitation, and to understand the optical principle of fluorescence relevant to biomedical imaging and sensing.II. Experimental Equipment1. Clear glass cups (2 identical)2. Tonic water containing quinine (sufficient to fill one glass)3. Plain drinking water (sufficient to fill one glass)4. Handheld UV lamp (long-wave UV, ~365 nm)5. Dark room or darkened environmentIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Darken the room to minimize ambient light. Place two clear glasses on a flat surface.2. Liquid Setup: Pour tonic water into the left glass and plain water into the right glass. Ensure both are clear and at similar fill levels.3. Initial Observation: With the UV lamp off, observe both glasses; both should appear colorless and transparent.4. Core Operation: Aim the handheld UV lamp at both glasses simultaneously and switch the UV lamp on.5. Comparison Observation: Observe the appearance of both liquids under UV illumination.6. Control Action: Switch the UV lamp off and on once more to confirm repeatability of the phenomenon.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. UV Off: Both tonic water and plain water appear clear and colorless in the dark.2. UV On: The tonic water in the left glass emits a bright blue glow, while the plain water in the right glass remains dark or shows no visible glow.3. UV Off Again: The blue glow from the tonic water disappears immediately.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleQuinine molecules in tonic water absorb ultraviolet light and are excited to a higher electronic energy state. When these molecules return to a lower energy state, they emit visible blue light, a phenomenon known as fluorescence. Plain water lacks fluorescent molecules and therefore does not emit visible light under UV illumination. This principle is widely applied in biomedical engineering, such as in fluorescence imaging and biochemical assays.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Avoid direct eye exposure to UV light.2. Ensure both glasses are clean and identical to avoid optical bias.3. Conduct the experiment in a sufficiently dark environment for clear observation.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Plastic Flow of a Modeling Clay Cylinder Under CompressionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Plastic Flow of a Modeling Clay Cylinder Under Plate Compression2. Subject: Engineering - Geotechnical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate plastic deformation and flow behavior of a ductile material under compressive stress, and to understand the basic concept of plastic flow relevant to soil and geomaterial behavior.II. Experimental EquipmentModeling clay (homogeneous, medium softness), cylindrical mold (or hand-shaped cylinder, height approximately equal to diameter), two flat metal plates (top and bottom), compression frame or manual loading device, stable base, camera or smartphone with tripod, constant lighting source.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Shape the modeling clay into a smooth vertical cylinder with flat top and bottom surfaces. Place it centrally on the lower metal plate.2. Setup: Position the upper flat metal plate directly above the clay cylinder, ensuring parallel alignment. Fix the camera on a tripod facing the side of the specimen and lock focus for time-lapse recording.3. Core Operation: Start recording. Slowly and continuously lower the top plate to apply compressive load to the clay cylinder. Maintain a steady, gradual loading rate.4. Observation Stage: Continue compression until clear deformation and lateral expansion are visible. Avoid sudden loading or unloading.5. Completion: Stop the compression and recording. Remove the load and document the final shape of the clay.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The clay cylinder has a regular shape with smooth surfaces and vertical sides.2. During Compression: As the top plate lowers, the cylinder shortens in height and expands laterally. The deformation is continuous and irreversible.3. Final State: The clay shows a barrel-shaped profile, indicating plastic flow under compressive stress.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleModeling clay behaves as a ductile material under low strain rates. When compressive stress exceeds its yield strength, elastic deformation transitions into plastic deformation. The applied vertical stress causes irreversible rearrangement of material, resulting in lateral flow due to volume conservation and shear yielding. This behavior is analogous to plastic flow in soils and soft geomaterials under load.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure plates are flat and parallel to avoid uneven stress.2. Apply load slowly to emphasize plastic flow rather than brittle failure.3. Keep camera focus fixed to ensure consistent time-lapse observation.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Minimum Value Search VisualizationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Minimum Value Search Visualization in an Array2. Subject: Engineering - Software Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the process of finding the minimum value in a simple array by sequential traversal, helping learners understand comparison-based algorithms and state tracking.II. Experimental Materials1. Display screen or visualization interface.2. A simple array of numbers: [4, 3, 2, 1].3. Visual cursor to indicate the current element.4. Minimum value marker (highlighted in blue).III. Experimental Procedure1. Initialization: Display the array [4, 3, 2, 1] horizontally on the screen. Place the cursor at the first element (4). Initialize the tracked minimum as the first element and mark it in blue.2. Traversal Step 1: Compare the first element (4) with the tracked minimum (4). Since they are equal, keep the minimum unchanged.3. Traversal Step 2: Move the cursor to the second element (3). Compare it with the tracked minimum (4). Since 3 is smaller, update the tracked minimum to 3 and move the blue marker to 3.4. Traversal Step 3: Move the cursor to the third element (2). Compare it with the tracked minimum (3). Since 2 is smaller, update the tracked minimum to 2 and update the blue marker accordingly.5. Traversal Step 4: Move the cursor to the fourth element (1). Compare it with the tracked minimum (2). Since 1 is smaller, update the tracked minimum to 1 and mark it in blue.6. Completion: Continue traversal until the last element is processed. End the experiment with the minimum value clearly marked.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initially, the first element (4) is marked as the minimum.2. As the cursor moves right, each element is compared with the current minimum.3. When a smaller number appears, the blue minimum marker shifts to the new value.4. At the end of traversal, the smallest number (1) remains marked in blue.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the principle of minimum value search in software engineering. By traversing an array sequentially and maintaining a tracked minimum, the algorithm ensures that each element is compared exactly once. The minimum value is updated only when a smaller element is found, resulting in a time complexity of O(n). The visualization reinforces the causal relationship between comparison operations and state updates.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Evaporation Rate Comparison: Ethanol vs Diethyl Ether Droplets on GlassSubject: Engineering – Chemical EngineeringObjective: To visually compare the evaporation rates of ethanol and diethyl ether under identical conditions and understand the relationship between evaporation rate, volatility, and vapor pressure.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentClean glass plate (flat and transparent);Micropipette or dropper;Ethanol (analytical grade);Diethyl ether (analytical grade);Permanent marker or label tape;Camera or smartphone with tripod (fixed focus, time-lapse mode);Well-ventilated laboratory environment.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Clean and dry the glass plate to ensure no contaminants remain. Place it horizontally on a stable surface in still air.2. Labeling: Mark the left side of the glass plate as Ethanol and the right side as Diethyl Ether.3. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Ice Melting Rate on Metal Plate vs Wooden SurfaceI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Ice Melting Rate Comparison on Metal Plate and Wooden Board2. Subject: Engineering – Energy Engineering (Heat Transfer)3. Experiment Objective: To compare the melting rates of identical ice cubes placed on a bare metal plate and a bare wooden board under the same room conditions, and to understand the effect of thermal conductivity on heat transfer. Through fixed-camera time-lapse observation, learners recognize how different materials transfer heat at different rates.II. Experimental Equipment- Identical ice cubes (2 cubes, same size and shape)- Bare metal plate (room temperature, clean and dry)- Bare wooden board (room temperature, clean and dry)- Flat table or experimental bench- Camera or mobile phone with time-lapse function- Tripod or fixed stand for camera- Timer or clock (optional, for reference)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the metal plate and wooden board side by side on the same flat table, ensuring both are exposed to identical room conditions (same air temperature, airflow, and lighting). Confirm both surfaces are dry and at room temperature.2. Camera Setup: Fix the camera on a tripod directly above or at a stable angle facing both surfaces. Adjust the frame so that both the metal plate and wooden board are clearly visible in the same shot. Fix the focus and exposure; do not adjust them during recording.3. Placement of Ice Cubes: Simultaneously place one identical ice cube at the center of the metal plate and the other at the center of the wooden board. Ensure they are placed at the same time to maintain fairness.4. Recording: Start time-lapse recording immediately after placing the ice cubes. Keep the camera fixed and avoid touching the setup during the experiment.5. Completion: Continue recording until a clear difference in melting progress is observed, or until one ice cube has nearly completely melted.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both ice cubes have the same shape, size, and transparency, resting solidly on their respective surfaces.2. Early Stage: The ice cube on the metal plate begins to show faster edge rounding and water formation at the base, while the ice cube on the wooden board melts more slowly.3. Mid Stage: A visible pool of meltwater forms around the ice cube on the metal plate, and its height decreases明显 faster. The ice cube on the wooden board remains larger with less surrounding water.4. Final Stage: The ice cube on the metal plate is mostly or completely melted, while the ice cube on the wooden board still partially retains its solid form.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates the role of thermal conductivity in heat transfer. Metal has a high thermal conductivity, allowing it to transfer heat quickly from the surrounding environment to the ice cube, accelerating melting. Wood has low thermal conductivity and acts as an insulator, slowing the transfer of heat to the ice cube. Under identical room conditions, differences in melting rates are therefore caused by the different abilities of materials to conduct heat, illustrating a key principle of energy engineering and heat transfer.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Dry Spaghetti Bent Until It Snaps (Brittle Fracture)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Dry Spaghetti Brittle Fracture by Bending2. Subject: Engineering - Materials Science & Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate brittle fracture behavior in dry spaghetti under bending load, observe fracture characteristics, and understand stress concentration and elastic failure.II. Experimental EquipmentSingle strand of dry spaghetti (uncooked), plain tabletop, two hands (operator), camera or smartphone fixed on a tripod, adequate lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the plain tabletop in a well-lit area. Fix the camera position and focus on the center region above the tabletop; do not adjust focus during recording.2. Setup: Hold one single dry spaghetti strand horizontally with both hands, positioning it over the tabletop at approximately mid-height.3. Core Operation: In one smooth and continuous motion, bend the spaghetti inward at the center by moving both hands symmetrically toward each other.4. Observation: Continue bending smoothly until the spaghetti suddenly snaps.5. Completion: Allow the broken pieces to fall or remain held briefly for clear visualization, then stop recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The dry spaghetti is straight, rigid, and unchanged in shape.2. During Bending: The spaghetti bends elastically with very little visible deformation.3. Fracture Moment: The spaghetti suddenly snaps, usually near the center, producing a sharp break with minimal prior warning.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesDry spaghetti behaves as a brittle material. Under bending, tensile stress concentrates on the outer surface at the center of the strand. When the tensile stress exceeds the material strength, a crack initiates and propagates rapidly, causing sudden fracture with negligible plastic deformation. This demonstrates classic brittle fracture behavior in materials science.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use only dry, uncooked spaghetti.2. Bend smoothly to avoid introducing torsion or uneven loading.3. Maintain a fixed camera focus to clearly capture the fracture moment.

Experiment Title: Comparison of Radiative Heating Rates of Matte Black and Shiny Metallic Surfaces Using Thermochromic Paint2. Subject: Engineering – Chemical Engineering (Heat Transfer)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that surfaces with different emissivity and absorptivity exhibit different heating rates under thermal radiation, and to visually compare radiative heat absorption using thermochromic paint.II. Experimental EquipmentInfrared heat lamp (overhead, fixed height); two identical metal plates of the same material and thickness; thermochromic paint applied uniformly to both plates; one plate finished as matte black, the other as shiny metallic; insulating stand or holder; fixed camera or smartphone with tripod; timer or time-lapse recording function.III. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Belleville Washer Stack Compressing as a Bolt Is TightenedI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Compression Behavior of a Belleville Washer Stack During Bolt Tightening2. Subject: Engineering - Mechanical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe how a stack of Belleville (disc spring) washers compresses as a bolt is tightened, understand the relationship between tightening torque, washer deformation, and preload force, and recognize the spring-like function of Belleville washers in bolted joints.II. Experimental EquipmentHex bolt and matching nut (1 set), Belleville washers (4–6 pieces, identical), flat washers (2 pieces), wrench or spanner, ruler or caliper (optional, for displacement observation), rigid base plate or fixture, safety gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the bolt vertically through the base plate. Put on safety gloves. Ensure all Belleville washers are clean and undamaged.2. Washer Stacking: Stack the Belleville washers on the bolt in a defined orientation (e.g., all facing the same direction) to form a disc spring stack. Place a flat washer on top to distribute load evenly.3. Assembly: Thread the nut onto the bolt by hand until it contacts the washer stack.4. Core Operation (Tightening): Using a wrench, gradually tighten the nut in small, continuous rotations. Pause briefly after each partial turn to observe the washer stack.5. Observation: Observe the change in height and curvature of the Belleville washer stack as tightening continues.6. Completion: Stop tightening once a clear compression state is achieved. Do not overtighten. Loosen the nut slightly to observe elastic recovery (optional).IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Belleville washers have a visible conical shape with gaps between adjacent washers.2. During Tightening: As the nut is tightened, the washers gradually flatten, and the overall stack height decreases.3. Advanced Compression: With further tightening, the washers approach a flatter shape, indicating increased preload force.4. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Bubble Sort Algorithm Execution Process DemonstrationSubject: Engineering - Computer ScienceExperiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the execution process of the Bubble Sort algorithm by creating a short educational animation that shows how an array of vertical bars labeled with numbers becomes sorted through repeated comparisons and swaps.II. Experimental Materials and Environment1. A predefined array of integers (e.g., [5, 3, 8, 4, 2]).2. Visualization environment or animation tool capable of displaying vertical bars.3. Each integer represented as a vertical bar, with bar height proportional to its value and a number label.III. Experimental Procedure1. Initialization: Display the initial unsorted array as a row of vertical bars aligned horizontally, each bar labeled with its corresponding number.2. First Pass Comparison: Starting from the left, compare the first two adjacent bars. Highlight them to indicate comparison.3. Swap Operation: If the left bar represents a larger number than the right bar, swap their positions with a smooth animation.4. Continue Comparisons: Move to the next pair of adjacent bars and repeat the comparison and swap process until reaching the end of the array.5. Pass Completion: Mark the last bar as sorted (optional visual cue), as it now contains the largest value of the current pass.6. Repeated Passes: Repeat steps 2–5 for the remaining unsorted portion of the array until no swaps are needed.7. Termination: End the animation when the entire array is in ascending order.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Vertical bars appear in an unsorted order, with varying heights and number labels.2. During Sorting: Adjacent bars are repeatedly highlighted, compared, and swapped when out of order. Larger bars gradually move toward the right side of the array.3. Final State: All bars are arranged from shortest to tallest (or smallest to largest number), indicating a sorted array.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesBubble Sort is a comparison-based sorting algorithm. Its core principle is to repeatedly traverse the array, compare adjacent elements, and swap them if they are in the wrong order. Each pass places the largest unsorted element at the end of the array. Through multiple passes, the array becomes fully sorted. The animation visually encodes this principle by showing comparisons, swaps, and the gradual emergence of order from an initially disordered array.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept Definition: The video should clearly represent the Bubble Sort algorithm, assuming only basic knowledge of arrays and comparison-based sorting. Bars symbolize array elements, and adjacent comparison with conditional swapping is the only required mechanism.Phased Storyline: (1) Present an unsorted array of numbered vertical bars; (2) show repeated adjacent comparisons with visual highlights; (3) animate swaps when left value exceeds right value; (4) illustrate repeated passes with larger values moving rightward; (5) conclude with a fully sorted array. The camera view should remain fixed and fully visible to allow verification of order, comparisons, and swaps within a short, accelerated timeframe.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Zinc–Copper Galvanic Cell LED Brightness Change after Adding SaltI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Zinc–Copper Galvanic Cell LED Brightness Change after Adding Copper Sulfate2. Subject: Engineering – Energy Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To construct a zinc–copper galvanic cell, observe electrical energy generation, and understand how increasing electrolyte ion concentration affects current and LED brightness.II. Experimental EquipmentZinc metal strip, copper metal strip, two beakers, zinc sulfate solution (colorless), copper sulfate solution (blue), copper sulfate crystals, salt bridge (filter paper soaked in potassium nitrate or sodium chloride solution), connecting wires with clips, LED, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear safety goggles. Place two beakers side by side on the bench.2. Left Half-Cell Setup: Pour zinc sulfate solution into the left beaker. Insert the zinc strip into the solution, ensuring good contact.3. Right Half-Cell Setup: Pour copper sulfate solution into the right beaker. Insert the copper strip into the blue solution.4. Circuit Connection: Connect the zinc strip to one terminal of the LED using a wire. Connect the copper strip to the other terminal of the LED.5. Salt Bridge: Place the soaked salt bridge so that one end is immersed in each beaker, completing the internal circuit.6. Initial Observation: Observe the LED; it should light dimly, indicating current flow.7. Core Operation: Carefully add a small amount of copper sulfate crystals to the blue copper sulfate beaker.8. Final Observation: Observe the LED brightness change.9. Conclusion and Cleanup: Record observations, disconnect the circuit, dispose of solutions properly, and clean equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Zinc solution is colorless, copper solution is blue, LED is off before circuit completion.2. After Circuit Completion: LED lights with low or moderate brightness.3. After Adding Copper Sulfate Crystals: Blue color deepens, and the LED becomes noticeably brighter.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates a zinc–copper galvanic cell converting chemical energy into electrical energy. Zinc undergoes oxidation at the anode, releasing electrons, while copper ions are reduced at the cathode. Adding copper sulfate increases Cu²⁺ ion concentration and solution conductivity, reducing internal resistance, increasing current, and thus increasing LED brightness.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Neon-Lamp Relaxation Oscillator in XY DisplayI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Observation of a Neon-Lamp Relaxation Oscillator Using Oscilloscope XY Mode2. Subject: Engineering – Control & Automation3. Experiment Objective: To set up a neon-lamp relaxation oscillator, observe its charge–discharge behavior, display the capacitor voltage versus lamp current as a closed loop on an oscilloscope in XY mode, and understand the operating principle of relaxation oscillation.II. Experimental EquipmentDC power supply (0–200 V adjustable), series resistor (100 kΩ–1 MΩ), neon lamp, capacitor (0.01–1 µF, rated voltage sufficient), sense resistor (e.g., 100 Ω–1 kΩ), oscilloscope with XY mode, connecting wires, camera on tripod (for time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ensure the power supply is off. Fix the camera on a tripod facing the oscilloscope screen and lock focus.2. Circuit Connection: Connect the DC supply, series resistor, neon lamp, and capacitor in series to form a relaxation oscillator loop. Insert the sense resistor in series with the neon lamp to measure current.3. Oscilloscope Connection: Connect the capacitor voltage across the capacitor to the oscilloscope X input. Connect the voltage across the sense resistor (proportional to lamp current) to the Y input. Set the oscilloscope to XY mode.4. Operation: Slowly increase the DC supply voltage until periodic flashing of the neon lamp occurs and a stable trace appears on the oscilloscope.5. Recording: Allow the system to run steadily. Record the XY display over time using time-lapse photography or accelerated recording.6. Shutdown: Reduce the supply voltage to zero, turn off power, and disconnect the circuit.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Lamp off; no trace or a single point on the XY display.2. Oscillation: The lamp periodically flashes. The XY display shows a closed loop corresponding to the capacitor charging and sudden discharge through the lamp.3. Steady State: A stable, repetitive closed curve is maintained as oscillation continues.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates a relaxation oscillator. The capacitor charges through the series resistor until the neon lamp reaches its breakdown voltage and conducts. The capacitor then discharges rapidly, causing the lamp to extinguish once the voltage falls below the sustaining level. This cycle repeats. Plotting capacitor voltage (X) against lamp current (Y) produces a closed-loop trajectory, visually representing the non-linear charge–discharge dynamics.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use resistors to limit current and protect the neon lamp.2. Ensure capacitor voltage rating exceeds the supply voltage.3. Do not touch live circuits; discharge the capacitor before handling.4. Keep camera focus fixed to ensure consistent time-lapse recording.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: River Model Demonstrating Different Surface Speeds in Shallow and Deep SectionsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: River Model with Shallow and Deep Sections Showing Different Surface Speeds2. Subject: Engineering – Civil & Environmental Engineering (Hydraulics)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how water depth and channel roughness affect surface flow velocity in a river, and to understand the basic hydraulic principle that deeper and smoother channels generally have higher flow velocities.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent river flume (rectangular), shallow section with gravel bed, deeper section with smooth bed, water supply with steady flow control, identical floating beads (light-colored, same size), stopwatch or visual timing reference (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the transparent flume on a level surface. Ensure one side of the flume contains a shallow gravel bed and the other side a deeper smooth channel. Adjust the water supply to produce a steady, clear, and uniform flow.2. Flow Stabilization: Allow water to flow for a short time until the water depth and flow speed in both sections become stable and free of waves or disturbances.3. Bead Release: Align several identical floating beads across the width of the flume at the upstream end, positioning beads simultaneously above the shallow gravel side and the deep smooth side.4. Core Operation: Release all beads at the same time onto the water surface without adding extra force.5. Observation: Observe and compare the downstream movement of beads on the shallow gravel side and the deep smooth side.6. Completion: After beads reach the downstream end, stop the water flow and collect the beads.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Water flows steadily and clearly through the flume; beads float motionless at the release point before release.2. During Motion: After release, all beads move downstream with the flow. Beads above the deeper smooth channel move noticeably faster than those above the shallow gravel side.3. Comparative Result: Over the same time interval, beads in the deep channel travel a longer distance than beads in the shallow gravel section.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment illustrates basic open-channel flow principles in hydraulics. Flow velocity at the water surface is influenced by channel depth and boundary roughness. The deeper smooth channel has a larger hydraulic radius and lower relative frictional resistance, allowing water to flow faster. In contrast, the shallow gravel section has higher friction due to roughness and reduced depth, resulting in lower surface velocity. Therefore, even under the same slope and discharge, surface flow speeds differ across the river cross-section.

manual: Experiment Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Thermistor Temperature Sensor Changing LED Brightness When Heated by a Hand2. Subject: Engineering – Mechatronics & Robotics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how a thermistor senses temperature changes and converts them into an electrical signal that changes LED brightness. By moving a bare hand close to and around the thermistor and then away, learners observe the relationship between temperature, resistance, and light intensity, and understand basic sensor–actuator interaction in mechatronic systems.II. Experimental Equipment1. NTC thermistor (one, room-temperature type)2. LED (one, visible color such as red)3. Fixed resistor (appropriate value for current limiting, e.g., 220–1kΩ)4. DC power supply or battery (3–5 V)5. Breadboard and connecting wires6. Tabletop working surface7. Camera mounted above the tabletop with fixed focus (for time-lapse or continuous recording)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the breadboard on a stable tabletop. Fix the camera above the tabletop, ensure the entire circuit is in frame, and lock the camera focus so it does not change during recording.2. Circuit Setup: Connect the thermistor and fixed resistor in series with the LED and the power supply, forming a simple closed circuit. Ensure correct LED polarity so that it can light when powered.3. Initial State Check: Power on the circuit. Confirm that the LED is lit at a baseline brightness when the thermistor is at room temperature and no hand is nearby.4. Core Operation – Heating by Hand: Slowly move a bare hand close to the thermistor without touching it. Hold the hand near and gently move it around the thermistor for several seconds.5. Core Operation – Withdrawal: Gradually move the hand away from the thermistor and keep it away until the system returns toward its initial state.6. End of Experiment: Turn off the power supply. Stop recording. Leave the circuit components in place for final observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The LED shows a steady baseline brightness when the thermistor is at room temperature.2. Hand Approaches Thermistor: As the bare hand comes close and warms the thermistor, the LED brightness gradually changes (typically becoming brighter for an NTC thermistor in a suitable circuit).3. Hand Near and Moving Around: While the hand remains close and moves around the thermistor, the LED brightness remains altered and may fluctuate slightly with hand distance and position.4. Hand Moves Away: As the hand is withdrawn and the thermistor cools, the LED brightness gradually returns toward its original baseline level.V. Summary of Experimental Principle1. Core Principle: A thermistor is a temperature-sensitive resistor. For an NTC thermistor, resistance decreases as temperature increases.2. Electrical Effect: When the thermistor is warmed by a nearby hand, its resistance changes, altering the current in the circuit.3. Output Response: The LED brightness depends on the current flowing through it. Therefore, temperature change (input) → resistance change (sensor response) → current change → LED brightness change (output).4. Mechatronics Significance: This experiment demonstrates a basic sensing-and-actuation loop, where a physical quantity (temperature) is converted into an electrical signal and then into a visible output, illustrating fundamental mechatronic system behavior.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Do not touch the thermistor directly to avoid mechanical damage or unstable readings.2. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Heated Metal Wire Immersed in Room-Temperature Water Showing Surface Bubble NucleationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Surface Bubble Nucleation on an Electrically Heated Metal Wire in Water2. Subject: Engineering – Nuclear Engineering (Thermal-Hydraulics / Boiling Heat Transfer)3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate surface bubble nucleation and early-stage boiling phenomena on a heated metal surface immersed in room-temperature water, and to understand the basic mechanism of nucleate boiling relevant to nuclear reactor thermal-hydraulics. The experiment emphasizes clear visualization using fixed-focus, time-lapse photography.II. Experimental Equipment1. Clear glass tank (rectangular, transparent, clean)2. Room-temperature water (approximately 20–25 °C, degassed not required)3. Thin metal wire (e.g., nichrome or stainless steel, diameter ~0.2–0.5 mm)4. Insulating supports to stretch the wire horizontally across the tank5. Adjustable DC power supply with leads and switch6. Electrical connectors and clamps (insulated)7. Camera or smartphone with tripod (fixed focus and fixed position)8. Safety equipment: insulated gloves, dry working surfaceIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   (1) Clean the glass tank to ensure no visible impurities on the walls.   (2) Fill the tank with room-temperature water to a level where the wire will be fully submerged.   (3) Mount the thin metal wire horizontally across the center of the tank using insulating supports, ensuring the wire is taut and not touching the tank walls.2. Electrical and Optical Setup:   (1) Connect both ends of the metal wire to the external DC power supply using insulated leads.   (2) Keep the power supply switched off during setup.   (3) Position the camera perpendicular to the wire, ensuring the wire is clearly visible through the glass.   (4) Fix the camera focus, exposure, and framing; do not adjust during the experiment.3. Core Operation:   (1) Switch on the camera and start time-lapse or continuous recording.   (2) Gradually turn on the power supply and slowly increase the current to heat the wire.   (3) Maintain a steady power level once visible phenomena appear on the wire surface.4. Observation and Shutdown:   (1) Observe the wire and surrounding water without disturbing the setup.   (2) After sufficient observation, gradually reduce the current to zero.   (3) Turn off the power supply and stop the camera recording.   (4) Allow the wire to cool before draining the tank or disassembling equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The metal wire is clearly visible in still, transparent water with no bubbles present.2. Early Heating Stage: As electrical power increases, tiny discrete bubbles begin to appear at localized points on the wire surface.3. Nucleation Stage: Small bubbles repeatedly form, grow slightly, and detach from the wire, rising vertically due to buoyancy.4. Sustained Heating: The number of active nucleation sites increases, forming a regular pattern of bubble generation along the wire.5. Cooling Stage: After power reduction, bubble formation weakens and eventually disappears, returning the water to a quiescent state.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Electrical Heating Principle: When electric current passes through the metal wire, resistive (Joule) heating raises the wire temperature above that of the surrounding water.2. Nucleate Boiling Mechanism: When the wire surface temperature locally exceeds the saturation temperature corresponding to the surrounding pressure, vapor bubbles form at microscopic surface cavities (nucleation sites).3. Bubble Dynamics: The bubbles grow by evaporation at the solid–liquid interface and detach when buoyancy and hydrodynamic forces overcome surface tension.4. Engineering Significance: This experiment illustrates nucleate boiling, a highly efficient heat transfer mode that is critically important in nuclear reactor fuel rod cooling.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure all electrical connections remain dry and insulated.2. Increase current gradually to avoid sudden overheating of the wire.3. Do not touch the wire during or immediately after heating.4. Keep camera position and focus fixed to ensure valid time-lapse comparison.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Nucleate boiling on a heated solid surface in liquid water. Minimum assumptions: a thin conductive wire generates heat uniformly when powered; water is initially subcooled or near saturation at atmospheric pressure; vapor bubbles originate only from the heated surface. Expected phased storyline: (1) Static initial state with clear water and visible wire; (2) gradual heating without visible change; (3) onset of surface bubble nucleation at discrete points on the wire; (4) repeated bubble growth and detachment rising upward; (5) reduction and disappearance of bubbles after power-off. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Steel Pile Driven into Sand by Drop HammerSubject: Engineering – Geotechnical EngineeringExperiment Objective: To demonstrate the pile driving process in sandy soil using a crane-mounted drop hammer, observe pile penetration and sand densification, and understand the basic principle of impact pile driving. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Level the sandy ground and place the steel pile vertically using a guide frame. Mark depth increments on the pile. manual: Experiment Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Behavior of Parallel Light Bulbs When One Bulb Is Removed During Operation2. Subject: Engineering – Systems Engineering (Basic Electrical Systems)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that in a parallel circuit, each load operates independently. By observing two identical light bulbs connected in parallel to a power source, students verify that removing one bulb while the circuit is powered does not affect the operation or brightness of the remaining bulb. The experiment also supports time-lapse or fixed-focus video recording of system behavior.II. Experimental Equipment1. DC power source or low-voltage AC power supply (rated to match bulbs)2. Two identical light bulbs with sockets (same model, same rated voltage and power)3. Parallel circuit wiring (conductive wires, connectors)4. Switch (optional, for initial power control)5. Stable mounting board for circuit components6. Camera or recording device mounted on a tripod (focus fixed for time-lapse photography)7. Insulated gloves (optional, for safe bulb handling)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:- Securely mount the two identical bulb sockets on the circuit board, labeling them left bulb and right bulb.- Connect the two bulbs in parallel to the power source, ensuring both bulbs share the same voltage.- Place the camera in front of the circuit, adjust framing so both bulbs and the left bulb socket are clearly visible, and fix the focus. Do not change focus during recording.2. Initial Operation:- Turn on the power source.- Confirm that both the left and right bulbs light up simultaneously and appear equally bright.- Begin continuous or time-lapse recording.3. Core Operation:- While the power remains on, slowly reach in with a hand and unscrew the left bulb counterclockwise.- Continue unscrewing until the left bulb is completely removed from its socket.- Ensure no other wires or components are disturbed during removal.4. Completion:- Keep the power on for a short period after removal to observe the state of the remaining bulb.- Turn off the power source after observation is complete.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both identical bulbs are on, emitting steady light with similar brightness.2. During Removal: As the left bulb is unscrewed, it gradually dims and then turns off when fully disconnected.3. After Removal: The right bulb remains lit throughout the entire process, with no visible flicker or change in brightness.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesIn a parallel circuit, each branch is connected directly across the power source. Therefore, each bulb receives the full supply voltage independently of the other branch. Removing one bulb opens only its own branch, stopping current in that path, but does not interrupt current flow in the remaining branch. This demonstrates the independence and reliability of parallel system design, a key principle in systems engineering and electrical engineering.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use bulbs and a power source with compatible voltage ratings to avoid damage.2. Do not touch exposed conductors while the power is on.3. Unscrew the bulb slowly to clearly capture the phenomenon on video.4. Keep the camera fixed to ensure accurate comparison of brightness over time.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Independence of branches in a parallel electrical system. Minimum assumptions: two identical bulbs, equal voltage supply, true parallel wiring, and continuous power during bulb removal.Phased Storyline: (1) Establishment phase – camera fixed, two identical bulbs in parallel both steadily lit. (2) Intervention phase – a hand enters the frame and unscrews the left bulb while power remains on, causing only the left bulb to go out. (3) Result phase – the right bulb remains continuously illuminated with unchanged brightness. Visibility constraints: both bulbs, wiring context, and the left-hand removal action must stay in frame, with no camera refocus or scene cuts, enabling clear verification of causal independence.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Cantilever Beam Test—Carbon Fiber vs AluminumI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Cantilever Beam Deflection Test under Identical Hanging Load (Carbon Fiber vs Aluminum)2. Subject: Engineering – Aerospace Engineering / Structural Mechanics3. Experiment Objective: To visually and quantitatively compare the bending stiffness of a carbon fiber cantilever beam and an aluminum cantilever beam under the same end load; to understand how material properties, especially Young’s modulus and density, affect structural deformation.II. Experimental Equipment1. Carbon fiber beam (black, identical geometry to aluminum beam)2. Aluminum beam (silver, identical geometry to carbon fiber beam)3. Rigid clamp or vise (capable of firmly fixing both beams)4. Laboratory bench or support frame5. Identical hanging weights (one weight per beam, same mass)6. Hooks or strings for attaching weights7. Ruler or scale (optional, for deflection comparison)8. Fixed camera or tripod (for recording and observation)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:- Place the clamp securely on the lab bench.- Align the carbon fiber beam and aluminum beam side by side, ensuring they have the same length exposed beyond the clamp.- Insert one end of each beam into the clamp and tighten firmly so both beams are fixed horizontally and cannot slip.2. Initial State Verification:- Confirm that both beams are initially straight and level.- Ensure no load is attached and that the camera position is fixed, capturing both beams clearly in the same frame.3. Core Operation:- Attach an identical hanging weight to the free end of the carbon fiber beam.- Attach the same type and mass of hanging weight to the free end of the aluminum beam.- Release both weights carefully so the loads are applied smoothly and simultaneously.4. Observation Stage:- Keep the camera fixed and allow the beams to reach a stable deflected shape.- Observe and compare the vertical deflection of the free ends of the two beams.5. Experiment Completion:- Remove the weights from both beams.- Loosen the clamp and remove the beams.- Store all equipment properly.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both the black carbon fiber beam and the silver aluminum beam are straight, horizontal, and undeformed.2. After Loading:- Both beams bend downward due to the applied hanging load.- The aluminum beam exhibits a visibly larger downward deflection at its free end.- The carbon fiber beam shows a smaller deflection, appearing stiffer under the same load.3. Comparative Result: Under identical loading and geometry, the carbon fiber beam resists bending more effectively than the aluminum beam.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Core Principle: Cantilever beam bending theory from strength of materials.2. When a load is applied at the free end of a cantilever beam, bending occurs due to the generated bending moment.3. The end deflection of a cantilever beam is given by δ = FL³ / (3EI), where F is the applied load, L is beam length, E is Young’s modulus, and I is the second moment of area.4. Since both beams have identical geometry and loading, differences in deflection are primarily due to differences in material properties.5. Carbon fiber composites generally have a higher stiffness-to-weight ratio and higher effective Young’s modulus along the fiber direction than aluminum, resulting in smaller deflection under the same load.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both beams have identical dimensions and clamping length.2. Apply loads gently to avoid dynamic effects.3. Confirm the clamp is rigid to prevent rotation or slipping.4. Maintain a fixed camera position to ensure valid visual comparison.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Comparison of cantilever beam bending behavior under identical end loads, emphasizing material stiffness differences between carbon fiber and aluminum. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: both beams have identical geometry, are rigidly clamped at one end, and experience the same gravitational load at the free end; deflection arises from elastic bending governed by cantilever beam theory.Phased storyline: (1) Initial static scene—two straight, horizontal beams (black carbon fiber, silver aluminum) clamped side by side with no load, camera fixed. (2) Load application—identical weights are attached smoothly to both free ends. (3) Deformation phase—both beams bend downward; aluminum shows visibly larger deflection. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Ball Rolling in a Smooth Bowl with FrictionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Ball Rolling in a Smooth Concave Bowl with Friction2. Subject: Engineering - Control & Automation3. Experiment Objective: To observe the motion of identical balls released from different positions in a smooth concave bowl with friction, and to understand how friction causes energy dissipation and leads to a stable equilibrium state. Time-lapse photography is used to clearly record the motion process.II. Experimental EquipmentSmooth concave bowl (hemispherical or similar), identical solid balls (same size, mass, and material), stable horizontal table, camera or smartphone with tripod, time-lapse recording function, marker tape (optional, to indicate release positions).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the concave bowl on a stable horizontal table. Check that the inner surface of the bowl is smooth and clean. Set up the camera on a tripod above the bowl, fix the focus and field of view, and enable time-lapse recording.2. Position Setting: Select at least two different release positions at different heights along the inner surface of the bowl. Ensure the positions are clearly distinguishable.3. Release Operation: Place one identical ball gently at a selected position on the bowl’s inner surface. Release the ball without any push or initial velocity. Repeat for other balls from different positions, either sequentially or simultaneously.4. Recording: Allow the balls to roll freely while the camera records continuously. Do not touch the bowl or balls during motion.5. End of Experiment: Stop recording after all balls have come to rest at the bottom of the bowl.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Balls are stationary at different heights on the inner surface of the bowl.2. Motion Process: After release, each ball rolls downward toward the lowest point of the bowl, passes through it, and oscillates back and forth along the bowl surface.3. Energy Dissipation: Due to friction, the oscillation amplitude gradually decreases with time.4. Final State: Regardless of the initial release position, all balls eventually come to rest at the same lowest point of the bowl.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesUnder gravity, a ball on a concave surface experiences a component of force driving it toward the lowest point, which corresponds to a stable equilibrium. Friction converts part of the mechanical energy into thermal energy, causing gradual loss of kinetic energy. Therefore, although balls released from different initial positions have different initial potential energies, friction causes all motions to decay, and the system finally settles at the same equilibrium position. This illustrates stability and damping concepts commonly used in control and automation systems.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure balls are released without any push; keep the camera focus fixed throughout recording; avoid vibrations of the table; use identical balls to ensure comparability.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstrate damped motion and stable equilibrium in a mechanical system, using identical balls rolling in a smooth concave bowl with friction. Minimum assumptions include constant gravity, identical ball properties, a fixed bowl, and the presence of friction.Expected phenomenon storyline: (1) Setup phase: a smooth concave bowl with identical balls at different heights, camera fixed. (2) Release phase: balls are released without push and begin rolling downward. (3) Dynamic phase: balls oscillate through the lowest point with visibly decreasing amplitude due to friction. (4) Final phase: all balls settle at the same lowest point, showing convergence to equilibrium. Visibility constraints: the bowl interior, ball trajectories, and fixed camera perspective must remain clear throughout for verification.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: RC Low-Pass Circuit Driven by Frequency Sweep with LED Amplitude Indication2. Subject: Engineering - Control & Automation3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the frequency-domain behavior of an RC low-pass filter by driving it with a sine-wave frequency sweep from low to high, and to visually compare input and output amplitudes using LEDs. Through observation, learners understand how low-pass filters attenuate high-frequency signals and how amplitude changes relate to frequency.II. Experimental Equipment- Signal generator capable of sine-wave output with continuous frequency sweep (low to high)- RC low-pass circuit (resistor R in series, capacitor C to ground)- Red LED with current-limiting resistor connected to input signal- Blue LED with current-limiting resistor connected across the capacitor output- DC power supply or function generator output as required- Breadboard and connecting wires- Oscilloscope (optional, for reference)- Camera mounted on tripod with fixed focus for time-lapse photographyIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation:   - Assemble the RC low-pass circuit on a breadboard: connect the resistor in series with the signal input, and connect the capacitor from the resistor output node to ground.   - Connect the red LED (with resistor) to the input signal so that its brightness reflects the input amplitude.   - Connect the blue LED (with resistor) across the capacitor output so that its brightness reflects the filtered output amplitude.   - Mount the camera on a tripod facing the circuit. Fix focus, exposure, and framing to avoid changes during recording.2. Signal Setup:   - Set the signal generator to output a sine wave with constant amplitude.   - Configure the generator to perform a frequency sweep from low frequency (well below the cutoff frequency) to high frequency (well above the cutoff frequency).3. Core Operation:   - Start the camera recording or time-lapse capture.   - Start the sine-wave frequency sweep.   - Allow the sweep to run continuously from low to high frequency while keeping all connections stable.4. Completion:   - Stop the frequency sweep and camera recording.   - Power off the signal generator and disconnect the circuit safely.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial Low-Frequency State:   - The red LED at the input blinks or glows with stable brightness.   - The blue LED at the capacitor output shows similar brightness, indicating minimal attenuation at low frequency.2. During Frequency Increase:   - As frequency increases, the red LED brightness remains approximately constant.   - The blue LED gradually becomes dimmer and may blink less intensely, showing increasing attenuation of the output signal.3. High-Frequency State:   - At frequencies much higher than the cutoff frequency, the blue LED is very dim or nearly off.   - The red LED remains clearly visible, indicating that attenuation occurs mainly at the output.V. Summary of Experimental Principle1. Core Principle:   - An RC low-pass filter allows low-frequency signals to pass with little attenuation while attenuating high-frequency signals.2. Mechanism Explanation:   - The capacitive reactance decreases with increasing frequency, causing the capacitor to increasingly shunt high-frequency components to ground.   - The output voltage across the capacitor therefore decreases as frequency increases.3. Visual Interpretation:   - LED brightness is proportional to signal amplitude. The red LED shows constant input amplitude, while the blue LED visualizes the frequency-dependent attenuation at the output.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure current-limiting resistors are used with both LEDs to prevent damage.2. Keep camera focus and exposure fixed to ensure valid time-lapse comparison.3. Avoid touching or moving components during the sweep to maintain spatiotemporal consistency.4. Verify correct polarity of LEDs before powering the circuit.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Demonstrate the frequency response of an RC low-pass filter using a sine-wave frequency sweep, with LED brightness as a proxy for signal amplitude. Minimum assumptions: a correctly wired RC circuit, constant input amplitude, frequency-dependent capacitive reactance, and LEDs that visibly respond to amplitude changes.Phased Storyline: (1) Setup phase shows a stable RC circuit with a red input LED and blue output LED in fixed camera view. (2) Low-frequency phase where both LEDs appear similarly bright, indicating minimal attenuation. (3) Transition phase where frequency increases and the blue LED gradually dims while the red LED stays stable, showing causal filtering action. (4) High-frequency phase where the blue LED is very dim or off, confirming low-pass behavior. Visibility constraints: LED colors must be distinguishable, circuit layout must remain fixed, and the sweep must progress monotonically from low to high frequency for verification.

Basic InformationExperiment Title: Unidirectional Conduction of a Silicon DiodeSubject: Engineering – Materials Science & EngineeringObjective: Demonstrate that a silicon diode conducts current in one direction (forward bias) and blocks current when polarity is reversed (reverse bias) using a simple series circuit.II. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place all components on a tabletop. Identify the diode anode and cathode.2. Circuit Connection: Connect the battery, diode, and bulb in series: battery positive → diode anode → bulb → battery negative.3. Observation A: Ensure secure contacts. Observe the bulb state.4. Polarity Reversal: Without changing other connections, flip the battery orientation to reverse the diode polarity.5. Observation B: Observe the bulb state after reversal.6. Finish: Disconnect the circuit.IV. Observation of PhenomenaInitial connection (forward bias): The bulb lights up, indicating current flow.After battery flip (reverse bias): The bulb goes out or remains dark, indicating current is blocked.V. Experimental PrincipleA silicon diode has a PN junction that allows current under forward bias by lowering the potential barrier, enabling charge carrier flow. PrecautionsUse appropriate voltage to avoid bulb damage; ensure correct diode identification; avoid short circuits.
