manual: Instructions for the Experiment: LEDs of Different Colors Turning On Only Above Specific VoltagesI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: LEDs of Different Colors Turning On Only Above Specific Voltages2. Subject: Engineering – Electrical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe that LEDs of different colors have different forward turn-on voltages by gradually increasing a DC supply voltage and visually comparing the lighting sequence of red, green, and blue LEDs.II. Experimental EquipmentVariable DC power supply with current-limiting function; red LED, green LED, blue LED (one of each); current-limiting resistors or built-in current limit; breadboard or terminal block; connecting wires; lab bench; camera with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the power supply on the lab bench and ensure current limiting is enabled. Set the output voltage to zero.2. Circuit Connection: Connect the red, green, and blue LEDs in parallel to the DC supply, arranged physically from left to right as red, green, blue. Ensure correct polarity for each LED.3. Camera Setup: Position the camera facing the LEDs, fix the focus and framing, and start time-lapse recording.4. Core Operation: Slowly and continuously increase the supply voltage from zero while keeping current limited.5. Observation and Completion: Continue increasing voltage until all three LEDs are lit, then stop increasing voltage and end recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: At low voltage, none of the LEDs emit light.2. As voltage increases: The red LED lights first, followed by the green LED, and finally the blue LED.3. Final State: At higher voltage, all three LEDs are illuminated.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesLEDs emit light only when the applied forward voltage exceeds a color-dependent threshold. Red LEDs have the lowest forward voltage, green LEDs are higher, and blue LEDs are highest. As the supply voltage increases, LEDs turn on sequentially according to these forward voltage differences, demonstrating the relationship between semiconductor bandgap energy and emitted light color.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure current limiting to prevent LED damage; verify correct LED polarity before powering on; increase voltage slowly; keep the camera fixed throughout the experiment.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Different-colored LEDs have different forward voltages, causing sequential illumination as voltage increases. Minimum assumptions: LEDs are correctly wired in parallel with current limiting; a variable DC supply increases voltage smoothly; camera viewpoint is fixed. Expected phased storyline: Phase 1—initial low voltage with all LEDs off; Phase 2—voltage rises and red LED turns on first; Phase 3—further increase lights green LED; Phase 4—highest voltage lights blue LED; all phases must occur in order with stable spatial layout and clear visibility of LED colors.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Geiger Counter Needle Deflection Near a Weak Radiation SourceI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Geiger Counter Needle Deflection Near a Weak Radiation Source2. Subject: Engineering – Nuclear Engineering3. Experiment Objective: Observe how radiation intensity affects the indication of an analog Geiger counter by changing the distance between a weak sealed radioactive check source and the detector; understand distance dependence and counting statistics.II. Experimental EquipmentAnalog Geiger–Müller counter with visible needle and scale; small sealed radioactive check source (low activity, approved for teaching); disposable laboratory gloves; lab bench; camera on tripod with fixed focus (for time-lapse or continuous recording).III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place the Geiger counter on the lab bench, power it on, and allow it to stabilize. Put on gloves. Position the camera facing the meter so the needle and scale are clearly visible; fix focus and do not adjust during recording.Background Measurement: With no source nearby, observe and note the background needle position and natural fluctuations.Core Operation: Holding the sealed check source with a gloved hand, slowly move it from a far position toward the detector window of the Geiger counter, pausing briefly at a close position.Withdrawal: Slowly move the source away from the detector back to the far position.Completion: Keep the source stored at a safe distance; turn off the instrument if finished.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: With only background radiation, the needle shows a low reading with small random fluctuations.Approach: As the source approaches the detector, the needle deflects to a higher value, with visible statistical fluctuations.Withdrawal: As the source is moved away, the needle deflection decreases and returns toward the background level.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesA Geiger–Müller counter detects ionizing radiation events and converts them into electrical pulses that drive an analog meter. Bringing a radioactive source closer increases the radiation intensity at the detector due to reduced distance and geometric spreading, increasing the count rate and needle deflection. Moving the source away reduces intensity and the count rate. Random fluctuations arise from the statistical nature of radioactive decay.VI. Experimental PrecautionsUse only sealed, low-activity check sources; do not open sources. Wear gloves and minimize handling time. Do not touch the detector window with the source. Follow institutional radiation safety rules.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstrate distance-dependent response of an analog Geiger counter to a weak sealed radioactive source. Minimum assumptions: a functioning analog GM counter with a visible needle, a low-activity sealed check source, and fixed camera focus. Phased storyline: (1) Establish background with needle at low fluctuating level; (2) Gloved hand approaches source toward detector causing increased needle deflection; (3) Brief hold at close distance with higher average deflection; (4) Withdrawal of source causing needle to decrease toward background. Visibility constraints: meter face and needle must remain readable; source-hand distance change must be clear; camera remains static with consistent lighting.
